docs.title: Khue's Homelab
docs.text:
Features • Get Started • Documentation

This project utilizes Infrastructure as Code and GitOps to automate provisioning, operating, and updating self-hosted services in my homelab. It can be used as a highly customizable framework to build your own homelab.

What is a homelab?

Homelab is a laboratory at home where you can self-host, experiment with new technologies, practice for certifications, and so on. For more information, please see the r/homelab introduction and the Home Operations Discord community (formerly known as k8s-at-home).

If you encounter an issue, please create a bug report (avoid asking for support about issues specific to this project in other communication channels).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Project status: ALPHA

This project is still in the experimental stage, and I don't use anything critical on it. Expect breaking changes that may require a complete redeployment. A proper upgrade path is planned for the stable release. More information can be found in the roadmap below.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Common applications: Forgejo, Jellyfin, Paperless, OpenCloud...
  • Automated bare metal provisioning with PXE boot
  • Automated Kubernetes installation and management
  • Installing and managing applications using GitOps
  • Automatic rolling upgrade for OS and Kubernetes
  • Automatically update apps (with approval)
  • Modular architecture, easy to add or remove features/components
  • Automated certificate management
  • Automatically update DNS records for exposed services
  • VPN (Tailscale or Wireguard)
  • Expose services to the internet securely with Cloudflare Tunnel
  • CI/CD platform
  • Private container registry
  • Distributed storage
  • Support multiple environments (dev, prod)
  • Monitoring and alerting
  • Automated backup and restore
  • Single sign-on
  • Infrastructure testing

Some demo videos and screenshots are shown here. They can't capture all the project's features, but they are sufficient to get a concept of it.

Demo Deploy with a single command (after updating the configuration files) PXE boot Homepage powered by... Homepage Monitoring dashboard powered by Grafana Matrix chat server Continuous deployment with ArgoCD ntfy displaying received alerts

docs.title: Certificate management
docs.text:
Certificates are generated and managed by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt. By default certificates are valid for 90 days and will be renewed after 60 days.

Apps do not request certificates. One wildcard Certificate in namespace gateway (system/gateway/templates/certificate.yaml) covers every app host, and both Gateways terminate TLS with its secret:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: homelab-wildcard
spec:
  secretName: homelab-wildcard-tls
  dnsNames:
    - "*.example.com"
  issuerRef:
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    name: letsencrypt-prod

Kanidm also has its own Certificate, because it serves TLS itself: the Gateway re-encrypts to it and checks its certificate (BackendTLSPolicy).

flowchart LR
  User -- 6 --> Gateway

  subgraph cluster[Homelab cluster]
    Gateway --- Secret
    Certificate -. 5 .-> Secret
    Certificate -- 2 --> CertificateRequest -- 3 --> Order -- 4 --> Challenge
  end

  Order -.- ACMEServer[ACME server]

  subgraph dnsprovider[DNS provider]
    TXT
  end

  Challenge -- 4.a --> TXT
  ACMEServer -.- Challenge
  ACMEServer -. 4.b .-> TXT
  1. The Certificate resource is in git (system/gateway)
  2. Based on the Certificate resource, cert-manager creates a CertificateRequest resource to request a signed certificate from the configured ClusterIssuer
  3. The CertificateRequest will create an order with an ACME server (we use Let's Encrypt), which is represented by the Order resource
  4. Then cert-manager will perform a DNS-01 Challenge:
    1. Create a DNS TXT record (contains a computed key)
    2. The ACME server retrieve this key via a DNS lookup and validate that we own the domain for the requested certificate
  5. cert-manager stores the certificate (typically tls.crt and tls.key) in the Secret named in the Certificate, which the Gateways reference
  6. Now you can access the HTTPS website with a valid certificate

A much more detailed diagram can be found in the official documentation under certificate lifecycle.

docs.title: Development shell
docs.text: The development shell makes it easy to get all of the dependencies needed to interact with the homelab.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Info

NixOS users can skip this step.

Install Nix using one of the following methods:

  • Official Nix installer
  • Determinate Nix Installer

If you're using the official installer, add the following to your ~/.config/nix/nix.conf to enable Flakes:

experimental-features = nix-command flakes

docs.title: How to open it
docs.text:
Run the following command:

nix develop

It will open a shell with all the dependencies defined in ./flake.nix:

[khuedoan@ryzentower:~/Documents/homelab]$ which kubectl
/nix/store/0558zzzqynzw7rx9dp2i7jymvznd1cqx-kubectl-1.30.1/bin/kubectl

Tip

If you have direnv installed, you can run direnv allow once and it will automatically enter the Nix shell every time you cd into the project.

docs.title: PXE boot
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Nixie
    participant Router as Router (DHCP)
    participant Machines

    Nixie->>Nixie: Load hosts.json
    Nixie->>Machines: Check recorded machine IDs over SSH
    Note over Nixie: Skip recorded hosts, even if unreachable<br/>or their identity differs. Stop if all are recorded.

    Nixie->>Nixie: Build NixOS installer with Nix
    Nixie->>Nixie: Start ProxyDHCP, TFTP, HTTP, and API services
    loop Each uninstalled machine
        Nixie->>Machines: Send Wake-on-LAN packet
    end

    par Machines boot and install concurrently
        Note over Machines: UEFI PXE boot
        Machines->>Router: Broadcast DHCP discovery
        Machines->>Nixie: Same broadcast
        par IP configuration
            Router-->>Machines: Assign IP address
        and PXE discovery
            Nixie-->>Machines: Offer PXE boot server (ProxyDHCP)
        end
        Machines->>Nixie: Discover boot file (UDP 4011)
        Nixie-->>Machines: iPXE bootloader path
        Machines->>Nixie: Request bootloader (TFTP)
        Nixie-->>Machines: iPXE bootloader

        Note over Router,Machines: iPXE repeats DHCP discovery<br/>ProxyDHCP supplies the boot-script URL
        Machines->>Nixie: Request boot script, then kernel and initrd (HTTP)
        Nixie-->>Machines: Boot script, kernel, and initrd
        Note over Machines: Boot NixOS installer<br/>systemd starts nixie-agent

        Machines->>Nixie: POST /install with MAC address
        Nixie->>Nixie: Select host flake by MAC<br/>Use request's source IP for SSH
        Nixie->>Machines: Run nixos-anywhere to install NixOS over SSH
        Note over Machines: Reboot into installed system
        Nixie->>Machines: Read installed /etc/machine-id over SSH
        Machines-->>Nixie: Machine ID
        Nixie->>Nixie: Save IP and machine ID hash to hosts.json<br/>Mark host installed
    end

    Note over Nixie: Shut down after all hosts are installed

docs.title: From WSL
docs.text:
Under WSL with mirrored networking, nixie runs on the laptop and reaches the machines' LAN over the laptop's own interface (Wi-Fi works). Two things differ from a Linux machine on the LAN:

  • WSL receives no broadcast from the LAN until the Hyper-V firewall lets nixie's ports in (UDP 67, 69, 4011 and TCP 80, 5000): the rules, and their removal after the install, are in the deployment guide.
  • Broadcasts sent from WSL without a source address may leave by another interface (Docker's bridges): nixie binds its own (--address, HOMELAB_PXE_ADDRESS), and the specs' Wake-on-LAN binds the workstation's LAN address.

Here's how it looks like in action (this is an old clip so the logs look different now):

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• OpenBao (platform/openbao) holds the cluster's secrets in its KV store secret/.
  • Every namespace reads its own branch, secret/<namespace>/<name>, through its SecretStore openbao (system/secret-store, rendered by every Application) and External Secrets ExternalSecrets. OpenBao refuses a read of another namespace's branch.
  • Values come from three places:
  • generated secrets: platform/generated-secrets pushes each one to its readers' branches, under secret/<namespace>/generated/, the only paths its role writer reaches;
  • OpenTofu's secrets (Cloudflare's tokens and Tunnel credentials, WireGuard's key, the backup bucket's credentials file and Kopia's repository password from infra/<env>/backup): the unit infra/<env>/secrets writes them as Secrets into namespace infra-secrets, and platform/infra-secrets pushes them anywhere except generated/ (role infra);
  • Kanidm's OAuth2 client secrets: the kaniop operator, directly in each client's namespace.
flowchart TD
  subgraph generated-secrets[generated-secrets namespace]
    generators[Password generators] -- PushSecret generatorRef, IfNotExists --> writer[SecretStore openbao-writer]
  end
  writer -- role writer: generated/ --> openbao[(OpenBao secret/)]
  subgraph infra-secrets[infra-secrets namespace]
    tofu[OpenTofu infra/env/secrets] -- server-side apply --> tofusecrets[Secrets]
    tofusecrets -- PushSecret, Replace --> infra[SecretStore openbao-infra]
  end
  infra -- role infra: all but generated/ --> openbao
  subgraph app[application namespace]
    store[SecretStore openbao] -- role apps: secret/<namespace>/ --> openbao
    ExternalSecret --- store
    ExternalSecret -- create --> Secret
    App -- read --> Secret
  end

docs.title: Reading a secret
docs.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: grafana-admin
spec:
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: SecretStore
    name: openbao
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: grafana/generated/admin  # secret/grafana/generated/admin: the namespace's own branch
        property: password

scripts/check-secret-stores refuses, before merge, an ExternalSecret that reads another store or another namespace's branch, and a generated secret that nobody reads or that is read but never pushed. A secret two namespaces need is pushed to both branches (destinations in platform/generated-secrets/values.yaml).

docs.title: Unsealing and configuration
docs.text:
• OpenBao unseals itself (seal "static") with a 32-byte key that the OpenTofu unit infra/<env>/openbao creates, keeps in its state (.state/, readable only by you; Cloudflare R2 with state encryption from step 8c) and writes into Secret openbao/openbao-unseal. Losing the key loses everything OpenBao holds.
  • On first start OpenBao configures itself from platform/openbao/values.yaml (initialize stanzas):
  • the KV v2 store secret/ and Kubernetes auth;
  • the policies apps (read secret/<namespace>/), writer (push: create, read, update on secret/<namespace>/generated/ only, because External Secrets reads before it writes; no delete), infra (the same everywhere except generated/), snapshot (read sys/storage/raft/snapshot) and admin;
  • their roles: apps for every namespace's default service account, writer for generated-secrets', infra for infra-secrets/openbao-infra, snapshot for openbao/openbao-snapshot (the hourly raft snapshot) and admin for openbao/openbao-admin. They accept only service account tokens issued for audience openbao (the SecretStores ask for it), so a token sent to OpenBao never works against the API server.
  • These stanzas run only on an empty storage: editing them later changes nothing on a running OpenBao. Apply the change by hand with the admin role (below), or, in the sandbox, just dev-clean.
  • No root token and no recovery keys exist.
  • OpenBao's data is backed up as its hourly raft snapshot (CronJob openbao/openbao-snapshot, volume openbao-snapshots), copied off-site daily (Backup and restore). The snapshot is useless without the unseal key, and the Kopia password that encrypts the copies lives in OpenTofu's state, never only in OpenBao.

docs.title: Emergency access
docs.text:
No root token exists: log in with the admin role, as service account openbao/openbao-admin.

# Logs the bao CLI in OpenBao's pod in with the admin role for an hour; neither token reaches an argument or your
# shell history
kubectl -n openbao create token openbao-admin --audience=openbao --duration=1h |
  kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -c openbao -- \
    sh -c 'bao write -field=token auth/kubernetes/login role=admin jwt=- | bao login -no-print -'
kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -c openbao -- sh
# Inside, when you are done
bao token revoke -self && rm ~/.vault-token

The OpenBao token stays in ~/.vault-token in the pod until you revoke it, it expires or the pod restarts. Anyone who can create tokens for openbao-admin or exec into OpenBao's pod (cluster admins) holds every secret.

docs.title: Generated secrets
docs.text:
Random secrets (admin passwords and other random app secrets; kaniop generates the OAuth2 client secrets) are listed in platform/generated-secrets/values.yaml. Each one is an external-secrets Password generator and a PushSecret that runs it (selector.generatorRef) and writes the value to each of its destinations in OpenBao (updatePolicy: IfNotExists): every reconcile (hourly, a force-sync, an ESO restart) generates a value and writes it only where none exists, so an existing value never changes and a missing one (an OpenBao that lost its data, a rotation) is written within the hour. The destinations of a first push all get the same value. Namespace generated-secrets holds no Secret: OpenBao's value is the only one. (Until step 8e a Secret in global-secrets held a copy: ESO's refreshPolicy: CreatedOnce regenerates under a stale cache, so the copy could differ from what every app reads.)

./platform/generated-secrets/values.yaml
# Random secrets generated for this cluster and written straight into OpenBao, once per destination
# (secret/<namespace>/generated/<name>, the only paths the writer reaches): a Password generator and a PushSecret
# each (templates/), no Secret in this namespace. Readers use their namespace's SecretStore openbao. A value two
# namespaces need is two destinations of one entry, written by the same push; a destination added later gets the
# existing value by hand first (docs/concepts/secrets-management.md). Never rotated automatically.
secrets:
  - name: forgejo.admin
    key: password
    special: true
    destinations: [forgejo/generated/admin]
  - name: paperless.admin
    key: PAPERLESS_ADMIN_PASSWORD
    special: true
    destinations: [paperless/generated/admin]
  # paperless 3 refuses to start without it
  - name: paperless.secret-key
    key: PAPERLESS_SECRET_KEY
    length: 64
    destinations: [paperless/generated/secret-key]
  # Kiali signs its session cookies with it (AES: 32 characters)
  - name: kiali.signing-key
    key: key
    length: 32
    destinations: [kiali/generated/signing-key]
  - name: grafana.admin
    key: password
    special: true
    destinations: [grafana/generated/admin]
  # zot's machine account ci (its htpasswd) and the golden path's push (platform/ci)
  - name: registry.ci
    key: password
    destinations: [zot/generated/ci, ci/generated/registry]
  # Forgejo's org ci webhook to Argo Events (Authorization: Bearer, set by lab infra forgejo sync)
  - name: ci.webhook
    key: token
    destinations: [ci/generated/webhook]
  # ntfy (apps/ntfy.yaml): user alerts publishes (Alertmanager), user phone subscribes (people's apps). No symbols:
  # ntfy's lists are comma-separated. ntfy tokens are tk_ plus 29 characters: the readers add the prefix
  - name: ntfy.alerts-token
    key: token
    length: 29
    destinations: [ntfy/generated/alerts-token, monitoring-system/generated/ntfy]
  - name: ntfy.alerts-password
    key: password
    destinations: [ntfy/generated/alerts-password]
  - name: ntfy.phone-token
    key: token
    length: 29
    destinations: [ntfy/generated/phone-token]
  - name: ntfy.phone-password
    key: password
    destinations: [ntfy/generated/phone-password]
  # Argo CD's local account backstage (system/argocd-config bcrypts it into argocd-secret), and Backstage's Argo CD
  # plugin signing in with it
  - name: argocd.backstage-password
    key: password
    destinations: [argocd/generated/backstage-password, backstage/generated/argocd-password]
  # Backstage's session cookies
  - name: backstage.session-secret
    key: secret
    length: 64
    destinations: [backstage/generated/session-secret]
# Environment-specific additions, so the list above does not have to be restated
extraSecrets: []

docs.title: Reading a generated value
docs.text:
Read it where the apps read it, in OpenBao, with the admin role (the token never reaches your shell):

kubectl -n openbao create token openbao-admin --audience=openbao --duration=10m |
  kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -c openbao -- \
    sh -c 'export BAO_TOKEN=$(bao write -field=token auth/kubernetes/login role=admin jwt=-); bao kv get -field=<property> secret/<namespace>/generated/<name>; bao token revoke -self >/dev/null'

For example -field=password secret/ntfy/generated/phone-password. Or read the Secret the app's own ExternalSecret writes in its namespace.

docs.title: Adding a destination
docs.text:
A destination added to an existing entry would get a new value (the push writes a missing destination with what it generates). Copy the existing value there first, inside OpenBao's pod so it never reaches your terminal, and mark the copy as External Secrets' (it refuses to write a path without that mark later); then add the destination to values.yaml: the push finds it and leaves it. For ntfy.alerts-token gaining <namespace>/generated/ntfy:

kubectl -n openbao create token openbao-admin --audience=openbao --duration=10m |
  kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -c openbao -- \
    sh -c 'export BAO_TOKEN=$(bao write -field=token auth/kubernetes/login role=admin jwt=-) &&
      bao kv get -field=token secret/ntfy/generated/alerts-token | bao kv put secret/<namespace>/generated/ntfy token=- &&
      bao kv metadata put -custom-metadata=managed-by=external-secrets secret/<namespace>/generated/ntfy;
      bao token revoke -self >/dev/null'

docs.title: Rotating
docs.text: lab secrets rotate <name> replaces any secret, generated or not, by its own method; a daily CronJob rotates the ones with a period (Rotating secrets). Kanidm OAuth2 client secrets are generated by the kaniop operator instead, as <client>-kanidm-oauth2-credentials in the client's namespace.

docs.title: Forgejo's deploy tokens and org ci's bot
docs.text:
lab infra forgejo sync writes two records with the admin role: secret/forgejo/deploy (user deploy's token, which lab infra forgejo push uses) and secret/argocd/forgejo (user argocd's read-only token, which the ExternalSecret argocd/argocd-repo-forgejo reads). Running sync again keeps a token Forgejo still accepts and replaces one it does not (for example after Forgejo's data was lost), then refreshes Argo CD's credential.

It also keeps ci-bot's token in secret/ci/forgejo-token (the golden path's clones and commit statuses), and records in secret/ci/forgejo-webhook the hash of the webhook header it gave org ci's hook, whose secret is the generated secret/ci/generated/webhook (In-cluster CI).

docs.title: Secrets from OpenTofu
docs.text:
The unit infra/<env>/secrets (infra/_modules/secrets) writes one Secret per OpenBao path into namespace infra-secrets (<namespace>.<name>, one key per property) on every just infra deploy … (the sandbox's in just dev). platform/infra-secrets pushes each entry of its values.yaml to secret/<namespace>/<name> with updatePolicy: Replace: OpenTofu is the source, a changed value replaces OpenBao's within an hour, a lost one comes back.

OpenBao path Source cert-manager/cloudflare, external-dns/cloudflare, cloudflared/cloudflare infra/production/cloudflare's output secrets (production) wireguard/private-key generated by the unit (wireguard_asymmetric_key); peers need terragrunt output wireguard_public_key in infra/<env>/secrets

Tailscale's auth key (tailscale/auth-key) comes from Headscale in step 13. OpenTofu's Cloudflare login (cf auth login) never reaches the cluster.

  • Adding one: produce it in OpenTofu (an input of the unit, or a resource in the module), add its path and properties to platform/infra-secrets/values.yaml (and values-dev.yaml if the sandbox has it), and read it from its namespace. scripts/check-secret-stores refuses a push nobody reads.
  • Rotating one: change it in OpenTofu (for a Cloudflare token, terragrunt apply -replace=cloudflare_account_token.cert_manager in infra/production/cloudflare), run just infra deploy production, then kubectl -n infra-secrets annotate pushsecret <namespace>.<name> force-sync=$(date +%s) --overwrite or wait an hour, and restart the consumer.
  • Removing one: delete its entry, then its OpenBao value with the admin role (bao kv metadata delete …).

Please see the official documentation for more information:

  • OpenBao
  • External Secrets Operator and its Vault provider

docs.title: User onboarding
docs.text:
For userFor admin

Add the person to one of the three role groups (admins, editors or users), and optionally to the access groups budget, documents and files:

./scripts/onboard-user johndoe "John Doe" "johndoe@example.com" users budget files

The script prints the idm_admin password for the login prompt and ends with a credential reset link. Let the user scan the QR code or follow the link to set up a passkey or password + TOTP (Kanidm requires MFA).

The role group decides access to the admin tools: admins administer Grafana, Argo CD and the registry; editors edit Grafana dashboards, sync Argo CD apps and push images; users view and pull. In Forgejo, every role group gets an account on first login; admins are site admins.

Apps with personal data only admit their access group, whatever the role group:

Kanidm group App Access homelab-budget Actual Budget an account on first login (the first one becomes the server owner) homelab-documents paperless an account on first login with the permissions of the paperless group homelab-documents (documents, tags, mail rules…, created at every start; groups set in the paperless UI are replaced at each login); members of homelab-admins also become superusers homelab-files OpenCloud an account on first login (Kanidm asks once to consent); members of homelab-admins get the Admin role, the others User; the role follows the groups at each login

To grant access to an existing person later: kanidm group add-members homelab-budget johndoe --name idm_admin.

To offboard someone, remove them from their groups (or delete the person) in Kanidm and delete their API keys in the registry: zot keeps the groups from their last login for existing keys. Also disable the user in Forgejo: their access tokens and SSH keys keep working after Kanidm removes the person. OpenCloud keeps the files of removed people; delete their account in OpenCloud's user management.

docs.title: VPN setup
docs.text: You can choose between Tailscale, Wireguard, or use both like me. I primarily use WireGuard but keep Tailscale as a backup for when the WireGuard server is down.

docs.title: Tailscale (requires third-party account)
docs.text:
The auth key will come from Headscale (roadmap step 13), which replaces Tailscale's service; until then apps/tailscale.yaml waits for secret/tailscale/auth-key in OpenBao. To use Tailscale's service before that, write a key from the admin console with the admin role (emergency access): bao kv put secret/tailscale/auth-key auth-key=- (the key on stdin).

Finally, enable subnet routes for homelab-router from the admin console.

You can now connect to your homelab via Tailscale and invite user to your Tailscale network.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Find your public IP address using:

curl -4 ifconfig.me

If you don’t have a static IP address, use dynamic DNS and replace the IP with your domain name.

Next, configure port forwarding in your router for the WireGuard service.

Example

Each router is different, here's mine for reference:

  • Protocol: UDP
  • Start Port: 51820
  • End Port: 51820
  • Local IP Address: 192.168.0.3, the wireguard VIP (service_vips.wireguard in infra/production/cluster/config.json; check it with kubectl get service -n wireguard wireguard)
  • Start Port Local: 51820
  • End Port Local: 51820

The server's key pair comes from OpenTofu (infra/production/secrets): its private key reaches the cluster through OpenBao, and its public key, which every peer needs, is

cd infra/production/secrets && terragrunt output -raw wireguard_public_key

I use 172.16.0.0/12 as the private IP range for WireGuard, but you can choose any private IP address range you prefer in ./apps/wireguard.yaml. I also recommend removing my peers and adding your own.

docs.title: Add a new device to the server
docs.text:
Info

Each device requires its own configuration.

Generate a new key pair for the device. You can generate it for the user, or they can generate it themselves if they prefer to keep the private key confidential:

wg genkey | tee /dev/tty | wg pubkey

This will generate a private key and a public key, in that order. The private key must be saved in a secure password manager, and save the public key for the next step.

Update the list of peers in ./apps/wireguard.yaml, make sure you replace all of my peers with yours.

Example

Example configuration for my phone:

[Peer]
PublicKey = nITHFdgTkNZOTWeSWqnGXjgwlCJMKRCnnUsjMx2yp2U=
AllowedIPs = 172.16.0.12/32
  • The public key is the one generated in the previous step.
  • 172.16.0.12/32 is the device's private IP address, manually selected from the 172.16.0.0/12 range mentioned above.

docs.title: Add the Wireguard config to the device
docs.text:
Create a new configuration file for the device:

[Interface]
Address = <CLIENT PRIVATE IP>/32
PrivateKey = <CLIENT PRIVATE KEY>

[Peer]
PublicKey = <SERVER PUBLIC KEY>
Endpoint = <SERVER PUBLIC IP>:51820
AllowedIPs = <SERVER PRIVATE IP>/32, <LOAD BALANCER IP RANGE>

Replace placeholders with actual values and save as wg0.conf.

Example

Example configuration for my phone:

[Interface]
Address = 172.16.0.12/32
PrivateKey = <REDACTED>

[Peer]
PublicKey = <the server's public key: the homelab peer in apps/wireguard.yaml>
Endpoint = <HOME IP>:51820
AllowedIPs = 172.16.0.1/32, 192.168.0.10/32, 192.168.0.2/32

Use the vip and service_vips.gateway of infra/production/cluster/config.json in AllowedIPs.

The client can now import this configuration and connect to your WireGuard mesh. Make sure you clean up the wg0.conf file after importing it to the client.

MobileLinux

Generate a QR code from the configuration file:

qrencode -t ansiutf8 -r wg0.conf

Then scan the QR code using the official WireGuard app.

Import the WireGuard configuration using NetworkManager:

nmcli connection import type wireguard file wg0.conf

Activate the connection:

nmcli connection up wg0

docs.title: Headscale
docs.text: Headscale is a self-hosted implementation of the Tailscale control server that does not require a third-party account. To set it up, take a look at the changes proposed by this PR.

docs.title: Add or remove nodes
docs.text: Or how to scale horizontally. To replace the same node with a clean OS, remove it and add it again.

docs.title: Add new nodes
docs.text:
Tip

You can add multiple nodes at the same time

Add its details to the inventory:

infra/production/metal/hosts.json
 {
   "homelab-1": {"ip": "192.168.1.110", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:01"},
   "homelab-2": {"ip": "192.168.1.111", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:02"},
   "homelab-3": {"ip": "192.168.1.112", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:03"},
+  "homelab-4": {"ip": "192.168.1.113", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:04"},
 }

Install the OS (nixie) and join the cluster (lab cluster enroll):

just infra deploy production

Then verify the new node:

export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/infra/production/kubeconfig.yaml"
kubectl get nodes

That's it!

docs.title: Remove a node
docs.text:
Warning

It is recommended to remove nodes one at a time

Use the environment's kubeconfig:

export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/infra/production/kubeconfig.yaml"

Drain the node:

kubectl drain ${NODE_NAME} --delete-emptydir-data --ignore-daemonsets --force

Remove the node from the cluster

kubectl delete node ${NODE_NAME}

Shutdown the node:

ssh root@${NODE_IP} poweroff

Remove it from the inventory:

infra/production/metal/hosts.json
 {
   "homelab-1": {"ip": "192.168.1.110", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:01"},
   "homelab-2": {"ip": "192.168.1.111", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:02"},
   "homelab-3": {"ip": "192.168.1.112", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:03"},
-  "homelab-4": {"ip": "192.168.1.113", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:04"},
 }

Reapply the environment with just infra deploy production. Don't replace the initializer with a fresh server in an existing cluster.

Optionally, after Ceph finishes recovering, clean up the removed node's OSD records using the Rook guide.

Testbed is the same with infra/testbed/metal/hosts.json and just testbed, which also creates the VM.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: Alertmanager posts alerts to ntfy (apps/ntfy.yaml), topic alerts, published at https://ntfy.<domain> through the Cloudflare Tunnel. Nothing is readable or writable without a user: phone reads, alerts (Alertmanager) publishes.

docs.title: Subscribe on a phone
docs.text:
1. Install ntfy (Android or iOS).
  2. Settings → Users → add server https://ntfy.<domain>, user phone, password: secret/ntfy/generated/phone-password, property password, read from OpenBao with the admin role
  3. Subscribe to topic alerts on that server.

iOS gets instant notifications through ntfy.sh, which only receives a poll request (a hash of the topic), never the message. The sandbox runs ntfy without it.

docs.title: Telegram, the second path (production)
docs.text:
Every alert also goes to Telegram, so it still arrives while ntfy is down and the cluster is up (a cluster that is down entirely sends nothing on either path). Alertmanager reads the bot token and the chat id from OpenBao (secret/monitoring-system/telegram), never from git: the chat id names a person's chat.

  1. In Telegram, ask @BotFather for a new bot (/newbot): it answers with the bot's token.
  2. Send the bot any message, then read the chat id from https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates (message.chat.id).
  3. Open OpenBao with the admin role (Emergency access) and write both without them showing:
bao kv put secret/monitoring-system/telegram bot_token=-    # paste the token, then Ctrl-D
bao kv patch secret/monitoring-system/telegram chat_id=-    # paste the chat id, then Ctrl-D

Until then Alertmanager runs without it and reports the failed Telegram notifications (AlertmanagerFailedToSendAlerts). A new token: lab secrets rotate telegram.bot-token gives the steps (BotFather's /revoke ends the old one at once).

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text: The Watchdog alert fires all the time. Each heartbeat replaces a message scheduled 15 minutes ahead ("Monitoring heartbeat missing"): if Prometheus or Alertmanager stop, it is delivered. If ntfy, the Tunnel or the whole cluster stop, nothing is: an external dead man's switch is an idea in CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: VeleroNoRecentBackup fires when no daily off-site copy succeeded for 26 hours: the schedule fails, or the cluster was never enabled (every new cluster starts read-only: lab backup enable, Backup and restore).

docs.title: Alternate DNS setup
docs.text:
Info

Skip this step if you already use the included Cloudflare setup

Before you can access the home page at https://home.example.com, you'll need to update your DNS config.

Some options for DNS config (choose one):

  • Change the DNS config at your domain registrar (already included and automated)
  • Change the DNS config in your router (also works if you don't own a domain)
  • Use nip.io (suitable for a test environment)

docs.title: At your domain registrar (recommended)
docs.text: The default configuration is for Cloudflare DNS, but you can change the code to use other providers.

docs.title: In your router
docs.text:
Tip

If you don't have a domain, you can use the home.arpa domain (according to RFC-8375).

You can add each subdomain one by one, or use a wildcard *.example.com and point it to the IP address of the load balancer. To acquire a list of subdomains and their addresses, use this command:

./scripts/get-dns-config

docs.title: Use nip.io
docs.text: Preconfigured in the dev branch.

docs.title: Backstage
docs.text: Backstage (backstage.<domain>, LAN only) is the homelab's developer portal: a catalog of every app and component, this repository's docs (TechDocs), and a template that starts a repository in Forgejo's org ci (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-16-backstage-design.md). Homepage stays the family's start page; Backstage is for whoever runs the homelab.

docs.title: Who signs in
docs.text: Only homelab-admins and homelab-editors (Kanidm's client backstage admits no one else). Backstage takes who you are from Kanidm's token: your name and those groups (backstage/packages/backend/src/auth/identity.ts); people are not in the catalog. Admins may do everything; editors read and refresh, but neither run templates nor add or remove what the catalog reads (permissions/policy.ts). Even an admin's template runs only fetch:*, publish:gitea, catalog:register and debug:log.

docs.title: What the catalog shows
docs.text:
Every app and component describes itself once, in its own files: a homelab: list in apps/<name>.yaml (one item per route) or homelab/* annotations in a chart's Chart.yaml. lab catalog generate writes the catalog (catalog/, catalog-info.yaml) and Homepage's services from them; the basic check catalog fails when either is stale.

homelab:
  - route: main            # the app-template route whose host Homepage links (omit: no page)
    name: Jellyfin
    description: Media system (movies, music, etc.)
    group: Popular         # Homepage's group (omit: not on Homepage)
    icon: jellyfin.svg

Backstage reads the catalog from the repository Argo CD syncs (global.gitRepository at global.gitRevision): GitHub's branch sandbox in the sandbox, Forgejo's ops/homelab in production. A component's page shows its pods (the Kubernetes plugin: no Secrets, ConfigMaps, logs or exec) and its Argo CD Application (account backstage, read-only).

docs.title: A new repository
docs.text: Create → "A repository in org ci" (admins): a name and a description make a repository in Forgejo's org ci with a Containerfile, a README.md and its catalog-info.yaml, registered in the catalog. Its first push runs the golden path (in-cluster-ci.md). Backstage publishes as Forgejo's user backstage (team templates: creates repositories, holds no other), whose token lab infra forgejo sync writes.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text: TechDocs builds this repository's MkDocs site on first view, inside Backstage's pod, from the Domain homelab.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
Backstage's app is backstage/ (Backstage 1.56, made by @backstage/create-app). The sandbox builds it from the checkout (scripts/build-backstage-image, run by just dev when Backstage is among its optional apps); production runs the image .github/workflows/backstage-image.yaml builds from master, signed keyless with its SBOM attested, which Kyverno's verify-backstage-image checks. After the first release builds it, pin its digest in platform/backstage/values.yaml and drop platform/backstage's exclusion from system/argocd/values.yaml.

The sandbox always runs it (just dev builds its image each time; Docker reuses the layers that did not change). Its specs are labelled backstage (just dev --tests backstage).

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text: Git rebuilds every resource of the cluster: Argo CD applies it all from the repository, and OpenTofu's state (with OpenBao's unseal key) is already on R2, encrypted. What git cannot rebuild is the data in the volumes, and that is what backups hold, never Kubernetes resources.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
Layer Where Covers Does not cover Ceph's replicas the nodes' disks power loss, a sudden shutdown, one disk or node lost a deletion or corruption (copied to every replica) Hourly local snapshots, kept 48 hours Ceph, on the nodes a deletion, corruption, a failed upgrade: back one hour losing several nodes or Ceph itself, new hardware Off-site copies, the newest 30 kept R2 bucket homelab-production-backup losing every node, new hardware losing R2 or the state passphrase
  • Switching the nodes off or losing power only restarts the cluster that exists: nothing is restored.
  • Local snapshots are VolumeSnapshots taken by the CronJob velero/snapshots. Taking them and restoring from them needs no internet.
  • Off-site copies are Velero's (system/velero): CSI snapshots moved into a Kopia repository (deduplicated, compressed, encrypted with a password from OpenTofu) on R2.

docs.title: Which volumes
docs.text:
Every volume claim declares its group with the label homelab/backup (scripts/check-backup-groups fails the basic checks otherwise):

Group Volumes Off-site daily OpenBao (its hourly raft snapshot, openbao-snapshots), Kanidm, Forgejo (forgejo-data and PostgreSQL forgejo-db), ntfy, Matrix (tuwunel's database) every day at 02:00 manual Actual Budget, paperless, OpenCloud only with lab backup push <app> none zot, Loki, jellyfin, everything else never: rebuilt or downloaded again

Both daily and manual get local snapshots.

To add a volume:

  1. Label its claim (in an app file persistence.<name>.labels, or the chart's PVC labels).
  2. Add it to EXPECTED in scripts/check-backup-groups (claims it does not name must be none).

A database's volume is copied as it is: PostgreSQL and SQLite recover from a crash-consistent snapshot. Forgejo's two volumes come from the same run, snapshotted one right after the other. A few seconds between them can leave Forgejo slightly behind its repositories, which forgejo doctor check --all --fix repairs.

docs.title: lab backup
docs.text:
Every command takes --env production (the default) or --env sandbox.

lab backup list                    # the off-site copies, newest first, and whether backups are on
lab backup enable                  # writable location, schedules on (asks first)
lab backup disable                 # read-only, schedules paused
lab backup push paperless          # one app off-site now: prints its size against R2's free tier, asks first
lab backup restore forgejo         # one app from its newest local snapshot (--at <RFC 3339>, --from offsite)
lab backup restore                 # the whole cluster after a fresh install (see below)

Without a terminal, enable, push and restore refuse unless given --yes.

docs.title: Read-only until enabled
docs.text:
Every new cluster starts with the location ReadOnly and the schedule paused: git declares both, and Argo CD ignores the two fields afterwards. Velero then writes and deletes nothing, so a new cluster can never replace or prune the backups it may need to restore from.

  • A brand-new homelab: run lab backup enable once after the first deploy.
  • After a restore: run it once the restored data was checked.
  • Retention by count: the CronJob velero/prune keeps the newest 30 completed copies of the schedule and of each app. It runs only while the location is writable. Velero's own expiry is ten years, so a cluster that was down for months loses nothing.
  • A copy cut short (a power cut while its data movers copied) ends Failed, and prune deletes it once a newer copy of its group completed. Velero may leave a VolumeSnapshot it made for that copy (labelled velero.io/backup-name): prune deletes every such snapshot whose backup no longer exists, in either mode, since no restore can need it.
  • The alert VeleroNoRecentBackup (through ntfy) fires when no daily copy succeeded for 26 hours. That includes a cluster never enabled.

docs.title: Check the space on R2
docs.text: R2's free tier is 10 GB-month, account-wide (the state bucket uses a few MB). lab backup push prints the app's volumes and the bucket's current size against it before it uploads. Kopia deduplicates, so keeping 30 copies costs little more than one copy plus what changed. Beyond 10 GB, R2 charges about $0.015 per GB-month.

docs.title: Restore one app
docs.text:
From the newest local snapshot, back one hour at most (no internet needed):

lab backup restore forgejo                                   # newest snapshot
lab backup restore forgejo --at 2026-10-22T14:00:00+07:00   # newest at or before that time
lab backup restore forgejo --from offsite                    # the newest off-site copy holding it (--backup <name>)

lab does the following:

  1. Pauses Argo CD's automated sync of the app.
  2. Stops its workloads. CloudNativePG clusters are hibernated with their reconciliation paused, and kaniop's Kanidm is stopped through its replicas.
  3. Replaces the claims, giving back the owner references Velero drops.
  4. Starts the app again.
  5. Resumes the sync, then waits for Argo CD to report the app Synced and Healthy.

If a step fails, the app stays paused and stopped, and the error says so. Fix the cause and run the same command again.

After restoring Kanidm, lab deletes the Secrets kaniop writes only once (kanidm-admin-passwords and every *-kanidm-oauth2-credentials), so kaniop writes them again from the restored data, and it restarts their readers.

docs.title: Restore the whole cluster (new hardware, every node lost)
docs.text:
1. Keep the state passphrase (~/.config/homelab/state.env). Without it, OpenTofu's state on R2 cannot be read, and with it OpenBao's unseal key, the Kopia password and the R2 credentials.
  2. Build the nodes and run just infra deploy production, as for a first install. Argo CD builds everything from git. Velero starts read-only and paused, so it syncs the backup list from R2 and touches nothing.
  3. Check what is there: lab backup list.
  4. Run lab backup restore. It takes the newest scheduled copy that completed before this cluster was created (or --backup <name>). It restores OpenBao first, from its raft snapshot, then every app with a daily volume, then each manual app from its newest push. Finally it refreshes every ExternalSecret and restarts every reader.
  5. Run just infra deploy production again. The restored Forgejo holds ops/homelab as it was at the backup, so Argo CD would otherwise run that older commit; this pushes master again.
  6. Check the data:
  7. sign in through Kanidm (passwords and passkeys come back);
  8. open Forgejo's repositories and issues; if a repository looks behind, run kubectl -n forgejo exec deploy/forgejo -- forgejo doctor check --all --fix;
  9. check that the other apps have their data;
  10. confirm every Argo CD Application is Synced and Healthy.
  11. Run lab backup enable. Daily copies start again, and the prune job keeps the newest 30.

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text: The sandbox runs the same path: - csi-driver-host-path gives it CSI snapshots (system/csi-hostpath, its default StorageClass); - an S3 server in namespace velero (versitygw) stands in for R2; - TestBackupRestore backs up, loses a repository, its issue and an OpenBao key, and restores them, the whole cluster and then Forgejo alone.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every pull request into dev or master, and every push to them, runs the basic checks on GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/checks.yaml), in the same Nix dev shell as the workstation.

Job Command render, go, cli, infra, docs, mesh, backup-groups, rotation-catalog, env-config, secret-stores, lint, leaks, iac, images, workflows scripts/ci-check <job> checks succeeds only when every job above did: the one status the ruleset requires

Run them all locally before a commit (the basic checks), in the dev shell:

scripts/ci-check all

render renders the charts the branch changes, uncommitted changes included (cd cli && go run ./cmd/lab test charts lists them).

go vets the whole suite and runs the offline tests: packages test/offline (renders, scripts, checks) and test/internal/* (the helpers both sides use). test/e2e holds only the specs that need a cluster (Ginkgo, which just dev runs by label): a test that needs none goes in test/offline, and runs in the basic checks by being there. TestE2EKeepsSelection there checks that every scope group and recipe still selects the specs it selected before the move to labels (test/offline/fixtures/e2e-selection.json).

docs.title: Detection (step 15a)
docs.text:
Four jobs look for what a change brings that should not reach dev. Kubernetes manifests (privileged, root, RBAC) are Kyverno's (step 15b), not these jobs'.

Job Fails on Scans leaks a secret gitleaks recognises (.gitleaks.toml: its default rules), printed redacted the commits from the base (the pull request's, origin/dev locally) to HEAD iac a HIGH or CRITICAL Trivy finding every Dockerfile and OpenTofu (infra/), from the root images a CRITICAL vulnerability that has a fix the images new in the renders of the charts and app files the change touches workflows any weakness zizmor finds offline (template injection, dangerous triggers, unpinned actions, credentials left in the checkout) .github/

GitHub's secret scanning and push protection are on as well (the repository is public): a push holding a known provider's token is refused before any job runs.

What to do about a finding:

  • A leaked secret: it is public once pushed. Rotate it (lab secrets rotate <name>, or the provider's console), then remove it from the branch. Rewriting history does not take it back.
  • An image: bump it to a release that fixes the CVE (Renovate usually has one). If none exists and the risk is understood, add the CVE to .trivyignore.yaml under vulnerabilities with a statement naming the image and an expired_at at most 90 days away (an entry ignores the CVE in every image).
  • A workflow finding: fix it (zizmor's --fix applies the safe ones), or add it to .github/zizmor.yml under its rule's ignore as <file>:<line> with the reason on the same line.
  • A Dockerfile or OpenTofu finding: fix it, or add it to .trivyignore.yaml under misconfigurations with the file's path from the root and a statement.

Trivy keeps its databases in ~/.cache/trivy and downloads them again when they are older than its refresh period. GitHub Actions restores them from a cache per job, keyed by day.

docs.title: A failed run
docs.text: Open the failed job in the pull request's checks: its last step is the scripts/ci-check command, which reproduces locally. A newer push cancels the older run of a pull request: its jobs show as cancelled and its checks as failed.

docs.title: Protected branches
docs.text:
The ruleset protect-dev-master (.github/rulesets/protect-dev-master.json): changes reach dev and master only through pull requests whose checks passed (no approval needed), never by a direct push, a force-push or a deletion. Repository admins may merge a pull request whose checks failed (gh pr merge --admin), for a GitHub Actions outage only: run scripts/ci-check all first. Branch sandbox is not protected (just dev force-pushes it).

# Create it (once)
gh api --method POST 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets' --input .github/rulesets/protect-dev-master.json
# Its ID
id=$(gh api 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets' --jq '.[] | select(.name == "protect-dev-master") | .id')
# Update it after editing the file
gh api --method PUT "repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/$id" --input .github/rulesets/protect-dev-master.json
# Show it, and the rules a branch gets
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/$id"
gh api 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/dev'
# Remove it
gh api --method DELETE "repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/$id"

The ruleset protect-master-sandbox (.github/rulesets/protect-master-sandbox.json) adds the check sandbox to master; the same commands apply with its file and name.

gh fills {owner}/{repo} from the repository you are in.

docs.title: Adding a check
docs.text: Add a case to scripts/ci-check and its name to the checks list there and to the workflow's matrix.

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text:
Four workflows build a fresh sandbox on a GitHub-hosted runner and run the suite with just dev --revision <sha> (their steps are the composite action .github/actions/sandbox): Argo CD syncs that commit (the bootstrap writes it as the revision of Argo CD's cluster Secret, infra/_modules/argocd/cluster-secret.sh), so nothing is pushed to branch sandbox and a local sandbox is not disturbed. A run takes about 30 minutes; it needs no secret (the state passphrase is random).

Workflow Trigger Runs sandbox workflow_dispatch only (Actions tab, or gh workflow run sandbox.yaml --ref <branch>) scope full or auto, or exactly tests (a label filter: gh workflow run sandbox.yaml --ref dev -f tests='logs \|\| mesh'); revision picks another commit sandbox-release A pull request into master (a release): opened, reopened or a new commit The whole suite; its check sandbox is required by the ruleset protect-master-sandbox sandbox-retarget A pull request retargeted to master (its base changed) The whole suite, reported as the check sandbox through the checks API sandbox-label The label sandbox on a pull request into anything but master What just dev would run for the pull request (its base to its head)

Labels never trigger sandbox-release: a label event would replace the running check with a skipped one, which GitHub counts as passing. For the same reason no other job is named sandbox (sandbox's is sandbox-dev): a run that tests nothing would pass the required check on the same commit. A pull request retargeted to master from a fork gets a read-only token, which cannot create the check: push to it (or close and reopen it). Labelling needs Triage or more on the repository. A new commit on a labelled pull request does not rerun sandbox-label (except Renovate's own commits on its labelled pull requests): remove the label and add it again (read the new code first: it runs on the runner); other labels never cancel it. Pull requests from forks get a read-only token, which is all the run needs.

Label your own pull requests only when they change what the local sandbox cannot prove (the first install, CI): just dev already ran their scope. Renovate labels its pull requests itself (renovate.json5; its App has Issues and Pull requests write, and a label added by an App triggers workflows), because nobody runs just dev for them.

A failed run uploads the artifact sandbox-state: the just dev output, the pods, the events, the Applications and the logs and descriptions of the pods that are not ready, why each unhealthy Application is unhealthy (applications-unhealthy.yaml), and whether the node restarted and why: its container's state (node-container.json: restarts, OOMKilled, exit code), the runner's memory and kernel OOM kills (memory.txt, oom.txt) and k3s's own errors and starts (k3s-errors.log; only those lines, since the artifact is public).

gh run download <run-id> --name sandbox-state

Every run, passed or failed, also uploads e2e-reports: Ginkgo's JUnit and JSON reports of each run of the suite (test/reports/e2e/<env>-<filter>.xml|json), with each spec's time and failure.

A push to dev (a merge) runs only the basic checks: just dev already ran the branch's scope locally, and the whole suite runs on every dev → master pull request (and locally with just dev-fresh). Run sandbox by hand to test dev in between. If dev breaks after a merge, fix it with a new pull request right away. A dev → master pull request runs the whole suite on its head and cannot merge until it passes.

GitHub disables the workflows of a fork now and then to save compute: no run starts, and a manual run answers Actions has been disabled for this repository, while Settings → Actions still shows them allowed. The Actions tab then shows "Workflows on this fork have been disabled": re-enable them there.

docs.title: Cluster scan
docs.text:
What is misconfigured in the cluster itself and in what it runs: the API server's and kubelets' flags, RBAC, and what workloads may do on a node (step 15d, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-05-cluster-scan-design.md). Two scanners, run by hand, each against the environment it can read:

Target Tool Where Reads just testbed-scan, or just test e2e --env production --labels scan kube-bench (CIS benchmark k3s-cis-1.11) the testbed's or production's three NixOS nodes k3s's flags, files and permissions on each node just dev-scan kubescape 4.0.17 (allcontrols, --keep-local) the sandbox, the only environment with the whole platform RBAC and workloads through the API

Run them before step 12b's hardware, and again when k3s, the node profile (infra/_modules/metal) or a component's RBAC changes. Neither is part of just dev, just testbed or a release's proof. Production's hardware ran the same Job in step 12b-1 (just test e2e --env production --labels scan).

Both read .cluster-scan-accepted.yaml: a finding it does not list fails the target. Each fails rather than passes when the scan did not really run (below).

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
just testbed            # VMs up (just testbed-stop after)
just testbed-scan       # one kube-bench Job per node, in a temporary privileged namespace, deleted afterwards

k3d cluster start homelab-dev   # every pod Ready first
just dev-scan

A failure names what nobody decided on: homelab-2: undecided, ...: 1.2.30 for kube-bench (one line per node), one C-0057 <namespace>/<Kind>/<name> per line for kubescape. Reports hold command lines and config: they stay in the test's temporary directory and the failures name only checks, controls and resources. kubescape downloads its controls at each run, so a new control can fail the target with no change here: read it like any other finding.

docs.title: Deciding a finding
docs.text:
Fix it if the fix is small and contained, otherwise accept it in .cluster-scan-accepted.yaml with its reason. A finding that would let someone reach a node, every Secret or the whole API and has no small fix is raised before it is accepted.

  • kube-bench, by check number (kubeBench). Only FAILs fail the target. WARNs are manual checks, read once below.
  • kubescape, two levels (kubescape):
  • controls: noise here, accepted whole (limits, labels, probes, signatures, what Kyverno already checks).
  • resources: a group of controls on a group of resources, for one reason. The resource is <namespace>/<Kind>/<name> (a cluster-scoped one starts with /), and a pattern only inside the name (kube-system/DaemonSet/svclb-*), so a new workload holding the same power fails the target. The dangerous controls (cluster-admin, wildcards, impersonation, bind and escalate, privileged, host path, network and PID, capabilities, credentials in configuration) can only be accepted here; the file is refused otherwise. So are who may read every Secret, exec, create pods or volumes, port-forward or reach the kubelets' proxy (Dangerous in test/internal/clusterscan/clusterscan.go), and a name pattern keeps at least three characters of its own.

Sort by what a finding would let someone do, not by the tool's score.

docs.title: Not fooled by the tools
docs.text:
The spike found each of these reporting clean or wrong; the targets now fail instead:

  • kube-bench's image has no journalctl, which every k3s check calls: 21 false FAILs until the node's /nix and /run/current-system are mounted and on PATH. A result whose audit command was not found fails the target.
  • Without run --targets master,etcd,controlplane,node,policies it detects no control plane on k3s and skips three sections with 0 fails. Each of sections 1 to 5 must have results on every node, and every node must report.
  • kube-bench v0.16.0's image has k3s benchmarks only up to 1.9: k3s-cis-1.11 is vendored from its main (test/kube-bench-cfg/, the commit in config.yaml's header). Drop the directory when a release has it.
  • No benchmark maps to Kubernetes 1.37 (the table ends at 1.35): this is the nearest, not an exact match.
  • kubescape must have seen at least 500 resources and istio-system/DaemonSet/ztunnel, or the target fails.

Each guard was seen to fail: without the /nix mount (1.2.1: its audit command was not found on every node), without --targets (section 1 did not run), and kubescape found a privileged Pod applied for the purpose (C-0057 scan-probe/Pod/scan-probe).

docs.title: What was found and decided (2026-11-05)
docs.text:
kube-bench: 64 pass, 5 fail, 49 warn on each node before this step.

Check Decision 1.2.30 service-account-extend-token-expiration Fixed: false on the nodes and k3d 1.3.7, 1.4.2 bind-address, 4.3.1 kube-proxy metrics Accepted: bound beyond localhost for Prometheus; nixos-fw admits only pods and nodes on those ports 4.2.4 read-only-port Accepted, a false report: the journal's line ends read-only-port=0", the check reads 0"; nothing listens on 10255

The fourteen warnings outside section 5's manual policy checks (section 5 is what Kyverno and kubescape read):

Warning Reading 1.2.3 DenyServiceExternalIPs Left: no Service sets externalIPs; Kyverno could refuse it if one ever does 1.2.9 EventRateLimit Left: an alpha admission plugin needing its own config file 1.2.11 AlwaysPullImages Left: every image is pinned, and pulling at every start would make a power cut's recovery wait on the registries 1.2.17 audit-log-maxage Fixed: 30 days, on the nodes and k3d (the size and backup limits still bound it) 1.2.18 audit-log-maxbackup Left at 3: the OpenTelemetry agent ships the audit log to Loki, which keeps 60 days (Security logs) 1.2.20 request-timeout Left at the default 1.3.1 terminated-pod-gc-threshold Left at the default 3.1.1 to 3.1.3 authentication for users People sign in through Kanidm to the apps; only the admin kubeconfig uses a client certificate, kept on the workstation 3.2.2 audit policy Read in step 15c (infra/_modules/metal/flake/audit-policy.yaml) 4.2.12 kubelet ciphers Left: Go's defaults are strong; pinning a list would need updating as Go changes them 4.2.13 pod PID limit Fixed: pod-max-pids=4096, on the nodes and k3d 4.2.14 seccomp-default Fixed (step 15h): on, on the nodes and k3d, so a pod naming no profile gets RuntimeDefault. The golden path's Buildah step needs unshare, which it refuses: a native MutatingAdmissionPolicy gives it the Localhost profile homelab/buildah.json (RuntimeDefault plus unshare, mount, umount2 and pivot_root, infra/_modules/metal/flake/seccomp), and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy refuses any Localhost profile to every other pod in namespace ci (In-cluster CI); other namespaces have no such guard, their pods come from git

kubescape: 87 failed controls on the sandbox, about 2,100 control and resource pairs. Fixed:

  • Velero was bound to cluster-admin, though it moves only volumes: its own ClusterRole now (system/velero/templates/rbac.yaml). Two tries were short of what it needs: its ServiceAccount plugin lists ClusterRoleBindings when it starts, and its controllers watch its own kinds (datauploads) at cluster scope, so a restore waited for them forever. It may not create volumes: one could be a hostPath volume a pod in its own namespace mounts, which is the node (restored claims get theirs from the CSI provisioner). TestBackupRestore is the proof.
  • Grafana could read every Secret (the chart's ClusterRole for its sidecars): a Role reading only ConfigMaps in grafana and monitoring-system now.
  • kube-state-metrics listed every Secret for kube_secret_*, which nothing here reads: that collector is off.

TestScanNarrowedRBAC keeps the three narrow. "Credentials in configuration" (C-0012, C-0259) matched names only: each value was read and none is a credential (the file says what each is). kyverno-migrate-resources names a missing ServiceAccount because both are the chart's post-upgrade hooks and only the ServiceAccount is deleted afterwards.

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
k3s encrypts Secrets in etcd (--secrets-encryption, AES-CBC, in infra/_modules/metal/flake/profiles/k3s-server.nix since step 12a-1). TestTestbedSecretsEncrypted (part of just testbed) writes a Secret and reads it raw from etcd with etcdctl: it must start with k8s:enc:aescbc: and hold no trace of the value. The sandbox (k3d) has no such flag.

It protects a copy of etcd's data taken without the key: an etcd snapshot, a disk image of the database alone. It does not protect against:

  • someone with the cluster's credentials or a pod that may read Secrets: the API server decrypts for them;
  • a stolen or thrown-away disk: the key is on the same disk (/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/cred/encryption-config.json, mode 0600). Disk encryption (LUKS) would; it is set aside for now, an accepted risk on the before-production list (adding it later means reinstalling each disk).

Public clouds' "encryption at rest" works the same way at the storage layer, with the key in a separate KMS: it guards the media, not against valid credentials.

docs.title: Rotating the key
docs.text:
Only by a person, when there is a reason (k3s.encryption-key in cli/internal/rotate/catalog.yaml): k3s warns a wrong rotation can corrupt the cluster for good, and with stolen disks set aside a schedule guards little. Run once on the testbed (2026-11-05):

ssh root@<a server> k3s secrets-encrypt status       # Enabled, All hashes match
ssh root@<a server> k3s secrets-encrypt rotate-keys  # "keys rotated, reencryption finished"
# restart k3s on each server in turn, waiting for it to be Ready
ssh root@<each server> systemctl restart k3s
ssh root@<a server> k3s secrets-encrypt status       # All hashes match, a little after the last restart

rotate-keys reports reencrypt_finished at once, but the hashes differ until every server has restarted: the status said hash does not match for minutes before the restarts and for a little after the last one. Afterwards each node had one key, dated that run; every Secret in etcd (27) began with the new key's name, every node listed them through the API, and TestTestbedSecretsEncrypted passed.

The k3s token (k3s.token) has an entry too, with k3s's documented steps (k3s token rotate); it was never run here.

docs.title: Deploy to Forgejo
docs.text:
GitHub is where work happens (pull requests, checks, the sandbox). Production's Argo CD syncs ops/homelab on Forgejo, which changes only when a commit is deployed:

just infra deploy production       # the infrastructure, Forgejo's orgs ops and ci, the push, the Argo CD bootstrap
cd cli && go run ./cmd/lab infra forgejo push   # only the push

Both refuse anything but origin/master checked out without changes (and no untracked file under infra/ or system/argocd/) whose check checks passed and whose merged pull request's check sandbox passed (lab infra forgejo verify). Nothing force-pushes: roll back with a revert through a pull request.

docs.title: What proved the release
docs.text:
infra/production/cluster/config.json names the environment that proves a release: "release_proof": "testbed" or "staging"; without the key verify refuses. A release changing what that environment runs needs a commit carrying its mark, the commit status of that name, written when just testbed passes: infra/testbed/release-paths.yaml's paths and the components system/argocd/values-testbed.yaml lists, less not_run. A mark on an earlier commit, a merged branch's tip included, counts when those paths are the same. verify always says how far the testbed goes: "only the testbed proved this: no production-like environment did".

Without the mark verify refuses and names the paths; just infra deploy production --skip-proof "<reason>" (--skip-proof=<reason>) releases anyway and records the reason as the commit status testbed/skipped, which proves nothing to a later release.

docs.title: What lab infra forgejo sync owns
docs.text:
sync (part of just infra deploy production) owns orgs ops and ci, ci's bot and its webhook; nothing declares other orgs, teams or repositories. Running it again keeps what is right, fixes what is wrong and creates what is missing:

  • orgs ops and ci, private (made private again if someone changed that);
  • ops/homelab, private, default branch master, created empty: the first deploy fills it;
  • local users deploy (write) and argocd (read), restricted to the repositories they collaborate on; sync refuses a user of that name who signed in with Kanidm, and a team granting either of them more;
  • master's protection: only deploy may push, nobody force-pushes or deletes it, Forgejo's site admins included (they can still edit the protection, which the next sync restores);
  • their tokens in OpenBao: secret/forgejo/deploy (the push) and secret/argocd/forgejo (Argo CD's read-only credential, argocd-repo-forgejo);
  • in org ci, its team developers (write on code and pull requests, may create repositories in ci, not all of them): Forgejo's Kanidm login source makes homelab-admins its owners and homelab-editors its developers; no team of ci reaches ops;
  • the local user ci-bot, alone in ci's team pipeline (write on code of every repository of ci: the golden path's clones and commit statuses), and its token in secret/ci/forgejo-token;
  • ci's webhook to Argo Events (http://forgejo-eventsource-svc.ci:12000/forgejo, push and pull request events, Authorization: Bearer with secret/ci/generated/webhook), rewritten when that secret or the hook changed (In-cluster CI).

Other repositories (for example the blog) live in org ci, created there or mirrored, not through push.

docs.title: Break-glass: GitHub or the internet is down
docs.text:
Production keeps running without GitHub: Argo CD reads Forgejo. A fix that cannot wait for GitHub skips verify's GitHub checks, and nothing else:

direnv exec . scripts/ci-check all             # the checks GitHub would have run, locally
git switch -c fix/<what> && git commit ...     # a branch: master stays GitHub's
just infra deploy production --break-glass "<why>"  # verify without GitHub, the infrastructure, sync, the push, the bootstrap

Before anything is applied, verify --break-glass still refuses uncommitted changes, untracked files under infra/ or system/argocd/ and a commit that does not descend from what ops/homelab's master holds (so production never runs infrastructure from a commit the push would then refuse); the push prints the reason. --break-glass cannot be combined with --force. When GitHub is back, push the branch and open a pull request into dev that says why, then the release pull request into master: merge commits only (never squash or rebase), so master contains the deployed commit and the next normal deploy fast-forwards.

What still depends on the internet:

  • OpenTofu's state is on R2: with no internet just infra deploy cannot run. Push alone: cd cli && go run ./cmd/lab infra forgejo push --break-glass="<why>".
  • Charts served from *.github.io (app-template, Argo CD's) and images on ghcr.io are GitHub too: Argo CD renders only charts its repo server still caches, and a node runs only images it already pulled.
  • Kanidm and Forgejo work on the LAN; Cloudflare's Tunnel (the public routes) does not.

The last resort, when nothing can be pushed: pause the Application's auto-sync in Argo CD (an admin, in its UI), change the resource with kubectl, then commit the same change and resume auto-sync once it is deployed; Argo CD would revert a manual change while auto-sync runs.

docs.title: Expose services to the internet
docs.text:
Info

This tutorial is for Cloudflare Tunnel users, please skip if you use port forwarding.

Apply the ./external layer to create a tunnel if you haven't already, then attach the app's HTTPRoute to the public Gateway public (replace example.com with your domain):

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  annotations:
    external-dns.kubernetes.io/cloudflare-proxied: "true"
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: istio-system
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - foo.example.com
# ...

external-dns points the hostname at the tunnel (the public Gateway carries the external-dns.kubernetes.io/target annotation), and cloudflared forwards tunnel traffic to that Gateway only. Routes on the LAN Gateway gateway stay off the internet.

docs.title: In-cluster CI: Argo Workflows and Argo Events
docs.text: Repositories in Forgejo's org ci build their images in the cluster: a push runs the golden path, a template in this repository (platform/ci/templates/pipeline.yaml), never a pipeline the repository writes. This repository itself is not one of them: its CI is GitHub Actions (CI), and ops/homelab only receives deploys (Deploy to Forgejo). The design and its reasons: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-13-argo-ci-design.md.

docs.title: How a push becomes an image
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  push[push or pull request in org ci] -->|webhook, Bearer secret| es[EventSource forgejo]
  es --> bus[EventBus JetStream] --> sensor[Sensor forgejo]
  sensor -->|Workflow from template pipeline| wf[Workflow in namespace ci]
  wf --> clone --> settings --> build
  build -->|default branch only| sbom --> sign
  wf -->|commit status ci/pipeline| forgejo[Forgejo]
  • lab infra forgejo sync keeps org ci's webhook (push and pull request events) pointing at the EventSource, with Authorization: Bearer and the secret at secret/ci/generated/webhook; the EventSource refuses anything else, and only Forgejo's pods may reach it (namespace ci's allow).
  • The Sensor starts the template pipeline on a push to a branch (not its deletion) and on a pull request opened, updated or reopened. Tags and other events start nothing.
  • Each run has its own volume, deleted with it. Steps: clone the commit as ci-bot, read .ci.yaml, build with Buildah; on a push to the default branch also push registry.<domain>/<image>:<commit> to zot, make an SPDX SBOM, sign the image and attest the SBOM and an SLSA provenance with OpenBao's transit key ci-signing (role ci-signer; the key never leaves OpenBao). Pull requests and other branches build only.
  • The commit status ci/pipeline goes pending, then success, failure or error, linking the run's page.
  • Workflows stay a week; pods of steps that passed go at once, failed ones stay with their Workflow. Logs also reach Loki, like every pod's.

docs.title: Bring a repository
docs.text:
1. Create it in Forgejo's org ci (or a pull mirror of a GitHub repository, owner ci). Org ci's webhook covers every repository: nothing to enable.
  2. Give it a Containerfile (or Dockerfile) at its root. A repository with neither builds nothing (the run passes).

  3. Optionally, .ci.yaml at its root, with only these keys (anything else fails the run):

    context: web                       # the build context, inside the repository (default: .)
containerfile: web/Containerfile   # default: <context>/Containerfile, else <context>/Dockerfile
image: site                        # zot repository name, [a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]* (default: the repository's name)

Builds run with Buildah in their own user namespace under the seccomp profile homelab/buildah.json (infra/_modules/metal/flake/seccomp), unprivileged; vfs storage, so no layer cache between runs.

docs.title: Who signs in
docs.text:
https://ci.<domain> (LAN only) signs people in with Kanidm:

Kanidm group In Argo's UI homelab-admins everything in namespace ci, the templates included homelab-editors runs, resubmits and reads Workflows and their logs homelab-users reads Workflows and templates anyone else refused by Kanidm

Forgejo's Kanidm login source also makes homelab-admins the owners of org ci and homelab-editors its team developers (create and push repositories). Whatever the UI or the API is asked, the controller runs only Workflows that reference the golden path's templates (templateReferencing: Strict).

Only Forgejo's events publish. A run started from the UI or the API (Submit on the template pipeline) builds and reports its status but never pushes or signs: the admission policy ci-workflow-arguments refuses event=push from anyone but the Sensor, any entrypoint but main, and any change to a run's arguments afterwards, so resubmitting a push's run is refused too (push again instead). A signature therefore always means "built by the golden path from the default branch".

docs.title: Verify an image
docs.text:
The public key is the ConfigMap ci/ci-signing-public-key, copied from OpenBao after every sync of platform/ci. Kyverno's verify-ci-images (Audit until step 15b-2) checks every pod's registry.<domain>/* image with it:

kubectl -n ci get configmap ci-signing-public-key -o jsonpath='{.data.cosign\.pub}' > cosign.pub
cosign verify --key cosign.pub --insecure-ignore-tlog=true registry.<domain>/<image>@<digest>
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --insecure-ignore-tlog=true --type slsaprovenance1 registry.<domain>/<image>@<digest>
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --insecure-ignore-tlog=true --type spdxjson registry.<domain>/<image>@<digest>

No signature goes to a public transparency log: the registry and its image names are the homelab's.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
All in OpenBao and the rotation catalog (Secrets rotation):

Secret Path Rotation the webhook's secret ci/generated/webhook ci.webhook, manual: a new value, lab infra forgejo sync, the EventSource restarted ci-bot's Forgejo token ci/forgejo-token forgejo.ci-bot-token, with overlap, from the workstation zot's ci password zot/generated/ci, ci/generated/registry registry.ci, once no run is unfinished Kanidm client argo-workflows kaniop's Secret kanidm-client.argo-workflows the signing key OpenBao transit ci-signing ci.signing-key, manual (Kyverno needs the new public key)

docs.title: See the mesh with Kiali
docs.text:
Kiali (system/kiali) draws the mesh from Prometheus and checks Istio's config. Open https://kiali.<domain>/kiali on the LAN (in the sandbox https://kiali.127-0-0-1.nip.io/kiali) and sign in with Kanidm.

  • Who: only homelab-admins. Kanidm refuses everyone else (the client kiali gives no other group a scope).
  • Read-only: Kiali shows config and traffic but changes nothing: its service account can only read (the API server refuses a write), and view_only_mode hides the UI's write actions. Change the mesh in git.
  • Not public: its route is on the LAN Gateway only, never the Cloudflare Tunnel.

docs.title: What the graph shows
docs.text:
• Inside the mesh, L4 only: the ambient mesh has no sidecars and no waypoints, so ztunnel reports TCP connections and bytes between workloads, not HTTP requests, codes or latency.
  • At the Gateways, L7: requests entering through gateway and public are HTTP to the Gateways' Envoy, so the edges from gateway-istio carry request rates, codes and latency.
  • Istio config: validation of AuthorizationPolicy, Gateway API routes and the rest, per namespace.

The data comes from Prometheus scraping ztunnel, istiod and the Gateways (system/istio-system's PodMonitors), which Grafana can also query.

docs.title: Not here
docs.text: Traces (no Tempo), Kiali's write features, and L7 inside the mesh (it needs waypoints).

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Every pod's log, the audit logs and the cluster's Kubernetes events are in Loki (system/loki) for 30 days (7 in the sandbox). Grafana → Explore → data source Loki.

Labels follow OpenTelemetry's conventions (the Collector sends over OTLP):

Query Shows {k8s_namespace_name="forgejo"} every container of a namespace {k8s_namespace_name="forgejo", k8s_container_name="forgejo"} \|= "error" lines containing "error" {service_name="grafana"} one app (its app.kubernetes.io/name) {service_name="kubernetes-events"} \|= "paperless" the events naming a namespace (scheduling, pulls, probe failures, OOM kills) {k8s_namespace_name="istio-system"} \|= "<trace id>" the Gateways' access log lines of one request (Traces)

Other attributes (the node, the pod's uid, the workload) are structured metadata: filter them after the selector, e.g. {k8s_namespace_name="loki"} | k8s_node_name="homelab-1".

The OpenTelemetry agent (a DaemonSet in namespace opentelemetry) reads /var/log/pods and the API server's audit log on each node, remembers where it stopped and queues what Loki has not taken yet in /var/lib/otelcol on the node, so a Loki outage plus a restart of the agent loses no line. The gateway Collector gathers the cluster's events once. Logs have no backup (step 11 decides).

docs.title: Media management
docs.text:
Warning

This is for educational purposes only Use it at your own risk!

docs.title: Initial setup
docs.text:
• Jellyfin https://jellyfin.example.com:
    • Create an admin user and save the credentials to your password manager
    • Add media libraries:
      • Movies at /media/movies
      • Shows at /media/shows
  • Radarr https://radarr.example.com:
    • Authentication method: Forms
    • Create an admin user and save the credentials to your password manager
    • Navigate to Settings -> Download Clients -> Add -> Transmission (you can keep the default address and port)
    • Navigate to Settings -> Media Management -> Add Root Folder /movies
    • Navigate to Settings -> General -> API Key -> copy it for the next steps (or save it to your password manager)
  • Sonarr https://sonarr.example.com: same as Radarr but use /shows for the root folder
  • Prowlarr https://prowlarr.example.com:
    • Authentication method: Forms
    • Create an admin user and save the credentials to your password manager
    • Navigate to Settings -> Apps -> Add:
      • Radarr: paste the API key (you can keep the default address and port)
      • Sonarr: same as Radarr
    • Go back to Indexers -> Add New Indexers
  • Jellyseerr https://jellyseerr.example.com:
    • Sign In
      • Use your Jellyfin account
      • URL: https://jellyfin.example.com
      • Email: you can enter anything
      • Username: admin
      • Password: same as Jellyfin
    • Configure Media Server
      • Enable Movies and Shows
    • Configure Services:
      • Add Radarr Server:
        • Default Server: true
        • Name: Radarr
        • Hostname: localhost
        • Port: use default
        • API Key: from previous step
        • Click Test
        • Quality Profile: choose whatever suits you
        • Root folder: /movies
        • External URL: https://radarr.example.com
        • Enable Scan: true
      • Add Sonarr Server: similar to Radarr

Optionally, for convenience, you can add a guest account without a password in Jellyfin, allow access to all libraries, and allow that account to manage requests in Jellyseerr.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Here's a suggested flow:

  • Users using the guest account can request media in Jellyseerr
  • Admins approve the request (or you can enable auto-approve)
  • Wait for the media to be downloaded
  • Watch on Jellyfin

You may need to increase the volume size depending on your usage.

docs.title: Policy: Kyverno and Pod Security Admission
docs.text:
Two layers keep workloads within the rules (step 15b, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-27-policy-design.md).

  • Kyverno (system/kyverno) applies the Pod Security Standards at restricted, plus two rules of this repository: every image is pinned (a tag other than latest, or a digest), and comes from an allowed registry (registries in system/kyverno/values.yaml, plus zot). It runs in Audit: violations land in PolicyReports; nothing is refused yet (Enforce is step 15b-2).
