  • Pod Security Admission (Kubernetes itself) enforces baseline on every managed namespace, and stays in force if Kyverno is down. Namespaces whose pods need the node are privileged: the mesh (istio-system), Ceph (rook-ceph), opentelemetry (its agent), monitoring-system (node-exporter), the sandbox's csi-hostpath, and the VPN routers (tailscale, wireguard). The labels come from Argo CD's ApplicationSets (system/argocd/values.yaml).

docs.title: The policy check
docs.text: scripts/ci-check policy (a basic check, also in CI) renders every chart and app file for both environments and runs the same policies with the kyverno CLI. A pull request whose workload breaks one fails before it merges.

docs.title: A new workload
docs.text:
Set its securityContext:

  • The pod: seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}, and runAsNonRoot: true with the image's numeric user (runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup) when the image has a non-root user.
  • Each container: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and capabilities: {drop: [ALL]} when it runs as non-root.

In app files, use defaultPodOptions.securityContext and each controller's defaultContainerOptions (defaultContainerOptionsStrategy: merge).

docs.title: An exception
docs.text:
When the image cannot meet a rule (it runs only as root, it needs the node), write a PolicyException beside the workload, in its own chart (templates/policy-exception.yaml) or app file (rawResources.policy-exception):

apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: PolicyException
metadata:
  name: pod-security
  annotations:
    homelab/reason: "the image runs as root (no USER)"
spec:
  policyRefs:
    - {name: require-run-as-nonroot, kind: ValidatingPolicy}
  matchConditions:
    - name: app
      expression: "object.metadata.name.startsWith('app')"

Name only the policies it breaks, and match only its workload by name. Read the current exceptions with kubectl get policyexceptions.policies.kyverno.io -A. If the workload also breaks baseline (hostPath, host namespaces, privileged, added capabilities), its namespace must be privileged in Argo CD's templatePatch.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
kubectl get policyreports -A                      # one per resource (its scope)
kubectl -n <namespace> get policyreports -o yaml  # each result: fail, error or warn (passes are not kept)

TestPolicy checks that no workload of this repository fails. That is the condition for switching to Enforce.

On a fresh cluster a pod can start before Kyverno has cached the PolicyException beside it, so its report (and its Deployment's) shows a fail the exception excuses, until the next background scan (every 6 hours in the sandbox, every hour in production) or the pod is recreated. TestPolicy therefore judges only the reports of pods created a minute after the newest exception was created or changed (k3s's own pods in kube-system are not the repository's). On a fresh sandbox that is few pods (often only CronJob runs): there TestPolicy does not prove the renders clean, scripts/ci-check policy does. Before Enforce (15b-2), read the reports of a sandbox that has run a background scan since its first sync.

docs.title: Power
docs.text: The homelab comes back by itself after losing power, with nobody home. There is no UPS for now, so every outage is a sudden cut of every node, and that is the main path. Nothing runs on the cluster to recover from one.

docs.title: After an outage
docs.text:
Set each node's BIOS "Restore on AC power loss" to Last State: a node running when the power went comes back, and one turned off on purpose stays off, even through an outage.

The nodes boot, k3s and etcd form a cluster again, then Ceph and the mesh follow. On the testbed this takes about 3 minutes from the VMs starting, with only Ceph and the mesh on it. The whole platform takes longer: on the one-node sandbox a cut took from 5.5 to 23 minutes, the mesh's restart deadlock accounting for the slowest (docs/reference/architecture/networking.md), so wait that long before going home to look. Hardware has its own numbers: the testbed does not prove a real disk keeps what it acknowledged, so 12b prefers SSDs with power-loss protection and repeats the cut before real data.

docs.title: Turning the homelab off
docs.text:
lab cluster shutdown --environment production

In order:

  1. It writes the marker, ConfigMap kube-system/cluster-shutdown, naming what it is about to change.
  2. It stops Argo CD's application controller, which would undo the next step.
  3. It suspends every CronJob that is not already suspended, except those labelled homelab/power-keep: "true" (the mesh's istio-cni-watchdog).
  4. It waits for running Jobs, at most --job-wait (5 minutes), and names those it left.
  5. It sets Ceph's noout.
  6. It powers off every node at once, without draining.

Velero's Schedule is left alone: a backup the shutdown cuts ends Failed and the next one runs.

A node's poweroff can hang: one holding a Ceph volume waits for OSDs that are gone. A unit started with the poweroff (poweroff-deadline) cuts its power after 180 seconds without syncing. For what was left to write that is a sudden cut, which the power tests prove survivable. On the testbed a node with no volume is off in 20 to 90 seconds.

Running it again after a partial run finishes the job and keeps what the first run recorded. If it fails with the nodes up, it says to run lab cluster startup.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Power on the nodes (Wake-on-LAN or the button). Nobody needs to run anything: the unit cluster-startup runs on every node at boot.

  • No marker: it does nothing, as after a sudden cut.
  • A marker, with most of its nodes still on the boot it recorded: it does nothing yet, so one node rebooting during a shutdown does not resume what is being stopped.
  • A marker, with most of its nodes on a new boot: it waits for the API, resumes the CronJobs the marker names and starts Argo CD's controller. It then takes noout off and removes the marker.

To run it by hand and wait for it, whatever the boot IDs say:

lab cluster startup --environment production

docs.title: A node that does not return
docs.text:
Two nodes are enough. CronJobs and Argo CD come back without the third, so backups and rotation do not stay off.

noout stays until every OSD answers, or for 30 minutes from startup's first run. After that Ceph copies what the dead node held rather than staying short of a replica. The marker goes last, so it lasts as long as noout.

docs.title: When the marker stays
docs.text:
The alert ClusterShutdownMarkerStuck fires when the marker is over two hours old: what the shutdown stopped may still be stopped.

ssh root@<node> journalctl -u cluster-startup
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap cluster-shutdown -o yaml
lab cluster startup --environment production

docs.title: With a UPS
docs.text: A separate step, when a UPS is bought. An ordered shutdown leaves the last state "off", so Last State would never bring the nodes back. That step sets the BIOS to Power On and has NUT tell the UPS to cut and restore its output (shutdown.return), which also covers the power returning during a shutdown. The cost: a node turned off on purpose comes back after an outage. Choose a UPS that NUT drives with that command.

docs.title: Public surface
docs.text:
What the internet reaches, and how it is guarded (step 15f, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-public-surface-design.md). The Cloudflare Tunnel publishes the public apps only; every admin app (Argo CD, Grafana, Kiali, Forgejo, Argo Workflows, zot, Kanidm) stays on the LAN Gateway.

Host App Namespace www. blog blog draw. excalidraw excalidraw ntfy. ntfy ntfy

Matrix (matrix. and chat.) stays on the LAN: it signs in through Kanidm, which is LAN-only until step 13 (VPN from outside).

Three guards:

  • The allow-list. Gateway istio-system/public admits routes only from the namespaces of the public map (public in system/istio-system/values.yaml); a route from any other namespace stays NotAllowedByListeners. TestPublicRoutes (basic checks) renders production and fails a route on public from a namespace off the map, with a host the map does not list for it, or without external-dns.kubernetes.io/cloudflare-proxied: "true": a Tunnel host works only proxied (external-dns makes records DNS-only otherwise), and only then gets the WAF and the rate limit. TestGatewayPublicAllowList proves the Gateway's refusal in the sandbox.
  • Cloudflare's edge (infra/_modules/cloudflare, applied by infra/production/cloudflare): one rate limit and the WAF's managed rules, below.
  • A weekly scan (system/public-scan): nuclei against the public hosts from inside the cluster, below.

docs.title: Publishing an app
docs.text:
1. Its route: parentRefs istio-system/public, its host <label>.{{ .Values.global.baseDomain }}, and the annotation external-dns.kubernetes.io/cloudflare-proxied: "true".
  2. Its namespace and host label in public (system/istio-system/values.yaml).
  3. The label in targets (system/public-scan/values.yaml; TestPublicScanTargets keeps the two equal).

The pull request then shows the new surface in one place. An admin app never goes there: publish it on the LAN Gateway, and reach it from outside through the VPN.

docs.title: Cloudflare's edge
docs.text:
The Free plan (Cloudflare's docs, read 2026-11-06) allows one rate-limiting rule, counted per client IP over 10 seconds, blocking for 10 seconds, whose expression may use only the path: it cannot name a host. So the rule (cloudflare_ruleset.rate_limit) covers the whole zone: 200 requests per 10 seconds per IP (rate_limit_requests), far above a browser's cold load of a public app. Nothing else in the zone is proxied; a proxied host added later outside the Tunnel gets the same rule. Per-account limits stay the apps' own (ntfy's per-visitor limits read CF-Connecting-IP). The rule also counts cached assets: the Free plan cannot exclude them.

The WAF's managed rules are the Free Managed Ruleset. Cloudflare creates no entry point for it on a Free zone (a plan on 2026-11-07 found none, and the dashboard's WAF page offers only paid add-ons), so the module declares the zone's http_request_firewall_managed entry point (cloudflare_ruleset.managed) running it. Its id is not published: the module finds it by name (Free) among the managed rulesets the zone may run, and a plan fails, naming those it found, when there is not exactly one.

Apply with the rest of production (just infra deploy production), or the unit alone:

cf auth login          # Account API Tokens enabled on its consent page
terragrunt --working-dir infra/production/cloudflare plan

docs.title: The weekly scan
docs.text:
system/public-scan's CronJob runs Sunday at 04:00 (global.timezone). For each host of targets, through public DNS and Cloudflare, as an outsider's requests arrive:

  1. Preflight, right before the host's scan and again right after it: the host's first page must answer normally. An error, a block, or a Cloudflare challenge (a 403, or a "Just a moment..." page) fails the run: the scan would see Cloudflare, not the app, and a challenge that began mid-scan would otherwise end as a clean run.
  2. nuclei (image) with a pinned templates release (templates: a tarball checked against its sha256), throttled to rateLimit (8 requests per second, under half the rate limit: TestPublicScanRateBelowLimit), so a run never blocks the household. About 29 000 requests a host, an hour each. Excluded: dos, fuzz and intrusive templates, and out-of-band ones (-no-interactsh: they would send probes' data to ProjectDiscovery's servers). The WAF blocks some probes: the protection working, not a failure.
  3. A run that loaded fewer than minTemplates templates (90% of the release's count) fails, and so does one with a finding the report cannot read.

The Job's log holds one line per finding, {"public_scan":"finding","template":...,"host":...,"severity":...}, and a last {"public_scan":"done","templates":N}. nuclei's own output (its requests as curl commands, what templates extracted) stays in the pod.

Alert Means Do PublicScanFinding (Loki) A finding at medium or above that nobody accepted Read the template (its id names it in the templates), then fix the app or accept it PublicScanFailed The newest run failed kubectl -n public-scan logs job/<job> names the host it could not see, or the count PublicScanMissing No run succeeded for eight days The runs fail, or the pod cannot start

Info and low findings (technology detection, missing headers) stay in the log only.

docs.title: Accepting a finding
docs.text:
In system/public-scan/values.yaml's accepted (or values-dev.yaml for the sandbox only), one entry per template and host, with the reason:

accepted:
  - template: <template-id>
    host: draw
    reason: why it is not a risk here

It hides that template on that host only. TestPublicScanAccepted refuses an entry without a reason or for a host the scan does not have.

docs.title: A Cloudflare challenge
docs.text: When the preflight reports did not answer normally (a 403) or Cloudflare challenged the scan, find out why before loosening anything: Cloudflare saw the home connection as hostile (a shared CGNAT address with a bad reputation, or the rate limit). The scan never gets a way around the edge: it would then test a surface no outsider sees.

docs.title: Bumping nuclei or its templates
docs.text: Pin the image's digest, the templates' tag and its tarball's sha256 (curl -sSL https://github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei-templates/archive/refs/tags/<tag>.tar.gz | sha256sum), and set minTemplates to 90% of the new count (a run's last line, or TestPublicScan's log).

docs.title: In the sandbox
docs.text: The CronJob runs there against the public map's hosts the sandbox serves (draw, ntfy), through the LAN Gateway, at 150 requests per second (values-dev.yaml: no Cloudflare). TestPublicScan runs it once: it completes, loads its templates, finds nothing at medium or above, and Loki's ruler holds PublicScanFinding. What Cloudflare does to the scan is seen only in production.

docs.title: Renovate
docs.text: Renovate runs in the production cluster (platform/renovate, daily at 05:00) and opens pull requests into dev on GitHub as the GitHub App duongle-lab-renovate. Its pull requests run checks and, labelled sandbox, the sandbox. The App's private key goes through OpenTofu into OpenBao and External Secrets into the Secret renovate-github-app. Each run mints its own installation token: the CronJob's initContainer github-token (the only container that mounts the key; platform/renovate/files/github-token.js) signs a JWT and asks GitHub for a token with Renovate's permissions, the Renovate container reads it from memory and revokes it when the run ends, failed or not. Passing trouble (the network, GitHub's 5xx or 429) is retried three times; a refused token (a wrong key, App ID or permission) fails the Job at once with GitHub's status and message (kubectl -n renovate logs job/<job> -c github-token). A failed run is retried once, a run stops after 55 minutes (its token lives an hour), and a failed Job reaches ntfy (KubeJobFailed). The pod runs as the image's user (uid 12021, gid 0) without privileges or a service account token.

docs.title: Create the App (once)
docs.text:
1. GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App: a name of your own (App names are global; this repository's is duongle-lab-renovate), homepage the repository's URL, Webhook: off (Renovate runs as a CronJob and polls; nothing listens for events).
  2. Repository permissions: Contents, Pull requests, Workflows, Issues (Renovate's Dependency Dashboard): Read and write; Commit statuses, Checks: Read-only; Metadata: Read-only (always). No organization or account permissions. "Only on this account".
  3. Create it, note the App ID, then Generate a private key (a .pem downloads once).
  4. Install App → your account → Only select repositories → homelab. The installation's URL ends with its installation ID (.../settings/installations/<id>).
  5. The bot's user id, for Renovate's commit author: gh api '/users/<app-name>[bot]' --jq .id.

App ID, installation ID and bot id are not secrets: they live in platform/renovate/values.yaml.

docs.title: Give the key to production (once, and after a rotation)
docs.text:
HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY=~/Downloads/<app-name>.<date>.private-key.pem just infra deploy production

The path comes from the environment, relative (to where just runs), absolute or ~/, spaces included. OpenTofu keeps the key in its encrypted state (infra/production/secrets); later runs need no file, so delete it. If the unit was applied before the key existed, apply once with the key and -replace=module.github_app_key.terraform_data.kept in infra/production/secrets (terragrunt apply -replace=...); the plain run refuses rather than ignoring the key.

docs.title: Rotate the key
docs.text:
Generate a new key on the App's page, then in infra/production/secrets:

HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY=<new.pem> terragrunt apply -replace=module.github_app_key.terraform_data.kept

Delete the old key on GitHub once Renovate ran with the new one.

docs.title: What it updates
docs.text: renovate.json5 adds to Renovate's defaults (charts, values*.yaml images, Go, OpenTofu providers, GitHub Actions): the images in apps/*.yaml, the app-template pin in system/argocd/values*.yaml (a regex manager) and flake.lock (the nix manager, every Monday's lock file maintenance; schedules use the time zone in the global config), and the sandbox's k3s image and Gateway API CRDs (infra/_modules/k3d, regex managers). TestRenovateManagers checks what Renovate finds, offline. A new commit from Renovate on its labelled pull request (a rebase, a newer version) runs sandbox-label again.

docs.title: Add a repository
docs.text: Install the App on it (App → Configure → Repository access) and add a renovate.json5; the next run finds it (autodiscover, limited to duongle-steven/*). Renovate skips repositories without a config.

docs.title: Runtime detection
docs.text:
Falco (system/falco) watches every node's system calls through its modern eBPF probe. It reports what happens inside running containers that should not: a shell nobody expected, a read of /etc/shadow, a binary that was not in the image, a reverse shell, a kernel module loaded, ptrace on another process, a container escape, a miner naming its pool. It only detects; nothing is blocked (step 15g-2 will respond to a short list of rules, after production's first weeks).

Its rules are the stable ruleset in Falco's image, plus one vendored file (system/falco/files/miners.yaml: the Stratum rule from falcosecurity/rules' sandbox set, with its tag). Nothing is downloaded while it runs. A miner that hides its pool's URI evades that rule, and egress does not stop one in a namespace allowed out on 443 (the golden path's builds, for one).

Its events are in Loki, beside the other logs (Logs), and on the dashboard Security (row "Runtime (Falco)"). Error and above raise alerts, which reach ntfy and Telegram like every other alert (Alerts).

Priority Where it goes emergency, alert, critical alert FalcoCriticalEvent (severity critical) error alert FalcoErrorEvent (severity warning) warning the dashboard only notice and below not logged

docs.title: Reading an event
docs.text:
Grafana → Explore → data source Loki:

{k8s_namespace_name="falco"} | json rule="rule", priority="priority", ns=`output_fields["k8s.ns.name"]` | __error__=""

Each line is one event: rule, priority, output (one sentence with the process, its command line, the user, the container and the pod) and output_fields (the same as fields). An event without k8s.ns.name came from a process outside Kubernetes. On the nodes that is the node itself. In the sandbox, which shares WSL's kernel, it can also be the workstation or another Docker container. Falco cannot see Windows.

docs.title: When an alert fires
docs.text:
• FalcoCriticalEvent or FalcoErrorEvent.
  • Open the event (the alert's description has the query).
  • Find out who or what ran the process: the pod, its image, the command line, the parent process. For an exec, the API server's audit log names the person (Security logs).
  • If it was an attack, isolate the pod (scale it to 0, or a NetworkPolicy denying all), keep its logs, then follow Secrets rotation for what the pod could read.
  • If it is expected, accept it (below). Never accept an event you cannot explain.
  • FalcoNotRunning: a node has no ready Falco, so nothing watches it. kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide shows which; its events (kubectl -n falco describe pod) say why.
  • FalcoStalled: Prometheus cannot scrape a Falco, or its syscall counter has not moved for 10 minutes. The probe may have detached. Read its log and restart the pod.
  • FalcoEventsDropped: Falco's ring buffer overflowed on a busy node, so rules may have missed events. Raise its CPU limit or its buffer (falco.driver.modernEbpf.bufSizePreset).

docs.title: Accepting an event
docs.text:
An accepted event narrows its rule with a Falco exception; it never disables the rule. Add it to accepted in system/falco/values.yaml, with its reason:

accepted:
  # ...the entries already there
  - rule: Read sensitive file untrusted
    name: backup-reads-shadow
    fields: [k8s.ns.name, proc.name]
    comps: ["=", "="]
    values: [["velero", "kopia"]]
    reason: "Velero's data mover reads every file of the volumes it backs up"

fields and comps are Falco's field names and comparisons (=, in, startswith…), and values holds one row per match (a value under in is a list). A process seen only on the workstation goes in acceptedWorkstation in values-dev.yaml, never in values.yaml (Helm would replace accepted itself). Every entry needs rule, name and reason (TestFalcoAccepted).

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
In the sandbox, Falco's pod was measured during a full suite on a fresh sandbox (just dev-fresh). Its requests in values-local.yaml are near the median and its limits about twice the peak (production keeps the chart's: 100m and 512Mi requested, 1 core and 1Gi at most).

Median Peak Request Limit Memory 145Mi 165Mi 160Mi 384Mi CPU 0.036 core 0.095 core 40m 200m

No event was dropped during that run, so base_syscalls stays at Falco's default. If FalcoEventsDropped fires on a busy node, raise the CPU limit first.

docs.title: What is proven where
docs.text:
• Sandbox (Falco): a read of /etc/shadow and a dropped binary in a test pod reach Loki with their rules, and FalcoCriticalEvent's expression selects them.
  • Testbed (TestbedFalco, once by hand): Falco runs on the three NixOS nodes with the modern eBPF probe and reports a dropped binary. It is off the testbed's list: on its 2-vCPU VMs the probe more than doubled k3s server's CPU (the measurement).
  • Production: its own workloads (cloudflared, the VPN routers, jellyfin, Ceph's daemons, kube-vip) were never watched. Review Falco's events in the first days after the first deploy, and accept each with its reason or fix its cause.

docs.title: Sandbox tests
docs.text:
just dev builds or updates the sandbox and runs the specs the branch's changes can affect. The cluster tests are Ginkgo specs in test/e2e (one top-level Describe each, named after the test it was); each carries labels, on its top-level container only, from the fixed list in test/scopes.yaml (labels:): where it may run (sandbox, testbed, production), what it proves (logs, sso, kiali, …) and alone for those that run by themselves.

Command Runs just dev The specs test/scopes.yaml maps the branch's changes to (git diff origin/dev...HEAD), plus smoke; nothing when every change is skipped (docs and the like); the whole suite when a file is in no entry just dev --full The whole suite on the existing sandbox: after merging into dev just dev-fresh just dev-clean, then the whole suite on a new sandbox: before a dev → master PR or a release just dev --tests '<label filter>' Exactly those specs (a Ginkgo label filter, examples below); a filter that does not parse, names a label outside labels: or selects no sandbox spec is refused just dev --revision <sha> The same selection, syncing that commit without pushing branch sandbox (what GitHub Actions runs, CI); it must be the commit checked out (HEAD), because the specs and their scope come from the checkout just test e2e --env <sandbox\|testbed\|production> [--labels '<filter>'] [--focus <regex>] [--verbose] The suite against an environment's cluster as it is, no build; --env is required, and && <env> is added to the filter

docs.title: Optional apps
docs.text:
Paperless and OpenCloud take about 900 MB, so the local sandbox runs them only when asked (the justfile's optional_apps; Backstage always runs, its image built by every just dev):

  • automatically, when the branch changes their app file (apps/paperless.yaml, apps/opencloud.yaml) outside its homelab: description: an upgrade is tested before production;
  • on request: just dev --apps paperless, --apps paperless,opencloud, or --apps all, for example with just dev-fresh --apps all.

--apps none (alone, never with names) leaves both out even when the branch changes their files: a branch that touches every app can then be proved in two runs that each fit in memory, just dev --full --apps none and then just dev --apps all --tests 'paperless || opencloud || smoke'.

just dev prints the list (optional apps '...') and refuses a name that is not an optional app. An app left out is removed: Argo CD deletes its Application, and just dev deletes its namespace (Argo CD keeps namespaces it created), volumes included. Its specs skip (SSOPaperless, SSOOpenCloud, its smoke spec), and in the sandbox lab secrets rotate --all skips its secrets ("not deployed here"). An app the list names but that is absent fails its specs instead. GitHub Actions' release, retarget and on-demand sandboxes run with --apps all, so paperless and OpenCloud are proved before every release; a pull request labelled sandbox deploys them only when it changes their files, as just dev does.

For example, the Loki and OpenBao specs only, then Kiali's (sso && kiali: a family and an extra label):

just dev --tests 'logs || secrets'
just dev --tests 'sso && kiali'

Specs labelled alone (NodeRestart restarts the node) never run with the others: just dev runs the main run with && !alone, then each alone spec the filter reaches in its own Ginkgo run, in alone:'s order, so a failure or a timeout names its own spec (--tests 'logs || node-restart' runs logs, then node-restart alone).

Each spec has its own timeout (SpecTimeout, sized from the measured durations), and Ginkgo prints a progress report for a spec still running after a minute, every 30 seconds; a filter that selects nothing fails (--fail-on-empty). JUnit and JSON reports land in test/reports/e2e/ (git-ignored; GitHub Actions uploads them as e2e-reports).

To see what a branch would run without running it:

cd cli && go run ./cmd/lab test scope                  # the main run's filter
cd cli && go run ./cmd/lab test scope --alone --each   # the alone runs afterwards, one per line
cd test && go tool ginkgo run --dry-run -v --label-filter '(logs) && sandbox' ./e2e   # the specs a filter selects

docs.title: Adding a component or a spec
docs.text: Add a component's paths to a group in test/scopes.yaml (a label filter of the specs that cover it), or to skip. A new spec is a top-level var _ = Describe("Name", Label(...), func() { ... }) in test/e2e with its environment labels and its family, each It with SpecTimeout, every wait on the spec's context (kube.*, Eventually(ctx, …), exec.CommandContext). just cli check (a basic check) fails while a component is in no entry, a label is outside labels: or labels no spec, or a filter selects no spec.

docs.title: Rotating secrets
docs.text: Every secret the homelab makes is in a catalog (cli/internal/rotate/catalog.yaml) that says where it lives, who reads it, how it is replaced and how often. lab replaces it by its own method, with no outage where the other side allows two values at once (several tokens per user, a new token before the old one goes), and otherwise with the shortest one it can: a restart of the readers, after waiting for the golden path to have no running step. The design is step 11b's.

docs.title: What is due
docs.text:
go -C cli run ./cmd/lab secrets list                 # every secret: its method, class, period, last rotation, next due date

just infra deploy production ends by naming the secrets due for rotation from the workstation (lab secrets list --due --workstation): OpenTofu's (Cloudflare's tokens, R2's), since the cluster holds no Cloudflare credentials, and Forgejo's deploy and argocd tokens, whose rotation needs Forgejo's admin password, which the CronJob never holds. lab shows the unit's plan with the replacement and applies it only once you approve: anything else pending in that unit is applied with it.

docs.title: Rotate one, or all
docs.text:
go -C cli run ./cmd/lab secrets rotate grafana.admin    # one (or several names)
go -C cli run ./cmd/lab secrets rotate --all            # assume everything leaked

lab prints the plan first: what restarts (a workload with one replica stops briefly), who must act, and what it skips with the reason (never rotated, another environment's, a person's step). It wants a completed off-site backup from the last 30 hours (a day, plus the daily run still copying at 03:00), so a failed rotation can be restored; --skip-backup-check='<reason>' overrides it and keeps the reason. It stops at the first failure and says what is done and what is left; running the same command again resumes an interrupted rotation where it stopped, without making a third value. A rotation by a person and the CronJob's never run at once on one secret (a Lease secrets-rotation/rotate-<name>).

docs.title: A run that died
docs.text:
A run killed with its node (a power cut) or one whose release found the API server restarting leaves its Lease, and the next run is refused, naming the holder, until the Lease expires (the run's 30-minute wait plus 5 minutes). A run that ends while the API server is back within two minutes releases its lock itself. When you know that run is dead, remove its lock as tofu force-unlock does, then resume:

go -C cli run ./cmd/lab secrets force-unlock ntfy.alerts-token steven@workstation/3f9a1c2e   # the holder the refusal printed
go -C cli run ./cmd/lab secrets rotate ntfy.alerts-token                                  # resumes from the recorded phase

force-unlock shows the holder and its times and asks first (--yes without a terminal). It refuses another holder: a live run (the CronJob's, or someone else's) keeps its lock.

Some steps need a person, and lab stops to give them:

  • Renovate's GitHub App key: generate a new key in the App's settings (GitHub has no API for it), give it to OpenTofu (docs/how-to-guides/renovate.md), run just infra deploy production, then delete the old key.
  • Telegram's bot token: BotFather's /revoke, then write the new one (Alerts).
  • ntfy's phone token and password: people re-enter them in their apps; the old token stays valid until a person confirms they did (lab secrets rotate ntfy.phone-token again on a terminal).

Never rotated, with the reason in the catalog: OpenBao's unseal key (it holds every secret), WireGuard's key (every peer has it) and Kopia's repository password (Velero cannot change it; after a leak, new repositories). The state passphrase has its own script (scripts/rotate-state-passphrase).

docs.title: The daily rotation
docs.text:
The CronJob secrets-rotation/secrets-rotation runs lab secrets rotate --scheduled at 03:00 (in global.timezone): the entries with a period (90 days) whose turn came, counted from their creation until their first rotation, and the interrupted ones. It never runs manual or workstation entries (OpenTofu's, Forgejo's tokens), and leaves an interrupted rotation by command to a person. Its Kubernetes access names what those entries need (each namespace's ExternalSecrets, workloads and the golden path's pods it waits on) and OpenBao's role rotator their paths; lab secrets check keeps both in step with the catalog. It never holds Forgejo's admin password (which reaches ops/homelab, what Argo CD deploys): taken over, it reaches the scheduled entries' secrets (ntfy's, zot's ci password), not the cluster.

  • A failed run alerts (SecretRotationFailed, through ntfy and Telegram): kubectl -n secrets-rotation logs job/<job> names the secret; fix the cause, then lab secrets rotate <name> finishes it.
  • No successful run for three days alerts (SecretRotationOverdue).
  • A run the cluster missed (it was off at 03:00) starts as soon as it is back, often before OpenBao: it waits up to 15 minutes for OpenBao before it fails.
  • Production's image comes from GitHub Actions (lab-image, on master when cli/ changes): set its digest in platform/secrets-rotation/values.yaml after the release; the CronJob stays suspended until then.

docs.title: A new secret
docs.text: Add its entry to the catalog in the same change: lab secrets check (in scripts/ci-check) fails while a generated secret, an infra-secrets path, a confidential Kanidm client or a Forgejo token has none.

docs.title: Security logs
docs.text:
Who did what to the cluster and to OpenBao is in Loki, beside the other logs (Logs): Grafana → Explore → data source Loki, or the dashboard Security. A few dangerous events raise alerts, which reach ntfy and Telegram like every other alert (Alerts).

Stream What Kept {service_name="k3s-audit"} the API server's audit log: one JSON event per request (who, verb, object, response code) 60 days (7 in the sandbox) {service_name="openbao-audit"} OpenBao's audit device: every request and response (who, path, operation); secret values are HMACed 60 days (7 in the sandbox)

docs.title: Where they come from
docs.text:
• k3s: the API server writes /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log on each server node (100 MB, 3 rotated files) under one policy, infra/_modules/metal/flake/audit-policy.yaml, used by production's nodes and by the sandbox's k3d node. Read-only noise from the control plane, leases, events and health checks is not logged. Secrets, ConfigMaps, token and access reviews, exec, attach and port-forward are logged at Metadata (never a body). Service accounts' other reads (get, list, watch) are not logged: controllers watching what they manage were 41% of the volume. Changes to RBAC, Kyverno's policies and exceptions, admission webhooks, namespaces and CRDs carry the body sent (Kyverno rewriting its own webhooks only Metadata). Everything else is Metadata. An event over 100KiB (a large CRD) loses its bodies, keeping who and what (audit.k8s.io/truncated): Loki refuses a line over 256KB. The OpenTelemetry agent reads the file on the node.
  • OpenBao: a file audit device writing to stdout, declared in its config (platform/openbao), so OpenBao creates it at every start. The OpenTelemetry agent routes these lines to service_name="openbao-audit" and leaves OpenBao's server log an ordinary pod log (k8s_namespace_name="openbao"). If every audit device fails OpenBao refuses requests; stdout does not fill up.

Command lines are logged

An exec's command is part of its request URL, which the audit log records. Pass a secret on stdin (bao kv put secret/x key=-), never as an argument.

Loki runs in the cluster: someone with cluster-admin can delete what it holds. Shipping the logs off the cluster is not done (accepted for a homelab).

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
The JSON fields come out with | json (user_username, verb, objectRef_resource, objectRef_namespace, objectRef_name, responseStatus_code, sourceIPs; OpenBao: type, auth_display_name, auth_policies, request_path, request_operation, request_remote_address, error).

Query Shows {service_name="k3s-audit"} \| json \| objectRef_subresource=~"exec\|attach\|portforward" who opened a shell, attached or port-forwarded, into which pod {service_name="k3s-audit"} \| json \| objectRef_resource="secrets" \| user_username!~"system:serviceaccount:.*" Secret reads by people {service_name="k3s-audit"} \| json \| objectRef_resource=~".*rolebindings\|.*roles" \| verb!~"get\|list\|watch" RBAC changes, with the body {service_name="k3s-audit"} \| json \| responseStatus_code=~"401\|403" refused requests {service_name="k3s-audit"} \| json \| user_username="system:admin" everything done with the admin kubeconfig {service_name="openbao-audit"} \| json \| type="request" \| auth_policies=~".*admin.*" OpenBao requests with the admin role {service_name="openbao-audit"} \| json \| request_path=~"auth/.+/login" \| error!="" failed OpenBao logins {service_name="openbao-audit"} \|= "secret/data/forgejo/" who read Forgejo's secrets

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Loki's ruler evaluates system/loki/files/audit-rules.yaml every minute and sends to Alertmanager. "A person" is any user but service accounts, nodes and the control plane; system:admin, the admin kubeconfig, is a person. Tools using that kubeconfig (the sandbox's tests, lab, OpenTofu) exec and read Secrets too, so they raise the first two alerts: this is accepted, and Alertmanager groups the audit alerts by alert and user, so one run notifies once.

Alert Severity Meaning What to do AuditExecByPerson warning a person exec'd, attached or port-forwarded into a pod (Argo CD's web terminal shows as argocd-server: the person is in its log) expected if it was you or your tool; otherwise find the user and the session, revoke the credential AuditSecretReadByPerson warning a person read a Secret same AuditClusterAdminBinding critical a binding to cluster-admin was created or changed, not by Argo CD read the body (requestObject); delete the binding unless it is in git AuditAnonymousAllowed critical an unauthenticated request succeeded (outside the public OIDC discovery URLs) check the URL; anonymous access should only reach health and discovery AuditManyDenied warning more than 20 requests from one address refused in 5 minutes a broken client or someone probing: find the address and the user AuditPolicyExceptionChanged warning a PolicyException changed outside Argo CD an exception bypasses policy; revert it unless it is in git OpenBaoRootToken critical root token generation started or went on (sys/generate-root); OpenBao's self-initialisation uses a root token of its own at every fresh start and revokes it, which does not alert nothing needs a root token: find who and why, cancel the generation or revoke the token OpenBaoManyFailedLogins warning more than 10 failed logins at one auth path in 5 minutes a misconfigured role or someone guessing OpenBaoConfigChanged critical a policy, an auth method or role, or an audit device changed (not with a root token: OpenBaoRootToken covers those) expected only when a person changes OpenBao with the admin role (docs/concepts/secrets-management.md) AuditLogsMissing critical no line from k3s for 15 minutes, or from OpenBao for 2 hours an audit trail stopped: check the OpenTelemetry agent on the server nodes, the audit flags, bao audit list

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Audit streams are kept 60 days (retention_stream in system/loki/values.yaml), other logs 30: 90 days would not fit Loki's 10Gi volume. The sandbox, idle on one node, writes about 520MiB of audit lines a day and 370MiB of the rest, which Loki compresses at least 5.7 times (measured): about 5.4GiB for 60 days of audit and 1.9GiB for the rest, 7.3GiB of 10Gi. Production has more nodes and apps; KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp warns before the volume fills. If they outgrow it, the period is shortened (45 days, then 30), not the volume raised.

docs.title: Single node cluster adjustments
docs.text:
Danger

This is not officially supported and I don't regularly test it, I highly recommend using multiple nodes.

Using a single node could lead to data loss unless your backup strategy is rock solid, make sure you are ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN this is what you want.

Update the following changes, then commit and push.

docs.title: Remove storage redundancy
docs.text:
Set pod counts and number of data copies to 1:

system/rook-ceph/values.yaml
rook-ceph-cluster:
  cephClusterSpec:
    mon:
      count: 1
    mgr:
      count: 1
  cephBlockPools:
    - name: standard-rwo
      spec:
        replicated:
          size: 1
          requireSafeReplicaSize: false
  cephFileSystems:
    - name: standard-rwx
      spec:
        metadataPool:
          replicated:
            size: 1
        dataPools:
          - name: data0
            replicated:
              size: 1
        metadataServer:
          activeCount: 1
          activeStandby: false

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
What runs in the cluster is watched for known vulnerabilities and baked-in secrets, our own image is signed where it is built, and the workflows that build it are checked on every pull request (step 15e, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-29-supply-chain-design.md).

What Where Checks Images already running the Trivy Operator (system/trivy-operator) CVEs, fixed or not, at HIGH and CRITICAL; secrets inside images Images new in a pull request the basic check images (CI) CRITICAL CVEs with a fix lab's image .github/workflows/lab-image.yaml, Kyverno's verify-lab-image a keyless signature and an SPDX SBOM from that workflow on master GitHub Actions workflows the basic check workflows (zizmor, offline) template injection, dangerous triggers, unpinned actions, credentials left in the checkout

Manifests are Kyverno's (Policy) and the cluster's configuration is kube-bench's and kubescape's (Cluster scan): the operator's config audit, RBAC, infra and compliance scanners are off.

docs.title: The Trivy Operator
docs.text:
The operator scans each image a workload runs, once, and again when the image changes or its report is a day old. One Trivy server in namespace trivy-operator keeps the vulnerability database (about 80 MB, from ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db, on an emptyDir: downloaded again when it restarts); the scan Jobs ask it. The scans pull the images from their registries (egress 443). In the sandbox one Job runs at a time, with memory limits (values-dev.yaml). Measured there: a scan Job peaks under 80Mi (the server does the work), the server at about 100Mi, the operator at about 160Mi.

kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A                 # one per container image, with its counts
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -n <ns> <name> -o yaml
kubectl get exposedsecretreports -A

Grafana's dashboard Security lists every finding, HIGH included.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
They reach ntfy and Telegram like every alert (Alerts), after an hour:

Alert Fires when Do ImageCriticalVulnerability a running image has a CRITICAL CVE with a fixed release bump the image ImageCriticalVulnerabilityUnfixed a running image has a CRITICAL CVE with no fix decide: accept it (below) or replace the app ImageExposedSecret a secret was found inside a running image kubectl get exposedsecretreports -n <ns>; rotate it if it is ours ImageScanMissing a running ReplicaSet, StatefulSet or DaemonSet has had no report for 6 hours: its scans fail (out of memory, timed out, an image it cannot pull), so it would show no finding read the operator's log for the workload (kubectl logs -n trivy-operator deploy/trivy-operator); a log that never names it means the operator dropped it at start (seen in the sandbox): kubectl annotate -n <ns> <kind> <name> homelab/trivy-rescan=$(date +%s) --overwrite queues its scan

HIGH findings alert on nothing: base images carry many, and they would bury these. A rollout leaves the old ReplicaSet at 0 replicas, with its report, as the Deployment's history: the alerts and the dashboard leave those out.

docs.title: Accepting a finding
docs.text:
When no image fixes a CVE yet (or the fix is not reachable here), accept it in system/trivy-operator/values.yaml under trivy.ignoreFile.vulnerabilities, and the same entry in .trivyignore.yaml (read by the basic checks):

        - id: CVE-2026-12345
          statement: >-
            <package and version> in <image and tag> (the latest): why it cannot be exploited here, or what limits
            it (default-deny egress, mTLS, Pod Security, who can reach the app). Bump when <image> is rebuilt
          expired_at: "2026-12-31T00:00:00Z"
  • expired_at at most 90 days away. In values.yaml write it in RFC 3339 and quoted: the chart writes the file with toYaml, which turns a bare date into a string, and Trivy reads a string only in RFC 3339 (any other form stops every scan Job). .trivyignore.yaml keeps the bare date.
  • Trivy ignores by id: one entry hides that CVE in every image. Name every image it covers in the statement.
  • The operator reads Trivy's settings only at start: TestTrivyOperatorRender prints the new value of the pod annotation homelab/trivy-config (in values.yaml and values-dev.yaml), which restarts it when Argo CD syncs.
  • An expired entry no longer applies: the finding is reported and alerts again.
  • The operator applies the ignore file only to new scans, and rescans a report once it is a day old (OPERATOR_SCANNER_REPORT_TTL): to clear an alert now, delete the workload's reports and it is scanned again (kubectl delete vulnerabilityreports -n <ns> -l trivy-operator.resource.name=<workload>).

TestTrivyOperator fails while any running image in the sandbox has a CRITICAL finding that is neither fixed nor accepted.

docs.title: lab's image: signature and SBOM
docs.text:
.github/workflows/lab-image.yaml builds lab's image on master, generates its SBOM with Syft (SPDX), signs the image by digest with cosign keyless (GitHub's OIDC token, Sigstore's Fulcio and Rekor) and attests the SBOM. No key is kept.

cosign verify ghcr.io/duongle-steven/homelab-lab@sha256:<digest> \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/duongle-steven/homelab/.github/workflows/lab-image.yaml@refs/heads/master
cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson <same arguments>

Kyverno's ImageValidatingPolicy verify-lab-image (system/kyverno/templates/lab-image-policy.yaml, production only: the sandbox runs lab's image built from the checkout, unsigned) checks both for every pod running ghcr.io/duongle-steven/homelab-lab. It audits, like every policy until step 15b-2:

kubectl get policyreports -n secrets-rotation -o yaml | grep -B2 -A6 verify-lab-image

In the sandbox, TestSupplyChain proves the same path with zot: it signs a test image with a key it generates, runs a signed and an unsigned pod under an Audit policy with that key, and expects the unsigned pod's fail (Kyverno keeps no pass results, --allowedResults). Kyverno's admission and reports controllers trust the sandbox CA for that (system/kyverno/values-local.yaml).

The blog's image will be signed by the in-cluster CI's golden path (OpenBao's transit key ci-signing, checked by Kyverno's verify-ci-images) when its repository comes (In-cluster CI).

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text: scripts/ci-check workflows runs zizmor --offline .github/; any finding fails it. Fix it, or ignore it in .github/zizmor.yml with the reason (CI).

docs.title: Traces
docs.text: Traces are in Tempo (system/tempo) for 7 days (1 in the sandbox). Grafana → Explore → data source Tempo.

docs.title: What sends spans
docs.text:
Source How The Istio Gateways (gateway, public) Istio's Telemetry API (system/istio-system/templates/telemetry.yaml): every request in the sandbox, a tenth in production Argo CD otlp.address in its params (system/argocd/values.yaml) Grafana tracing.opentelemetry.otlp in grafana.ini (platform/grafana/values.yaml)

Everything goes to the gateway Collector (gateway-collector.opentelemetry, OTLP gRPC 4317 or HTTP 4318), which only the senders above may call (allow-otlp in system/opentelemetry: OTLP is never published). A new sender adds its namespace to gateway.senders in system/opentelemetry/values.yaml.

Not traced: the ambient mesh's ztunnel makes no spans (L4 only), so calls between services inside the mesh show no span until waypoints come; Loki, Tempo and Kanidm send none (their own telemetry would mostly trace the telemetry path, and Kanidm's OTLP is not in kaniop's resources). Apps of our own get an SDK through the Operator's Instrumentation (Backstage, the next step, is the first).

docs.title: From a log line to its trace, and back
docs.text:
The Gateways write a JSON access log line per request with its trace_id. In Explore with Loki:

{k8s_namespace_name="istio-system"} |= "/api/health"

Each line's trace_id field is a link that opens the trace in Tempo; a trace in Tempo has "Logs for this span", which queries Loki for its trace id.

A request can carry its own trace id (W3C traceparent), to find it later:

curl -H "traceparent: 00-$(openssl rand -hex 16)-$(openssl rand -hex 8)-01" https://grafana.<domain>/api/health

docs.title: Updating documentation (this website)
docs.text:
This project uses the Diátaxis technical documentation framework. The website is generated using Material for MkDocs and can be viewed at homelab.khuedoan.com.

There are 4 main parts:

  • Getting started (tutorials): learning-oriented
  • Concepts (explanation): understanding-oriented
  • How-to guides: goal-oriented
  • Reference: information-oriented

docs.title: Local development
docs.text:
To edit and view locally, run:

just docs

Then visit localhost:8000

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: It's running on my other cluster in the khuedoan/horus project (so if the homelab goes down everyone can still read the documentation).

docs.title: PXE server logs
docs.text:
View the Nixie output in the terminal running just infra deploy production (or just testbed). To retry metal provisioning:

cd infra/production/metal
terragrunt run apply

docs.title: Nodes not booting from the network
docs.text:
• Plug a monitor and a keyboard to one of the bare metal node if possible to make the debugging process easier
  • Check if the controller (PXE server) is on the same subnet with bare metal nodes (sometimes Wifi will not work or conflict with wired Ethernet, try to turn it off)
  • Check if bare metal nodes are configured to boot from the network
  • Check if Wake-on-LAN is enabled
  • Check the controller's firewall config to make sure that the following ports are open:
    • UDP 67 and 68 for DHCP
    • UDP 69 for TFTP
    • UDP 4011 for the PXE boot service
    • TCP 80 for the boot files
    • TCP 5000 for the installer callback API
  • Check if the servers are booting to the correct OS (NixOS installer instead of the previously installed OS), if not try to select it manually or remove the previous OS boot entry
  • Examine the network boot process with Wireshark or Termshark

Verify your authorized SSH keys and trusted host keys if provisioning succeeds but enrollment fails.

docs.title: Backup secrets
docs.text:
Save the following files to a safe location like a password manager (if you're using the sandbox, you can skip this step):

  • ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  • ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
  • ./infra/production/kubeconfig.yaml
  • ~/.config/homelab/state.env (the state passphrase: without it production's state on R2, which holds OpenBao's unseal key, the Cloudflare tokens and the WireGuard key, cannot be read)

docs.title: Admin credentials
docs.text:
• ArgoCD:
    • Username: admin
    • Password: run ./scripts/argocd-admin-password
  • Forgejo (people log in with Kanidm; forgejo_admin works only while the Forgejo pod keeps running: it does not start while Kanidm is unreachable, so bring Kanidm back first after an outage):
    • Username: forgejo_admin
    • Password: OpenBao secret/forgejo/generated/admin (password), read with the admin role
  • Kanidm:
    • Usernames: admin and idm_admin
    • Password: kept by the kaniop operator, kubectl -n kanidm get secret kanidm-admin-passwords -o jsonpath='{.data.IDM_ADMIN_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d (ADMIN_PASSWORD for admin)
  • Jellyfin and other applications in the *arr stack: see the dedicated guide for media management
  • zot: people log in with Kanidm; the ci account (htpasswd, password in OpenBao secret/zot/generated/ci) is for automation
  • Other apps:
    • Username: admin
    • Password: OpenBao secret/<app>/generated/admin (the property is the entry's key in platform/generated-secrets/values.yaml), read with the admin role

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Now is a good time to set up backups for your homelab. Follow the backup and restore guide to get started.

docs.title: Run the full test suite
docs.text:
After the homelab has been stabilized, you can run the specs that run against production (those labelled production: the smoke checks and Argo CD's) to ensure that everything is working properly:

just test e2e --env production

Info

The "full" test suit is still in its early stages, so any contribution is greatly appreciated.

docs.title: Development sandbox
docs.text: The sandbox is a local k3d cluster (one k3s server) for testing changes on the dev branch before they are merged into master.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linux, or Windows with WSL 2 (NAT or mirrored networking). macOS does not work: the development shell includes Linux-only packages, and Docker runs in a VM there, so the host cannot reach the k3d network.
  • Docker and Nix (see development shell)
  • About 10 GiB of free RAM for Docker (the sandbox uses about 8 GiB, see resource usage)
  • Ports 80, 443 and 22 free on the host's 127.0.0.1

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git switch dev
nix develop
just dev

just dev runs Terragrunt in infra/sandbox: the unit cluster creates the k3d cluster with k3s's own networking (Flannel, kube-proxy, ServiceLB) and the localhost proxy, the unit argocd bootstraps ArgoCD; then it runs the tests. State stays on your machine (.state/).

The node pulls images through pull-through caches, one per registry (docker.io, ghcr.io, quay.io, registry.k8s.io, code.forgejo.org: k3d-homelab-cache-*, each with its own Docker volume). They are k3d registries outside the cluster, so just dev-clean and just dev-fresh keep them and a rebuilt sandbox downloads only what changed. A cached image expires a week after the cache first fetched it (registry:3 does not count later pulls), and the next build fetches it again; a new release is another tag, fetched on its first use, so after an upgrade the old one stays at most a week. An image from another registry, or one the cache fails to fetch, comes from its registry directly. Before it builds a cluster, just dev fills the caches one image at a time (scripts/warm-image-cache: every image the sandbox renders, plus k3s's, the operators' and the tests'; what a cache holds is skipped; --list prints them): the node pulls dozens of images at once, and on a slow link the cache's own request to the registry times out after 15 seconds (registry:3, not configurable), so the node would pull that image directly and the cache never get it. After the tests, scripts/warm-image-cache --node adds what the node holds and the caches miss, so the next build finds it. GitHub Actions runs without caches (HOMELAB_SANDBOX_CACHE=0: each runner starts empty). Empty one with k3d registry delete homelab-cache-docker-io (and docker volume rm homelab-cache-docker-io).

Note

The first build takes about 25 minutes. Running just dev again on an existing sandbox takes about a minute.

Warning

A sandbox built before step 8e (namespace global-secrets) needs just dev-fresh once: its OpenBao configured itself on first start with role writer bound to global-secrets, so generated-secrets cannot push to it.

docs.title: Explore
docs.text:
just uses the sandbox kubeconfig automatically. For kubectl in your own shell, point it at the same file first:

export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/infra/sandbox/kubeconfig.yaml  # from the repository root
  • https://argocd.127-0-0-1.nip.io (user admin, password: kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d)
  • https://draw.127-0-0-1.nip.io
  • https://grafana.127-0-0-1.nip.io ("Sign in with Kanidm", or user admin with kubectl -n grafana get secret grafana-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d)
  • https://registry.127-0-0-1.nip.io (zot; log in with Kanidm, then create an API key under your user menu and docker login registry.127-0-0-1.nip.io -u <username> -p <key>)
  • https://git.127-0-0-1.nip.io (Forgejo; "Sign in with Kanidm", or user forgejo_admin with kubectl -n forgejo get secret forgejo-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; ops/homelab stays empty until TestForgejoDeploy runs lab infra forgejo sync and push; SSH on 127.0.0.1:22)
  • https://budget.127-0-0-1.nip.io (Actual Budget) and https://paperless.127-0-0-1.nip.io (only with just dev --apps paperless: paperless and OpenCloud are optional here, Sandbox tests): log in with Kanidm (paperless also has a local admin, password in OpenBao secret/paperless/generated/admin, property PAPERLESS_ADMIN_PASSWORD)
  • https://drive.127-0-0-1.nip.io (OpenCloud): log in with Kanidm and accept the consent page once
  • https://home.127-0-0-1.nip.io, https://drop.127-0-0-1.nip.io, https://speedtest.127-0-0-1.nip.io

On Windows with WSL, open these from the Windows browser.

Everything goes through the Gateway istio-system/gateway (Istio), which ServiceLB serves on the k3d node; a localhost proxy (homelab-dev-proxy, recreated by just dev) forwards 127.0.0.1:80/443/22 to it, because Windows cannot reach ports Docker publishes under WSL mirrored networking. The tests connect to the node directly. The Argo CD CLI works through it with --grpc-web.

Certificates are issued by a local CA that is recreated with the cluster. To remove the browser warning, export it and import it into your trust store (on Windows: double-click homelab-dev-ca.crt → Install Certificate → Local Machine → Trusted Root Certification Authorities):

kubectl -n cert-manager get secret homelab-dev-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > homelab-dev-ca.crt

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Kanidm (https://auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io) runs in the sandbox, and every app logs in to it directly with its own OAuth2 client. The test accounts and their groups:

Test account Role group Access groups dev-admin homelab-admins homelab-budget, homelab-documents, homelab-files dev-editor homelab-editors homelab-documents, homelab-files dev-viewer homelab-users homelab-budget dev-outsider (none, refused) (none)

The identity tests use the sandbox-only client smoke (platform/kanidm).

The identity tests give each test account a password and TOTP the first time they run, and store them in the identity-test-credentials Secret in namespace kanidm:

kubectl -n kanidm get secret identity-test-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.dev-admin}' | base64 -d

What each group may do:

Group Grafana Argo CD zot Forgejo homelab-admins Admin, server admin admin read, push, delete site admin homelab-editors Editor view, sync, actions, logs, exec into apps/* read, push user homelab-users Viewer read-only read user

Actual Budget admits only homelab-budget, paperless only homelab-documents (members of homelab-admins become paperless superusers), OpenCloud only homelab-files (members of homelab-admins get the Admin role, the others User).

Argo CD and Grafana keep their local admin account, Forgejo its forgejo_admin; zot has a ci account for automation (password in OpenBao secret/zot/generated/ci; reading it).

Use the totpSecret there in any authenticator app to log in by hand. Kanidm asks for the TOTP code before the password.

If an account has credentials in Kanidm but none in that Secret (for example a run stopped mid-way), the tests cannot log in. Recreate the account so kaniop issues a new reset token:

kubectl -n kanidm delete kanidmpersonaccount dev-admin  # ArgoCD recreates it
kubectl -n kanidm patch secret identity-test-credentials --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/data/dev-admin"}]'

Group membership in the sandbox is declared in platform/kanidm/values-dev.yaml; people added by hand with scripts/onboard-user are removed from those groups on the next reconcile.

docs.title: Make changes
docs.text:
Work on a feature branch created from dev, and run the basic checks before opening a pull request into dev:

git switch dev && git pull
git switch -c feat/harness-the-sun
# ...edit, then for every changed chart or app file:
scripts/render-chart platform/kanidm
scripts/render-chart platform/kanidm dev
# the basic checks: the offline tests among them (test/e2e's specs need a cluster)
direnv exec . scripts/ci-check all
mkdocs build --strict
git commit -am "feat: harness the sun"
just dev   # pushes this commit to the branch sandbox and runs every sandbox test on it
git push -u origin feat/harness-the-sun   # then open a PR into dev

ArgoCD in the sandbox syncs the GitHub branch sandbox. just dev force-pushes the commit you are on to it (so commit first) and runs the specs the branch's changes can affect (test/scopes.yaml; nothing when only docs or comments changed), so a branch is tested before its pull request (sandbox tests).

Only the components listed in system/argocd/values-dev.yaml are synced: system and platform charts in the root ApplicationSet, apps in the apps ApplicationSet.

  • Apps are app-template values files, apps/<name>.yaml. The apps ApplicationSet pins the app-template version and passes the environment: write hosts as <host>.{{ .Values.global.baseDomain }}, and attach public apps to {{ .Values.global.publicGateway }} (the Cloudflare Tunnel Gateway in production, the LAN Gateway in the sandbox).
  • System and platform components are wrapper charts; one that needs sandbox-specific settings gets a values-dev.yaml next to its values.yaml, and what the sandbox shares with the testbed (the local CA, the tests' fixtures, no Telegram or Cloudflare) goes in values-local.yaml, loaded before it.

Check how ArgoCD will render something with:

scripts/render-chart apps/excalidraw.yaml dev
scripts/render-chart platform/kanidm dev

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
The sandbox runs every component and app except what needs real hardware, the internet's side of the homelab or production's data. The authoritative lists are system/argocd/values-dev.yaml (sandbox), values-testbed.yaml (testbed) and values.yaml (production: every system/* and platform/*, every app).

Sandbox Testbed Production Networking: Istio (Gateways, ambient mesh), egress, cert-manager yes Istio, cert-manager yes Storage csi-driver-host-path Ceph Ceph Addresses ServiceLB on the k3d node kube-vip kube-vip Security: Kyverno, Falco, Trivy Operator, the public scan yes no yes Observability: Prometheus, Alertmanager, Loki, OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Kiali, Grafana yes no yes Backups: Velero (to versitygw), CloudNativePG yes no yes (to R2) Identity and secrets: Kanidm, OpenBao, External Secrets, rotation yes no yes Git and CI: Forgejo, zot, Argo Workflows and Events, the golden path yes no yes Backstage (built from the checkout) yes no after its first release Apps: Actual Budget, Excalidraw, Homepage, Matrix, ntfy, PairDrop, Speedtest yes no yes Optional: paperless, OpenCloud when asked or changed no yes Cloudflare Tunnel, external-dns, Renovate, Jellyfin and its *arr apps, Tailscale, WireGuard, the blog no no yes

"Changed" means the branch changes the app's file, not only its homelab: description.

docs.title: Resource usage
docs.text:
Measured on a fresh k3d sandbox with all components running and every namespace in the ambient mesh (working-set memory per namespace from Prometheus; the node total from docker stats of k3d-homelab-dev-server-0; the k3d load balancer and the localhost proxy add about 25 MiB):

Namespace RAM paperless (with Redis) 926 MiB grafana 833 MiB monitoring-system 790 MiB argocd 637 MiB istio-system (istiod 103, Gateways 110, istio-cni 59, ztunnel 25) 300 MiB cert-manager (with trust-manager) 228 MiB opencloud 205 MiB forgejo 175 MiB external-secrets 158 MiB homepage 141 MiB kanidm 122 MiB zot 119 MiB kube-system (CoreDNS, local-path, metrics-server, ServiceLB) 116 MiB actualbudget 83 MiB pairdrop 69 MiB speedtest 22 MiB excalidraw 13 MiB k3s itself (API server, etcd, controllers, kubelet, containerd; outside any container: node total minus the rows above) about 3.1 GiB Node total 7.89 GiB

docs.title: After a restart
docs.text:
The sandbox survives a WSL or Docker restart: its containers start again (k3d cluster start homelab-dev if they do not) and keep their addresses. just dev makes each container's address on the k3d network static when it builds the cluster, because Docker otherwise gives a restarted container any free address, and k3s's etcd then refuses to start ("not a member of the etcd cluster": its member address is the old one). A sandbox built before that needs just dev-fresh once after such a restart; check with docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' k3d-homelab-dev-server-0 (a static address shows in IPAMConfig).

On WSL, a full C: drive crashes the whole VM (kernel panics with SIGBUS, reports in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\wsl-crashes): the sandbox's disk grows inside WSL's virtual disk on C:, so keep about 30 GB free there during the suite.

Never beside testbed: just dev refuses while testbed's VMs run (just testbed-stop), and both refuse with less than 30 GB free on C:.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text: just dev-clean  # terragrunt run --all destroy in infra/sandbox: the cluster, the proxy and the kubeconfig (not the image caches)

docs.title: Differences from production
docs.text:
• Certificates come from a local CA instead of Let's Encrypt
  • Only accessible from the host machine
  • No Renovate (production only)
  • Forgejo runs one PostgreSQL instance (CloudNativePG) instead of three; Argo CD syncs GitHub branch sandbox, not Forgejo (the tests push a commit with the checkout's tree to ops/homelab)
  • No Cloudflare Tunnel: excalidraw uses the LAN Gateway gateway instead of public
  • No kube-vip: ServiceLB serves the Gateway on the k3d node instead of a kube-vip address

docs.title: Staging (optional)
docs.text: A staging is an environment on its own hardware, run like production. It proves everything as production runs it, which the testbed cannot, and whoever has one needs no testbed. Nobody has built one yet: this page is a guide, not a record, and nothing in it has run.

docs.title: What it takes
docs.text:
1. Hardware in infra/staging/metal/hosts.json (name, MAC, address), with its own SSH key (infra/staging/metal/authorized_keys)
  2. Its own domain and addresses in infra/staging/cluster/config.json
  3. The same units as production under infra/staging
  4. values-staging.yaml next to a component's values.yaml, only where it must differ. A staging never loads values-local.yaml, which means "runs on the workstation"
  5. "release_proof": "staging" in infra/production/cluster/config.json

docs.title: What is built
docs.text: lab infra forgejo verify reads the environment release_proof names, and the commit status of that name is its mark. For staging it reads infra/staging/release-paths.yaml and values-staging.yaml; with an empty exclusion list every release needs the mark. This gate is unit-tested, never run.

docs.title: What you still write
docs.text:
• A target that deploys staging: just infra deploy runs verify, sync and push only for production
  • lab's environments: env.Load refuses --env staging today
  • Its state's backend: infra/root.hcl gives only production R2
  • A step that writes the mark when its run passes (scripts/mark-proof staging <commit>)
  • A test suite. The suite's fixtures (Kanidm's smoke client, dev-admin, the local CA) live in values-local.yaml, so most sandbox tests would not run there: a staging needs its own, less intrusive suite the first time one exists

docs.title: Testbed
docs.text:
The testbed is three NixOS VMs in WSL, installed and configured the way production's machines are: the same node definition (infra/_modules/metal), installed from the network by nixie, joined into one k3s cluster by lab cluster enroll, every node a k3s server with etcd, kube-vip holding the API's address. Argo CD deploys what runs on it. It proves what the one-node sandbox cannot: etcd with three members, addresses moving between nodes, Ceph replicating, the ambient mesh across nodes, the nodes themselves and their upgrades (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-02-testbed-design.md).

It is not like production, and nothing here says it is: a release it proved is printed by lab infra forgejo verify as "only the testbed proved this: no production-like environment did". Someone with spare hardware runs a staging instead, and needs no testbed.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Windows with WSL 2 and KVM (/dev/kvm), libvirt on the workstation (in ~/nixos-config: virtualisation.libvirtd.enable = true; and your user in group libvirtd), and an SSH agent (programs.ssh.startAgent = true;)
  • WSL at 13 GB with 4 GB of swap (.wslconfig)
  • The testbed's SSH key loaded in the agent; its public key is infra/testbed/metal/authorized_keys (the testbed only: production's nodes accept only infra/production/metal/authorized_keys)
  • The sandbox stopped (k3d cluster stop homelab-dev): just testbed refuses while the sandbox runs, and just dev while the testbed does (just testbed-stop)
  • 30 GB free on C: (WSL's virtual disk, where the VMs' disks grow)

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
just testbed

It force-pushes the commit you are on to GitHub branch testbed, which the testbed's Argo CD syncs, and applies infra/testbed:

  1. vms: a libvirt network (homelab-testbed, 192.168.100.0/24, NAT, one fixed DHCP lease per MAC address of infra/testbed/metal/hosts.json) and three VMs (homelab-1..3: 3.5 GB, 2 vCPUs, UEFI, a sparse 100 GB raw disk, cache=unsafe, safe against virsh destroy: only a crash of WSL itself loses data)
  2. metal: nixie boots the VMs it has not installed from the network, one at a time, and installs them with nixos-anywhere (PXE boot); scripts/testbed-wake turns its Wake-on-LAN into a power cycle of the VM. Then lab cluster enroll joins them (the first, init_host, starts the cluster), lab cluster kubeconfig writes infra/testbed/kubeconfig.yaml, and lab cluster upgrade rebuilds the nodes already installed whose system differs from the flake's, one at a time
  3. argocd: Argo CD and its ApplicationSets (system/argocd with values-testbed.yaml)

Then it runs the testbed's specs (just test e2e --env testbed --labels proof: the Testbed* specs; the first waits for every listed Application to have synced this commit and be healthy) and, when they pass, writes the commit status testbed on the commit it started from, the mark lab infra forgejo verify reads.

nixie records what it installed in .state/testbed/metal/nixie-hosts.json and never installs those machines again; just testbed-fresh removes the VMs, their disks and that record, then builds from empty disks. just testbed-clean removes them without building, just testbed-stop shuts the VMs down (they keep their disks).

The nodes' host keys are trusted on first contact (only on the workstation's own libvirt network); just testbed-clean forgets them with the disks.

Warning

Nothing watches memory during a run: a person stops it. A run stopped for low memory is not restarted without understanding why. A testbed that crashes WSL or makes the workstation unusable has failed.

docs.title: What runs
docs.text:
system/argocd/values-testbed.yaml lists it, by layers, each measured from a fresh install. A layer is stable when, over 30 minutes after the last Application is healthy, there is no k3s restart, no etcd leader change, no API server or lease error, and WSL keeps at least 2 GB available. leader failed to send out heartbeat warnings are counted, not failed.

Layer Adds Proves Here (i5-12500H, WSL 13 GB) 1 Argo CD, rook-ceph Ceph on three nodes through Argo CD holds, 2 vCPUs 2 cert-manager, Istio the ambient mesh across nodes, the Gateway at its VIP holds, 2 vCPUs 3 CloudNativePG, three instances failing over what otherwise only production runs does not hold beside 2 Falco (system/falco) the modern eBPF driver on NixOS's kernel does not hold

Measured from just testbed-fresh:

Layer 1 Layer 2 Layer 3, 2 vCPUs Layer 3, 4 vCPUs Tests pass pass pass Ceph (a test race, fixed), Mesh fail; Postgres cut by go test's hour TestTestbedCeph, which starts about a minute after the bootstrap 12.6 min 19.7 min 29.4 min 22 min k3s exits, install and tests 0 0 4 1 In the 30 minutes: k3s exits, leader changes 0, 0 0, 0 1, 1 not measured In the 30 minutes: heartbeat warnings 2 (35 ms, 2.3 s over) 0 about 20 (up to 3.2 s over) not measured CPU idle in each node at the end 86–93% 62–82% 17–67% not measured WSL's lowest available: window; first sync 2.38 GB; 2.50 GB; 1.61–1.85 GB 2.83 GB; 1.86 GB not measured; 1.68 GB WSL's swap in use 1.95 GB 2.04 GB

Layer 3's failover itself passes, in about 19 minutes at 2 vCPUs. What fails is the control plane around it: under the install and Postgres on Ceph, k3s lost its leases and left. At 4 vCPUs the nodes were 41–84% idle on average and k3s left once, so CPU alone does not explain it. The Gateway's address also stopped answering at 4 vCPUs: most likely k3s's ServiceLB writing the Service's status empty (reproduced at 2 vCPUs, matched at 4 only by its symptom), since fixed by turning it off on the nodes (TestTestbedGatewayKeepsItsAddress). So the list stops at layer 2 on this machine.

Another machine extends the list in system/argocd/values-testbed.yaml and its VM size in infra/testbed/vms/terragrunt.hcl (vcpus, up to 4 before measuring why more is needed). For layer 3 add platform/cloudnative-pg and a values-testbed.yaml beside it with cloudnative-pg.monitoring.podMonitorEnabled: false; TestTestbedPostgresFailover runs once it is listed.

"Up to everything" is a direction, not a promise: past these layers, components need more than the list (OpenBao and its units, Forgejo, tests made general for them).

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
just testbed-power

On a healthy testbed, from the main checkout, alone: it wrecks the cluster's availability, so it is never part of just testbed and gives no mark. Run it when lab cluster shutdown|startup, the node profile or the recovery path change, and before step 12b. --tests picks the specs by label, one run each (cut-every-node, shutdown-startup, node-not-returning: PowerCutEveryNode, PowerShutdownStartup, PowerNodeNotReturning). A probe on a Ceph volume writes numbered lines, flushing each, and every number it reported must be in its file afterwards (what they cover).

Measured at 2 vCPUs from a fresh install, from the moment the VMs start:

Test Time Every node cut (virsh destroy) the API at its VIP, every node Ready on a new boot, etcd whole 1m07s Ceph HEALTH_OK with every OSD answering, the Gateway at its VIP 3m02s 58 acknowledged lines intact, the probe writing again 5m25s, with the checks Ordered shutdown the nodes off, after lab returned: the one holding the probe's volume cut at 180 s, the others in 20 and 90 s 3m05s back on: every node Ready 1m15s the marker gone (CronJobs, Argo CD's controller and noout undone), Applications Synced 3m18s A node not returning CronJobs and Argo CD's controller back, with two nodes 1m23s noout off and the marker gone, at its limit 31m23s

WSL's lowest available across these runs was 1.66 GB.

Two status fields read wrong after a cut, so the tests and cluster-startup ask the thing itself. An OSD's pod stays Ready and ceph osd stat counts it up for a while after its node died (only ceph tell osd.N version tells), and a CephCluster's or CloudNativePG Cluster's status says what the operator saw before.

What this does not prove. virsh destroy kills QEMU, and with cache=unsafe what the guest handed to QEMU survives in WSL's page cache, a flush forced to no disk. So it proves the software recovers and that writes the guest never flushed do not count as acknowledged, not that a real disk keeps what it acknowledged. Without a UPS that risk sits entirely in the hardware: step 12b prefers SSDs with power-loss protection and repeats the cut before real data.

docs.title: Falco, one measurement
docs.text:
Once, on layers 1 and 2 after just testbed (2026-11-10, 2 vCPUs, the nodes just upgraded and rebooted), with system/falco on the list; it is off the list since. TestbedFalco passed: the modern eBPF probe loaded on all three nodes and a dropped binary was reported. Then 10-minute windows, with Falco, without it, and with it again:

With Falco (30 min) Without Falco Falco added again k3s exits, leader changes 0, 0 0, 0 1 exit (homelab-2), the API's VIP briefly gone API or lease errors (deadline exceeded) 3, 12, 0 0, 0, 0 Heartbeat warnings 0, 30, 0 0, 4, 0 k3s server's CPU, of 2 vCPUs 50–88% 17–33% load average 11–18 CPU idle in each node 0–20% 74–77% (one node 12%, Argo CD catching up) WSL's lowest available 2.18 GB

Falco itself used 7–12% CPU per node; the cost is the probe on every system call, which k3s server makes the most of. So the driver's proof on NixOS is this run, by hand: add system/falco to system/argocd/values-testbed.yaml on a branch, run just testbed, then just test e2e --env testbed --labels falco, and take it off again. Taking it off the list leaves it running: root keeps the resources of a path it drops (preserveResourcesOnDeletion), so delete them too (kubectl -n argocd delete application falco, kubectl delete namespace falco). 15h's upgrade found it still on the nodes, where it restarted kube-vip and lost the API's address during a drain. Production's nodes are larger; its own numbers come from FalcoEventsDropped and the nodes' load in the first days.

docs.title: CloudNativePG, one measurement
docs.text:
Once, not on the list and not in the mark (just testbed-power --tests cut-postgres, PowerCutPostgres, the operator rendered and applied by hand with its PodMonitor removed, an instance on each node, 2 vCPUs):

Result pass: the same primary with the write after 4m20s, two replicas streaming after 5m37s k3s exits 1, on one node, 49 s after its boot (below) CPU idle in each node, average over 15 minutes (lowest 0) 10–30% I/O wait, average; highest 0–3%; 21% MemAvailable in each node, lowest 1.08–1.21 GB Disk, average per sample of about a minute written 120–140 MB, read 330–890 MB WSL's lowest available 1.69 GB

The nodes ran short of CPU, not of disk or memory, while everything restarted at once, and rode it out. No lease was lost: 12a-2's finding did not recur, so it says nothing about that and was not repeated at 4 vCPUs. k3s stopped itself twice across the two runs, both on one node shortly after a boot, and systemd restarted it: failed to start networking: unable to initialize network policy controller: error getting node subnet here, and in a first run (failed by a test reading stale status) a nil pointer in Flannel 0.28.4's watchVXLANDevice. Neither stopped the recovery; both go with k3s's own updates.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The VMs hand the pages they free back to WSL (virtio balloon with free page reporting), but not their page cache: on a VM only, a timer (profiles/vm-memory.nix) reclaims cache each minute until a quarter of the node's memory is free, so that quarter goes back to WSL (without it each VM grew to 3.0–3.4 GB and WSL ran out). Each node also runs zram swap. QEMU holds 2.8–3.4 GB per VM.

docs.title: Differences from production
docs.text:
• VMs on one workstation: no real power loss (Power), no real Wake-on-LAN (scripts/testbed-wake plays it), one disk per node (SCSI, /dev/sda) shared by the system and Ceph's OSD
