  • slow_control_plane (infra/testbed/cluster/config.json): etcd heartbeat 500 ms and election 5 s, controller leases 60 s. Production keeps the defaults, so a stall this environment rides out would be an election there
  • Ceph: one mgr, a 1.25 GiB OSD, no CephFS
  • UDP tunnel offload off on VMs (vm-tunnel-offload): their peers refused it (bad gso)
  • Certificates from the local CA, no Cloudflare or Telegram (values-local.yaml), no image cache, Argo CD's limits in values-testbed.yaml
  • No Kyverno and no monitoring operator: the PolicyExceptions and PodMonitors of the charts it runs are off, listed as not_run in infra/testbed/release-paths.yaml, so a release changing only those needs no testbed run
  • ServiceLB is off on the nodes, as in production; the sandbox keeps it
  • No Forgejo: the sandbox proves Argo CD reading ops/homelab (TestForgejoArgoCDSyncs)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Open the development shell, which includes all the tools needed:

nix develop

Everything that depends on where your homelab runs lives in infra/production/cluster/config.json; edit it:

  • domain: your domain (apps are served as <app>.<domain>)
  • zone: the Cloudflare zone holding it (the domain itself, or its parent for a subdomain such as home.example.com)
  • timezone: your time zone (the charts receive it as global.timezone)
  • seed_repository: the Git repository (your fork) the first install copies into Forgejo
  • vip: the Kubernetes API address; network.gateway, network.prefix_length: your router and LAN prefix
  • service_vips: the LAN addresses of the Gateway and wireguard, outside your router's DHCP range

Charts read these from there (scripts/check-env-config checks that none is written into a chart or app file). One setting still needs a hand edit, because its chart cannot take it from config.json: the time zone in platform/renovate/values.yaml (Renovate's schedule). The nodes read the time zone from config.json.

Example

infra/production/cluster/config.json
{
  "release_proof": "testbed",
  "init_host": "homelab-1",
  "vip": "192.168.0.10",
  "disk": "/dev/nvme0n1",
  "network": {
    "prefix_length": 24,
    "gateway": "192.168.0.1",
    "dns": [
      "192.168.0.1"
    ]
  },
  "service_vips": {
    "gateway": "192.168.0.2",
    "wireguard": "192.168.0.3"
  },
  "domain": "hoangduong.dev",
  "zone": "hoangduong.dev",
  "timezone": "Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh",
  "seed_repository": "https://github.com/duongle-steven/homelab"
}

Then list the machines in infra/production/metal/hosts.json: the address each node will have (not its current one: the machines have no operating system yet) and the lowercase, colon separated MAC address of the interface it boots from. nixie rewrites this file after each install: it adds the machine's machine_id_hash (commit it: a recorded machine is never installed again) and keeps no other field.

In infra/production/cluster/config.json, set:

  • init_host: the node that starts the cluster.
  • disk: the disk every node installs on. Installation erases it, and the rest of the disk after the system becomes Ceph's OSD. A node whose disk differs names its own disk in hosts.json, but nixie drops that field at its next install, so prefer machines alike.
  • network.dns: the resolvers the nodes and, through k3s's CoreDNS, the pods use. Name your router when the ISP's equipment intercepts DNS on UDP/53. Without the field, the nodes use 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1.

Example

infra/production/metal/hosts.json
{
  "homelab-1": {"ip": "192.168.0.11", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:01"},
  "homelab-2": {"ip": "192.168.0.12", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:02"},
  "homelab-3": {"ip": "192.168.0.13", "mac_address": "02:00:00:00:00:03"}
}

Then review the diff (git diff), commit and push the changes.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Open the development shell if you haven't already:

nix develop

docs.title: The nodes, the first time
docs.text:
infra/production/metal installs the machines of infra/production/metal/hosts.json the first time (nixie wakes them by Wake-on-LAN, boots them from the network and installs each with nixos-anywhere; PXE boot), joins them into one k3s cluster (lab cluster enroll), writes infra/production/kubeconfig.yaml, then upgrades nodes already installed in place, one at a time (lab cluster upgrade). Before the first run:

  1. Make production's own SSH key, with a passphrase, and load it; its public half goes in infra/production/metal/authorized_keys (commit it):

    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/homelab-production -C homelab-production
ssh-add ~/.ssh/homelab-production

  2. Under WSL (mirrored networking), let nixie's ports in: without these rules WSL sees no broadcast from the LAN. In an administrator PowerShell:

    New-NetFirewallHyperVRule -Name nixie-pxe-udp -DisplayName "nixie PXE (UDP)" -Direction Inbound -VMCreatorId '{40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}' -Protocol UDP -LocalPorts 67,69,4011
New-NetFirewallHyperVRule -Name nixie-pxe-tcp -DisplayName "nixie PXE (TCP)" -Direction Inbound -VMCreatorId '{40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}' -Protocol TCP -LocalPorts 80,5000

  3. Log in to Cloudflare for production's state (cf auth login, Account API Tokens enabled on its consent page).

  4. Switch the machines off: nixie wakes them.

Then, with your machine's LAN address:

cd infra/production/metal
HOMELAB_PXE_ADDRESS=192.168.0.224 terragrunt apply

nixie writes each machine's machine_id_hash into hosts.json: commit it. A recorded machine is never installed again, and once every machine is recorded the hook neither asks for sudo nor needs HOMELAB_PXE_ADDRESS, so just infra deploy production runs it every time.

To reinstall a node:

  1. Drain it and take it out of the cluster (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, then kubectl delete node <node>). Its etcd member leaves too: k3s removes a deleted server's member.
  2. Power it off: nixie wakes only machines that are off.
  3. Delete its machine_id_hash in hosts.json (the key, not just the value), commit.
  4. Forget its old host key: ssh-keygen -R <address>.
  5. Apply as for the first install, with the firewall rules and HOMELAB_PXE_ADDRESS.

If the trust step stops with "no SSH from …", it prints ssh's own error: a changed host key needs step 4, and "Permission denied" a key missing from the agent (ssh-add ~/.ssh/homelab-production).

Afterwards, remove the firewall rules:

Remove-NetFirewallHyperVRule -Name nixie-pxe-udp, nixie-pxe-tcp

The nodes' host keys were trusted on first contact (scripts/testbed-trust, for hosts.json's addresses only). To check one, compare ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub on the machine's console with ssh-keygen -lF <address> on yours.

Then prove the nodes:

just test e2e --env production --labels proof          # etcd, Secrets encrypted, seccomp
just test e2e --env production --focus NodesResolveQuickly
just test e2e --env production --labels scan           # kube-bench
scripts/node-fio <address>                              # once per node, before Ceph takes rook-data
just test e2e --env production --labels hardware-proof --verbose  # powers nodes off: never once real data is there

--labels hardware-proof runs ProductionVIPMoves (a node powered off, woken by Wake-on-LAN) and ProductionPowerCut (you switch the power strip off and on). A routine just test e2e --env production never runs them, nor kube-bench.

docs.title: Measured on the hardware (2026-11-11)
docs.text:
Three HP EliteDesk Minis (one 800 G4, two 800 G3), one 256 GB NVMe each, on a TP-Link Archer C64:

  • Install: the three in parallel in about 3 minutes, from nixie waking them to the record, over the laptop's Wi-Fi.
  • DNS through the Archer (DoH): an NXDOMAIN and an AAAA-less name in 110–140 ms on the nodes, 60–110 ms in a pod. Through 8.8.8.8 on UDP, the ISP modem's interception made the NXDOMAIN take 5 s.
  • fio, etcd's pattern (p99 fdatasync, budget 10 ms): homelab-2 and homelab-3 (Samsung MZAL8256HDJD) 5.1–5.7 ms; homelab-1 (SK hynix BC901) 10.7, 16.4 and 14.1 ms in three runs, over the budget every time. Its etcd's own WAL fsync averaged about 4 times the others'. A finding for step 12b-2.
  • fio on rook-data (173.5 GB per node): about 2.5 GiB/s sequential write, 3 GiB/s sequential read, 185–210k random 4k write IOPS and 260–277k random read IOPS on every node.
  • kube-bench: no finding outside .cluster-scan-accepted.yaml.
  • The VIP: the API answered through it 3–4 s after its holder powered off; Wake-on-LAN brought the node back in 2m43s (it tries the network first, finds no nixie, then boots its NVMe).
  • A power cut of the three nodes and the Archer together: every node booted by itself and the API answered at its VIP 1m11s after it went. Data written before a cut is checked in 12b-2, with Ceph.

docs.title: The rest
docs.text:
Build the lab:

just infra deploy production

It runs the nodes' unit above (nothing to install once every machine is recorded), then the rest of the deploy below.

Yes it's that simple!

Note

just infra deploy production deploys. It refuses anything but origin/master checked out without changes whose check checks passed and whose pull request's check sandbox passed (lab infra forgejo verify), applies infra/production, provisions Forgejo's org ops (lab infra forgejo sync: the users deploy and argocd, master's protection, their tokens in OpenBao), pushes the commit to ops/homelab (lab infra forgejo push), then applies the Argo CD bootstrap again. Argo CD does not manage itself, so a change to system/argocd reaches the cluster this way too. The first install is the same command: Argo CD reads the seed repository until its read-only token reads ops/homelab's master, then switches to Forgejo and never back (not even while Forgejo restarts). lab infra forgejo push alone deploys without touching the infrastructure. Only deploy can push to master, and nobody can force-push or delete it, Forgejo's site admins (forgejo_admin, homelab-admins) included; a site admin can still edit or remove the branch protection itself, a deliberate bypass the next lab infra forgejo sync (every just infra deploy production) undoes. Roll back with a revert through a pull request. --force applies the infrastructure only and deploys nothing (a state migration from another commit).

Example

It will take a while to download everything, you can read the architecture document while waiting for the deployment to complete.

docs.title: External resources
docs.text:
Info

These resources are optional, the homelab still works without them but will lack some features like trusted certificates and offsite backup

Although I try to keep the amount of external resources to the minimum, there's still need for a few of them. Below is a list of external resources and why we need them (also see some alternatives below).

Provider Resource Purpose Cloudflare DNS DNS and DNS-01 challenge for certificates Cloudflare Tunnel Public services to the internet without port forwarding ntfy.sh Relay Instant push to iOS for the self-hosted ntfy (poll requests only, no message content)

docs.title: Create credentials
docs.text: You'll be asked to provide these credentials on first build.

docs.title: Cloudflare
docs.text:
infra/production/cloudflare (OpenTofu, infra/_modules/cloudflare) creates the Tunnel, its DNS record homelab-production-tunnel.<domain> and two DNS tokens (cert-manager's DNS-01 challenge and external-dns), for the domain and zone in infra/production/cluster/config.json. Their secrets are the unit's sensitive output secrets (infra/production/secrets writes them into namespace infra-secrets, from where they reach OpenBao; secrets management).

  1. Buy a domain on Cloudflare, or transfer it to Cloudflare; set domain and zone in config.json.
  2. Enable Zero Trust (any team name, the Free plan) so the account can create tunnels.
  3. Enable R2 (R2 Object Storage in the dashboard; it asks for a payment method even on the free tier, which OpenTofu's state stays far below).
  4. terragrunt plan in infra/production/cloudflare, then terragrunt apply (just infra deploy production applies every production unit).

docs.title: Cloudflare login
docs.text:
OpenTofu takes the account and an OAuth token from cf, Cloudflare's CLI (in the dev shell), and cf refreshes the token. Log in once, with no CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN in the environment (cf would use it instead):

env -u CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN cf auth login --no-browser

On the consent page, enable Account API Tokens (it is off by default): OpenTofu manages the DNS tokens and lab creates the expiring R2 credentials with it. cf auth whoami must list account_api_tokens:create; otherwise run cf auth login --force and enable it.

--no-browser prints a link and a code (handy under WSL). CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID picks the account when the login sees several. just infra check needs no login.

docs.title: State passphrase
docs.text:
Every OpenTofu state is encrypted (OpenTofu's state encryption, PBKDF2 and AES-GCM) with HOMELAB_STATE_PASSPHRASE, which .envrc loads from ~/.config/homelab/state.env:

sh -c 'umask 077; mkdir -p ~/.config/homelab; printf "export HOMELAB_STATE_PASSPHRASE=%s\n" "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" > ~/.config/homelab/state.env'
direnv allow

Keep a copy in a password manager. Losing it makes every state unreadable, including OpenBao's unseal key and the WireGuard private key, and with the unseal key every secret in OpenBao.

A state written before encryption (an older sandbox, or production before step 8c) is refused; run the first command once with HOMELAB_STATE_MIGRATE=1 (for example HOMELAB_STATE_MIGRATE=1 just dev), which reads it unencrypted and writes it encrypted.

docs.title: Rotating the passphrase
docs.text:
1. Set HOMELAB_STATE_PASSPHRASE to the new passphrase and HOMELAB_STATE_PASSPHRASE_PREVIOUS to the old one.
  2. Run scripts/rotate-state-passphrase production (and sandbox). It reads every unit's state with the old passphrase before it writes any, so a wrong old passphrase changes nothing; for production it names the Cloudflare account first. An interrupted rotation can be rerun with the same variables.
  3. Update the password manager and state.env, then unset HOMELAB_STATE_PASSPHRASE_PREVIOUS.

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text: Production's state is on R2 through its S3 API (OpenTofu's s3 backend): bucket homelab-production-tfstate (created on the first init by lab infra state ensure), one object per unit (<unit>/tfstate.json) and a lock file (<unit>/tfstate.json.tflock) while a command runs. Its credentials last one hour and come from lab infra state credentials (an account token for that bucket only, created with the cf login), so no token is written to disk; lab keeps the current one in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (memory-backed, user-only) and reuses it while it lasts 15 more minutes. lab runs with go run: after a fresh clone or a dependency bump, build it once (go -C cli build ./cmd/lab; just infra deploy does) so the first credential is not cut off by a cold build. An interrupted command can leave the lock behind: run terragrunt force-unlock <ID> in the unit with the ID OpenTofu prints. The sandbox's state stays in .state/sandbox/ (git-ignored, readable by the user only). Both are encrypted.

docs.title: ntfy
docs.text: Nothing to create: ntfy runs in the cluster (alerts); iOS notifications go through ntfy.sh's free relay.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
To avoid vendor lock-in, each external provider must have an equivalent alternative that is easy to replace:

  • Cloudflare DNS:
    • Update cert-manager and external-dns to use a different provider
    • Alternate DNS setup
  • Cloudflare Tunnel:
    • Use port forwarding if it's available
    • Create a small VPS in the cloud and utilize Wireguard to route traffic via it
    • Access everything via VPN
    • See also awesome tunneling
  • ntfy.sh (iOS relay):
    • Android only, or an Apple push setup of your own (see ntfy's docs on upstream-base-url)
    • Any other integration supported by Grafana Alerting

docs.title: Initial controller
docs.text:
Info

The initial controller is the machine used to bootstrap the cluster, we only need it once, you can use your laptop or desktop

  • A Linux machine that can run Docker (because the host networking driver used for PXE boot only supports Linux, you can use a Linux virtual machine with bridged networking if you're on macOS or Windows).

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
Any modern x86_64 computer(s) should work, you can use old PCs, laptops or servers.

Info

This is the requirements for each node

Component Minimum Recommended CPU 2 cores 4 cores RAM 8 GB 16 GB Hard drive 128 GB 512 GB (depending on your storage usage, the base installation will not use more than 128GB) Node count 1 (checkout the single node cluster adjustments tutorial) 3 or more for high availability

Additional capabilities:

  • Ability to boot from the network (PXE boot)
  • Wake-on-LAN capability, used to wake the machines up automatically without physically touching the power button

docs.title: Network setup
docs.text:
• All servers must be connected to the same wired network with the initial controller
  • You have the access to change DNS config (on your router or at your domain registrar)

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: Buying a domain is highly recommended, but if you don't have one, see alternate DNS setup.

docs.title: BIOS setup
docs.text:
Info

You need to do it once per machine if the default config is not sufficent, usually for consumer hardware this can not be automated (it requires something like IPMI to automate).

Common settings:

  • Enable Wake-on-LAN (WoL) and network boot
  • Use UEFI mode and disable CSM (legacy) mode
  • Disable secure boot

Boot order options (select one, each has their pros and cons):

  1. Only boot from the network if no operating system found: works on most hardware but you need to manually wipe your hard drive or delete the existing boot record for the current OS
  2. Prefer booting from the network if turned on via WoL: more convenience but your BIOS must support it, and you must test it throughly to ensure you don't accidentally wipe your servers

Example

Below is my BIOS setup for reference. Your motherboard may have a different name for the options, so you'll need to adapt it to your hardware.

Devices:
  NetworkSetup:
    PXEIPv4: true
    PXEIPv6: false
Advanced:
  CPUSetup:
    VT-d: true
Power:
  AutomaticPowerOn:
    WoL: Automatic  # Use network boot if Wake-on-LAN
Security:
  SecureBoot: false
Startup:
  CSM: false

This homelab's HP EliteDesk Minis (800 G3, 800 G4)

Set on each machine in F10 (BIOS Setup), and checked from nixie's installer in step 12b-1:

  • BIOS updated to HP's latest for the model (G3: P21, G4: Q21). One G3 shipped with P21 Ver. 02.15 from 2018, which kept no change made in F10 (Secure Boot, After Power Loss) until it was updated.
  • Secure Boot off ("Legacy Support Disable and Secure Boot Disable"): nixie's iPXE is unsigned, and the firmware refused it with "Selected boot image did not authenticate". No BIOS administrator password: the disks are not encrypted, so it would guard little, and a forgotten HP password is hard to reset.
  • After Power Loss: Previous State, so a node cut by an outage boots when the power returns.
  • S4/S5 Wake on LAN: Boot to Network (option 2 above). A node woken this way tries the network first; with no nixie answering it boots its NVMe about 75 seconds later.
  • Boot order: the M.2 drive first, then IPv4 network boot; IPv6 network boot off, USB last or off.
  • F12 starts a network boot by hand, if Wake-on-LAN does not; the startup menu (Esc) ignored one USB keyboard.

docs.title: Gather information
docs.text:
• MAC address for each machine
  • OS disk name (for example /dev/sda)
  • Network interface name (for example eth0)
  • Choose a static IP address for each machine (just the desired address, we don't set anything up yet)

docs.title: Bug report
docs.text: You can create a new GitHub issue with the bug report template.

docs.title: Submitting patches
docs.text:
Because you may have a lot of changes in your fork, you can't create a pull request directly from your master branch. Instead, create a branch from the upstream repository and commit your changes there:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/khuedoan/homelab
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/master
git checkout -b contrib-fix-something

# Make your changes here
#
# nvim README.md
# git cherry-pick a1b2c3
#
# commit, push, etc. as usual

Then you can send the patch using GitHub pull request or git send-email to mail@khuedoan.com.

docs.title: Is it necessary to install Linux on my servers before setting up the homelab?
docs.text: No, and that's the beauty of this setup. You start with empty hard drives, type a single command on your laptop/PC, and it will install the operating system for you automatically and in parallel over the network.

docs.title: Is it necessary to keep the PXE server running?
docs.text: No, the ephemeral PXE server is stateless, once Linux is installed on your servers, you can shut it down (or not, ideally, you don't even need to be aware of its existence). The Terragrunt metal unit runs nixie when you apply it.

docs.title: Use Velero for volumes only
docs.text:
Context

The cluster's resources all come from git (Argo CD) and OpenTofu's state is on R2; what git cannot rebuild is the data in some volumes. Upstream nixos replaced VolSync with Velero (VolSync needs a resource and credentials per volume) and backs up the whole cluster hourly, restoring by hand with a read-only location.

Decision

  • Velero (CSI snapshots moved by its data mover into Kopia on R2) copies only the PersistentVolumeClaims labelled homelab/backup: daily, once a day; manual ones only on lab backup push. Resources are never backed up: restoring them over Argo CD would fight it.
  • Hourly local VolumeSnapshots, kept 48 hours, need no internet.
  • Every new cluster starts read-only with the schedule paused (in git; Argo CD ignores the two fields) until lab backup enable. Retention is by count (the newest 30), never by age, so a long outage or a fresh install deletes no backup.
  • Restore is a command (lab backup restore), never automatic.
  • No point-in-time recovery (CloudNativePG's barman-cloud): it restores a database to any second, but Forgejo's repositories live on another volume that only has the backup moments, and both must match, so Forgejo could only go back to those moments anyway. A crash-consistent snapshot of PostgreSQL is enough.

Consequences

  • Every claim must declare its group (scripts/check-backup-groups); a new volume is not backed up by accident.
  • A restore drives each operator itself (CloudNativePG's owner references, kaniop's Secrets, OpenBao's raft snapshot): lab backup restore holds that knowledge, and TestBackupRestore proves it in the sandbox.
  • Velero needs broad cluster permissions, like upstream's.

docs.title: Remove the Docker wrapper for Nix shell
docs.text:
Context

The Docker wrapper was originally added because not everyone has Nix installed. However, it is not a good abstraction. Depending on how Docker (or Podman) was installed, there may be permission issues, and it is slower than running Nix directly on the host.

Decision

Remove the Docker wrapper and run the Nix development shell directly. While not everyone has Nix installed, not everyone has the same Docker setup either.

Consequences

  • Requires an additional step to install Nix, but this is a one-time setup.
  • The make tools command has been removed, you now need to run nix develop directly. Although it can be added to the Makefile, this requires make to be installed, and not everyone has the same version of make.

docs.title: Remove HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
Context

  • HashiCorp changed their license, and it's no longer free/libre software. One of the highest priorities of this project is to minimize the usage of non-free software as much as possible, so I don't really want to keep Vault, especially considering the next point.
  • Vault is fairly complex to maintain properly. This project only uses Vault for two things: basic key-value secret store and its API to create and manage secrets dynamically. With the new Kubernetes secret provider in External Secrets, both features can be replaced with Kubernetes's built-in secrets and API server.
  • A related goal of using Vault as an identity provider for SSO will be discarded, and we'll use Authelia instead, which has a beta identity provider feature (or use another alternative).

Decision

Replace Vault with a simplier in-cluster global secret store.

Consequences

Unlike secret path in Vault, Kubernetes does not support / in object name. We need to change secret convention from path to name and replace / with ..

Update secret generator config:

-- path: gitea/admin
+- name: gitea.admin
   data:
     - key: password
       length: 32

Update secret references in kind: ExternalSecret:

 remoteRef:
-  key: /gitea/admin
+  key: gitea.admin

docs.title: Manage package versions in development shell
docs.text:
Context

While Nix is reproducible, we need a way to control the versions of the tools and keep them up-to-date. For example, if we update the nixpkgs hash (in flake.nix) from abcd1234 to defa5678:

  • ansible: 2.12.1 -> 2.12.6
  • terraform: 1.2.0 -> 1.2.2
  • foobar: 1.8.0 -> 1.9.0

That looks good. But when we update it from defa5678 to cdef9012:

  • ansible: 2.12.6 -> 2.13.0
  • terraform: 1.2.2 -> 1.3.1
  • foobar: 1.9.0 -> 2.0.0

This time it breaks foobar because the new major version contains a breaking change.

We can pin the specific version of each dependency in flake.nix, however, the maintenance burden is too high (even with Renovate) because we need to update the version of each package regularly rather than just the nixpkgs hash. Instead, we can just bump the nixpkgs hash and run some tests to ensure there is no breaking change.

Decision

Update the tests to ensure that the versions remain within the desired range (i.e. no breaking change).

Consequences

We have the rail guard from the tests to ensure that we don't upgrade to a new major version with breaking changes, and we can make a conscious decision to take the necessary steps prior to upgrading to the new major version.

docs.title: Refactor the tools container from plain Dockerfile to Nix
docs.text:
Context

The previous implementation of the tools container is not reproducible, if someone builds it a few weeks after me, they will receive different versions of the tools. Also, if you change something in the tool list, everything will be downloaded again, with no caching.

Decision

Move to Nix shell with a Docker wrapper, in case Nix is not available (see commit adbaf32).

Consequences

  • All versions are pinned
  • When you change the list of tools, rebuilding is much faster

docs.title: Combine dhcpd and tftpd to dnsmasq in PXE server
docs.text:
Context

Original proposal from @Bourne-ID:

Issue statement

The use of dhcpd is great for air-gap solutions where a new DHCP is required. However for some home networks which does not have the VLAN capability or for users who would like to use common router DHCP services, the use of DHCPD will cause duplicate DHCP servers and will result in potential network disruption, or will limit the ability to auto-provision the Metal stage of this project.

Proposed Solution: DHCP Proxy

Use DHCP Proxy services to add PXE features such as Next Server into this project. This allows for users to use the existing DHCP servers which may be locked down or incapable of using Next Server/PXE settings on their network to be able to auto-provision hardware through PXE (with certain common configurations, like static IP allocation or reduction in DHCP request ranges on the DHCP server)

Proposed Application: DNSMasq

DNSMasq in Proxy mode interoperates with existing DHCP servers over IPv4 to add features such as next-server, TFTP, etc. where such hardware is either locked or unconfigurable for such services. This would be an opt-in change, configurable through the pxe_server defaults file.

Proposed Target Audience

Users who either do not want to create their own VLAN or lack the hardware to configure such services. Users who want to use common router services for DHCP and have router access to configure static IP and/or DHCP allocation ranges.

Additional Risks with Proposed Change

  • Additional Surface Area for Break-Out Attacks: Originally this project is locked to its own DHCP/VLAN, so any break-outs should be contained accordingly. Using common home networks increases the surface area of break-out attacks if the deployment is compromised.
  • Mitigation: Enrolment into this change is opt in only.

Proposed Next Steps

  1. Trial/Adopt/Halt - A discussion with all or a decision by the project maintainers to identify if this change should exist in this project or live on a fork.
  2. Documentation (This is in flight in any situation).

Decision

Migrate to dnsmasq (see commit f650c89, thanks to @Bourne-ID)

Consequences

  • DHCP proxy is enabled by default because most people have a standard home network with existing DHCP server, but it can still be disabled to restore the previous behavior

docs.title: Migrate documentation from mdBook to MkDocs
docs.text:
Context

mdBook is very minimal and light weight, which I personally prefer. However, Backstage TechDocs which I plan to use currently only supports mkDocs.

Decision

Migrate documentation from mdBook to MkDocs (see commit cd41343).

Consequences

  • We can no longer include only a portion of a file, see facelessuser/pymdown-extensions#1462.

docs.title: Choosing the base OS
docs.text:
Context

I've tried several distributions, and each has advantages and disadvantages. Fedora has a good (enough) balance between stability and new features.

Alternatives considered:

  • Fedora CoreOS (moved to Rocky in 7667254):
    • Pros: automatic and atomic upgrade, immutable, quick installation
    • Cons: hard to run Ansible on (Python is not included)
  • CentOS/Rocky Linux (moved to Fedora in 022b816):
    • Pros: relatively stable (however we did encounter a breaking change #63, still not sure why)
    • Cons: kernel and packages are too old
  • Debian: couldn't get it to work with PXE boot and Rocky Linux was sufficient so I didn't push any further
  • Cluster API (previous attempt in a8e4a85, I hope to get this to work someday):
    • Pros: control bare metal machines via Kubernetes API, open the possibility for autoscaling and autohealing
    • Cons: doesn't support simple WoL and shutdown via SSH (or similar)

Decision

Use Fedora as the base OS.

Consequences

¯\_(ツ)_/¯

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  subgraph LAN
    laptop/desktop/phone <--> LoadBalancer
    subgraph k8s[Kubernetes cluster]
      Pod --> Service
      Service --> HTTPRoute
      HTTPRoute --> gateway[Gateway gateway]
      HTTPRoute --> public[Gateway public]
      LoadBalancer <--> gateway
      cloudflared <--> public
    end
  end

  cloudflared -- outbound --> Cloudflare
  Internet -- inbound --> Cloudflare

The cluster uses k3s's own networking: Flannel, kube-proxy and the network policy controller (and ServiceLB in the sandbox; on the nodes it would overwrite kube-vip's addresses, so it is off). Istio serves two Gateway API Gateways in namespace istio-system (system/istio-system):

  • gateway is for the LAN. In production kube-vip gives its LoadBalancer Service its own address (192.168.0.2, announced with ARP and moved to another node when one fails); external-dns points each route's hostname at it. It also redirects HTTP to HTTPS and carries Forgejo SSH (port 22, TCPRoute), which the nodes' own SSH would block on their addresses. In the sandbox, ServiceLB serves it on the k3d node.
  • public is published through the Cloudflare Tunnel: its Service is ClusterIP, cloudflared forwards to it in the cluster, and external-dns points its routes' hostnames at the tunnel. Only apps that attach to it are reachable from the internet.

kube-vip also holds the Kubernetes API address (192.168.0.10) and serves LoadBalancer Services of class kube-vip.io/kube-vip-class, the only LoadBalancer Services the nodes have.

These addresses are set in infra/<env>/cluster/config.json (upstream's format: vip, network, plus service_vips); Argo CD passes them to every chart as global.addresses.*, and scripts/check-env-config keeps addresses out of charts and app files.

Both terminate TLS with one wildcard certificate. Apps attach an HTTPRoute to one of them; there are no Ingress objects.

docs.title: Service mesh
docs.text:
Every namespace Argo CD manages joins Istio's ambient mesh (istio.io/dataplane-mode: ambient, set through Argo CD's managedNamespaceMetadata): istio-cni redirects each pod's traffic to the ztunnel on its node, which wraps it in mutual TLS with the workload's SPIFFE identity. A mesh-wide PeerAuthentication (STRICT) makes meshed pods refuse plaintext. There are no sidecars; apps need no changes.

Outside the mesh:

  • istio-system (the mesh itself) and rook-ceph (some host-network pods, Ceph's own encryption), labelled none by the root ApplicationSet's templatePatch
  • kube-system, which Argo CD does not manage
  • the pods the Kubernetes API server calls as webhooks (cert-manager, trust-manager, External Secrets, the Prometheus operator, CloudNativePG), labelled none on the pod; scripts/check-mesh-policies fails if a chart adds a webhook that is still meshed
  • the VPN routers (WireGuard, Tailscale), labelled none on the pod: ambient would hand the clients' forwarded TCP to ztunnel, which refuses it

The CloudNativePG operator, outside the mesh, polls its PostgreSQL instances' status port (8000); a PeerAuthentication on forgejo-db lets that port accept plaintext.

The Istio Gateways reach meshed pods over HBONE, so inbound traffic is unchanged. Meshed connections arrive on ztunnel's HBONE port (TCP 15008), so a chart that ships NetworkPolicies (Argo CD) also gets a policy allow-hbone that lets that port in. If ztunnel is down on a node, meshed pods there cannot open connections.

Inside the mesh nothing is reachable unless allowed: deny-all in istio-system (the Gateways keep allow-gateways) and one AuthorizationPolicy allow per namespace, in the namespace's chart or app file: pods of the same namespace, the Gateway its routes attach to (on the pod ports behind them), Prometheus on the metrics ports, and a few named callers (Grafana to Prometheus and Loki, Argo CD's repo server to Forgejo, CloudNativePG's operator to its instances). Pods outside the mesh get a NetworkPolicy that opens only their webhook, VPN or metrics ports. A new app needs its allow policy; scripts/check-mesh-policies fails without it. Outbound traffic is restricted too (see Egress).

docs.title: Node restarts
docs.text: When a node restarts, the kubelet recreates its pods while the node's ztunnel may still be waiting for istiod. istio-cni cannot hand those pods to ztunnel within its 5-second limit, containerd tears their sandboxes down, and istio-cni's snapshot keeps their dead network namespaces, which ztunnel then retries forever: the node's meshed pods stay Pending and ztunnel stays not Ready. istio-cni works through those pods one at a time, and while each takes more than 5 seconds none ever succeeds. Two settings get the node out: istio-cni skips IPv6 rules (cni.ambient.ipv6: false; pods only get IPv4), which halves its work per pod, and the CronJob istio-system/istio-cni-watchdog clears a stuck node: one whose ztunnel has run for 3 minutes without becoming Ready, or where a pod has had no sandbox for 3 minutes while istio-cni's add keeps failing for it (its FailedCreatePodSandBox events; ztunnel can report Ready while it still retries dead network namespaces). It deletes the node's istio-cni pod, so the new istio-cni builds its snapshot again, or both istio-cni and ztunnel when istio-cni was already restarted after ztunnel's start and the node is still stuck (the sandbox's power cuts cleared only once both were new); it waits 3 minutes after either restart. The sandbox recovers in 5 to 14 minutes. Look at kubectl -n istio-system get pods and the watchdog Jobs' logs. istio-cni writes its own CNI config file (istioOwnedCNIConfig), because k3s rewrites 10-flannel.conflist at every start.

docs.title: Egress
docs.text:
Every namespace Argo CD manages (except istio-system and rook-ceph) gets system/egress: egress is denied except to the cluster (pod and Service ranges: DNS, the Gateway, pods outside the mesh), the Kubernetes API (the node network, port 6443) and the LAN Gateway's VIP. Namespaces listed in system/egress/values.yaml also reach the internet (any address except the private ranges) on their ports, and monitoring-system the nodes' metrics ports. Nothing reaches the rest of the LAN. Traffic between meshed pods and in-cluster DNS go through ztunnel and are governed by the mesh's AuthorizationPolicies, not by these policies. k3s's network policy controller applies policies to a new pod asynchronously, so a pod's first seconds are not yet restricted.

ESO's controller reads every namespace's Secrets, so it never reaches the internet: anything that needs a token from outside mints it in its own namespace (Renovate's GitHub token, in Renovate's pod; docs/how-to-guides/renovate.md).

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
+--------------+
|    ./apps    |
|--------------|
|  ./platform  |
|--------------|       +------------+
|   ./system   |- - - -| ./external |
|--------------|       +------------+
|   ./infra    |
|--------------|
|   HARDWARE   |
+--------------+

Main components:

  • ./infra: OpenTofu and Terragrunt: the nodes (infra/<env>/metal: NixOS and k3s), the sandbox's cluster, Argo CD's bootstrap and the cloud resources
  • ./system: critical system components for the cluster (load balancer, storage, Gateway API gateways, operation tools...)
  • ./platform: essential components for service hosting platform (git, build runners, dashboards...)
  • ./apps: user facing applications
  • ./external (optional): externally managed services

Support components:

  • ./docs: all documentation go here, this will generate a searchable web UI
  • ./scripts: scripts to automate common tasks

docs.title: Provisioning flow
docs.text:
Everything is automated, after you edit the configuration files, you just need to run a single just infra deploy production command and it will:

  • (1) Apply the metal unit (infra/<env>/metal):
    • Create an ephemeral, stateless PXE server (nixie)
    • Install NixOS on all servers in parallel
    • Build a Kubernetes cluster (based on k3s) and export its kubeconfig
  • (2) Bootstrap the ./system layer:
    • Install Argo CD and its ApplicationSets with OpenTofu (infra/<env>/argocd, applied again whenever system/argocd changes); Argo CD syncs every other layer from git
    • Install the remaining components (storage, monitoring, etc)
  • (3) Build the ./platform layer (Forgejo, Grafana, SSO, etc)
  • (4) Deploy applications in the ./apps layer
flowchart TD
  subgraph metal[infra/env/metal]
    pxe[PXE Server] -.-> linux[NixOS Server] --> k3s
  end

  subgraph system[./system]
    argocd[ArgoCD and root app]
    istio[Istio gateways]
    rook-ceph[Rook Ceph]
    cert-manager
    external-dns[External DNS]
    cloudflared
  end

  subgraph external[External services]
    letsencrypt[Let's Encrypt]
    cloudflare[Cloudflare]
  end

  letsencrypt -.-> cert-manager
  cloudflare -.-> cert-manager
  cloudflare -.-> external-dns
  cloudflare -.-> cloudflared

  subgraph platform[./platform]
    Forgejo
    argo-workflows[Argo Workflows and Events]
    Grafana
  end

  subgraph apps[./apps]
    homepage[Homepage]
    jellyfin[Jellyfin]
    matrix[Matrix]
    paperless[Paperless]
  end

  just[Run just infra deploy] -- 1 --> metal -- 2 --> system -. 3 .-> platform -. 4 .-> apps

Logs: the OpenTelemetry agent on every node reads the pods' and the API server's audit logs into Loki over OTLP, and the gateway Collector the cluster's events and every trace (system/opentelemetry, Loki in system/loki, traces in system/tempo), which Grafana queries (logs).

Portal: Backstage (platform/backstage, LAN only) catalogs every app and component from the descriptions in their own files (lab catalog generate, which also writes Homepage's services), serves these docs (TechDocs) and starts repositories in Forgejo's org ci from a template; admins and editors sign in with Kanidm (Backstage).

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/woodpecker-agent-0 would not any 15g TestFalcoAccepted renders only an = fixture: the real entries (an in with a nested list) are never rendered and checked, field, comp and value counts are not compared, fields/values are not required, and accepted in values-dev.yaml/values-local.yaml (which drops production's list) does not fail any 15g The Buildah memfd exception could also require proc.aname buildah, narrowing it further 15g-2 15g Falco's DaemonSet has no checksum annotation for falco-accepted-rules: a change relies on Falco's watch_config_files reload (it reloaded live in the sandbox) any 15g TestFalcoRender reads the chart's appVersion with helm show chart --repo, so the offline test needs the network any 15g The Falco spec runs its probe at once: right after just dev syncs a change to the rules, Falco may reload them (kubelet updates the ConfigMap within about a minute) after the probe ran, so the spec fails once; it could wait for the rendered rules in the pod first any 15h woodpecker-localhost-seccomp matches pod CREATE only: an ephemeral container (pods/ephemeralcontainers, kubectl debug) added to a running pod in woodpecker may name a Localhost profile unchecked; it needs the pods/ephemeralcontainers subresource in its rules, and only people who may update that subresource can try any 12b-1 The testbed's VMs query 8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1 through NAT, which the ISP modem may intercept like production's (slow negative answers): give the testbed network.dns its libvirt gateway if its network serves DNS, and run NodesResolveQuickly there any 12b-1 lab cluster upgrade on production ran only with nothing to change: its first real upgrade (drain, nixos-rebuild, Ceph healthy) on the hardware comes with 12b-2's first node change 12b-2 12b-1 scripts/metal-nixie counts "machine_id_hash": "" as recorded while nixie treats it as unrecorded, and a missing jq falls through to a confusing message instead of failing any 12b-1 ProductionVIPMoves powers its node off before checking it can wake it (no workstation address in the nodes' /24 leaves the node off), and assumes a /24 rather than config.json's prefix_length any 12b-1 just test e2e --env production --labels <broad filter> (e.g. production, !kiali) still selects hardware-proof: only the empty filter excludes it 12b-2 12b-1 metalEnv() treats any ENV other than testbed as production, and the production recipe leaves ENV as the shell has it: export ENV=production and fail on anything else any 12b-1 TestProductionMetalUnit and TestProductionConfig hard-code the machines' MACs, addresses and config values: replacing a machine means editing a test any 12b-2 EtcdLeaderChanges overlaps kube-prometheus-stack's etcdHighNumberOfLeaderChanges and fires once per member: aggregate it (max without (instance, pod)) or keep only EtcdSlowDisk any 12b-2 ProductionPowerCutWithData reads OpenBao once after the cut; wrap it in Eventually like the PostgreSQL read 12b-2 12b-2 TestStageGatesApps passes trivially if no apps cluster generator is rendered: assert one for production and dev any Matrix (#89) The Matrix spec leaves a private room for dev-admin per run in the daily volume: leave and forget it in a DeferCleanup any Matrix (#89) The Matrix spec finds tuwunel's "Continue sign-in" button by its text; a text or language change breaks it (its failure says where the browser stopped) any Matrix (#89) tuwunel 2.0's media.upload_min_free_space (1 GiB) refuses uploads once about 4 GiB of matrix-data's 5Gi is used: size it or note it 12b-3 Matrix (#89) Matrix joins the sandbox's default apps (requests 272Mi, limits about 1.1Gi) unmeasured under the full suite, and Falco's clean baseline has not run with it any 10f (Argo CI) infra/_modules/metal/flake/profiles/k3s-server.nix and infra/_modules/metal/flake/seccomp/README.md still say Woodpecker's Buildah steps get homelab/buildah.json (the golden path's build does now): infra/_modules/metal/** gates releases on the testbed, so a comment is not worth a run (TestNoWoodpecker excludes them) the next change there 10f (Argo CI) lab infra forgejo sync compares the webhook's events with reflect.DeepEqual, but Forgejo expands pull_request into its whole group (assign, label, review, sync…), so every sync rewrites the hook and its applied-hash record; compare after normalising, and make the fake echo what Forgejo returns any 10f (Argo CI) The build step has zot's ci credentials in its environment on every run, pull requests included, while the Containerfile's RUN steps run in that pod: move the push into its own step that runs only when publishing any 10f (Argo CI) sign.sh signs first and attests after: a failed attestation (e.g. a context/containerfile with ", which settings.sh allows and the heredoc JSON does not escape) leaves a signed image without provenance; restrict those values to a safe charset, or attest first any 10f (Argo CI) Any repository in org ci may name image: <another repository's name> in .ci.yaml and get it published and signed under that name; verify-ci-images checks only that a signature exists: keep the repository's own name, or match the provenance's repository to the image path 15b-2 10f (Argo CI) A branch push and its open pull request's synchronized event build the same commit twice and both post ci/pipeline on it (the last to end wins): build pull requests and default-branch pushes only, or use distinct contexts any 10f (Argo CI) The Sensor's string filters are unanchored regexes (push and opened match substrings); no Forgejo event misfires today, ^…$ costs nothing any 10f (Argo CI) No spec shows verify-ci-images returning pass for a golden-path image (no pod in the sandbox runs one): run the CI-built image as a pod and assert its PolicyReport has no fail or error 15b-2 10f (Argo CI) scripts/ci-check policy cannot see Workflow templates' pods (a WorkflowTemplate is not a pod kind), so the build step's missing allowPrivilegeEscalation went unnoticed until the final review; render the golden path's step pods for the policy check 15b-2 10f (Argo CI) Argo CD's repo-server hung 27 minutes on an orphaned git remote-https to GitHub (parent killed, TCP established and idle, keepalive answered): every Application went Unknown until it was killed; find why it outlived its fetch and bound it (git's http.lowSpeedTime, Argo CD's exec timeout) any OpenTelemetry infra/_modules/metal/flake/profiles/k3s-server.nix and infra/_modules/k3d/k3d.yaml still say Alloy sends the audit log to Loki (the OpenTelemetry agent does): the first gates releases on the testbed, the second recreates the sandbox's cluster when it changes, so a comment is not worth either (TestNoAlloy excludes them) the next change there OpenTelemetry The agent batches in the batch processor between the readers and the persistent queue: lines held there after the readers saved their positions are lost on an OOM kill, and 1000 records of up to 100KB audit events can exceed Loki's 16MB burst; batch in the exporter's sending_queue with a bytes sizer instead any OpenTelemetry The OpenBao route matches any pod in openbao (the snapshot jobs too), not only container openbao as Alloy did: add k8s.container.name == "openbao" any OpenTelemetry Nothing alerts on one node's agent (down, 429 forever, queue growing): AuditLogsMissing covers the cluster only; alert on up of agent-collector, otelcol_exporter_send_failed_log_records or a growing otelcol_exporter_queue_size 12b-3 OpenTelemetry The Operator's pod webhook sees every pod creation with a 10 s timeout: when its node loses power, pods wait until the endpoint goes; lower admissionWebhooks.timeoutSeconds to about 3 any Backstage-1 A component's open Alertmanager alerts: Roadie's backstage-plugin-prometheus has no new-frontend-system export; write the view in Backstage-2's own plugin Backstage-2 Backstage-1 The sandbox's SSO specs failed one at a time under load (SSOArgoWorkflows dev-admin, then SSOOpenCloud dev-editor) while k3s lost its lease twice in 40 minutes: watch whether they pass on a calm sandbox sandbox stability Backstage-1 backstage-db's CloudNativePG status reads "HTTP communication issue" (the operator polling the instance's port 8000 through the mesh) though the database works: check backstage-db-status's PeerAuthentication as forgejo-db-status's Backstage-2 Backstage-1 Production's egress table opens 443 for namespace backstage, which only the sandbox needs (GitHub): the table has no environment egress per environment

docs.title: kind + Cilium Sandbox (1a) Implementation Plan
docs.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: make dev builds a local kind + Cilium cluster that bootstraps ArgoCD from the dev branch on GitHub and runs ingress-nginx, cert-manager (dev CA), kube-prometheus-stack and excalidraw, reachable at https://*.127-0-0-1.nip.io from Windows.

Architecture: metal/ creates the kind cluster on a fixed Docker network, installs Cilium through the existing Ansible role, and starts a socat proxy from 127.0.0.1:80/443 to the ingress LoadBalancer IP. system/bootstrap.yml installs ArgoCD with values-dev.yaml. The dev ApplicationSet syncs an allowlist of components from GitHub, each rendered with values.yaml + an optional values-dev.yaml.

Tech Stack: Nix flake (nixos-26.05 + nixos-unstable for kind/cilium-cli), kind 0.32.0 (node v1.36.1), Cilium 1.20.2, Helm 3.20, Ansible 13 (core 2.21), ArgoCD (chart 10.10.3), ingress-nginx (4.15.1), cert-manager (v1.21.2), kube-prometheus-stack (92.3.0), app-template (5.3.0), Go + terratest.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-12-kind-cilium-sandbox-design.md

docs.title: Global Constraints
docs.text:
• Work on branch dev. Never touch master in this plan.
  • One concern per commit; chart bumps are one commit per chart.
  • Every tool and chart touched uses its current stable release, pinned exactly. Versions verified on 2026-10-12:
  • nixpkgs nixos-26.05; kind 0.32.0 and cilium-cli 0.19.7 from nixos-unstable (26.05 has kind 0.31, whose newest node image v1.35 is older than Cilium's supported maximum)
  • kind node image kindest/node:v1.36.1@sha256:3489c7674813ba5d8b1a9977baea8a6e553784dab7b84759d1014dbd78f7ebd5 (Cilium 1.20 supports Kubernetes 1.33–1.36; 1.37 is not supported yet)
  • Cilium chart 1.20.2
  • argo-cd 10.10.3, argocd-apps 2.0.6, ingress-nginx 4.15.1, cert-manager v1.21.2, kube-prometheus-stack 92.3.0, app-template 5.3.0 (excalidraw only)
  • alpine/socat:1.8.1.3
  • Helm stays at 3.20.2 from 26.05 (Helm 4 is only in unstable and is a major change; out of scope)
  • Fixed addresses: Docker network kind = 172.30.0.0/16; LB pool 172.30.255.200/29; ingress-nginx LB IP 172.30.255.200.
  • Names: cluster homelab-dev; proxy container homelab-dev-proxy; kubeconfig metal/kubeconfig.yaml.
  • Make variable env (prod default, dev). Ansible extra var homelab_env. Go test env var ENV.
  • Dev GitOps source: https://github.com/duongle-steven/homelab, revision dev. Allowlist: system/argocd, system/ingress-nginx, system/cert-manager, system/monitoring-system, apps/excalidraw.
  • Prod values.yaml changes only where a chart bump forces it.
  • All commands run inside the dev shell (nix develop, or direnv in ~/homelab).
  • Commits end with Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>.
  • git push origin dev publishes to GitHub; the user approved this flow in the spec (ArgoCD reads from origin dev).

docs.title: Review Focus
docs.text:
1. Second make dev on an existing sandbox must succeed without recreating anything (network, cluster, proxy, Cilium, ArgoCD) → checked in Task 11 step "run again".
  2. Ports 80/443 already taken on the WSL host (another web server, an old proxy) → the proxy must fail loudly, not silently → Task 4 checks ss before starting and the target errors out.
  3. ArgoCD self-management dropping dev settings (after bootstrap, ArgoCD re-renders itself only from the ApplicationSet) → Task 9 asserts the live ApplicationSet still points to GitHub dev after ArgoCD has synced itself.
  4. Plain make (prod) path changed by accident → Task 10 renders the prod ArgoCD/apps values and diffs the generator against master.
  5. make dev-clean on a half-built sandbox (cluster missing, proxy missing) must not fail → Task 4 runs clean twice in a row.

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
File Responsibility flake.nix, flake.lock dev shell tools metal/kind-dev.yaml (new) kind cluster definition metal/k3d-dev.yaml (delete) replaced by the file above metal/Makefile env-dependent default; kind, proxy, clean targets metal/inventories/dev.yml (new) dev vars: API endpoint, LB pool; empty metal group metal/inventories/prod.yml, stag.yml add Cilium API endpoint vars metal/roles/cilium/defaults/main.yml version bump, API endpoint from vars metal/roles/cilium/templates/ciliumloadbalancerippool.yaml cilium.io/v2 system/ingress-nginx/{Chart.yaml,Chart.lock,values-dev.yaml} bump, dev LB IP system/cert-manager/{Chart.yaml,Chart.lock,values.yaml,values-dev.yaml,templates/clusterissuer.yaml} bump, dev CA issuer system/monitoring-system/{Chart.yaml,Chart.lock,values-dev.yaml} bump, dev overrides apps/excalidraw/{Chart.yaml,Chart.lock,values.yaml,values-dev.yaml} bump, schema fix, dev host system/argocd/{Chart.yaml,Chart.lock,values-dev.yaml} bump, dev ApplicationSet system/bootstrap.yml, system/Makefile env-aware bootstrap Makefile dev, dev-clean test/smoke_test.go, test/apps_test.go (new) env-aware app list CLAUDE.md (new), docs/installation/sandbox.md docs

Helper used by render checks in several tasks (run from repo root, inside the dev shell). Write it once in Task 5 as scripts/render-chart:

#!/bin/sh
# Render a wrapper chart the same way ArgoCD does: values.yaml, then values-<env>.yaml if it exists.
# Usage: scripts/render-chart <chart-dir> [env]
set -eu
dir="$1"
env="${2:-prod}"
name="$(basename "$dir")"
set -- -f "$dir/values.yaml"
[ "$env" != prod ] && [ -f "$dir/values-$env.yaml" ] && set -- "$@" -f "$dir/values-$env.yaml"
helm dependency build "$dir" >/dev/null
helm template "$name" "$dir" --namespace "$name" --include-crds "$@"

docs.title: Task 1: Dev shell on current stable tools
docs.text:
Files: - Modify: flake.nix - Modify: flake.lock

Interfaces: - Produces: kind, cilium-cli, helm, kubectl, ansible, yq on PATH in the dev shell.

  • Step 1: Show the current state fails the requirement

Run: nix develop -c sh -c 'kind version' Expected: FAIL, kind: command not found (the shell ships kube3d).

  • Step 2: Edit flake.nix

Replace the whole file with:

{
  description = "Homelab";

  inputs = {
    nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05";
    nixpkgs-unstable.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable";
    flake-utils.url = "github:numtide/flake-utils";
  };

  outputs = { self, nixpkgs, nixpkgs-unstable, flake-utils }:
    flake-utils.lib.eachDefaultSystem (system:
      let
        pkgs = import nixpkgs { inherit system; };
        # Only for tools whose stable release is newer than nixos-26.05 ships
        unstable = import nixpkgs-unstable { inherit system; };
      in
      with pkgs;
      {
        devShells.default = mkShell {
          packages = [
            ansible
            ansible-lint
            bmake
            diffutils
            docker
            docker-compose
            dyff
            git
            glibcLocales
            go
            gotestsum
            iproute2
            jq
            k9s
            kanidm_1_11
            kubectl
            kubernetes-helm
            kustomize
            libisoburn
            neovim
            openssh_gssapi
            opentofu # Drop-in replacement for Terraform
            p7zip
            pre-commit
            qrencode
            shellcheck
            unstable.cilium-cli
            unstable.kind
            wireguard-tools
            yamllint
            yq-go

            (python3.withPackages (p: with p; [
              jinja2
              kubernetes
              mkdocs-material
              netaddr
              pexpect
              rich
            ]))
          ];
        };
      }
    );
}
  • Step 3: Update the lock file

Run: nix flake update Expected: flake.lock now has nixpkgs on nixos-26.05 and a nixpkgs-unstable node.

  • Step 4: Verify tool versions

Run: nix develop -c sh -c 'kind version; cilium version --client | head -1; helm version --short; kubectl version --client | head -1; ansible --version | head -1' Expected: kind v0.32.0, cilium-cli: v0.19.7, v3.20.2, Client Version: v1.36.3, ansible [core 2.21.x].

If kind or cilium-cli in unstable has moved past the versions in Global Constraints, keep what unstable provides, but check that the kind release notes still list kindest/node:v1.36.x and update the node image digest in Task 2 to match.

  • Step 5: Commit
git add flake.nix flake.lock
git commit -m "build: move dev shell to nixos-26.05, replace k3d with kind

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>"

docs.title: Task 2: Preflight — WSL localhost forwarding and free ports
docs.text:
Throwaway probe; nothing is committed. It decides the proxy bind address used in Task 4.

Files: none

Interfaces: - Produces: PROXY_BIND decision, either 127.0.0.1 (default) or 0.0.0.0, recorded in Task 4.

  • Step 1: Ports 80 and 443 are free on the WSL host

Run: ss -ltnH '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )' Expected: empty output. If not empty, stop and report what is listening.

  • Step 2: Start a probe on 127.0.0.1:80 from a host-network container

Run: 

docker run -d --rm --name homelab-probe --network host alpine/socat:1.8.1.3 \
  TCP-LISTEN:80,bind=127.0.0.1,fork,reuseaddr SYSTEM:'printf "HTTP/1.0 200 OK

probe-ok
"'

  • Step 3: Reach it from Windows

Run: /mnt/c/Windows/System32/curl.exe -s --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1/ Expected: probe-ok

If it fails: docker rm -f homelab-probe, rerun Step 2 with bind=0.0.0.0, and repeat Step 3. If 0.0.0.0 works, use PROXY_BIND=0.0.0.0 in Task 4. If neither works, stop and report: Windows access needs a different approach (spec risk 1).

  • Step 4: Clean up

Run: docker rm -f homelab-probe

docs.title: Task 3: kind cluster on a fixed Docker network
docs.text:
Files: - Create: metal/kind-dev.yaml - Delete: metal/k3d-dev.yaml - Create: metal/inventories/dev.yml - Modify: metal/Makefile

Interfaces: - Produces: make -C metal env=dev kind creates network kind (172.30.0.0/16) and cluster homelab-dev and writes metal/kubeconfig.yaml. Node name homelab-dev-control-plane. Inventory inventories/dev.yml with vars cilium_k8s_service_host, cilium_k8s_service_port, load_balancer_ip_pool.

  • Step 1: Confirm the target does not exist yet

Run: make -C metal env=dev kind Expected: FAIL, No rule to make target 'kind'.

  • Step 2: Create metal/kind-dev.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: homelab-dev
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    image: kindest/node:v1.36.1@sha256:3489c7674813ba5d8b1a9977baea8a6e553784dab7b84759d1014dbd78f7ebd5
networking:
  # Cilium is the CNI and replaces kube-proxy, same as production
  disableDefaultCNI: true
  kubeProxyMode: none
kubeadmConfigPatches:
  # Expose control plane metrics so kube-prometheus-stack can scrape them
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    controllerManager:
      extraArgs:
        - name: bind-address
          value: 0.0.0.0
    scheduler:
      extraArgs:
        - name: bind-address
          value: 0.0.0.0
    etcd:
      local:
        extraArgs:
          - name: listen-metrics-urls
            value: http://0.0.0.0:2381
  • Step 3: Create metal/inventories/dev.yml
all:
  vars:
    cilium_k8s_service_host: homelab-dev-control-plane
    cilium_k8s_service_port: 6443
    load_balancer_ip_pool:
      - 172.30.255.200/29
# The kind node is not managed over SSH, so the metal plays have no hosts
metal:
  children:
    masters:
      hosts: {}
    workers:
      hosts: {}
  • Step 4: Rewrite metal/Makefile
.POSIX:

env ?= prod
export KUBECONFIG = $(shell pwd)/kubeconfig.yaml

kind_cluster = homelab-dev
kind_subnet = 172.30.0.0/16

default: ${env}

prod: boot cluster

dev: kind cluster

~/.ssh/id_ed25519:
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -P '' -f "$@"

boot: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    ansible-playbook \
        --inventory inventories/${env}.yml \
        boot.yml

cluster:
    ansible-playbook \
        --inventory inventories/${env}.yml \
        cluster.yml

console:
    ansible-console \
        --inventory inventories/${env}.yml

kind:
    docker network inspect kind >/dev/null 2>&1 \
        || docker network create --subnet ${kind_subnet} kind
    kind get clusters | grep -qx ${kind_cluster} \
        || kind create cluster --config kind-dev.yaml
    kind get kubeconfig --name ${kind_cluster} > kubeconfig.yaml
  • Step 5: Delete the k3d config

Run: git rm metal/k3d-dev.yaml

  • Step 6: Create the cluster

Run: make -C metal env=dev kind Expected: kind prints Creating cluster "homelab-dev" and finishes.

  • Step 7: Verify network, node and control-plane flags

Run: 

docker network inspect kind -f '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Subnet}}'
KUBECONFIG=metal/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl get nodes
docker exec homelab-dev-control-plane sh -c 'ps -eo args | grep -E "kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd " | grep -oE "(bind-address|listen-metrics-urls)=[^ ]+"'
Expected: 172.30.0.0/16; node homelab-dev-control-plane with status NotReady (no CNI yet); bind-address=0.0.0.0 twice and listen-metrics-urls=http://0.0.0.0:2381.

  • Step 8: Verify it is idempotent

Run: make -C metal env=dev kind Expected: succeeds and does not print Creating cluster.

  • Step 9: Commit
git add metal/kind-dev.yaml metal/inventories/dev.yml metal/Makefile
git commit -m "feat(metal): create dev sandbox with kind instead of k3d

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>"

docs.title: Task 4: Cilium 1.20 on kind, L2 LB IPs, localhost proxy, clean target
docs.text:
Files: - Modify: metal/roles/cilium/defaults/main.yml - Modify: metal/roles/cilium/templates/ciliumloadbalancerippool.yaml - Modify: metal/inventories/prod.yml, metal/inventories/stag.yml - Modify: metal/Makefile

Interfaces: - Consumes: Task 3 cluster and inventories/dev.yml; Task 2 PROXY_BIND. - Produces: make -C metal env=dev gives a Ready node with Cilium, LB IPAM serving 172.30.255.200/29, and container homelab-dev-proxy forwarding ${PROXY_BIND}:80/443 → 172.30.255.200. make -C metal env=dev clean removes cluster, proxy and network.

  • Step 1: Run the Cilium play and see it fail on kind

Run: make -C metal env=dev cluster Expected: the play runs Cilium 1.16.1 with k8sServiceHost: 127.0.0.1 / 6444; agents never become ready (kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium shows CrashLoopBackOff or Init after 3 minutes). Uninstall before continuing: KUBECONFIG=metal/kubeconfig.yaml helm -n kube-system uninstall cilium.

  • Step 2: Edit metal/roles/cilium/defaults/main.yml
cilium_repo_url: https://helm.cilium.io
cilium_version: 1.20.2
cilium_namespace: kube-system
cilium_values:
  operator:
    replicas: 1
  kubeProxyReplacement: true
  l2announcements:
    enabled: true
  k8sServiceHost: "{{ cilium_k8s_service_host }}"
  k8sServicePort: "{{ cilium_k8s_service_port }}"
  hubble:
    relay:
      enabled: true
    ui:
      enabled: true
  • Step 3: Move the k3s endpoint into the prod and stag inventories

In both metal/inventories/prod.yml and metal/inventories/stag.yml, under all: vars: (create the all: vars: block at the top of stag.yml, which has none), add:

    # k3s-specific API endpoint, generic solution is in progress
    # https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/19038
    cilium_k8s_service_host: 127.0.0.1
    cilium_k8s_service_port: 6444
  • Step 4: Switch the IP pool to the v2 API

metal/roles/cilium/templates/ciliumloadbalancerippool.yaml:

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  blocks:
    {% for cidr in load_balancer_ip_pool %}
    - cidr: {{ cidr }}
    {% endfor %}

ciliuml2announcementpolicy.yaml stays on cilium.io/v2alpha1 (still the only version in 1.20).

  • Step 5: Add proxy and clean targets to metal/Makefile

Change the dev line and append the targets. Use the PROXY_BIND from Task 2 (default 127.0.0.1):

dev: kind cluster proxy

proxy_name = homelab-dev-proxy
proxy_bind = 127.0.0.1
ingress_ip = 172.30.255.200

proxy:
    @if docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -qx ${proxy_name}; then exit 0; fi; \
    docker rm -f ${proxy_name} >/dev/null 2>&1; \
    if ss -ltnH '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )' | grep -q .; then \
        echo "ports 80/443 are already in use on this host:"; ss -ltnp '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )'; exit 1; \
    fi; \
    docker run -d --name ${proxy_name} --network host --restart unless-stopped \
        --entrypoint sh alpine/socat:1.8.1.3 -c '\
            socat TCP-LISTEN:80,bind=${proxy_bind},fork,reuseaddr TCP:${ingress_ip}:80 & \
            exec socat TCP-LISTEN:443,bind=${proxy_bind},fork,reuseaddr TCP:${ingress_ip}:443'

clean:
    docker rm -f ${proxy_name} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    kind delete cluster --name ${kind_cluster}

{{- if .Values.issuer.dev }}

kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:

---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: homelab-dev-ca

  isCA: true

docs.text:

  • Step 1: Create CLAUDE.md
# Homelab (fork of khuedoan/homelab)

This fork diverges from upstream. Selected upstream changes are still cherry-picked, so keep the `apps/<name>/{Chart.yaml,values.yaml}` layout.

## Roadmap

Each step changes one thing, with its own spec and plan in `docs/superpowers/`.

0. Workstation: NixOS-WSL (done, outside this repo)
1. Sandbox: 1a kind + Cilium foundation, 1b platform (external-secrets, kanidm, dex, Grafana, zot)
2. Replace ingress-nginx and `Ingress` objects with Gateway API (Cilium Gateway), tested in the sandbox
3. Production: kubeadm instead of k3s, Ubuntu LTS instead of Fedora (rewrite `metal/`)

## Rules

- Use the current stable release of every tool and chart, pinned exactly. The versions in this repo are not a reference; check upstream when touching something.
- Branch `dev` is the integration branch: changes land there, are tested in the sandbox, then merged into `master`.
- Sandbox config lives next to production config and is selected with `env=dev`. Never fork config into a separate branch or directory.

## Sandbox

- `make dev` builds it, `make dev-clean` removes it. Pages: `https://<app>.127-0-0-1.nip.io`.
- ArgoCD in the sandbox syncs from `github.com/duongle-steven/homelab` branch `dev`; push to see changes.
- Components synced in the sandbox are listed in `system/argocd/values-dev.yaml`.
- A component that needs different settings in the sandbox gets a `values-dev.yaml` next to its `values.yaml`. It is loaded only in the sandbox.
- Fixed addresses: Docker network `kind` 172.30.0.0/16, LB pool 172.30.255.200/29, ingress 172.30.255.200.

# Development sandbox

The sandbox is a local kind cluster for testing changes on the `dev` branch before they are merged into `master`.

## Prerequisites

- Docker and Nix (see [development shell](../concepts/development-shell.md))
- About 12 GiB of RAM available to Docker (measured usage: <RAM from Task 11 Step 7>)
- Ports `80` and `443` free on the host

## Build

```sh
git switch dev
nix develop
make dev

make dev creates the kind cluster with Cilium, bootstraps ArgoCD, waits for it, and runs the smoke test.

docs.title: Sandbox Identity (1b) Implementation Plan
docs.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: The sandbox runs generated secrets (ESO), Kanidm managed by kaniop with three groups and four test accounts, and Dex in front of Kanidm. Go + chromedp tests prove that each test account logs in through Dex with the right groups claim and that an account in no group is refused.

Architecture: - Secrets. ESO Password generators in namespace global-secrets replace the Go Job; the existing ClusterSecretStore distributes them. - Identity. kaniop deploys Kanidm (Kanidm CR) and reconciles groups, persons and Dex's OAuth2 client from git. - Dex. Dex uses PKCE against Kanidm and trusts the dev CA through its own certificate's ca.crt. - Sandbox DNS. A CoreDNS rewrite, sandbox only, sends *.127-0-0-1.nip.io to ingress-nginx inside the cluster. - Tests. - Credentials: test accounts enrol a password and TOTP through Kanidm's credential-update API, using the reset token that kaniop publishes as an event. The credentials are kept in a Secret so reruns can log in again. - Login: chromedp drives the login and captures the authorization code from a Dex client named smoke.

Tech Stack: external-secrets chart 2.12.0, kaniop chart 0.18.0 (Kanidm 1.11.2), Dex chart 0.26.0 (Dex 2.46.0), Ansible (kubernetes.core), Go 1.26 + chromedp v0.21.0 + pquerna/otp v1.5.0, nixpkgs chromium.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-12-sandbox-identity-design.md

docs.title: Global Constraints
docs.text:
• Workflow:
  • Work on branch dev, and push to origin dev when a task says so (ArgoCD in the sandbox syncs from it).
  • One concern per commit. Commits end with Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>.
  • All commands run inside the dev shell (nix develop or direnv in ~/homelab). export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/metal/kubeconfig.yaml for kubectl.
  • Chart.lock is gitignored; never commit it.
  • Versions: current stable releases, pinned exactly (verified 2026-10-12): external-secrets 2.12.0, kaniop 0.18.0, Kanidm image docker.io/kanidm/server:1.11.2, Dex chart 0.26.0, chromedp v0.21.0, pquerna/otp v1.5.0.
  • Helm values: Helm replaces lists and cannot delete keys across values files; dev overrides restate whole lists.
  • Names:
  • Groups: homelab-admins, homelab-editors, homelab-users.
  • Test accounts: dev-admin, dev-editor, dev-viewer, dev-outsider, with mail <name>@example.com.
  • Kanidm CR kanidm in namespace kanidm; admin Secret kanidm-admin-passwords.
  • Dex OAuth2 client dex in namespace dex; its Secret dex-kanidm-oauth2-credentials gets aliases KANIDM_CLIENT_ID and KANIDM_CLIENT_SECRET.
  • Dex test client smoke with redirect https://smoke.127-0-0-1.nip.io/callback; its secret is dex.smoke (key client_secret) in namespace global-secrets.
  • Test credentials Secret identity-test-credentials in namespace kanidm.
  • Hosts (dev): auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io (Kanidm) and dex.127-0-0-1.nip.io (Dex). Production keeps the domains already in values.yaml.
  • Group membership: KanidmGroup.members replaces the whole membership. It is set only in dev; production groups never carry members, so people added by scripts/onboard-user are kept.
  • Make: make dev runs the smoke test with filter Smoke|Identity.

docs.title: Review Focus
docs.text:
1. Second make dev. Test accounts already have credentials, so kaniop publishes no new reset token, and the tests must log in with the stored credentials instead of failing. → Task 8, step "rerun".
  2. TOTP code reuse. Kanidm rejects a code from a 30 s step that was already used, for example enrolment followed at once by login. → Task 7, unit test TestIdentityTOTPWaitsForNextStep.
  3. Production group membership wiped. A prod render of KanidmGroup with members would remove every onboarded person. → Task 4 asserts that the prod render has no members.
  4. groups claim format. Kanidm may send SPNs (homelab-admins@auth…). The assertion must accept both forms, and the actual value is logged for 1c. → Task 7, unit test TestIdentityHasGroup.
  5. Dex starting before its Kanidm client Secret exists. Dex must converge without manual action. → Task 6 waits for Dex readiness after a cold sync and checks that the restarts settle.

{{- range concat .Values.secrets .Values.extraSecrets }}
---
apiVersion: generators.external-secrets.io/v1alpha1
kind: Password
metadata:
  name: {{ .name }}
  namespace: {{ $.Release.Namespace }}
spec:
  length: {{ .length | default 32 }}
  digits: 6
  symbols: {{ if .special }}6{{ else }}0{{ end }}
  allowRepeat: true
  noUpper: false
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: {{ .name }}
  namespace: {{ $.Release.Namespace }}
spec:
  # Generate once; regenerating would break consumers (see secrets-management docs)
  refreshInterval: "0"
  target:
    name: {{ .name }}

{{- end }}

docs.title: Task 3: CoreDNS rewrite for sandbox hostnames
docs.text:
Files: - Create: metal/roles/coredns_rewrite/tasks/main.yml - Modify: metal/cluster.yml, metal/inventories/dev.yml

Interfaces: - Produces: inside the sandbox, any *.127-0-0-1.nip.io name resolves to the ingress-nginx-controller ClusterIP.

  • Step 1: Failing check

Run: kubectl run dnstest --rm -i --restart=Never --image=docker.io/library/busybox:1.37 -- nslookup auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io 2>&1 | grep -A1 '^Name:'; kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc ingress-nginx-controller -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'; echo Expected: the answer is 127.0.0.1, not the ClusterIP printed on the last line.

  • Step 2: Create metal/roles/coredns_rewrite/tasks/main.yml
- name: Read the CoreDNS configuration
  kubernetes.core.k8s_info:
    kind: ConfigMap
    namespace: kube-system
    name: coredns
  register: coredns

- name: Add the rewrite rule
  vars:
    corefile: "{{ coredns.resources[0].data.Corefile }}"
  when: coredns_rewrite_rule not in corefile
  kubernetes.core.k8s:
    state: patched
    kind: ConfigMap
    namespace: kube-system
    name: coredns
    definition:
      data:
        Corefile: "{{ corefile | replace('    ready\n', '    ready\n    ' ~ coredns_rewrite_rule ~ '\n') }}"
  register: corefile_patch

- name: Restart CoreDNS to apply the rule now
  when: corefile_patch is changed
  kubernetes.core.k8s:
    state: patched
    kind: Deployment
    namespace: kube-system
    name: coredns
    definition:
      spec:
        template:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              homelab/corefile-patched: "{{ now(utc=true).isoformat() }}"
  • Step 3: Run the role from metal/cluster.yml only when the variable is set

Replace the second play with:

- name: Install Kubernetes addons
  hosts: localhost
  roles:
    - cilium
    - role: coredns_rewrite
      when: coredns_rewrite_rule is defined
  • Step 4: Set the rule in metal/inventories/dev.yml

Under all: vars: add:

    # Pods would otherwise resolve sandbox hostnames to their own loopback
    coredns_rewrite_rule: 'rewrite name regex (.*)\.127-0-0-1\.nip\.io ingress-nginx-controller.ingress-nginx.svc.cluster.local answer auto'
  • Step 5: Apply and verify

Run: 

make -C metal env=dev cluster
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy/coredns --timeout=3m
kubectl run dnstest --rm -i --restart=Never --image=docker.io/library/busybox:1.37 -- nslookup auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io 2>&1 | grep -A1 '^Name:'
make -C metal env=dev cluster | grep -c 'Add the rewrite rule.*changed'
Expected: - the answer is the ingress-nginx ClusterIP - the second run reports 0 changes for the rewrite task, because the rule is already present

git commit -m "feat(metal): resolve sandbox hostnames to ingress-nginx inside the cluster

kubectl -n kanidm get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=dev-admin,reason=TokenCreated -o jsonpath='{.items[0].message}' | grep -o '/ui/reset?token=' 
kubectl -n kanidm get ingress -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,HOST:.spec.rules[0].host

docs.title: Task 5: onboard-user by group; remove the hacks
docs.text:
Files: - Modify: scripts/onboard-user, Makefile - Delete: scripts/hacks, scripts/kanidm-reset-password

Interfaces: - Consumes: kanidm-admin-passwords, groups homelab-* (Task 4). - Produces: scripts/onboard-user <username> <fullname> <mail> <admins|editors|users>.

  • Step 1: Failing check

Run: scripts/onboard-user probe "Probe User" probe@example.com users; echo "exit=$?" Expected: fails. The old script reads the ingress kanidm and adds the person to editor, which no longer exists.

  • Step 2: Replace scripts/onboard-user
#!/bin/sh
# Usage: scripts/onboard-user <username> <fullname> <mail> <admins|editors|users>

set -eu

username="${1}"
fullname="${2}"
mail="${3}"
group="${4}"

case "${group}" in
    admins|editors|users) ;;
    *) echo "group must be one of: admins, editors, users" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

export KUBECONFIG="${KUBECONFIG:-./metal/kubeconfig.yaml}"
host="$(kubectl get kanidm --namespace kanidm kanidm --output jsonpath='{.spec.domain}')"
url="https://${host}"

# The sandbox CA is not in the system trust store; certificates from Let's Encrypt have no ca.crt
ca_file="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "${ca_file}"' EXIT
kubectl get secret --namespace kanidm kanidm-tls --output jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > "${ca_file}"
if [ -s "${ca_file}" ]; then
    export KANIDM_CA_PATH="${ca_file}"
fi

echo "Log in as idm_admin with this password:"
kubectl get secret --namespace kanidm kanidm-admin-passwords --output jsonpath='{.data.IDM_ADMIN_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
echo

kanidm login --url "${url}" --name idm_admin
kanidm person create "${username}" "${fullname}" --url "${url}" --name idm_admin
kanidm person update "${username}" --url "${url}" --name idm_admin --mail "${mail}"
kanidm group add-members "homelab-${group}" "${username}" --url "${url}" --name idm_admin
kanidm person credential create-reset-token "${username}" --url "${url}" --name idm_admin
  • Step 3: Remove the hacks and post-install

Run: git rm -q scripts/hacks scripts/kanidm-reset-password

In Makefile: - change default: metal system external smoke-test post-install clean to default: metal system external smoke-test clean - delete the post-install: target and its recipe line

  • Step 4: Verify against the sandbox, then remove the probe user

kanidm login reads the password from a terminal, so run it under script:

pw=$(kubectl -n kanidm get secret kanidm-admin-passwords -o jsonpath='{.data.IDM_ADMIN_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d)
printf '%s\n' "$pw" | script -qec 'scripts/onboard-user probe "Probe User" probe@example.com users' /dev/null | tail -5
printf '%s\n' "$pw" | script -qec 'sh -c "export KANIDM_CA_PATH=\$(mktemp); kubectl -n kanidm get secret kanidm-tls -o jsonpath={.data.ca\\.crt} | base64 -d > \$KANIDM_CA_PATH; kanidm login --url https://auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io --name idm_admin && kanidm group list-members homelab-users --url https://auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io --name idm_admin && kanidm person delete probe --url https://auth.127-0-0-1.nip.io --name idm_admin"' /dev/null | tail -4
grep -n 'post-install\|hacks' Makefile; echo "makefile-checked"
Expected: - the first command ends with a reset link (…/ui/reset?token=…) - the member list contains probe (next to dev-viewer), and the delete succeeds - makefile-checked with no matches above it

If the CLI cannot read the password through script, record a ruling and verify interactively, with the user, in Task 8.

The kaniop operator now owns groups, OAuth2 clients and admin credentials.
