After a leak: new repositories (new password, new prefix) while the old ones age out, by hand — — renovate.github-app-key Renovate's initContainer overlap: a GitHub App holds several private keys; generating one is manual (no API): lab stops and gives the steps, then deletes the old key n/a command only forgejo-db (CloudNativePG's forgejo-db-app) Forgejo CloudNativePG's way: write the new password (and the keys derived from it: uri, fqdn-uri, jdbc-uri, fqdn-jdbc-uri, pgpass) into forgejo-db-app; the instance manager applies it to the role; restart Forgejo right after (it reads the password at start; its open connections bridge the gap) 1 (2 at worst: a request fails while a new connection is refused) command only telegram.bot-token (new, decision 7) Alertmanager (bot_token_file, read at every notification) BotFather's /revoke (manual, no overlap), then the new token in OpenBao; no Alertmanager restart 1 (Alertmanager retries; ntfy still delivers) command only openbao.unseal-key, wireguard.private-key — never: the first holds all of OpenBao's data, the second is in every peer — — state.passphrase OpenTofu scripts/rotate-state-passphrase (existing); lab points to it — command only Renovate's token, R2's state credentials, TLS certificates — already short-lived — automatic

docs.title: 4. Safety around every rotation
docs.text:
Before rotating, lab checks for a completed off-site backup from the last 24 hours. Without one it stops and offers lab backup push (a manual group) or waits for the daily run. --skip-backup-check=<reason> overrides this; the reason is recorded.

lab then checks each reader after the change: the ExternalSecret has refreshed, the workloads are ready, and the credential works (an authenticated request where one is cheap).

On a failure lab keeps what it can roll back. With an overlap it never revokes the old value, so the readers keep working. It reports the failure (decision 7).

Restarts are rolling (kubectl rollout restart), so an app with several replicas has no outage. An app with one replica on a ReadWriteOnce volume has a short one, and lab names those apps in its confirmation.

docs.title: 5. Scheduled rotation
docs.text:
• Only catalog entries marked with a period rotate on a schedule. The starting default is 90 days, at a quiet hour (03:00 in global.timezone).
  • In the cluster this runs as a CronJob. It runs lab secrets rotate --scheduled, which picks the entries that are due, with a service account and OpenBao role allowed only those entries' paths and restarts.
  • This needs lab as a container image. My call: built by GitHub Actions from master into ghcr.io/duongle-steven/homelab-lab, pinned by digest, bumped by Renovate. The builder may propose another source if this one fights the deploy path.
  • OpenTofu's entries (Cloudflare, R2) cannot rotate from inside the cluster, which holds no Cloudflare account credentials. Their due date is checked by make infra env=production: it warns when one is due, and lab secrets rotate <name> runs the -replace.
  • A scheduled run that finds Woodpecker busy waits for it, within a limit, then fails and alerts.

docs.title: 6. Record
docs.text: Each rotation records the secret, the time, the method, the result and the person or job. OpenBao keeps every value's versions; lab adds the record in a place it can read back, e.g. custom metadata on the OpenBao entry or an annotation, chosen by the builder. lab secrets list shows the last rotation. There is no metric per secret (amendment 2): the scheduled Job's own kube-state-metrics series raise the alerts.

docs.title: 7. Reporting: alerts through ntfy and Telegram
docs.text:
• A failed rotation raises an alert through Alertmanager like any other, e.g. SecretRotationFailed.
  • A rotation more than a margin past its due date raises SecretRotationOverdue.
  • A successful one is only logged and recorded; it sends no message.
  • Alertmanager gains a second receiver, Telegram (telegram_configs), next to ntfy for every alert, so the existing alerts (VeleroNoRecentBackup and the others) also reach people while ntfy is down.
  • The bot token and the chat id live in OpenBao, never in git (the chat id identifies a person), and the person writes them with the admin role, as docs/how-to-guides/alerts.md will say.
  • Alertmanager reads them as files (bot_token_file, chat_id_file, both read at every notification), mounted from an ExternalSecret like the ntfy token: no rendered Alertmanager config Secret.
  • Egress: monitoring-system on 443 to the internet (system/egress).
  • The sandbox renders the receiver but does not deliver to Telegram.
  • An external dead man's switch (healthchecks.io) for a cluster that is down entirely is not part of 11b. It stays in the ideas, which gain one line: pause the check before switching the homelab off on purpose (the healthchecks.io API), e.g. in a shutdown command.

docs.title: 8. Not in this step
docs.text:
• More replicas for the apps that need them: each app and step 12 (three nodes) decide that.
  • Detecting leaks: GitHub secret scanning and push protection, gitleaks, audit logs of OpenBao, Cloudflare and GitHub. Record this as an idea or a later step.
  • People's own passwords (Kanidm accounts) and their zot or Woodpecker personal tokens: people change their own.
  • Matrix's signing key (its federation identity), if production has one: catalogued as never, with the reason.

docs.title: 9. Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A rotation that leaves a reader on a revoked value without saying so.
  • A rotation that silently changes something people must re-enter, like the phone's ntfy credentials, on a schedule.
  • Secrets or the chat id in git, in logs, in command arguments or in test output.
  • A scheduled job with more rights than its due entries need.

docs.title: 10. Tests and the spike
docs.text:
• Task 1 was a spike on the sandbox, as 11a's was. It confirmed the methods the catalog marked spike:
  • Woodpecker's agent tokens;
  • SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS in paperless;
  • how to trigger kaniop's rotation once, and whether its readers restart cleanly;
  • CloudNativePG's password rotation;
  • the Tunnel's secret;
  • Kopia's password through Velero;
  • whether Alertmanager re-reads credentials_file, so no restart is needed.

It also confirmed that no secret is class 3. Its findings are in the catalog above and in the Amendments. - make dev gains TestSecretsRotation. For each method, on at least one secret, it proves: - the new value works; - with an overlap, both values work during the window; - the old value is refused afterwards; - the readers are ready again.

It also proves --all on the sandbox's entries, and that a failing rotation raises SecretRotationFailed. The sandbox has one replica per app, so outages there are expected and not asserted. - Unit tests in cli/ cover the catalog check, the ordering, the backup check, the idle wait and the failure reports. - OpenTofu's rotations, the GitHub App key and Telegram can only be planned or rendered in the sandbox. They join the "Before the first production deploy" list.

docs.title: Amendments
docs.text:
From Task 1's spike on the sandbox (2026-10-23; the evidence is in the plan's ledger, never values). Each changes the catalog above or a decision:

  1. OpenTofu's Cloudflare and R2 tokens are class 1, not an overlap. cloudflare_account_token has no in-place roll, so a new value is a -replace, and one apply destroys the old token before infra-secrets pushes the new one and the readers switch, create_before_destroy or not. The readers recover alone: cert-manager reads the token at each DNS01 solve and retries a failed challenge (a renewal starts weeks before expiry); external-dns reads it as an environment variable, so it restarts, and it retries on its next sync; Velero retries at its next schedule (never rotate at 02:00, its daily run). This comes from the provider's, cert-manager's and external-dns's source; no plan ran against production's state. It joins the production checklist: confirm at the first production rotation.
  2. No metric per secret. The spike amended decision 6: it has no per-secret Prometheus metric. Failures and overdue rotations come from the scheduled Job and CronJob through kube-state-metrics (a failed Job, a CronJob without a recent success), and lab secrets list shows each secret's last rotation and due date.
  3. Woodpecker's agent secret becomes per-agent tokens. Changing the shared WOODPECKER_AGENT_SECRET never revokes the old value: a system agent stores the secret it registered with as its own token, and the server accepts that token from any agent. On the sandbox the agent's stored token was an earlier value, and it still authenticated. So the server's shared secret is dropped (empty) and every agent gets its own token from the admin API, which gives an official overlap: a new token beside the old, then the old agent deleted. Agent pods that share one token share one agent, so each replica needs its own token. lab needs a Woodpecker admin token for this (the admin is Forgejo's site admin, WOODPECKER_ADMIN): the catalog's new woodpecker.admin-token. A running step pod carries the label woodpecker-ci.org/step. woodpecker.agent's work (per-agent tokens, the emptied shared secret) moves to the plan's Task 8 (controller ruling).
  4. paperless's secret key has no fallback. paperless 3.3 does not expose SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS, so a new key ends every session (class 2). The key also signs paperless's Celery messages and its classifier file: restart while no task is queued; the classifier is retrained by its hourly task.
  5. kaniop's client secrets rotate by annotation, not by period. kaniop.rs/force-secret-rotation on a KanidmOAuth2Client regenerates its secret once; deleting the Secret only writes the same value again. Only Argo CD reads the new secret live; Grafana failed every login (401 at the token exchange) until it restarted, and Actual Budget, paperless and Forgejo read it at start too. kaniop's secretRotation period restarts nobody, so it is not used: lab annotates, then restarts the readers.
  6. CloudNativePG's password is written into its own Secret. The instance manager applies a new password in forgejo-db-app to the role within seconds, but leaves the derived keys (uri, pgpass, ...) stale, so lab writes them all. Forgejo keeps its open connections, so a restart right after makes it class 1.
  7. Kopia's repository password is never rotated. Velero has one password for every repository and no change-password; Kopia's own change-password keeps the data keys, so it gains nothing against a leak. A leak is handled by new repositories while the old ones age out, by hand.
  8. The Tunnel's secret rotates in place. Replacing random_password.tunnel_secret updates the same Tunnel (Cloudflare's token refresh, same id and record); connected cloudflared keeps serving until it restarts. Class 2 with today's single replica, seamless with two. To confirm in production.
  9. Alertmanager needs no restart. It reads credentials_file, bot_token_file and chat_id_file at every notification; ESO's refresh and kubelet's volume sync carry a new value. A rotation changes OpenBao and forces the ExternalSecret's refresh: ESO puts back a hand edit of its Secret at once.
  10. ntfy's overlap is confirmed, with restarts. ntfy accepts two tokens for one user, and drops a token no longer listed from auth.db at its next start; each step of the overlap is an ntfy restart (NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS is an environment variable). ntfy.alerts-password has no runtime reader.

  11. No class 3 secret. None of the secrets the spike covered loses data or stays stuck after a failed rotation.

  12. The final review: the backup check accepts a completed scheduled run started in the last 30 hours, not 24: the 03:00 rotation starts an hour after the 02:00 daily backup, which may still be copying to R2, so yesterday's run must count.

  13. The user's decision after the final review: Forgejo's deploy and argocd tokens rotate from the workstation (catalog workstation: true, named by make infra env=production when due), not the CronJob: their method needs Forgejo's admin password, which reaches ops/homelab and so the cluster. OpenBao's role rotator loses that password and both tokens' paths, and the CronJob its access to namespace argocd.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text: The catalog's format, the record's location, the CronJob's namespace and RBAC, the overdue margin, and the order --all uses. Pick sensible defaults and state them in the plan.

docs.title: Step 11c: what a sudden power cut does to the sandbox
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-25; spike run and decisions taken the same day. Branch: feat/power-cut from dev (after step 11b's PR #54).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Find out what a sudden power cut does, rather than require that the cluster survives one. The answers decide what to fix, what to accept and document, and whether a UPS (step 12) is needed:

  • does the cluster come back by itself, and how long does it take;
  • what is left stuck, and what a person must do;
  • what data is lost.

A power cut is a disaster, rarer than a planned shutdown. Losing what was in flight at the cut is acceptable; what matters is getting back to a working state with as little loss as possible.

TestNodeRestart already proves a graceful restart (docker restart). This step looks at the hard case on the one-node sandbox. The multi-node case (etcd's quorum, Ceph, CloudNativePG's failover, kube-vip, real disks) is step 12's, in staging and on the hardware.

docs.title: How (the user's decisions, in chat)
docs.text:
1. A spike first, on the sandbox, without a fixed test. Cut the power (docker kill of the k3d node's container: SIGKILL, no flush, no graceful stop), start it again, and watch. One cut per run; no second cut during the recovery.
  2. Situations, one cut each:
  3. idle;
  4. while writing (a loop creating Forgejo issues, ntfy messages, OpenBao secrets, Kanidm people);
  5. while an off-site backup runs (Velero's data mover copying);
  6. while a secret's rotation runs (lab secrets rotate, cut between its phases).
  7. For each, record: whether it recovered by itself and how long it took (the restartBlockers checks of TestNodeRestart: ztunnel Ready, pods running and redirected, apps answering as before, every Application Synced and Healthy); what stayed stuck and what was done by hand; which data written before the cut is missing (separating what was acknowledged seconds before the cut from what settled long before).
  8. Report to the user, item by item, with a proposal: fix (code, with a test), accept (documented), or a reason for a UPS. The user decides each.
  9. Then act on the decisions: the fixes with tests (e.g. lab secrets force-unlock <name> <holder>, like tofu force-unlock LOCK_ID, only if a rotation's lock left by a killed run turns out to need it); a fixed TestNodePowerCut (alone, after TestNodeRestart) only for what the user decides must hold; the UPS conclusion in step 12's roadmap line.

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• A second cut during the recovery.
  • Several nodes, Ceph, etcd's quorum, CloudNativePG's failover, kube-vip, the order network gear comes back, real disks without power-loss protection: step 12.
  • An ordered shutdown command and the UPS itself: step 12.

docs.title: Record
docs.text: Findings go in the plan's ledger as the spike runs, then into an "## Findings" section of this spec with the user's decision for each, before any code.

docs.title: Findings (spike, 2026-10-25, the sandbox built from step 11b)
docs.text:
Four cuts (docker kill, then docker start), one situation each:

Cut Recovered by itself Time What stayed Idle yes ~330 s nothing While writing (Forgejo issues on PostgreSQL, ntfy messages on SQLite, ~3 acknowledged writes a second) yes ~313 s nothing lost: Forgejo 80/80, ntfy 65/65, the last acknowledged about 4 s before the cut While an off-site backup ran (data movers in flight) yes ~331 s Velero marked the backup Failed and its DataUploads Canceled; a new backup completed; prune deleted the failed one once a newer one completed; a VolumeSnapshot Velero made for the failed backup stayed, owned by nothing While a rotation ran (ntfy.alerts-token, cut after its switch began) yes ~325 s the workstation's run failed ("apiserver not ready") and its lock release failed silently, so the Lease held for its full duration, 2100 s (35 minutes); then the rerun resumed from the recorded phase and finished, with no third value

Measurement: right after the restart the API server still reports the pods' states from before the cut, so Argo CD's Healthy alone is a false recovery. Recovery is the node Ready after the cut, no pod Unknown or not ready, and the apps answering through the Gateway.

docs.title: Decisions (the user's, after the findings)
docs.text:
1. Accepted: the cluster comes back by itself in about five and a half minutes, and acknowledged writes survive.
  2. Fixed: orphaned snapshots. prune also deletes the VolumeSnapshots Velero labelled with a backup that no longer exists, with a test.
  3. Fixed: a dead run's rotation lock. lab secrets force-unlock <name> <holder> (like tofu force-unlock LOCK_ID: the holder the "being rotated by" error prints; it asks first, --yes skips), and the lock's release retries while the API server comes back, so a run that survives the cut usually frees its own lock. Both with tests.
  4. A fixed test, TestNodePowerCut: alone after TestNodeRestart, one cut while idle, recovery measured as above within 20 minutes, and data written before the cut read back (a Forgejo issue, an ntfy message, an OpenBao secret).
  5. The UPS: on one node a power cut breaks nothing that matters once 2 and 3 are fixed, so a UPS is not needed for correctness; it would save the five-minute outage and spare real disks. The decision waits for step 12's staging cut of all three VMs (etcd's quorum, Ceph, CloudNativePG's failover), recorded in step 12's roadmap line.

docs.title: Step 15a: detection in the basic checks
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-27. Branch: feat/detection from dev. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat. The rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A pull request that adds a secret, an image with a fixable critical CVE, or a risky OpenTofu or Dockerfile setting fails its basic checks, before anything reaches dev.

docs.title: Scope against step 15b (user)
docs.text:
Kubernetes manifests (privileged, root, securityContext, RBAC) are 15b's: Kyverno's policies, also run in CI with the kyverno CLI on the renders. One rule set and one place for exceptions (PolicyException). So 15a does not run Trivy's Kubernetes checks. A spike counted 224 HIGH/CRITICAL findings on today's renders; that baseline is 15b's work.

15a covers what Kyverno cannot see: secrets in the diff, image CVEs, and OpenTofu and Dockerfile config.

docs.title: What exists (measured 2026-10-27)
docs.text:
• GitHub secret scanning and push protection are already on: the repository is public. Nothing to change in GitHub's settings.
  • gitleaks finds nothing in today's tree. Its 10 findings in the history are upstream's (2021–2022 values of khuedoan's homelab, variable references, test fixtures). Only the pull request's commits are scanned, so they do not matter.
  • Trivy finds nothing HIGH/CRITICAL in infra/. Four Dockerfiles run as root:
  • cli/Dockerfile: a false positive. distroless nonroot is already non-root, but has no USER line;
  • the root Dockerfile (upstream's docs image);
  • metal/'s dnsmasq and http images for PXE, where dnsmasq needs root.

docs.title: Design (Claude's calls)
docs.text:
1. Tools. Both come from the dev shell:
  2. gitleaks 8.30.1 from nixos-26.05, the latest;
  3. Trivy from unstable: 0.76.0. 0.76.1 is two days old and not packaged yet; note it next to the package.
  4. Three new checks in scripts/ci-check, each its own job in .github/workflows/checks.yaml's matrix. They feed the required checks.
  5. leaks: gitleaks git over the commits $BASE..HEAD, with the default rules. Any finding fails. .gitleaks.toml extends the defaults; an allowlist entry needs a reason, and none is expected now. Output is redacted.
  6. images:
    • Render each chart and app file the change touches, at the base and at HEAD (lab test charts lists them).
    • Collect the images (every image: in the renders) and scan only those new at HEAD with trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed. Any finding fails.
    • Images pinned by digest are scanned by digest.
    • .trivyignore.yaml lists accepted CVEs: each with the image, the reason and an expiry date at most 90 days away, so it is looked at again.
  7. iac: trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL over infra/ (OpenTofu), cli/, the root Dockerfile and metal/. These are small, so all of them are scanned every time, not only what changed.
    • cli/Dockerfile gains USER 65532:65532 (distroless' nonroot), which clears its finding.
    • The other three go in .trivyignore.yaml with their reasons: dnsmasq binds port 67; upstream's docs image is not deployed by this repository. The root Dockerfile's unpinned images go in deferred minors.
  8. Trivy's database in CI. Cached with actions/cache, keyed by day. Trivy reads it offline after the first download (--skip-db-update when the cache hit), so 11 parallel jobs do not each pull it, and GHCR's rate limit is not hit. Locally, Trivy's cache is in ~/.cache/trivy.
  9. Local runs. scripts/ci-check all runs the three like the rest. images pulls only the new images' layers, usually none or a few.
  10. Tests. Offline tests in test/ (TestCheckLeaks, TestCheckImages, TestCheckIaC) run the checks against fixture repositories or files. Each one shows:
  11. a planted fake secret fails leaks, and a clean diff passes;
  12. an image list diff picks only the new images, and a fake trivy that reports a finding fails images;
  13. a Dockerfile without USER fails iac, and the ignore file is honoured.

They are added to ci-check's offline_tests. The checks workflow proves the jobs on the pull request itself. 6. Docs. docs/how-to-guides/ci.md gains what each check does, how to handle a finding (rotate a leaked secret: lab secrets rotate; bump an image; add a reasoned, expiring ignore), and the ruleset note that checks covers the new jobs.

docs.title: Also recorded (user)
docs.text: CLAUDE.md, "Before the first production deploy": a scan found unencrypted production state under .state/production/cloudflare/ (terraform.tfstate and a .pre-r2 copy, git-ignored, holding Cloudflare tokens). Check that the state on R2 is complete, delete the local copies, and rotate the Cloudflare tokens they hold before the first deploy.

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• Kubernetes manifest policy (15b).
  • The Trivy Operator, SBOMs and signatures (15e).
  • Rewriting history (the upstream findings are not this repository's secrets).

docs.title: Step 14d: Kiali
docs.text: Status: designed 2026-10-27. Branch: feat/kiali from dev. The user asked to try Kiali in the cluster, before step 15, both to learn it and to see the mesh while steps 15b and 15c change policies. They left the design to Claude; every choice below not stated by the user is marked (Claude's call).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A Kiali that shows the mesh: which workloads talk to which, whether the Istio config is valid, and what the Gateways serve. It is reachable on the LAN Gateway, for admins only, read-only, in the sandbox too.

docs.title: What the user decided (in chat)
docs.text:
• Kiali before security (step 15). The order is recorded in CLAUDE.md's roadmap.
  • Read-only (view_only_mode), admins only, in the sandbox too.
  • The graph shows L4 only inside the mesh: in ambient mode without waypoints, ztunnel reports TCP metrics, not HTTP. Waypoints for L7 are not part of this step.

docs.title: Design (Claude's calls unless noted)
docs.text:
1. Chart. system/kiali, namespace kiali. It wraps kiali-server from https://kiali.org/helm-charts, version 2.33.0. That is the latest chart; Kiali's compatibility table tests Istio 1.31 with 2.31 and higher. The kiali-server chart is used, not the operator: one Deployment needs no CRD or operator. It is added to the root ApplicationSet in system/argocd/values-dev.yaml, so it runs in the sandbox, and to production's list.
  2. Sign-in. Kiali's openid strategy with a confidential KanidmOAuth2Client kiali in namespace kiali.
  3. Kiali 2.33 always sends PKCE, which Kanidm requires.
  4. Only homelab-admins gets a scope (scopeMap), so nobody else can sign in.
  5. Add kiali to oauth2ClientNamespaces. The client secret reaches Kiali from kaniop's Secret kiali-kanidm-oauth2-credentials. Kiali reads key oidc-secret from Secret kiali by default, so map it through the chart's own secret setting, or a small wrapper, whichever the chart supports.
  6. disable_rbac: true. k3s's API server has no OIDC, so Kiali cannot act as the user. Kiali's service account then needs read-only cluster access, the chart's viewer role.
  7. The sandbox trusts the dev CA as other Go apps do (SSL_CERT_DIR in values-dev.yaml).
  8. Read-only. deployment.view_only_mode: true. No write role is rendered.
  9. Route. HTTPRoute kiali.<baseDomain> on istio-system/gateway, the LAN Gateway only, never public.
  10. Data.
  11. Prometheus is monitoring-system's (prometheus-operated:9090).
  12. Tracing is off; Tempo is only an idea.
  13. The Grafana link uses grafana.<baseDomain> for the browser. Kiali needs no Grafana API access; turn off what calls it if the chart would.
  14. Istio's namespace is istio-system, and the root namespace is also istio-system.
  15. Istio metrics, new. Today nothing scrapes Istio, so Kiali's graph would be empty. system/istio-system gains scrape config for:
  16. ztunnel: TCP metrics between workloads (/stats/prometheus on 15020);
  17. istiod: control plane health and config pushes (15014);
  18. the Gateways' Envoy: L7 metrics for requests entering through gateway and public.

Each one gets whatever lets Prometheus reach it under deny-all. These metrics stay useful without Kiali, for Grafana. Keep the series count small where the charts allow, since the sandbox's Prometheus is small. 7. Mesh and network. - Namespace kiali joins the mesh like every managed namespace. - Its AuthorizationPolicy allow admits the Gateway on Kiali's port and Prometheus on its metrics. - monitoring-system's allow admits Kiali's service account for Prometheus queries. - Kiali also calls the API server and istiod (control plane status). Add whatever the renders cannot show to EXTRA in scripts/check-mesh-policies. - Egress: none to the internet. 8. Secrets catalog. The new Kanidm client's secret gets an entry in cli/internal/rotate/catalog.yaml, of kind kaniop-client like the other confidential clients, with Kiali as reader. 9. Backup. Kiali keeps no state and has no PVC. 10. Test. A sandbox test TestKiali, plus test/scopes.yaml entries for system/kiali/** and for the Istio scrape change. The test checks: - Kiali answers through the Gateway and redirects an anonymous visitor to Kanidm; - an admin signs in and Kiali's API answers (e.g. its namespaces and graph); - a non-admin cannot sign in; - Prometheus has ztunnel's TCP series, so the graph has data.

Use the existing SSO test helpers (Kanidm sign-in like `TestSSO*`).

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• Waypoints (L7 inside the mesh), tracing, Kiali's write features, multi-cluster.
  • Kiali through the Cloudflare Tunnel.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• The chart's exact keys for the secret mapping, the dev CA, and turning off Grafana calls.
  • PodMonitor versus ServiceMonitor, and the scrape intervals and relabelling.
  • Resources: requests sized for the sandbox.

docs.title: Step 15b: policy (Kyverno and Pod Security Admission)
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-27, after a spike. Branch: feat/policy from dev. Decisions marked (user) were agreed in chat. The rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Workloads that break the Pod Security Standards, run unpinned images, or pull from an unknown registry are refused. The refusal happens in the pull request (CI) and again at admission (the cluster). The few that must break a rule do so through a written exception with its reason.

docs.title: The spike (2026-10-27)
docs.text:
The official policies (kyverno-policies 3.9.2, Pod Security restricted, Audit) were applied with the kyverno CLI 1.19.2 to the workload renders of every chart and app file (36 files).

  • Baseline: 14 failures, all inherent.
  • istio-cni and ztunnel: capabilities, hostPath, AppArmor (the mesh);
  • tailscale and wireguard: NET_ADMIN (VPN routers);
  • node-exporter, kured and Alloy: host namespaces, hostPath, privileged (they read or reboot the node);
  • csi-hostpath (sandbox only): privileged, hostPath.
  • Restricted: 41 workloads, mostly missing declarations: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (40), seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (39), runAsNonRoot (33). Some images can only run as root.
  • Errors: woodpecker-agent's check failed with "no such overload" until user namespaces are allowed (podSecurityUserNamespaces; its step pods run with hostUsers: false).

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. (user) Kyverno 1.19.2 (chart 3.9.2) in system/kyverno, in the sandbox too, with three policy sets:
  2. the Pod Security Standards at restricted (the kyverno-policies chart 3.9.2, ValidatingPolicy);
  3. pinned images: a tag that is not latest, or a digest;
  4. allowed registries: the list of registries the renders use today, plus zot (registry.<domain>).
  5. (user) Two phases in step 15b.
  6. 15b-1 (this branch):
    • fix every violation that values can fix, by setting each workload's securityContext;
    • write a PolicyException for each inherent one, with its reason: the baseline list above, plus images that must run as root;
    • the policies run in Audit in the cluster, and block in CI: a new basic check policy runs kyverno apply with the policies and exceptions on the renders.
  7. 15b-2 (later): once the sandbox's PolicyReports show no failure, switch to Enforce.
  8. (user) Pod Security Admission as a second layer, in case Kyverno is down: every managed namespace gets pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline. A namespace with an inherent baseline exception gets privileged instead, through the same mechanism that labels namespaces for the mesh. kube-system is not managed.
  9. (Claude's call) Kyverno in the mesh. The API server calls its admission controller, so its pods carry istio.io/dataplane-mode: none, and its chart's NetworkPolicies, if any, let 15008 in. The webhooks are failurePolicy: Ignore while in Audit; Enforce in 15b-2 reconsiders that. Its CRDs follow the same SkipDryRun rules as the other operators, on a fresh cluster.
  10. (Claude's call) Exceptions live with the component they excuse: a templates/policy-exception.yaml in that chart, or a raw resource in its app file. Each names the policies and the workload, and carries a policies.kyverno.io/description-style reason. The policy check loads them with the policies.
  11. (Claude's call) The policy check (scripts/check-policy):
  12. render the policies (system/kyverno), the exceptions and the workloads of every chart and app file, both environments;
  13. keep workload kinds only, since the CLI's fake cluster refuses duplicate names of other kinds;
  14. fail on any fail or error result.

Policies change rarely and a full run takes about a minute, so everything is checked, not only what the change touches. The kyverno CLI comes from unstable (1.19.2); nixos-26.05 ships 1.18.2. 7. (Claude's call) Tests. - Offline TestCheckPolicy: a fixture workload without securityContext fails the check, and one with it passes. - A sandbox test TestPolicy: Kyverno is up, a PolicyReport for a workload exists, and a pod that breaks restricted is reported (Audit) but still admitted. PSA's baseline refuses a privileged pod in a namespace labelled baseline.

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• Enforce mode (15b-2), image signatures (15e), and runtime detection (15g).
  • Kyverno's mutation or generation policies.

docs.title: Step 14e: optional apps in the sandbox
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-28. Branch: feat/sandbox-optional-apps from dev. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; the rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The sandbox shares 12 GB (WSL) with everything else. Since 14d, 15a and 15b (Kiali, Istio's metrics, Kyverno), its node used 8.9 of 11.7 GB under the suite. k3s twice lost its own leader lease and restarted mid-run (2026-10-27/28), so TestBackupRestore and the SSO tests failed for want of memory, not for a bug.

Paperless and OpenCloud take about 900 MB together. They are apps, they were tested many times, and most changes never touch them.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. (user) Paperless and OpenCloud are optional in the local sandbox. They are deployed only when wanted:
  2. automatically, when the branch changes their app file (apps/paperless.yaml, apps/opencloud.yaml): an upgrade or a large change is tested before production;
  3. on request, with make dev apps=paperless,opencloud (or apps=all), e.g. with make dev-fresh.
  4. (Claude's call) The release sandbox keeps everything. GitHub Actions' runner has more memory: sandbox-release and sandbox-retarget (dev → master) run with apps=all, so nothing reaches production untested.
  5. (user) Prometheus is slimmer in the sandbox: one day of retention (values-dev.yaml). It is the largest component there (1.5 GB), and the tests read only recent series.
  6. (Claude's call) How.
  7. system/argocd/values-dev.yaml lists only the always-on apps.
  8. infra/sandbox/argocd reads HOMELAB_SANDBOX_APPS (space-separated names) into the module's optional_apps. infra/_modules/argocd/set-sandbox-apps.sh, beside set-revision.sh, adds apps/<name>.yaml to the apps ApplicationSet's git generator. The bootstrap re-applies when the list changes.
  9. make dev computes the list: the optional_apps named in the Makefile whose file changed since the base, plus apps=. It prints the list.
  10. Removing an app from the list deletes its Application. Argo CD keeps a namespace it created (CreateNamespace=true), so make dev deletes the namespaces of the optional apps it left out, volumes included; that is fine in the sandbox. (review)
  11. The tests get the list (HOMELAB_SANDBOX_APPS): an app it names that is absent fails, never skips, so the release sandbox cannot go green without them. (review)
  12. (Claude's call) Tests follow what is deployed.
  13. TestSSOPaperless, TestSSOOpenCloud and the smoke list skip an app whose Application does not exist, and say so.
  14. lab secrets rotate --all --env sandbox skips an entry whose readers' namespaces do not exist, reported as "not deployed", instead of failing. Production is unchanged: a missing namespace there is hit, not skipped.
  15. The scheduled rotation already rotates no paperless entry (they have no period).
  16. (Claude's call) Docs: docs/installation/sandbox.md and docs/how-to-guides/sandbox-tests.md (optional apps, apps=), and CLAUDE.md's Sandbox section.

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• Making other components optional, and limits on other pods.
  • Production: unchanged.

docs.title: Step 15c: security logs
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-28. Branch: feat/security-logs from dev. Decisions marked (user) were agreed in chat. The rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Who did what to the cluster and to OpenBao is written down, kept, and searchable in Grafana. A few dangerous events that no metric can show raise an alert.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
(user) Most of the use is looking back: search the logs while debugging or checking what happened, the way one searches Splunk. Alerts are only for events that are dangerous and invisible to metrics. The user did not pick the alerts; they asked for what the community and enterprises usually do. They then accepted the list below as a start.

Today Loki holds pod logs and Kubernetes events. Nothing records API calls (who exec'd into a pod, who read a Secret, who changed a role binding) or OpenBao requests (who read which secret, who logged in as admin).

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. k3s's API audit log. (Claude's call, following GKE's audit policy and the Kubernetes documentation's example)
  2. One audit policy file in the repository, used by the sandbox (k3d) and by production's k3s config (today metal/roles/k3s; NixOS in step 12). Production is only rendered here, as with the rest of step 15.
  3. Levels:
    • None: read-only noise. This covers watch/list/get by the node, controllers and the scheduler; leases; endpoints and EndpointSlices; events; /healthz, /readyz, /livez, /metrics, /version.
    • Metadata (who, when, verb, object, response code; never the body): Secrets, ConfigMaps, TokenReviews, SubjectAccessReviews, ServiceAccount tokens, pods/exec, pods/attach, pods/portforward.
    • Request (the body sent): writes to RBAC (Roles, ClusterRoles and their bindings), PolicyExceptions and Kyverno policies, admission webhook configurations, namespaces and CRDs.
    • Metadata for everything else. Stage RequestReceived is omitted.
  4. No secret value ever reaches Loki (anti-goal): a Secret's body is never logged, and neither is a ServiceAccount token request's response.
  5. The API server writes a file on the node with size-based rotation (e.g. 100 MB, 3 files). The server's own rotation is enough; Loki is the long-term copy.
  6. Alloy reads that file on server nodes and sends it with the label job="audit/k3s".
  7. OpenBao's audit device. (Claude's call)
  8. A file device writing to stdout, declared in OpenBao's config. OpenBao 2.x forbids creating audit devices through the API unless told otherwise; check that config-declared devices work on 2.7.1, and fall back to an initialize stanza if they do not.
  9. Its lines reach Loki through the pod-log path that already exists. Alloy labels them job="audit/openbao", kept apart from the server's own log lines.
  10. OpenBao HMACs secret values in audit entries by default; that stays on.
  11. If every audit device fails, OpenBao refuses requests. stdout cannot fill up, so this is accepted.
  12. Retention.
  13. Audit streams are kept 90 days, other logs 30 days as today (the sandbox keeps 7 days for everything). This uses Loki's retention_stream. (Claude's call)
  14. The sandbox measures the daily volume. If 90 days would not fit in production's Loki PVC (10Gi), the period is shortened, not the PVC raised: 60 days first, then 45 or 30 if 60 still does not fit (user). The plan records the measurement and the period chosen.
  15. Search. (user: Splunk-like search)
  16. Grafana's Explore on the Loki data source.
  17. A dashboard "Security" with the common questions: exec/attach/port-forward by user, Secret reads by non-service-accounts, RBAC changes, 401/403 by source, OpenBao logins and reads by role and path.
  18. The how-to guide lists the LogQL queries.
  19. Alerts from logs. (user accepted this list as a start)
  20. Loki's ruler evaluates LogQL rules and sends to the existing Alertmanager, so alerts reach ntfy and Telegram like every other alert.
  21. "A person" means a user that is not a ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:…) and not a node or control-plane component (system:node:…, system:kube-…, system:apiserver). The k3s admin (system:admin) counts as a person.
  22. Expected actors are left out of every rule: Argo CD, ESO, the rotation CronJob, Velero, kaniop and Kyverno.
Alert Source Severity A person exec'd, attached or port-forwarded into a pod k3s warning A person read a Secret k3s warning A binding to cluster-admin was created or changed, except by Argo CD k3s critical An anonymous request (system:anonymous) succeeded k3s critical Many 401/403 responses from one source in 5 minutes k3s warning A PolicyException was created or changed, except by Argo CD k3s warning A root token was used, or root token generation started OpenBao critical Many failed logins in 5 minutes OpenBao warning A policy, an auth method or an audit device changed outside the known flows OpenBao critical No audit line from k3s, or from OpenBao, for 15 minutes Loki critical

The last row matters most: an audit trail that stops silently is worse than none. OpenBao is quiet (ESO refreshes hourly, the raft snapshot runs hourly, health probes are not audited), so its window is 2 hours, not 15 minutes; k3s's stays 15 minutes (Claude's call: a longer window rather than a heartbeat component).

"Known flows" in OpenBao (Claude's call): the roles rotator, writer and infra and the stores' read roles are expected, and only on the paths their policies allow. A person using the admin role is not excluded: changing a running OpenBao is rare and deliberate, and an alert for one's own change is accepted, like a sudo notice.

Tools that use the admin kubeconfig (the sandbox tests, lab, OpenTofu) also exec into pods and read Secrets as a person, so they raise the first two alerts. This is accepted (user): the alert names the user, and Alertmanager groups these two alerts by user so one run sends one notification, not one per call (Claude's call). No separate identity for tooling in this step.

Thresholds ("many") are the builder's to set from the sandbox's normal traffic. Each rule carries a summary that names the user, the object and the query to open in Grafana. 6. Tests. (Claude's call) A sandbox test, TestSecurityLogs: - kubectl exec into a pod. A matching audit/k3s line with that user appears in Loki, and the exec alert reaches Alertmanager. - Read a secret in OpenBao. A matching audit/openbao line appears, and the secret's value is not in it. - Loki holds no line containing a known generated secret value, from either source. - Each rule's LogQL is checked offline: it parses, and the ruler's ConfigMap renders.

The scopes map gets an entry for the new paths. 7. Mesh and egress. Loki's ruler calls Alertmanager inside the cluster, so monitoring-system's allow admits Loki. Nothing calls the internet. 8. Docs. - docs/how-to-guides/security-logs.md: where the logs are, the queries, what each alert means and what to do. - CLAUDE.md: 15c done, the Sandbox section's Loki line, and the "before production" items (the audit policy on the real nodes, the audit volume against the 10Gi PVC).

docs.title: Not in this step
docs.text:
• Runtime detection (Falco, Tetragon): step 15g.
  • Audit logs of Cloudflare, GitHub and Kanidm: listed under Ideas.
  • Restricting who may create a PolicyException: step 15b-2. This step only alerts on it.
  • Shipping logs off the cluster. Loki is in-cluster: an attacker with cluster-admin can delete what Loki holds. Accepted for a homelab; noted in the guide.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• How Loki loads the rules (the ruler's local storage from a ConfigMap) and the exact Alertmanager URL.
  • Where the audit policy file lives and how k3d mounts it into the node.
  • How Alloy tells OpenBao's audit lines from its server log lines (JSON with type request/response).
  • The thresholds, after watching the sandbox's normal traffic.

docs.title: Step 15e: supply chain
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-29. Branch: feat/supply-chain from dev. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat. The rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
What runs in the cluster is known and watched:

  • an image with a fixable critical CVE, or a secret baked into an image, raises an alert;
  • our own image (lab's) is signed by the workflow that built it, with its SBOM attached, and Kyverno checks that signature;
  • the GitHub Actions workflows that build and sign it are checked for known weaknesses on every pull request.

docs.title: What exists (measured 2026-10-29)
docs.text:
• 15a's images check scans only the images new in a pull request's renders. Nothing watches the images already running when a CVE is published later.
  • lab's image is built by .github/workflows/lab-image.yaml from master and pushed to ghcr.io/duongle-steven/homelab-lab:<sha>. platform/secrets-rotation/values.yaml pins its digest by hand. It is neither signed nor shipped with an SBOM.
  • The blog's image (registry.<domain>/blog:latest) has no pipeline yet.
  • Kyverno 1.19 runs in Audit; Enforce is 15b-2.
  • zizmor 1.31.1 (offline) finds 14 issues in .github/: 10 suppressed, 4 low, none medium or high.

docs.title: Scope (user)
docs.text:
• Trivy Operator scans only what nothing else covers.
  • It scans image vulnerabilities and exposed secrets in images.
  • Config audit is off: Kyverno covers it (15b).
  • RBAC assessment, infra assessment and cluster compliance are off: kube-bench and kubescape cover them (15d).
  • The blog's signature waits for its pipeline (Woodpecker, org ci, a later step). That pipeline signs with a key in OpenBao. This step only records it in CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: 1. Trivy Operator (system/trivy-operator)
docs.text:
Version and setup - The trivy-operator chart at its latest release, from Aqua's repository. - One namespace trivy-operator (the directory name, as every component), inside the mesh. Its scan Jobs are short pods; they get the mesh's defaults. - ClientServer mode with the built-in Trivy server: the vulnerability DB is downloaded once and kept on the server.

Scanners - vulnerabilityScannerEnabled and exposedSecretScannerEnabled are on. - configAuditScannerEnabled, rbacAssessmentScannerEnabled, infraAssessmentScannerEnabled, clusterComplianceEnabled and sbomGenerationEnabled are off. - Cluster SBOM reports would grow etcd, one CRD object per image. Our own image's SBOM is in step 2.

Severity (user: unfixed findings are reported too, since they cannot be patched and stay exploitable) - Every finding is reported, fixed or not (ignoreUnfixed: false), at HIGH,CRITICAL. - The "Security" dashboard shows them all. - An unfixed CVE cannot be fixed by a bump. It is handled by one of these: - what already limits exploitation: default-deny egress, mTLS and deny-all, Pod Security, and 15g later; - replacing the app or turning off the vulnerable feature; - an acceptance with a reason and an expiry.

Accepted findings - Accepted findings go in the operator's ignore policy in values.yaml. Each one carries a reason and an expiry, like 15a's .trivyignore.yaml. - An expired acceptance no longer applies, so the alert fires again. - The baseline is measured in the sandbox and reported in chat before it is accepted: - a fixable finding is fixed by bumping the image; - an unfixed CRITICAL is accepted with its reason, or its app is replaced.

Metrics and alerts - Prometheus scrapes the operator through a ServiceMonitor. - Three PrometheusRule alerts, all warning and for: 1h, labelled by namespace, workload and image: - ImageCriticalVulnerability fires when a running image has a CRITICAL finding with a fix. The fix is a bump. - ImageCriticalVulnerabilityUnfixed fires when a running image has a CRITICAL finding with no fix and no acceptance. The fix is a decision: accept it with a reason and an expiry, or replace the app. - ImageExposedSecret fires when a secret is found in a running image. - HIGH findings alert on nothing and show only on the dashboard: base images carry many, and alerting on them would bury the alerts that matter. - Both reach ntfy and Telegram like every alert.

Sandbox: 12GB, already tight once Kiali and Kyverno joined - One scan Job at a time (scanJobsConcurrentLimit: 1) with memory limits. - Images are pulled through the sandbox's pull-through caches (Trivy's registry mirrors), not from the internet again. - If the suite's memory still does not fit, the sandbox's scans are scheduled outside the suite. That decision is made in the plan's sandbox task, ledgered.

Network - Egress 443 for trivy-operator (the DB and registries) in system/egress/values.yaml. - An allow AuthorizationPolicy for its namespace. - homelab/backup: none on any claim. - Pod Security restricted, or a PolicyException with its reason. - An entry in test/scopes.yaml.

docs.title: 2. lab's image: signature and SBOM
docs.text:
lab-image.yaml after the push - Generate an SPDX SBOM with Syft, pinned. - Sign the image by digest with cosign, keyless: GitHub's OIDC token, Sigstore's Fulcio and Rekor. - Attest the SBOM to the image (cosign attest --type spdxjson). - Permissions gain id-token: write. No key is kept, so cli/internal/rotate/catalog.yaml gets no new secret. - Actions are pinned by digest, as today.

Kyverno policy, in system/kyverno, production only - An ImageValidatingPolicy matching ghcr.io/duongle-steven/homelab-lab*. - It requires: - a keyless signature from issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com; - subject https://github.com/duongle-steven/homelab/.github/workflows/lab-image.yaml@refs/heads/master; - the SPDX attestation from the same identity. - In Audit, like every policy until 15b-2. - Kyverno gets egress 443 to ghcr.io and Sigstore's TUF and Rekor.

Sandbox - The sandbox runs lab's image built from the checkout, which is unsigned, so the production policy is not rendered there (values-dev.yaml). - TestSupplyChain proves Kyverno's verification path instead: - The test signs a small image in zot with a key pair it generates. - It creates its own Audit ImageValidatingPolicy for that image's repository, with that public key. - It runs a pod from the signed image, then one from an unsigned image in the same repository. Kyverno reads zot with the test's pull credentials (the policy's credentials). - It expects a pass report for the first and a fail report for the second. - The production policy is checked offline: it renders, with the identity fields above (TestLabImagePolicy). kyverno apply cannot check it offline, since verification fetches the image. - Its real verification against ghcr is listed under "Before the first production deploy". It needs the first signed release from master.

docs.title: 3. zizmor in the basic checks
docs.text:
• zizmor comes from the dev shell: unstable.zizmor 1.31.1, the latest.
  • A new check workflows in scripts/ci-check, and a job in checks.yaml's matrix that feeds the required checks.
  • It runs zizmor --offline .github/.
  • Any finding fails it. The 4 low findings today are fixed, or ignored in .github/zizmor.yml with a reason.
  • Online audits (they call GitHub's API) are not run: a token in the basic checks is not worth what they find here.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• TestTrivyOperatorRender (offline) checks:
  • only the two scanners are on;
  • ignoreUnfixed is false;
  • every ignore entry has a reason and an unexpired expiry;
  • the alerts' expressions use metrics the operator exports.
  • TestTrivyOperator (sandbox):
  • the operator is running;
  • a VulnerabilityReport appears for a known workload;
  • an image with a known fixable CRITICAL CVE, run in a test namespace, raises ImageCriticalVulnerability's expression in Prometheus;
  • after the suite, no other workload has an unaccepted CRITICAL finding, fixed or not.
  • TestSupplyChain (sandbox): the signed and unsigned pods, as in section 2.
  • TestLabImagePolicy (offline): the production policy with the identity above; the dev render has no policy.
  • The workflows check: a fixture workflow with a known finding (pull_request_target checking out the head) fails, and today's .github/ passes.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• The blog's pipeline and signature (later, with its repository).
  • Signing or verifying third-party images.
  • Enforce (15b-2).
  • Trivy's config, RBAC and compliance scans (15b and 15d).

docs.title: Step 12a: staging
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-10-31. Branch: feat/staging from dev. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; the rest are (Claude's call).

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The sandbox is k3s in Docker on one node (k3d). Production is k3s on NixOS on three nodes. What only exists with several real nodes has never run: etcd with three members, kube-vip moving the API and Service addresses, Ceph replicating across nodes, CloudNativePG's failover, a power cut of every node at once, and the NixOS nodes themselves (their install, their k3s configuration). Staging is three NixOS VMs in WSL, as close to production as the workstation allows (user), so a release that changes the infrastructure is proven there before production.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• One node definition for staging and production (user). Upstream nixos's layout replaces metal/ (Ansible, still written for Fedora): infra/_modules/metal (a NixOS flake: configuration.nix, disks.nix with disko, profiles k3s-server, kube-vip, network, rook-ceph, and the installer), a Terragrunt unit infra/<env>/metal with hosts.json, and lab cluster enroll and lab cluster kubeconfig ported from upstream. metal/, nix develop .#metal and make metal are removed in this step, not kept until 12b (user).
  • Installed the way production is: nixie (user). The VMs boot from the network (PXE), nixie serves its installer from the workstation, finds each machine by its MAC address and installs it with nixos-anywhere; then lab cluster enroll joins the nodes and lab cluster kubeconfig writes infra/staging/kubeconfig.yaml.
  • Three VMs of 3.5 GB each (user), measured as the work goes (user): memory is the constraint (the workstation has 16 GB, WSL 12 GB).
  • Ceph first, fewer apps (user): staging proves rook-ceph on three nodes; apps follow as far as memory allows ("the more apps the better if resources allow, fewer if not" (user)).
  • Staging stays installed and is upgraded in place (user), like the sandbox: make staging brings the running staging to the current commit, so a release is proven as production will take it (a running cluster with etcd, Ceph and CloudNativePG data moving to new NixOS, k3s, Istio and rook versions); make staging-fresh reinstalls the VMs with nixie from empty disks. Nodes are upgraded one at a time (drain, nixos-rebuild from the flake over SSH, wait for the node and Ceph to be healthy, uncordon): upstream has no such path, and production needs the same one, so it is part of infra/_modules/metal and make infra env=production too.
  • make staging upgrades staging to the current commit, runs the staging tests and marks the commit as proven; lab infra forgejo verify refuses a release touching infra/, nodes, k3s, kube-vip, Istio, storage or the deploy path without that mark, unless --skip-staging=<reason> (recorded) (the roadmap's 12a).
  • An ordered shutdown and a power cut of all three VMs, each measured (time to recover) and checked (data written before is intact), as the roadmap's step 12 describes: lab cluster shutdown / lab cluster startup, NUT's low-battery shutdown, and virsh destroy of every VM at once.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Real hardware, the UPS itself, BIOS settings, Wake-on-LAN on real machines: step 12b.
  • Step 15d (secrets encryption at rest checked, kube-bench, kubescape): it runs on staging after this step.
  • Reaching staging's pages from the Windows browser: the tests run in WSL. (Claude's call; a localhost proxy like the sandbox's can come later.)
  • Running staging in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A staging that differs from production where it matters: separate node definitions, another install method, k3d.
  • A staging that crashes WSL (memory, or C: filling up: memory/wsl-memory-limit): it runs only with the sandbox stopped and checks C:'s free space first.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• WSL has 12 GB and 3 GB of swap; the sandbox uses about 9 GB under its suite, so staging and the sandbox never run together: make staging refuses while the k3d cluster runs (and make dev while staging runs).
  • KVM works inside WSL (/dev/kvm, nested virtualisation).
  • nixie runs as root (ports 67/69/4011/80) and needs a DHCP server on the network it serves (it answers as a proxyDHCP).
  • C: keeps 30 GB free: staging's disks are sparse qcow2 files in WSL's virtual disk.
  • Latest stable pins everywhere (CLAUDE.md), so not upstream's pins as they are (Gateway API v1.6.3, not v1.4.0).

docs.title: Nodes (infra/_modules/metal)
docs.text:
Ported from upstream nixos (infra/_modules/metal/flake/), then adapted:

  • k3s keeps this repository's choices where they differ from upstream's: ServiceLB stays on and kube-vip serves only its class kube-vip.io/kube-vip-class (the Gateway's and WireGuard's addresses from config.json), the API server's audit policy and flags (step 15c: metal/roles/k3s/files/audit-policy.yaml moves into the module, and the k3d sandbox mounts it from there), --secrets-encryption, the control plane's metrics, the packaged Gateway API CRDs disabled and the latest installed through k3s's manifests, disable-helm-controller.
  • Each environment's infra/<env>/cluster/config.json keeps its current format and gains what the nodes need (upstream's init_host; the network is already there). infra/<env>/metal/hosts.json holds the machines (name, MAC, address, disk). Production's MAC addresses stay placeholders until 12b.
  • Upgrades: kured stays (cluster side); a node changes only through make infra / make staging, which rebuild it from the flake one node at a time (above) (user: in place); no unattended system.autoUpgrade (Claude's call).
  • zram swap on every node (Claude's call: it lets 3.5 GB nodes keep more in memory).

docs.title: Staging's VMs (infra/staging)
docs.text:
• Three VMs (homelab-1..3 or this repo's names), 3.5 GB, 2 vCPUs each (Claude's call), a system disk and the rook-data partition from disks.nix's layout (or a second disk: the plan picks what disko and rook need), on one bridge in WSL with fixed MAC addresses, booting from the network first.
  • libvirt manages them (user): a network with DHCP and NAT on the bridge, static leases by MAC, virsh destroy as the roadmap's power cut, created by an OpenTofu unit in infra/staging. The workstation's ~/nixos-config (outside the repository) gains virtualisation.libvirtd.enable and the user in group libvirtd; the exact change is shown to the user before it is made.
  • The sandbox's patterns where staging also needs them: a local CA for certificates, the k3d pull-through caches reused if the VMs can reach them, OpenTofu state local and encrypted like the sandbox's (.state/staging/).

docs.title: What runs on staging
docs.text:
• Production's values first; a values-staging.yaml only where staging must differ (local CA, Ceph's memory, replica counts that do not fit, the reduced app set). Ceph: osd_memory_target about 1 GB, one mgr.
  • If the core does not fit, in this order (user): drop apps (the core stays: k3s with etcd, Istio, Argo CD, cert-manager, ESO, OpenBao, rook-ceph); squeeze the core (Ceph's OSD toward 900 MB, Prometheus off); raise each VM to 3.75 GB with WSL at 12 GB; last, WSL to 13 GB. Three nodes stay (etcd's and Ceph's quorum and replicas) and so does Istio.
  • The app set grows by measurement, in this order (Claude's call): Argo CD, Istio, cert-manager, ESO and OpenBao, rook-ceph, Kanidm, Forgejo with CloudNativePG's three instances, Velero (an S3 stand-in like the sandbox's), then Prometheus with a short retention. Each addition is measured (each node's memory, idle and under the tests); one that does not fit is left out and written down.
  • Argo CD follows production's deploy path: the bootstrap, then ops/homelab on staging's Forgejo with the commit under test (lab infra forgejo sync|push), so the switch the sandbox cannot prove runs here.

docs.title: make staging and the mark
docs.text:
• make staging (main checkout only, like make dev): refuses while the sandbox runs or when C: has less than 30 GB free; applies infra/staging (VMs and nixie only when a VM is new or empty, enroll, the nodes' rolling upgrade, Argo CD); deploys the current commit; runs the staging tests; marks the commit. make staging-fresh destroys the VMs' disks first.
  • The mark must still hold for the release: the commit on master is a merge commit, not the one staging proved. (Claude's call, the plan decides the mechanism: a GitHub commit status staging on the proved commit, accepted by verify when the release's infrastructure paths equal the proved commit's.)

docs.title: Shutdown and power cut
docs.text:
• lab cluster shutdown: pause the external checks, suspend CronJobs, wait for running Jobs, Ceph noout, then the nodes; lab cluster startup undoes it and waits for etcd, Ceph and CloudNativePG to be healthy (roadmap step 12).
  • NUT through NixOS's power.ups: upsd on one node, upsmon on the others. Staging has no UPS: NUT's dummy-ups driver plays one and the test sets its low battery (Claude's call).
  • The tests: an ordered shutdown and startup, and virsh destroy of all three VMs at once then start, each measuring the recovery and checking data written before (Forgejo, OpenBao, a CloudNativePG write), like TestNodePowerCut does for one node.

docs.title: Order of work (Claude's call)
docs.text:
Three pull requests, like 6d or 15b:

  1. 12a-1 nodes: the metal module and flake, metal/ removed, staging's VMs, nixie, enroll, kubeconfig, the nodes' rolling upgrade, k3s on three nodes with kube-vip, rook-ceph; measured. The first task proves nixie on a WSL bridge.
  2. 12a-2 platform: what runs on staging, the deploy path through Forgejo, make staging, the mark and verify's check.
  3. 12a-3 power: lab cluster shutdown|startup, NUT, the shutdown and power-cut tests.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Node and network names and addresses, the libvirt network's range, VM disk sizes.
  • How lab cluster enroll/kubeconfig are ported (upstream's code, adapted to this cli/).
  • The test layout (staging tests beside the sandbox's in test/, selected by environment).
  • Docs: docs/installation/ (staging, production's install by nixie), CLAUDE.md's roadmap and the "before the first production deploy" list (what staging now proves).

docs.title: 2026 11 01 staging platform design
docs.text: Replaced by docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-02-testbed-design.md: this staging ran out of CPU on the workstation before the core was up.

docs.title: Step 12a-2: staging's platform, deploy path and release mark
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-01. Builds on 12a-1 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-31-staging-design.md, docs/installation/staging.md): three NixOS k3s VMs in WSL (3.5 GB, 2 vCPU each), kube-vip, rook-ceph with AES256K CephX keys, make staging, lab cluster enroll|kubeconfig|upgrade. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Staging exists to prove, before a release, what the one-node sandbox cannot: production's components on three nodes with Ceph, and production's deploy path. Ideally staging is production (user): the same components, the same values, the full suite. A workstation that cannot hold all of it runs less, and the reduction is a property of that machine, not of staging's design (user): someone with more memory, or real machines, empties the reduction and gets production's parity and the full test run, with no other change.

When it must shrink, it drops first what the sandbox already proves the same way, so no work is duplicated (user).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Argo CD, the platform and as many apps as the workstation holds, on staging, deployed the way production is.
  • Production's deploy path end to end: the bootstrap from the seed repository, Forgejo on staging, lab infra forgejo sync|push, Argo CD switching to ops/homelab (the switch the sandbox never proves).
  • make staging marks the commit it proved; lab infra forgejo verify refuses a release that changes anything staging runs without that mark.
  • Reuse the existing sandbox tests against staging where they apply; no second copy of a test.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Cloudflare: the Tunnel, cloudflared, external-dns, the public Gateway, ACME. Staging has a local CA like the sandbox. Renovate (production only).
  • The power work: lab cluster shutdown|startup, NUT, the power-cut tests (12a-3).
  • Running staging and the sandbox at once.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A staging that crashes WSL (memory, or C: below 30 GB free).
  • A gate that blocks a release over something staging does not run, or lets through a change to something it runs.
  • Staging-only copies of production config beyond what must differ (values-staging.yaml only where it must).

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text: Removed from the homelab (user), in its own small pull request before 12a-2: its app file, egress entry, volume group, catalog entries and docs. It can come back later.

docs.title: What runs on staging
docs.text:
The default is production's set. The reduction is one list of excluded components and apps (Claude's call: a list in system/argocd/values-staging.yaml that the root and apps ApplicationSets leave out, with a comment naming the machine it was sized for; a larger machine empties it in a pull request together with the VMs' size in infra/staging/vms).

What staging must run (the sandbox cannot prove it) (user agreed, "tạm thời vậy"):

  • rook-ceph, Istio on three nodes (the Gateway's VIP through kube-vip), Argo CD syncing from Forgejo
  • OpenBao, Kanidm, Forgejo with CloudNativePG's three instances (data on Ceph, failover)
  • Velero with real Ceph snapshots (an S3 stand-in like the sandbox's versitygw for the off-site copy)
  • Loki with Alloy reading the NixOS nodes' pod logs and audit file; Prometheus scraping the nodes and the control plane
  • cert-manager (local CA), ESO, Kyverno (every PolicyException needs its CRD), trust-manager

Dropped first when memory runs short (the sandbox proves them the same way): stateless apps (excalidraw, pairdrop, speedtest, homepage, blog), Kiali, ntfy; then the heavy apps (jellyfin, matrix, paperless, OpenCloud). Woodpecker's step pods in user namespaces on NixOS are unproven: it stays if it fits.

Cannot run on staging: cloudflared, external-dns, the public Gateway, Renovate.

If even the must-run set does not fit after the whole fallback order, 12a-2 still ships with what fits (user): whatever is left out (a whole component, or one switched off inside its values, such as Prometheus) goes in the exclusion list, so the gate knows staging did not prove it.

Memory, measured as each part joins (each node's memory and QEMU's in WSL, idle and under the tests); the fallback order is the 12a spec's (user): drop apps; squeeze the core (Ceph's OSD toward 900 MB, Prometheus off); 3.75 GB per VM with WSL at 12 GB; WSL at 13 GB last. Three nodes and Istio stay. An estimate (Claude's, unmeasured): the core platform adds about 1 GB per node, which brings QEMU near 3.3 GB per VM; expect the fallback to be needed.

docs.title: Values layers (user)
docs.text:
Every environment that is not production shares a layer, so staging gets the local CA and the tests' fixtures without copying them and without the sandbox's shrinks:

Environment Loads, in order production values.yaml staging values.yaml, values-local.yaml, values-staging.yaml (where it exists) sandbox values.yaml, values-local.yaml, values-dev.yaml
  • values-local.yaml: the local CA and its trust (homelab-dev-ca, trust-manager, SSL_CERT_DIR, global.devCA), the tests' fixtures (Kanidm's smoke client and dev-admin, Woodpecker's admin, the rotation CronJob on lab's image built from the checkout) and anything else both need.
  • values-dev.yaml: only what the one-node 12 GB sandbox shrinks or swaps (Prometheus's one day, Loki's 2Gi and 7 days, Kyverno's workers, versitygw, the CoreDNS rewrite of *.127-0-0-1.nip.io, the hostpath CSI).
  • values-staging.yaml: only where staging must differ (rook-ceph's memory today).
  • The split moves content out of the 17 values-dev.yaml files; scripts/env-values, scripts/render-chart and both ApplicationSets learn the layer. The sandbox's renders must be identical before and after (checked by rendering every component both ways).

docs.title: Deploy path
docs.text:
• infra/staging gains the units production has where staging needs them: openbao (the unseal key), secrets (OpenTofu's secrets for staging: no Cloudflare), argocd (the bootstrap: system/argocd with values-staging.yaml, the seed first, then ops/homelab once Argo CD's token reads it, as infra/_modules/argocd/choose-values.sh does). State stays local in .state/staging/, encrypted like the sandbox's.
  • make staging pushes the commit under test to staging's Forgejo with lab infra forgejo sync|push (staging as an environment, like the sandbox: a commit with HEAD's tree on top of what Forgejo holds), then waits for Argo CD.
  • Certificates from a local CA under the production issuer name, like the sandbox; domain 192-168-100-2.nip.io (infra/staging/cluster/config.json). The workstation trusts staging's CA for the tests as it does the sandbox's.

docs.title: The mark and the release gate
docs.text:
• make staging, when every staging test passed, marks the commit it proved: a GitHub commit status staging on that commit (12a spec, Claude's call).
  • The gate follows what staging runs (user). A release must carry the mark when it changes:
  • the infrastructure staging proves: the paths in infra/staging/release-paths.yaml (user: not in test/scopes.yaml, whose job is the sandbox's tests) (the node flake, infra/, k3s, kube-vip, Istio, storage, the deploy path);
  • any component or app staging deploys: production's set minus staging's exclusion list, derived, never listed by hand.

A change only to an app staging leaves out needs no mark: the dev → master pull request already runs it in a fresh sandbox. With an empty exclusion list every release needs the mark. - When: make staging runs on dev's head before a release (user). verify accepts a mark on an earlier commit whose gated paths equal the release's, so a docs merge into dev after the run needs no rerun (Claude's call). - What a change is compared against (Claude's call): the commit production runs, ops/homelab's master on Forgejo (read when verify runs; on a first install, with no Forgejo yet, everything counts as changed). The gated set comes from the proved commit's exclusion list: what staging actually ran. - Without the mark verify refuses, naming the gated paths that changed; --skip-staging=<reason> lets the release through and the reason is recorded where --break-glass's is. - A test checks every path in release-paths.yaml exists, so the list cannot go stale unnoticed.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• The existing suite runs against staging (ENV=staging) where a test applies there; a test that cannot (sandbox only: k3d, the hostpath CSI, the localhost proxy) skips with its reason. TestStaging* stay.
  • make staging runs TestStaging* plus the whole suite for what staging deployed, the destructive tests included (TestBackupRestore, TestNodeRestart, TestRotation, like the sandbox's scope=full) (user): about an hour more; a run that wrecks staging's state is recovered with make staging-fresh. The mark needs all of them green.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Everything the rules in CLAUDE.md say: pinned latest versions, config.json for environment settings, the secrets catalog (environments gains staging where an entry applies), the backup labels, PolicyExceptions, mesh policies.
  • Staging and the sandbox never run together (scripts/staging-guard); make staging from the main checkout only.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• How lab infra forgejo takes staging as an environment, and how the bootstrap's seed selection works there.
  • Which existing tests apply to staging and how they skip.
  • The exact mechanism of the commit status (who writes it, with which credential) and of the derived app set.
  • The measurement points and what to drop at each step, within the order above.
  • The pull request split: one, or platform then the gate.

docs.title: Step 12a-2: testbed, optional staging, and what a release must prove
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-02, approved by the user. It replaces docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-01-staging-platform-design.md, whose staging ran out of CPU on the workstation before the core was up (measurements below). Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
"Staging" named one thing that had to be like production and also fit inside WSL. It cannot be both. Three environments, each with one job (user):

Environment Runs on Proves Required sandbox k3d, one node, the workstation apps and the platform, accepting differences from production; the everyday dev and test environment yes testbed (staging in 12a-1) VMs, several nodes, the workstation what needs several nodes: nodes, their upgrades, etcd, the VIP, Ceph, and more as far as the machine allows one of these two (user); its size depends on the machine staging its own hardware, like production everything, as production runs it one of these two (user): whoever has the hardware turns it on

Someone with a staging needs no testbed: staging proves all of it on real machines, and nothing in the staging path depends on the testbed. A testbed stays useful to them only as a cheap place to break things (reinstalls, power cuts) (discussed 2026-11-02).

The repository should work for someone else by changing configuration (user): more resources run more in the sandbox and the testbed, and hardware adds a staging. This workstation has no staging, and nothing may assume it does or that a staging is local.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• testbed proves the multi-node path, and grows by measurement until the machine says stop.
  • Everything the sandbox and testbed share lives in values-local.yaml; a staging on hardware never loads it (user).
  • Argo CD reading ops/homelab on Forgejo, which happens at every release, is proven on the sandbox.
  • A release states what proved it: production's configuration names the environment, and lab infra forgejo verify checks that environment's mark and says plainly how far it goes.
  • Adding a staging later needs no change to the gate's code; it does need code to deploy it and write its mark, which its guide names (user).

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Building or testing a staging now: nobody here has the hardware. Its path is documented and marked unproven (user: optional; Claude's call: no test suite for it yet).
  • The whole switch of a cluster from the seed to Forgejo in any test: it happens once in a cluster's life, and a failure leaves the apps running and is fixed by running the bootstrap again. It stays on the before-production list with Forgejo on Ceph (discussed 2026-11-02).
  • Making the whole repository portable (see Portability).
  • The power work (12a-3), which runs on the testbed afterwards.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A testbed that crashes WSL or makes the workstation unusable while it runs.
  • A verify message that lets someone think the testbed proved what only production-like hardware can.
  • Calling anything "like production" that is not.

docs.title: The testbed
docs.text:
• infra/staging becomes infra/testbed, with its targets, scripts, tests and GitHub branch: make testbed, testbed-fresh, testbed-clean, testbed-stop, scripts/testbed-*, TestTestbed*, ENV=testbed, values-testbed.yaml (user: a better name than sandbox 2; the name is Claude's).
  • Three VMs on the workstation: 3.5 GB each, 2 vCPUs (discussed: the i5-12500H has 4 P-cores and 8 E-cores, so 16 threads overstate it; 12a-1's 2 vCPUs ran the nodes and rook-ceph). Memory and vCPUs are configuration; raising vCPUs needs a measurement showing CPU is the limit.
  • WSL at 13 GB with 4 GB of swap, as the workstation is now (user).
  • Keeps what the runs measured it needs: one install at a time, the installer reclaiming cache, raw disks with cache=unsafe, slow_control_plane (etcd heartbeat 500 ms, election 5 s, controller leases 60 s), scripts/testbed-trust waiting for SSH, make testbed-clean not asking the cluster, kernel 7.3 and AES256K keys.
  • No image cache (user: few deploys, and closer to a real deploy): nodes pull from the registries. Add one only if a measurement shows pulls dominate.
  • Argo CD deploys it (user), syncing GitHub branch testbed, which make testbed force-pushes, as the sandbox does. There is no Forgejo and no seed switch, so the testbed's seed machinery goes (seeded, seed_environment, seed_revision, set-seed.sh); the fix for a cluster without Argo CD's CRDs stays, since production's first install needs it. make testbed no longer applies rook-ceph by hand.

docs.title: What runs, by layer
docs.text:
Each layer must be stable and measured before the next joins (the spec's rule the last run broke by starting with almost everything). A layer passes from a fresh install with every listed layer syncing (user), since that is how a testbed is really rebuilt: each measurement is one make testbed-fresh plus the soak below. Sync ordering is added only if a measurement needs it:

Layer Adds Proves 1 Argo CD, rook-ceph Ceph on three nodes through Argo CD; the base measurement, at 2 vCPUs 2 Istio with what it needs (cert-manager, and the CRDs of Kyverno and the monitoring operator, as little of them as works) the ambient mesh and the Gateway's VIP on several nodes 3 CloudNativePG's three instances, failing over what only production otherwise runs
  • Stable means, over 30 minutes after the last Application is healthy: no k3s restart, no etcd leader change, no API server or lease error (leaderelection lost, request timed out, deadline exceeded), and WSL with at least 2 GB available (user, 2026-11-03). leader failed to send out heartbeat warnings are counted and recorded, not failed: layer 1 logged two (2.3 s and 35 ms over) with no leader change and no error, and the first followed a sign of the VM being stalled from outside. A delay close to the 5 s election timeout stops the run to ask.
  • The list stops where the machine stops (user: fit what fits), recorded with its numbers in docs/installation/testbed.md. Another machine extends the list in system/argocd/values-testbed.yaml, up to everything.
  • A vCPU ceiling of 4 per VM (user): a layer that fails at that stops the list at the layer before it, which is not a failure of 12a-2: the branch ships with the layers that fit.
  • Layer 1 is the floor (user): a testbed without Ceph through Argo CD has lost its purpose. If it fails the bar at 4 vCPUs, the work stops and asks; the bar is not relaxed and an empty branch does not ship.
  • "Up to everything" is a direction, not a promise (user): components past these layers need more than the list (OpenBao and its units, Forgejo, tests generalised for them). What is cheap and tested stays (the ENV helpers); the units and values for components the testbed does not deploy go. docs/installation/testbed.md says so.
  • The testbed runs on a workstation, not in GitHub Actions (user).

docs.title: Measured, 2026-11-01 (why it is built this way)
docs.text:
• Three parallel installs ran WSL out of memory; one at a time, WSL stayed above 5 GB.
  • At 2 vCPUs with qcow2: etcd fsync averaged 27 ms, up to a second, a node reached a load of 31, and k3s exited.
  • Raw and cache=unsafe brought fsync to 3–10 ms. The heartbeat and lease settings took k3s from 12 restarts in 35 minutes to 2 in 30.
  • With most of the platform, at 4 vCPUs and WSL at 13 GB: about 1% CPU idle on every node, repo-server restarting on its 1 s probe, rook-ceph unrendered after 48 minutes. Memory inside the guests was not the limit by then.
