  • Top processes: k3s-server about 1 GB on each node, the Argo CD controller up to 1 GB.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
Environment Loads, in order production, staging values.yaml, then values-staging.yaml for a staging where it exists testbed values.yaml, values-local.yaml, values-testbed.yaml sandbox values.yaml, values-local.yaml, values-dev.yaml

values-local.yaml means "runs on the workstation": the local CA and its trust, the tests' fixtures, the S3 stand-in, no Telegram or Cloudflare, and the limits on Kyverno and the Trivy Operator (user). Comments that say "staging and the sandbox" change accordingly. A file that holds only what one environment needs stays in that environment's file.

docs.title: The deploy path, on the sandbox
docs.text:
• A test pushes to the sandbox's Forgejo (lab infra forgejo sync|push), creates a temporary Application reading ops/homelab at Forgejo's in-cluster address with the argocd user's read-only token, checks that it syncs, then removes it (discussed 2026-11-02: this happens at every release; the whole switch does not).
  • The allow from Argo CD's repo server to Forgejo, production-only and only rendered until now, is enabled in the sandbox so the test proves it.
  • It runs when the deploy path changes and in fresh runs (test/scopes.yaml), not at every make dev.
  • lab infra forgejo --env needs no testbed: what 12a-2 added for --env staging goes (user), since it assumes the local CA.

docs.title: What a release must prove
docs.text:
• Production's infra/production/cluster/config.json names the proving environment: "release_proof": "testbed" or "staging" (Claude's call, approved in outline). The key is required: without it verify refuses and says to set it, so a release never goes unproven by omission (Claude's call). A commit status named after that environment is its mark, written when its run passes.
  • testbed: the mark is needed when a release changes infra/testbed/release-paths.yaml's paths or a component the testbed runs, derived from values-testbed.yaml as already built. verify always says: only the testbed proved this, and no production-like environment did.
  • staging: the same gate reads infra/staging/release-paths.yaml and values-staging.yaml, and with an empty exclusion list every release needs the mark. Unit-tested, never run.
  • A component switched off inside its chart counts as not run: release-paths.yaml gains a not_run list that GatedPaths subtracts (the gap left open in the last run).
  • --skip-staging becomes --skip-proof=<reason>, needing a reason and recording it as the release's status.
  • What the mark needs: every test of make testbed, which are TestTestbed* and the existing tests for the layers it runs (replaces "the whole suite with the destructive tests", which assumed a staging running the platform).

docs.title: Adding a staging
docs.text: docs/installation/staging.md becomes that guide: hardware in infra/staging/metal/hosts.json, its own domain and config.json, the same units as production, its own SSH key, values-staging.yaml only where it must differ, "release_proof": "staging". Nothing more is built now (user): the gate reads it and is unit-tested, and the guide names what that person must still write: a target that deploys staging (make infra runs verify, sync and push only for production) and runs the mark. It says what is unproven, including that the suite's fixtures live in values-local.yaml, so most sandbox tests would not run there and a staging needs its own less intrusive suite when one first exists (discussed 2026-11-02).

docs.title: Portability
docs.text: This step does what the design needs: VM size and each environment's app list in configuration. The rest becomes its own roadmap step (discussed 2026-11-02): the GitHub repository in system/argocd/values-dev.yaml, the domain in apps/matrix, the time zone in kured and renovate, and the assumptions of WSL (C:, .wslconfig).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md's rules: pinned latest versions, config.json for what depends on where it runs, the secrets catalog, backup labels, policy exceptions, mesh policies, test/scopes.yaml, deferred minors.
  • The sandbox's renders stay identical apart from the deploy-path allow.
  • Testbed and sandbox never run together. A run stopped for low memory is not restarted without asking: an operating rule for whoever runs it, with no watchdog in make testbed (Claude's call).
  • Live runs only from the main checkout.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• How the branch's existing commits are reworked, and whether the branch is renamed; 12a-2's tests for environments (localOnly, testDomain) stay if they still serve someone with a larger testbed.
  • How Istio gets the CRDs it needs in layer 2, and whether Argo CD's limits on the testbed stay, from measurements.
  • How CloudNativePG is exercised without Forgejo in layer 3.
  • The exact not_run format and its check that every entry is a real path.

docs.title: Step 12a-3: an ordered shutdown, startup, and every node losing power at once
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-03/04. Builds on 12a-1 and 12a-2 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-02-testbed-design.md, docs/installation/testbed.md): three NixOS k3s VMs, Argo CD, layers 1 and 2 (rook-ceph, cert-manager, Istio). It replaces the "Shutdown and power cut" section of docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-31-staging-design.md, written when staging was to run most of the platform. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: The homelab must come back by itself after losing power, with nothing it acknowledged writing lost, and nobody at home. Production has no UPS for now and may get one later (user), so every outage is a sudden cut of every node: that is the main path. An ordered shutdown is for when someone chooses to stop the homelab (maintenance, moving it); a UPS will reuse it later.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Every node cut at once comes back by itself: etcd, the API at its VIP, Ceph, the mesh, the Gateway at its VIP, with data acknowledged on Ceph intact. Measured: how long it takes.
  • lab cluster shutdown stops the cluster in order and turns the nodes off; they stay off until someone starts them.
  • When nodes boot after an ordered shutdown, startup runs by itself and undoes it (user); lab cluster startup runs the same thing by hand and waits for it.
  • One measurement of CloudNativePG's three instances through the same cut.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• NUT and a UPS: a separate step, when a UPS is bought (user). dummy-ups would only prove a few lines of configuration, not a driver or a real UPS.
  • BIOS settings, Wake-on-LAN and disks on hardware: step 12b.
  • Forgejo and OpenBao on the testbed (user). TestNodePowerCut proves on the sandbox that they keep acknowledged writes through a sudden cut; what several nodes add beneath them is Ceph, which this step tests directly. OpenBao's raft and Forgejo on Ceph first run on hardware and stay on the before-production list.
  • healthchecks.io: it is still under Ideas, so there is nothing to pause. Whoever adds it adds that step.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A startup that waits for something a suspended component would have fixed, and so never finishes (see the watchdog below).
  • Resuming a CronJob that was suspended on purpose before the shutdown (production's rotation CronJob is, until the first release).
  • A docs line that lets someone think the testbed proved real disks survive a power cut.
  • Node health stuck behind a person: backups and rotation silently off after an outage because nobody ran a command.

docs.title: What differs from a real cut
docs.text: virsh destroy kills QEMU. The VMs use cache=unsafe, so what the guest handed to QEMU survives in WSL's page cache, and a guest's flush is not forced to any disk. The test proves the software recovers and that writes the guest never flushed do not count as acknowledged. It does not prove that a real disk keeps what it acknowledged. Without a UPS that risk sits entirely in the hardware: docs/installation/testbed.md and CLAUDE.md's before-production list say so, and 12b prefers SSDs with power-loss protection and repeats the cut on hardware before real data (discussed 2026-11-04).

docs.title: lab cluster shutdown
docs.text:
Beside lab cluster upgrade, same flags (--environment, --flake, a timeout), reaching the nodes the same way. In order:

  1. Write the marker: a ConfigMap (kube-system, name left to the builder) listing what this shutdown changes, before changing it, so a shutdown cut halfway still gets undone. It also records each node's boot ID, which startup needs below, and the controller's replicas.
  2. Stop Argo CD's application controller (scale to zero). Applications self-heal, so it would undo the next step at once; Argo CD does not manage itself, so it stays stopped (Claude's call).
  3. Suspend every CronJob that is not already suspended, recording its name in the marker, except those labelled to keep running (below).
  4. Wait for running Jobs, at most 5 minutes by default (a flag), then go on and name the Jobs it left (Claude's call: a bounded wait, because a sudden cut is already proven survivable, and a UPS will have only 10-15 minutes).
  5. Ceph noout, when Ceph exists.
  6. Power off every node at about the same time, not one by one: losing them singly would make etcd and Ceph react to each loss. No drain. A node whose poweroff hangs (a volume's unmount stalling once the OSDs are gone) is forced off by a bounded systemd timeout, measured on the testbed: nobody is home to press the button, and a sudden cut is already proven survivable (Claude's call).

Velero's Schedule is left alone and its Backups are not waited for: a backup cut by the shutdown ends Failed and the next one runs, as 11c proved, and an off-site copy can outlast any wait worth having (Claude's call).

It is idempotent: a second run after a partial one finishes the job and never records as "suspended by shutdown" what the first run suspended twice over.

docs.title: The watchdog keeps running
docs.text: istio-system/istio-cni-watchdog is a CronJob that breaks the mesh's deadlock after a node restart (CLAUDE.md). Suspending it could leave the mesh deadlocked while startup waits. It carries a label that shutdown skips (Claude's call).

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
One implementation, on the nodes (Claude's call): a small script in the node flake (writeShellApplication, using k3s's kubectl and the node's /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml), run by a systemd unit at boot on every node, and run over SSH by lab cluster startup. lab is not on the nodes, and packaging it there would tie the flake to cli/'s Go module for a few kubectl calls.

  • No marker: do nothing and exit (a sudden cut recovers by itself, needs nothing undone).
  • Marker, but a majority of its nodes still on the boot it recorded: do nothing yet. One node rebooting during shutdown's wait must not resume what is being stopped; a cut halfway through a shutdown reboots them all, so it gets undone (Claude's call). A shutdown that fails with the nodes up says to run lab cluster startup, which undoes it whatever the boot IDs say.
  • Marker, and a majority of its nodes on a new boot: wait for the API (retrying with no limit: the other nodes may take any time to come back), then resume the CronJobs the marker names and scale Argo CD's controller back up. It does not wait for every node: a node that never returns must not leave backups and rotation off (user).
  • noout comes off when every OSD is back, or after 30 minutes at most, so Ceph copies what a dead node held instead of staying short of a replica forever (user). The marker goes last, after noout. Every step is idempotent, and three nodes may run it at once.
  • A marker that outlives its welcome raises an alert, so someone learns a node did not return or startup failed (user). Rendered only on the testbed, which runs no monitoring; the sandbox's TestMonitoring style can prove the rule loads.
  • CloudNativePG, when installed: report whether every Cluster is healthy, without holding the rest back. Unit-tested only here; the testbed does not list it (user).
  • lab cluster startup runs the script on the first node that answers and fails with a timeout, naming what it waits for.

A node booting with the marker does not wait for the Ceph that a marker-less boot would need nothing from; the unit must never hold up boot or k3s (ordered after k3s.service, no Before= or RequiredBy= on anything it needs).

docs.title: Power on after an outage
docs.text:
(user: without a UPS, Last State is right; the UPS step changes it.)

  • No UPS (now): BIOS "Restore on AC power loss" = Last State. Running when the power went: comes back. Turned off on purpose: stays off, even through an outage.
  • With a UPS (its own step): an ordered shutdown leaves the last state "off", so Last State would never bring the nodes back. That step sets "Power On" and has NUT tell the UPS to cut and restore its output (shutdown.return), which also covers the power returning during a shutdown. The cost: a node turned off on purpose comes back after an outage. Choose a UPS that NUT drives with that command.

The roadmap in CLAUDE.md changes accordingly. None of this can run on VMs.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
On the testbed, from the main checkout, alone and never in make testbed's run: they wreck its availability. A new target (make testbed-power) runs them on a healthy testbed. They do not count towards the release mark (Claude's call: the mark says a release deployed and passed; these run when cluster shutdown|startup, the node profile or the recovery path change, and always before 12b). TestTestbed* is make testbed's filter, so they need another prefix.

A write probe, shared: a small pod on a Ceph PVC appends numbered records, fdatasyncs each, and prints the number afterwards. The test follows its log from outside the VMs, so what it read is what was acknowledged. After recovery every number it read is in the file, in order. The probe's PVC, its namespace and its mesh label are the test's; it is removed at the end.

Every node cut (virsh destroy of all three, in one go, while the probe writes): start them, then measure and require, with no command run on the cluster:

  • the API at its VIP, every node on a new boot and Ready (the API first reports what it knew before: as TestNodePowerCut, a new bootID is the proof)
  • Ceph HEALTH_OK, mons and OSDs running
  • the mesh between two nodes and the Gateway at its VIP, as TestTestbedMesh checks; this is the check that would catch 12a-2's kube-vip finding (its lease held with the VIP not answering), so a failure there is reported as that finding, not waited through
  • the probe's data intact, and the probe able to write again
  • no etcd member lost, no marker involved

If the Gateway's address does not return (the kube-vip finding): one bounded investigation, about half a day of machine time. Fixed: the fix ships in this branch. Not fixed: the work stops and asks, with the logs. It is neither recorded as passing nor moved to 12b without the user (user), since coming back with nobody home is this step's whole point.

Limit: 30 minutes (Claude's call, from 12a-2's install times; the first run sets the real number, recorded in the docs). Then do it again during a Ceph-heavy moment only if the first run shows a reason.

Ordered shutdown and startup: before it, a fixture CronJob running, a fixture CronJob suspended on purpose, and a long Job. Run lab cluster shutdown. Check the marker's contents before the nodes go, then every VM shut off and staying so. Start them, without calling lab: the units undo it. Require: the running CronJob resumed, the suspended one still suspended, the watchdog never suspended, noout off, Argo CD's controller back and its Applications Synced, the marker gone, the probe's data intact. Then a second run: lab cluster startup by hand with no marker is a no-op that succeeds.

A node that does not return: shut down in order, start only two VMs. Require the CronJob resumed and Argo CD's controller back with the third still off, and noout off after its limit. Start the third last, so the testbed ends healthy.

Unit tests, in cli/internal/cluster beside upgrade_test.go's fakes: the order of shutdown, the marker written before anything changes, skipping what is suspended and what is labelled, the Job wait's limit, idempotence. The script gets a test through a fake kubectl in test/, offline and wired into scripts/ci-check's offline_tests.

docs.title: CloudNativePG, one measurement (user)
docs.text: Once, not on the list and not in the mark: with layer 2 stable, install platform/cloudnative-pg by hand and its three instances, write through the primary, cut every node, and check that a primary returns with the write. Also log I/O and memory inside each guest, alongside each node's vmstat: that answers what 12a-2 could not, why layer 3 lost its leases at 4 vCPUs with CPU idle. The result and the numbers go in docs/installation/testbed.md as one measurement, whichever way it goes. A failure does not block this step: it moves to 12b's list with its numbers. The bar is what the measurement reports, not a pass or fail of this step (discussed 2026-11-03). It runs at 2 vCPUs, what this workstation ships; 4 only if that run points at CPU (Claude's call).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md's rules: test/scopes.yaml for what make dev would run (these tests are not the sandbox's), deferred-minors.md, the before-production list.
  • The node profile is a gated path (infra/_modules/metal/**), and cli/internal/cluster/** too: this branch's own change needs make testbed's mark again.
  • Never beside the sandbox, 30 GB free on C:, WSL above 1.5 GB; a run stopped for low memory is not restarted without asking.
  • From the main checkout only. The VMs are the testbed's: virsh destroy is safe there and never used on anything else.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• The marker's name and format, the label's name, how noout is set (the toolbox or the operator's pod), the probe's image.
  • Whether the systemd unit needs a timer or a retry loop, as long as it survives the API being away for any length of time.
  • The test's file and prefix, and how many of its waits to share with TestTestbedMesh and TestTestbedCeph.
  • Where the roadmap names the UPS step (it runs when a UPS is bought).

docs.title: Step 15d: the cluster's configuration, scanned
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-05, after a spike on the testbed and the sandbox (numbers below). Builds on 12a (the testbed), 15b (Kyverno) and 15e (the Trivy Operator, whose config, RBAC and compliance scanners are off because this step covers them). Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Before the first production deploy, find out what is misconfigured in the cluster itself and in what it runs, handle each finding by its weight (user), and notice when something new appears. The threat this step answers is someone reaching the cluster over the network, so what matters is the API server's and the kubelets' settings, RBAC and what workloads may do on a node.

The step was named "secrets encryption at rest", but --secrets-encryption has been on the nodes since 12a-1 (profiles/k3s-server.nix, kept from upstream). What is missing there is proof and a procedure, not the setting.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. make testbed-scan runs kube-bench on every testbed node and make dev-scan runs kubescape on the sandbox. Each fails on a finding nobody has decided on, and each fails rather than passes when the tool could not really check.
  2. Every finding open today is decided: fixed, or accepted in one file with its reason.
  3. The fixes below are made and proven.
  4. A test proves Secrets are encrypted in etcd on the nodes, and the key has a procedure that ran once.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• LUKS, or any disk encryption (user): stolen machines and thrown-away disks are set aside for now, and it does nothing against someone who gets in while the cluster runs. It goes on the before-production list as an accepted risk, saying that adding it later means reinstalling each disk.
  • A scanner running in the cluster (the Kubescape operator) and scans on GitHub Actions.
  • Fixing all of kubescape's 86 failed controls: most are noise for a homelab (below) and get one line of reason.
  • Rotating the encryption key on a schedule: with disk loss set aside it guards little, and k3s's docs warn a wrong rotation can corrupt the cluster for good. Its 90 days would add risk, not safety.
  • Kyverno's Enforce (15b-2), and a scan as part of a release's proof. make testbed's mark does not depend on these targets.

docs.title: What the spike found
docs.text:
kube-bench v0.16.0 with k3s-cis-1.11, three nodes, the same on each: 64 pass, 5 fail, 49 warn (35 of them section 5's manual policy checks).

Fail Reading Decision 1.2.30 service-account-extend-token-expiration Real: not set, so the default Fix: set it false 1.3.7, 1.4.2 bind-address; 4.3.1 kube-proxy metrics Ours on purpose, for Prometheus; nixos-fw admits only pods and nodes on those ports Accept 4.2.4 read-only-port False: the journal's line ends read-only-port=0", the check sees 0"; nothing listens on 10255 Accept as a false report

Fourteen warnings outside section 5 need a reading: 1.2.3, 1.2.9, 1.2.11, 1.2.17, 1.2.18, 1.2.20, 1.3.1, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 3.1.3, 3.2.2, 4.2.12, 4.2.13, 4.2.14.

Four traps, each of which gave a clean or a wrong result:

  • v0.16.0's image has k3s benchmarks only up to 1.9. k3s-cis-1.11 is on main, in no release yet (2026-11-05).
  • The image has no journalctl, which every k3s check calls: 21 false FAILs until the node's /nix and /run/current-system are mounted and on PATH.
  • Without run --targets master,etcd,controlplane,node,policies it detects no control plane on k3s and skips three sections, reporting 0 fails.
  • No benchmark maps to Kubernetes 1.37 (main's table ends at 1.35), so this is the nearest, not an exact match.

kubescape 4.0.8 (nixpkgs), allcontrols: testbed 80 failed controls and 132 resources, sandbox 86 and 311. Its compliance score was 61 on both. Worth reading on the sandbox:

  • velero-server is bound to cluster-admin (C-0185), though Velero here backs up volumes only.
  • Wildcards and impersonation: Velero and Argo CD's controller (C-0187, C-0065).
  • kyverno-migrate-resources names a ServiceAccount that does not exist (C-0307).
  • "Credentials in configuration" in 7 resources (C-0012) looks name-matched (...KEY, ...SECRETS). Only names were read so far: read each, openbao-config first.

The rest is mostly limits, labels, probes and image signatures, or repeats Kyverno.

docs.title: Where each tool runs (user)
docs.text:
• kube-bench on the testbed: it reads the NixOS nodes, which the sandbox does not have. Production's hardware runs it in 12b.
  • kubescape on the sandbox: the only environment with the whole platform. On the testbed it adds little beyond rook-ceph (Claude's call).

Both run by hand: before 12b, and when k3s, the node profile or a component's RBAC change. Neither joins make dev or make testbed.

docs.title: One file of decisions
docs.text:
.cluster-scan-accepted.yaml at the root, beside .trivyignore.yaml. Every entry has a reason.

  • kube-bench, by check number. Any FAIL not listed fails the target. WARNs do not fail it: they get one reading in this step, recorded in the guide.
  • kubescape, two levels (Claude's call):
  • Noisy controls are accepted whole, by control ID (limits, labels, probes, signatures).
  • Dangerous controls are accepted by resource, so a new workload there fails the target: at least cluster-admin, wildcards, impersonation and bind/escalate, privileged, host path, host network and PID, capabilities, credentials in configuration (C-0185, C-0187, C-0035, C-0065, C-0191, C-0057, C-0045, C-0048, C-0041, C-0038, C-0046, C-0012, C-0259). A control not listed at all fails the target.

Which of the remaining controls is noisy or dangerous is decided while triaging, by what it would let someone do. Sort by effect, not by the tool's score.

docs.title: Not fooled by the tool
docs.text:
The targets fail when a check did not really run, because the spike showed these tools report clean otherwise:

  • kube-bench: every one of sections 1 to 5 must be present in the JSON on every node, and no result may contain not found from its audit command.
  • kubescape: the scan must have seen the resources (a floor on the count, and a known bad resource such as istio-system/ztunnel present in the results).

docs.title: How they run
docs.text:
• Go tests in test/, as make testbed-power runs its tests, named so test/scopes.yaml's full regex does not select them.
  • kube-bench is a Job per node in a temporary namespace (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged), deleted afterwards whatever the result. It needs hostPID, read-only mounts of /var/lib/rancher, /etc/rancher, /var/log/journal, /etc/machine-id, /etc/systemd, /nix and /run/current-system.
  • Versions, by the repository's rule, latest stable and pinned: kube-bench's image at its release, with k3s-cis-1.11's files vendored from a named main commit and the reason beside them (no release has them), dropped when one does. kubescape at v4.0.17 or later from its release, since nixpkgs has 4.0.8. Check upstream again when building.
  • kubescape always with --keep-local: nothing leaves the workstation. Its controls download at each run and are not pinned (Claude's call): a new failing control is then a thing to read, which is what the target is for, at the cost of a target that can fail with no change here.

docs.title: Fixes in this step
docs.text:
• Set --service-account-extend-token-expiration=false on the nodes and on k3d, unless the sandbox's suite shows a client that needs it.
  • Velero's cluster-admin: find what a restore needs and bind that. TestBackupRestore is the proof. If it truly needs nearly everything, accept it by resource with what was tried.
  • kyverno-migrate-resources' ServiceAccount: find out whether it is a chart's leftover hook or a real failure, then fix or accept.
  • Cheap warnings, if measured harmless: --seccomp-default (4.2.14), a pod PID limit (4.2.13), audit log age (1.2.17). make dev on the whole platform and make testbed are the measure, with the flags on both k3d and the nodes. Changing k3d's arguments rebuilds the sandbox's cluster. One that breaks a workload is accepted with the reason, not forced.

Everything else found while triaging: fix it here if it is small and contained; otherwise accept it and add a line to deferred-minors.md. A dangerous finding that cannot be fixed small is raised with the user before it is accepted.

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
• TestTestbedSecretsEncrypted, part of make testbed: create a Secret with a known value, read its key raw from etcd on a node, and require the prefix k8s:enc:aescbc: and no plain value. How to reach etcd is the builder's (the client certificates are under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/tls/etcd, and k3s ships no etcdctl). It guards against the flag being lost. The sandbox has no such flag and needs none.
  • k3s secrets-encrypt rotate-keys runs once on the testbed, with Secrets readable afterwards on all three nodes and through a restart of k3s. The steps and the result go in the guide. It is not a permanent test.
  • cli/internal/rotate/catalog.yaml gets the encryption key as manual, no period, reason as above. The k3s token is not in the catalog either: it gets an entry too, with k3s's documented steps, marked as never run (Claude's call).

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• docs/how-to-guides/cluster-scan.md, in mkdocs' nav: running each target, reading a failure, the file's two levels, what encryption at rest does and does not protect, the rotation.
  • CLAUDE.md: the roadmap's 15d line, and the before-production list: LUKS's accepted risk, kube-bench to run on hardware, the benchmark not matching 1.37.
  • docs/how-to-guides/supply-chain.md already points here; check it still reads true.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• make testbed-scan and make dev-scan pass with every finding decided, and each fails when a finding is added to the cluster or removed from the file.
  • Each "not fooled" guard was seen to fail (the image without journalctl, no --targets).
  • TestTestbedSecretsEncrypted fails without the flag or against a plain value. If removing the flag cannot be tried cheaply, a check on a plain value proves the test can fail.
  • make dev and make testbed pass with the fixes.

docs.title: What this does not prove
docs.text:
• CIS 1.11 for k3s is not written for Kubernetes 1.37, and the testbed's slow_control_plane differs from production's flags.
  • The sandbox's RBAC and workloads are not exactly production's: production-only apps (matrix, jellyfin, cloudflared and others) and paperless and OpenCloud unless apps=all. make dev-scan scans whatever the sandbox has running and installs nothing, and an accepted resource that is absent fails nothing. Production's first scan belongs after 12b.
  • Passing a benchmark is not being secure: it checks known settings, not whether the design is sound.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text: File and test names beyond those above, how the Job is rendered, the floor on resources, the order of triage, and the wording of each reason.

docs.title: Step 15f: the public surface
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-06. The roadmap line came from the OWASP check in chat 2026-10-25 ("Cloudflare Access in front of the admin apps published through the Tunnel, rate limits, a periodic nuclei/nmap scan of what the Tunnel exposes"); reading the code changed it, as below. Builds on 7c (infra/_modules/cloudflare), 15c (Loki's ruler) and 15d (scans that fail when they did not really run). Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The Cloudflare Tunnel exists for the public apps only (user). The admin apps (Argo CD, Grafana, Kiali, Forgejo, Woodpecker, zot, Kanidm) stay on the LAN Gateway. This step makes sure it stays that way, puts Cloudflare's edge protections in front of what is public, and looks at the public hosts the way someone outside does, on a schedule.

What is public today, through Gateway istio-system/public:

Host App Namespace Proxied annotation www. blog blog yes draw. excalidraw excalidraw yes ntfy. ntfy ntfy no chat. Element web (apps/matrix; the host is written in full in apps/matrix/values.yaml's elementHostname) matrix yes

Two gaps found while reading:

  • Gateway public's listener has allowedRoutes.namespaces.from: All: one parentRefs edit puts any app, an admin one included, on the internet, and nothing checks it.
  • ntfy's route lacks external-dns.kubernetes.io/cloudflare-proxied: "true", so external-dns makes its record DNS-only: a Tunnel host that is not proxied does not work, and would skip the WAF and the rate limit anyway.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Only an allow-list of namespaces can attach routes to Gateway public, enforced by the Gateway itself and checked offline in the basic checks. Every route on public is proxied by Cloudflare.
  2. Cloudflare's WAF managed rules and a rate limit protect the public hosts, declared in OpenTofu (infra/_modules/cloudflare).
  3. nuclei scans the public hosts on a schedule from inside production, through public DNS and Cloudflare, and alerts on a finding nobody accepted and on a scan that did not really run.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Cloudflare Access (user): no admin app goes through the Tunnel, and the four public apps are meant for anyone (ntfy's phone apps and Element could not pass Access anyway). Access comes back only if something admin-like is published: Kanidm goes through the Tunnel in step 13 for Headscale, and that step decides.
  • nmap (user): the Tunnel opens no port at home (CGNAT on top), so nmap would only see Cloudflare's edge. It moves to step 13, against the VPS's public address.
  • Paid Cloudflare features (more rate-limit rules, the full managed ruleset, Bot Management), other zone settings, and hosts outside the Tunnel.
  • Matrix: Element web is public while dendrite's route is on the LAN Gateway, so Element cannot sign in from outside. Recorded as a deferred minor, not fixed here.

docs.title: 1. The allow-list
docs.text:
• One map, public in system/istio-system/values.yaml, from namespace to its public hosts' first labels: blog: [www], excalidraw: [draw], ntfy: [ntfy], matrix: [chat] (Claude's call: a map, so the Gateway, the offline test and the scan's targets read one place). Gateway public's listener uses from: Selector on kubernetes.io/metadata.name In <the map's keys>, as the LAN Gateway's SSH listener already does for forgejo. A route from any other namespace stays Accepted: False (NotAllowedByListeners).
  • An offline test in test/ (run by scripts/ci-check) renders every chart and app file for production and fails when a route attaches to public from a namespace not in the map, with a hostname the map does not list for it (<label>.<baseDomain>), or without the proxied annotation. Adding a public app is one line in the map plus its annotation, reviewed in its pull request.
  • ntfy's route gets the annotation.
  • Sandbox proof: the sandbox renders Gateway public too. A test creates a route in a namespace off the list and checks the Gateway refuses it, and that a listed namespace's route is accepted.

docs.title: 2. Cloudflare's edge, in OpenTofu
docs.text:
In infra/_modules/cloudflare, applied by infra/production/cloudflare (state on R2):

  • WAF managed rules: the Free plan's managed ruleset, deployed on the zone and declared, so its state is visible and drift shows in a plan. The builder checks with Cloudflare's docs and provider 5.x how a Free zone deploys it (it may already be on by default, in which case the declaration only asserts it).
  • Rate limit: the Free plan allows one rule, counted per client IP over a short period (the builder confirms the current limits: period, mitigation time, fields allowed in the expression). It likely cannot match the hostname, so the rule and the managed rules cover the whole zone: nothing else in hoangduong.dev is proxied, now or planned (user). A proxied host added later outside the Tunnel gets them too; the guide says so. The rule blocks, and its threshold is generous enough that a browser's first load of Element web passes (Claude's call): per-account limits stay the apps' own (ntfy's per-visitor limits, which read CF-Connecting-IP).
  • The API token cf auth login gives OpenTofu may lack the rulesets permission: the builder finds out with a plan first and says so before asking for more.
  • Applying is the user's call (user): this touches the production zone. No public app runs yet (production is not deployed), so applying it now affects nothing live. The step's proof is a plan, then an apply after the user agrees, then reading the rules back.
  • make -C infra check covers the new resources as it does the module's others.

docs.title: 3. nuclei on a schedule
docs.text:
• A CronJob in a new component system/public-scan (Claude's call: in the cluster rather than GitHub Actions, so a finding alerts through Alertmanager like everything else, and the requests leave from the home connection as an outsider's would reach Cloudflare). Weekly.
  • Targets: https://<label>.<baseDomain> for each host in the map (not typed twice).
  • The scan goes through the WAF and the rate limit like anyone else's requests (user): no header or rule lets it past them, since that would scan a surface no outsider sees and add a secret to rotate. nuclei is throttled below the rate limit's threshold, so it never blocks the household's own requests; a weekly run may take hours. Probes the WAF blocks are the protection working, not a failure. nuclei's templates are a pinned release, checked, not fetched as "latest" at run time. Image pinned per the version rule.
  • Severities medium and above are findings (Claude's call); info and low go to the log only.
  • Accepted findings: a list beside the CronJob's values (template ID, host, reason), like 15e's accepted CVEs. An entry without a reason fails the basic checks.
  • Output: JSON lines to stdout, read by Alloy into Loki. Loki's ruler alerts on:
  • PublicScanFinding: a finding not accepted. The alert names the template ID and host only.
  • PublicScanMissing: no completed scan in the last 8 days, or a scan that did not really run: some host's first, ordinary request did not get the app's normal answer (an error, a Cloudflare block or challenge page) (user), or nuclei ran fewer templates than a floor the builder sets from a first run.
  • Egress: the namespace gets 443 out (system/egress/values.yaml), its own AuthorizationPolicy and the rest a component needs (test/scopes.yaml, policy securityContext).
  • Sandbox: the CronJob runs there against the map's hosts the sandbox serves (excalidraw and ntfy; blog and matrix do not run there), through the LAN Gateway they attach to (*.127-0-0-1.nip.io, the local CA), so the job, its parsing and both alerts are proven. A test triggers it once and checks it completed and found nothing unaccepted. What Cloudflare does to the scan is seen only in production.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Latest stable everything, pinned (nuclei, its templates, providers).
  • Never print Cloudflare tokens, the zone id or the account id.
  • Never apply to production without the user's go-ahead.
  • Alerts and reports name only template IDs and hosts, never response bodies.

docs.title: Done means
docs.text:
• The allow-list is enforced on Gateway public, the offline test and the sandbox test pass, and ntfy is proxied.
  • The WAF and rate-limit resources plan cleanly; applied and read back once the user agrees.
  • The scan CronJob runs in the sandbox, its alerts load, and the guide (docs/how-to-guides/public-surface.md) says how to read and accept findings and how to add a public app.
  • CLAUDE.md: 15f's line rewritten (no Access, nmap moved to step 13), the before-production list says what ran only as a plan or only in the sandbox (the rules' effect on real traffic, the scan through Cloudflare).

docs.title: Mesh watchdog: the stuck pods, not only ztunnel's Ready
docs.text: Before the first production deploy (CLAUDE.md: "Fix the watchdog in its own PR first"). Agreed in chat on 2026-11-07.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
istio-system/istio-cni-watchdog (system/istio-system/files/cni-watchdog.sh, step 6, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-18-mesh-node-restart-design.md) restarts a node's istio-cni when that node's ztunnel has run 180 s without becoming Ready. ztunnel reports Ready while the mesh on its node is still stuck:

  • 12a-3: one TestNodePowerCut of three took about 23 minutes, 15 of them with the watchdog seeing nothing to do, while ztunnel retried dead network namespaces (Bind [::1]:15053).
  • 15f: a sandbox started from stopped left pods in ContainerCreating for minutes, every sandbox failing with plugin type="istio-cni" name="istio-cni" failed (add): istio-cni cmdAdd failed to contact node Istio CNI agent, ztunnel Ready; deleting both istio-cni and ztunnel by hand cleared it.

docs.title: What
docs.text:
1. A second signal: the symptom. A node is stuck when a pod on it has had no sandbox for more than NOT_READY_SECONDS (180) (Pending with PodReadyToStartContainers False: not a pod waiting in an init container or an image pull) and a FailedCreatePodSandBox event for that pod, seen within the same window, says istio-cni's add failed (type="istio-cni" and failed (add)). The watchdog lists the events and the Pending pods once each, whatever their number: after a power cut there are hundreds, and its Job has 50 s. The first signal stays: ztunnel running and not Ready for more than 180 s. Events are read through the API: no log access, and no dependence on ztunnel's log wording, which changes between releases. A pod stuck for another reason (image pull, volume) has no such event and is left alone.
  2. Escalation, without state. For a stuck node, nothing happens while its istio-cni or its ztunnel started less than 180 s ago (a restart is still taking effect). Otherwise the watchdog restarts istio-cni if istio-cni started before ztunnel (as today), and both istio-cni and ztunnel if istio-cni started after it (istio-cni was already restarted and the node is still stuck); the pods' start times are the only state. First built as ztunnel alone: two recorded power cuts on the sandbox (2026-11-07) cleared only once both were new (istio-cni then ztunnel, or ztunnel then istio-cni), each step costing another 180 s, so the second step restarts both.
  3. RBAC. A ClusterRole to list events and pods in every namespace; deleting stays limited to istio-system's pods (the Role).

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
• TestIstioCNIWatchdog (offline, fake kubectl): the new signal, an event outside the window, an event for another plugin, a pod no longer Pending, a pod whose sandbox exists, a young pod, a pod of the same name elsewhere, the escalation to both pods, and the number of API calls with hundreds of events (TestIstioCNIWatchdogFewCalls).
  • The sandbox: TestNodeRestart and TestNodePowerCut (they rely on the watchdog), with the time each took.

docs.title: Not in scope
docs.text:
• ztunnel's own health (its admin port, its metrics): the stuck pods are what matter, and they are visible through the API.
  • Several nodes at once (each node is judged alone, as today); the testbed's multi-node runs come with 12b.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The Makefiles hold commands, not builds: every target is .PHONY, nothing uses make's dependency graph, and the cost is make's syntax: $$ everywhere, $(value …) to keep a $ in a regex, override/export lines to pass a reason with quotes, $(MAKE) var=… to call another target, and options as name=value strings with no help or checking. just is a command runner: recipes take real arguments (long options and flags since 1.46), run the system shell or a shebang script with no escaping layer, list themselves (just --list), and just --dry-run prints without running (make's -n runs $(MAKE) lines: it once applied the sandbox mid-test). Upstream moved to just on 2026-11-03. go-task was weighed in chat (2026-11-07) and set aside: its sources/generates would go unused here, it runs recipes in its own shell interpreter and writes shell inside YAML strings.

14b is two steps. This one (14b-1) swaps the runner and keeps every behaviour. 14b-2 (later) moves lab's glue commands into recipes or scripts.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A justfile at the root and one each in infra/, cli/ and test/ (mod), replacing the four Makefiles, which are deleted (no make shim).
  • Arguments in just's style: long options and flags instead of name=value (decided with the user on 2026-11-08).
  • Same behaviour as today for every command: guards, ordering, exit statuses, what runs and what is refused.
  • Every living reference moves in the same PR: CI (.github/actions/sandbox, the workflows' inputs), scripts/, messages in Go and scripts, the offline tests that drive make, test/scopes.yaml, docs/ (except docs/superpowers/specs and plans, which are history), README.md, CLAUDE.md, docs/superpowers/deferred-minors.md.
  • just pinned at its latest stable release, 1.59.0 (nixos-unstable's lock has 1.58.0): a nix/just.nix from the release binary, like nix/kubescape.nix.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No change to what lab does (14b-2), to the tests' content or to the sandbox, testbed or production.
  • No new commands, no renamed concepts beyond what the interface below lists (--env replaces make's env=).
  • Historical specs and plans keep saying make.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A recipe that silently does less than its target did (a guard dropped, an exit status swallowed, a refresh skipped).
  • Re-creating make's escaping problems in just: shell logic of more than a few lines goes in a shebang recipe (#!/usr/bin/env bash with set -euo pipefail) or a script in scripts/, never in long \-joined lines.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
make just make dev just dev make dev scope=full just dev --full make dev tests='<regex>' just dev --tests '<regex>' make dev apps=<names>\|all\|none just dev --apps <names>\|all\|none make dev revision=<sha> just dev --revision <sha> make dev base=<ref> just dev --base <ref> make dev-fresh [apps=…] [tests=…], dev-clean, dev-scan just dev-fresh [--apps …] [--tests …], dev-clean, dev-scan make testbed, testbed-fresh, testbed-clean, testbed-stop, testbed-scan same names make testbed-power [tests='A B'] just testbed-power [--tests 'A B'] make infra env=<env> [force=1] [break_glass=<r>] [skip_proof=<r>] just infra deploy <env> [--force] [--break-glass <r>] [--skip-proof <r>] make -C infra check just infra check make -C cli test, check just cli test, just cli check make test, make -C test filter=… format=… just test run [--env <env>] [--filter <regex>] [--format <f>] (or just test --filter … if just passes a module's default recipe its options; the builder checks) make docs just docs make (no target: production's infra then the smoke tests) just lists the recipes; the old default is dropped

infra becomes a module (infra/justfile): a root recipe infra would clash with mod infra. HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY keeps its path rules (absolute, ~/, or relative to where just runs; spaces allowed), from the environment only: the command-line assignment make infra HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY=… allowed goes (its test case too; docs/how-to-guides/renovate.md says HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY=… just infra deploy production, the shell's own form). (Builder check: my call.)

just test run keeps what make test did: --env defaults to production (make's env ?= production, so docs/installation/post-installation.md's check still reads production), and selects the kubeconfig (infra/<env>/kubeconfig.yaml), ENV (dev for the sandbox, testbed, unset for production) and INSECURE_SKIP_VERIFY=1 (sandbox and testbed), as the root targets passed them; the filter defaults to .. The root recipes call it with their environment and filter (the old smoke-test with Smoke is no longer a public command). dev-fresh passes --apps and --tests on to dev, as $(MAKE) passed apps= and tests= (a --tests there overrides --full, as before). (Builder check: my calls.)

The internal targets (sandbox-checkout, sandbox-clean, sandbox-push, sandbox-refresh, smoke-test) become private recipes or plain dependencies.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• just's recipes run in their justfile's directory; just finds the root justfile from any subdirectory.
  • The main-checkout guard (never a git worktree) and the clean-tree and --revision is HEAD guards run before any sandbox or testbed work, as today.
  • A reason (--break-glass, --skip-proof) and a regex (--tests) reach lab and go test unchanged, quotes and $ included: pass them through the environment or "$@", never through re-parsed strings.
  • The alone tests keep running one go test each (#78), from lab test scope --alone --each.
  • testbed records the commit it started from and refuses to mark another (proof_commit), and infra deploy verifies and pushes the commit it started from (deploy_commit).
  • scripts/ci-check and GitHub Actions call just inside the dev shell (nix develop --command just …); the job and check names do not change (sandbox stays the required check).
  • The offline tests in test/ci_scripts_test.go drive sandbox-clean and infra deploy with fake lab and terragrunt: the recipes must take those from overridable variables or the environment, and the tests move to just.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
• scripts/ci-check all (the offline tests drive the new recipes).
  • just dev --full on the sandbox from the branch (the root justfile is in test/scopes.yaml's run-everything group).
  • just --dry-run of testbed-clean, testbed-power, infra deploy production and dev-fresh, read against the old targets; just infra deploy sandbox applied for real.
  • just testbed once on the testbed (sandbox stopped, 30 GB free on C:): the testbed recipes are rewritten too.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• The exact just syntax ([arg(…, long)], value= flags, [private], set options, exported parameters).
  • Whether long shell bodies become shebang recipes or move to scripts/.
  • How ci_scripts_test.go overrides lab and terragrunt.
  • The wording of messages that named make targets.

docs.title: 14f: test layout, Ginkgo for the cluster tests, benchmarks
Intent
docs.text:
test/ is one Go package of 214 tests: 130 offline (renders, scripts, checks) and 84 that need a cluster (TestRookCephAES256K only renders a chart, but neither ci-check's regex nor any scope selects it: it runs nowhere today, the very bug below; and the regex's prefix TestSecurityLogsRules also runs TestSecurityLogsRulesLoaded, a cluster test that skips offline). 14f-1 leaves 131 offline (with TestRookCephAES256K and its own TestRootIsTheRepository) and 84 cluster tests. Three things hurt:

  • scripts/ci-check runs the offline tests through a hand-written -run regex of 130 names: a new offline test that the regex misses never runs anywhere, silently.
  • test/scopes.yaml and lab test scope pick cluster tests by test-name prefixes in a -run regex. A prefix matches more than meant (Rotation also matched TestStatePassphraseRotation, fixed in #78 by anchoring), and a run whose filter matches nothing passes.
  • go test's one -timeout covers a whole run: when the alone tests' run hit 60 minutes, the panic blamed whichever test was running (#77's post-merge run), and a slow test shows no progress until it ends.

The cluster tests move to Ginkgo, the framework of the Kubernetes ecosystem's e2e suites (Kubernetes' own test/e2e, Cluster API, kubebuilder's scaffold) and of upstream's tests/e2e: labels and a label filter instead of name regexes, Serial/Ordered for tests that need the cluster alone, a timeout per spec with progress reports, --fail-on-empty, --dry-run listing and JUnit/JSON reports. The offline tests stay plain go test with testify, the Go norm for unit and render tests, where Ginkgo's DSL adds nothing. A new benchmarks suite measures storage and the mesh, to compare the testbed with production's hardware in step 12b.

Decided with the user (2026-11-08): convert all 84 cluster tests (no long-lived mix of two styles); keep the directory test/ (Kubernetes' and Cluster API's test/e2e; upstream's tests/ is only its choice); add the benchmarks suite.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• test/offline/: the 131 offline tests, plain go test + testify. scripts/ci-check runs the package (go test ./offline/...) with no list of names; a new test there runs in the basic checks by being there.
  • test/e2e/: the 84 cluster tests as Ginkgo specs (Describe/It, Gomega's Eventually instead of testify's 106 assert.Eventually), one suite entry (TestE2E). Every spec carries labels naming what it proves (a component: identity, sso, kiali, forgejo, …), so test/scopes.yaml lists labels and lab test scope prints a Ginkgo label filter.
  • The alone tests (NodeRestart, NodePowerCut, BackupRestore, Rotation) carry the label alone and Serial; just dev runs the main specs (!alone within the selection), then each selected alone spec in its own Ginkgo run, in the order today's alone list gives (#78's behaviour: a run's failure or timeout names its own spec).
  • A timeout per spec (SpecTimeout/NodeTimeout from the spec's context) for every spec that waits on the cluster, sized from today's measured durations; Ginkgo's progress report after 60 s of a slow spec, every 30 s; the suite's --timeout long enough for the full run.
  • --fail-on-empty everywhere: a filter that selects nothing fails.
  • JUnit and JSON reports under test/reports/<suite>/ (git-ignored); GitHub Actions' sandbox jobs upload them as an artifact.
  • test/benchmarks/: a Ginkgo suite run by hand (just test benchmarks --env <env>), not in just dev or CI:
  • storage: fio on the environment's default StorageClass (Ceph on the testbed, the CSI host path in the sandbox): random 4k read/write IOPS and sequential throughput, ReadWriteOnce (and ReadWriteMany where the class offers it);
  • mesh: throughput and latency between two pods on different nodes, in the ambient mesh (through ztunnel) and out of it, so the mesh's cost is a number;
  • each run writes a JSON report (environment, commit, date, the numbers) to compare later; no pass/fail bar beyond "the benchmark ran" (the numbers are what step 12b reads). The old test/benchmark/ manifests (dbench with a latest tag, applied by hand) are removed.
  • test/internal/: helpers both suites (or both e2e and benchmarks) use, as packages: the environment (ENV, the kubeconfig, the domain), clients, OpenBao and Kanidm access, render helpers the offline tests share.
  • Ginkgo and Gomega pinned at their latest stable releases in test/go.mod (tool github.com/onsi/ginkgo/v2/ginkgo, run as go tool ginkgo, no separate install).
  • The testbed's tests (TestTestbed*), the power tests (testbed-power) and the scans (dev-scan, testbed-scan) become e2e specs with labels testbed, power and scan, run by the same recipes through label filters; the sandbox's runs exclude them, as ENV does today.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No change to what any test checks: each spec asserts what its test asserted, with the same waits (a conversion may tighten a wait into a spec timeout, never loosen what it proves).
  • No new e2e tests beyond the conversion (new behaviour gets its tests in its own step).
  • No change to which tests a change runs: every test/scopes.yaml group selects the same tests through labels as it did through names (lab test scope's output differs in form only).
  • Not upstream's layout beyond what is chosen here (its tests/, its Python recipe, its inventory package).

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Two runners on dev: dev never has some cluster tests on go test and others on Ginkgo. The conversion lands in one pull request (14f-2), converted group by group in its commits, each group proven on the sandbox as it goes.
  • A spec that passes because it ran nothing or skipped silently: an optional app's specs skip only as today (absent and not asked for), and fail when the app list names it.
  • Lost coverage: the e2e suite's dry run lists at least the 84 tests' worth of specs, and a check compares the converted list against the old test names (each old test maps to one or more specs).
  • Labels as free text: the label set is fixed in one place (a Go file of constants or scopes.yaml), and just cli check fails on a spec label or a scope label the other does not know.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. 14f-1 offline split: move the 131 offline tests and their fixtures to test/offline/, shared helpers to test/internal/; ci-check drops its regex; test/scopes.yaml's skip list names test/offline/** instead of each file. Proof: scripts/ci-check all runs the 129 offline tests it ran plus TestRookCephAES256K (count compared), just dev --full once.
  2. 14f-2 Ginkgo e2e: the suite, labels, scopes.yaml and lab test scope on labels, just dev/just test and the testbed recipes on Ginkgo, reports and the CI artifact; then the 84 tests converted group by group. Proof: each group with just dev --tests '<labels>' as it lands, just dev --full and just testbed at the end, and the old-name → spec check.
  3. 14f-3 benchmarks: the suite and just test benchmarks, run once on the sandbox and on the testbed; the old manifests removed. Proof: both reports written, read in the PR.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text: today after just dev --tests '<regex>' just dev --tests '<label filter>' (Ginkgo's syntax: logs, sso && kiali, mesh \|\| gateway) just test run [--env] [--filter <regex>] [--format] just test e2e [--env] [--labels <filter>] [--focus <regex>] (--focus on spec text, for one spec) none just test benchmarks --env <env> [--labels storage\|mesh] just testbed-power [--tests 'A B'] just testbed-power [--tests '<label filter>'], each power spec still one run lab test scope … [--alone --each] same flags; prints label filters instead of regexes

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The e2e specs read the environment as today (ENV, INSECURE_SKIP_VERIFY, the kubeconfig from just), and never target production unless the existing production checks did (docs/installation/post-installation.md's smoke run keeps working: just test e2e --labels smoke).
  • Serial and the alone runs keep the cluster to one spec at a time where today's suite ran tests one at a time (Ginkgo runs one process; no -p).
  • The benchmarks' workloads meet the policy (securityContext, pinned images by digest or version, allowed registries) and clean up their namespace; they create no PVC without homelab/backup: none.
  • Ginkgo's per-spec timeout uses the spec's context.Context: every wait inside a spec takes that context.

docs.title: Calls made after the builder check (mine, 2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• terratest goes. The suite calls it about 245 times (k8s.RunKubectlAndGetOutputE, KubectlApplyFromString, WaitUntil*, http_helper), and none takes a context: behind GinkgoT() a spec timeout would abandon the spec while its retries run on into the next one, the misattribution this step removes. test/internal gets a small layer that takes the spec's context (kubectl through exec.CommandContext, client-go, HTTP with the context), and every call site moves to it. This roughly doubles 14f-2; it is what makes per-spec timeouts real.
  • Environment gates become labels. Today's in-test gates (sandboxOnly, localOnly, meshSandboxOnly, secretsSandboxOnly, testbedOnly, skipUnlessSandbox) become labels naming where a spec may run (sandbox, testbed, production; a spec for both local environments carries both). just test e2e --env <env> adds && <env> to every filter itself, so a selected spec never skips for its environment; the only run-time skip left is an optional app absent and not asked for, as today. With --fail-on-empty, a filter that selects nothing for that environment fails.
  • No default environment. just test e2e requires --env (no silent production run); production runs only specs labelled production, which are exactly the tests that run against production today (those with no environment gate: TestSmoke, TestArgoCDCheck, the others the builder finds ungated), and docs/installation/post-installation.md says just test e2e --env production.
  • Benchmarks on the sandbox and the testbed now; production in 12b. Production needs policy exceptions and pull access the sandbox does not exercise, so 12b adds production to the suite. On the one-node sandbox the mesh benchmark measures two pods on the same node and records it as such in the report; the testbed measures across nodes.
  • Scopes keep today's effective selection. Each group selects what its regex matches today, not what its words meant: logs covers the TestSecurityLogs* specs (today Logs matches them). The differences that go: offline tests no longer run inside just dev (23 matched today, e.g. Policy, PublicScan; the basic checks run them), and TestTestbed* specs no longer get selected on the sandbox to skip there. The old-name → spec check compares against today's effective selection per group.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• The label names and how groups map onto them (given the anti-goal above: one fixed set, checked).
  • How lab test scope learns the spec labels for its checks (a ginkgo --dry-run --json-report it reads, or the constants file).
  • Each spec's timeout value, from the durations the full runs logged.
  • Which helpers become test/internal/ packages and their names.
  • fio's and the mesh benchmark's exact parameters and image (pinned), and the report's fields.

docs.title: Argo CD reads what OpenTofu knows from the cluster Secret (step 14g)
Intent
docs.text:
The bootstrap (infra/_modules/argocd) renders system/argocd and then rewrites the rendered ApplicationSets with yq for values that are not in git or are known only when OpenTofu runs:

  • set-revision.sh points every homelab source and generator at one commit. GitHub Actions uses this through just dev --revision.
  • set-sandbox-apps.sh adds the sandbox's optional apps (paperless, opencloud) to the apps generator.
  • set-backup-endpoint.sh sets global.backupS3Url, R2's endpoint, which holds the account id and is never in git.
  • choose-values.sh picks values-seed.yaml or values.yaml. The seed file restates both ApplicationSets' generators and sources only to change the repository. bootstrap.sh then replaces its placeholder with sed.

This step replaces those rewrites with the GitOps Bridge pattern:

  • OpenTofu writes these values as annotations and labels on Argo CD's in-cluster cluster Secret.
  • The ApplicationSets read them through a clusters generator.

The rendered chart then is what Argo CD runs. A value that changes is one Secret update, not a re-render plus a yq rewrite.

It is on the roadmap (step 14g). It does not answer a failure: it removes four rewrite scripts and most of values-seed.yaml.

docs.title: Spike (sandbox, Argo CD v3.5.5, 2026-11-09)
docs.text:
The spike was a throwaway on the running sandbox: a cluster Secret and two ApplicationSets named spike-*, all deleted afterwards. It found:

  • A clusters generator selecting the Secret by label, matrixed with a nested matrix (git directories × git files config.json), passes the Secret's parameters into both inner git generators. repoURL and revision templated from the Secret's annotations work, and so does valuesObject (global.backupS3Url, global.baseDomain from config.json).
  • Changing an annotation updated the generated Applications within 4 seconds. Adding or removing a label added or removed an app at once.
  • A brace glob in a git files path (apps/{paperless,opencloud}.yaml, built from an annotation) matched nothing. One generator per optional app, whose clusters selector also requires a label homelab/app-<name>: "true", works.
  • index .metadata.annotations "key" yields "" for a missing key, silently. Sprig's required is not available.
  • Dot access with missingkey=error makes the ApplicationSet report ErrorOccurred for a missing key and keep its existing Applications unchanged. This only works for keys without / or -, e.g. .metadata.annotations.backupS3Url.
  • A Secret that the selector no longer matches makes the ApplicationSet delete every Application it generated. root's preserveResourcesOnDeletion keeps their resources, but every Application goes until the Secret is back.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• set-revision.sh, set-sandbox-apps.sh and set-backup-endpoint.sh go. The bootstrap no longer rewrites rendered manifests.
  • The bootstrap writes Argo CD's in-cluster cluster Secret before it applies the ApplicationSets:
  • Name in-cluster, namespace argocd.
  • Label argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster.
  • server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, name in-cluster. Existing destination.name: in-cluster keeps working.
  • One label that every homelab clusters generator selects on. The name is the builder's choice, e.g. homelab/environment: <env>.
  • Annotations, camelCase without a prefix, so templates read them with dot access and fail closed:
    • repository: the homelab repository Argo CD syncs: GitHub for the sandbox and the testbed, the seed or ops/homelab on Forgejo for production.
    • revision: sandbox, testbed or master, or the commit just dev --revision asks for.
    • backupS3Url: production's R2 endpoint. Elsewhere it is an empty string, so the key always exists. The sandbox's endpoint stays in system/velero/values-dev.yaml.
  • Label homelab/app-<name>: "true" for each sandbox optional app that just dev asks for, and none otherwise.
  • The ApplicationSets read the Secret:
  • Every homelab generator and source in root and apps, in every values file, takes repoURL and revision / targetRevision from the annotations.
  • Velero's location already falls back to values-dev.yaml's endpoint when backupS3Url is empty (default .Values.backupStorageLocation.s3Url).
  • The outer matrix is clusters × the existing matrix (git directories or files × git files config.json).
  • global.backupS3Url comes from the annotation in every environment.
  • The sandbox's apps gets one extra generator per optional app, selecting on its label.
  • Other repositories' revisions, such as app-template's chart, stay literal.
  • values-seed.yaml keeps only what differs on a first install:
  • The metrics and ServiceMonitors stay off, because there are no Prometheus CRDs yet (TestArgoCDServiceMonitors).
  • It no longer restates the generators, the sources or the seed placeholder.
  • bootstrap.sh drops the sed and its placeholder check.
  • choose-values.sh keeps its decision but returns more:
  • The seed stays until Argo CD's credential reads ops/homelab's master, and never comes back once switched.
  • It also returns the repository to write: seed_repository or the Forgejo URL.
  • It reads "already switched" from the cluster Secret's repository annotation instead of root's generator.
  • A cluster from before 14g has no Secret yet. Falling back to root's generator there keeps production from going back to the seed. Whether that fallback is needed is left to the builder: production has never been deployed.
  • config.json stays in git and is read through the git files generator as now. Domain, time zone and addresses are public or private-LAN data: the domain is in DNS and Certificate Transparency logs, and the addresses are RFC 1918. Moving them into the Secret would hide nothing, since OpenTofu reads them from the same file, and would break scripts/env-values' offline rendering.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Moving config.json's settings into the Secret (see above).
  • Changing which components or apps each environment syncs: values-dev and values-testbed keep their allow-lists.
  • Letting Argo CD manage itself again, or managing the cluster Secret with Argo CD.
  • applicationsSync: create-update or any other ApplicationSet deletion policy change: an app directory removed from git still deletes its Application.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
These would make the step a failure even if it works:

  • A missing annotation silently rendering an empty repository or revision. Dot access with missingkey=error must cover repository and revision.
  • Anything that can leave the cluster Secret absent or unmatched on a running cluster, since every Application would be deleted:
  • OpenTofu destroying it.
  • The bootstrap applying ApplicationSets before it.
  • A label rename without both sides in one change.
  • Production going back to the seed after it switched to Forgejo, including across this upgrade.
  • The account id of R2 in git (it stays in OpenTofu's state).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Order: the bootstrap must write the Secret before the ApplicationSets on a new cluster, and before any ApplicationSet whose selector changed.
  • Ownership: the Secret is written with the same server-side apply and field manager as the rest of the bootstrap unless the builder finds a reason not to. Nothing else owns it.
  • Rule: charts and app files hold no IP address or domain (scripts/check-env-config checks this). A repository URL in values files is fine, as now.
  • Readers that follow the generators' shape must follow the new shape:
  • scripts/check-env-config: every ApplicationSet reads its environment's config.json.
  • cli/internal/guard/proof.go: the testbed's list, from values-testbed.yaml's generators.
  • cli/internal/scope/charts.go: the app-template pin.
  • infra/testbed/release-paths.yaml, which lists values-seed.yaml.
  • renovate.json5's app-template regex.
  • scripts/env-values, which bootstrap.sh and scripts/render-chart call. It resolves every {{ .x }} in valuesObject against config.json, so it must also resolve the Secret's keys, offline as well (render-chart has no cluster).
  • test/e2e/testbed_test.go's testbedList, which reads generators[0].matrix.generators[0].
  • Where values come from:
  • The sandbox's and the testbed's repository annotation comes from config.json's seed_repository, the GitHub repository. This was my call: the rule keeps settings that depend on where the homelab runs in config.json, and step 16 names that repository as configuration.
  • The values files' literal GitHub URL goes, since every homelab repoURL reads the annotation.
  • choose-values.sh no longer finds the Forgejo URL in values.yaml's generator. It gets it from the module, a variable set by production's unit.
  • Re-applies: OpenTofu re-applies when the revision, the optional apps or the backup endpoint change, as now. The builder decides whether the Secret gets its own resource, so these changes skip re-rendering the chart, or stays in bootstrap.sh.
  • Existing clusters: the sandbox and the testbed are rebuilt freely. An existing sandbox gets the Secret on the next just dev, which re-applies because the chart files change.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Offline (test/offline), replacing TestArgoCDRevision, TestArgoCDBackupEndpoint and TestSetSandboxApps:
  • The rendered ApplicationSets take every homelab repoURL / revision / targetRevision from the Secret's annotations, in every values file. Other repositories stay literal.
  • Optional apps come only through their labelled generators.
  • The bootstrap writes the Secret before the ApplicationSets.
  • The Secret carries every annotation the templates read.
  • TestArgoCDChooseValues keeps its cases and checks the repository returned. The "switched" case reads the annotation.
  • TestArgoCDServiceMonitors still holds for the seed.
  • e2e (test/e2e), labelled sandbox and argocd (and testbed if it fits):
  • The cluster Secret exists with its keys and its selector label.
  • Every Application's homelab source uses its annotations' repository and revision.
  • Sandbox runs:
  • just dev with and without --apps paperless, and --revision <sha>.
  • just dev-fresh once, for a first install with the Secret.
  • Testbed: just testbed once, since its values file changes.
  • Production: not deployed. The seed switch stays rendered and tested offline only, as now.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• The selector label's name and value.
  • Whether the Secret is its own terraform_data or part of bootstrap.sh.
  • Whether choose-values.sh needs the fallback for a cluster from before 14g.
  • How values-dev.yaml and values-testbed.yaml restate the nested matrix, since Helm replaces lists as before.
  • Where the docs change: docs/installation/sandbox.md, docs/how-to-guides/ci.md, the architecture page on Argo CD if one describes the bootstrap, and CLAUDE.md:
  • The Sandbox section names set-revision.sh and set-sandbox-apps.sh.
  • Roadmap step 14g is marked done, and so is 14f-2.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Steps 15a to 15f make an attack hard to start: detection in CI, policy, security logs, scans, the supply chain and the public surface. Nothing yet sees what happens inside a running container once something gets in: a shell nobody opened, a binary that was not in the image, a read of /etc/shadow, a call to the API server with a stolen token. Step 15g adds that last layer, following common security practice (the OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 checked in chat on 2026-10-25 lists runtime detection), before the first production deploy.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Falco, not Tetragon. Falco is a detection product (CNCF graduated) with a maintained ruleset mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Tetragon's strengths are enforcement and observability, and its detections are TracingPolicies we would write ourselves. This fork also dropped Cilium in step 6a.
  • Detection only, no blocking. A wrong kill stops a real workload, and one person watches this homelab. Woodpecker's Buildah steps, for one, run binaries created after the container started. Blocking is step 15g-2: Falco Talon responds, either deleting the pod (its controller recreates it from the image) or isolating it with a NetworkPolicy (kept for forensics). It covers a short list of rules with almost no false positives:
  • a reverse shell;
  • the execution of a binary that is not in the image (drift), outside Woodpecker's steps;
  • a crypto miner;
  • a container escape (a kernel module load, ptrace of another process, a write to /proc/sys, a host mount).

15g-2 waits for production's numbers: some weeks of detection only. This mirrors 15b-1 (Audit) then 15b-2 (Enforce). - Alerts follow 15c's path. - Falco writes JSON events to stdout, and Alloy already ships pod logs to Loki (job="pods", namespace="falco"). - Loki's ruler (system/loki/files/falco-rules.yaml, beside the audit and public-scan rules) alerts through Alertmanager to ntfy and Telegram. - No falcosidekick: it would be one more component for a path that already exists. - Priorities. - Falco logs from warning up. - error and above alert: critical, alert and emergency as severity critical, error as warning. - warning shows only on the dashboard Security. - No download at runtime. falcoctl's install and follow are off, so no egress is opened for Falco and every rule is pinned like every other version. - Rules come from the Falco image's stable ruleset, plus the rules 15g-2's list will need where they are not in the stable set. Those are vendored with their ruleset version, so 15g already reports what 15g-2 would act on. - Accepted events are Falco exceptions or overrides in system/falco/values.yaml, each with its reason, like the Trivy Operator's accepted findings. Expected sources include Woodpecker's steps, istio-cni, Velero's data mover, the rotation and backup Jobs, and kubectl exec by the tests. - A silent detector is a failure. - Falco's metrics are scraped (a ServiceMonitor). - FalcoNotRunning alerts when its DaemonSet does not run on every node (kube-state-metrics). - FalcoEventsDropped alerts on dropped syscall events (its drop counters). - FalcoStalled alerts when a node's Falco stops counting syscall events (its event counter does not rise for some minutes) or Prometheus cannot scrape it. Falco has no heartbeat log line, so this uses its metrics, not Loki (my call: a quiet node logs nothing at warning, so a log-based alert could not tell quiet from dead). - Runs everywhere, the sandbox included by default. Proving it with the whole platform shows whether it slows the suite. - Its requests and limits are small in values-local.yaml, as Kyverno's and the Trivy Operator's are. - They are measured during just dev-fresh, and the guide records the measurement. - If the sandbox runs out of memory, the fallbacks, in order, are: lower Falco's limits, scrape less in the sandbox, make Falco optional like paperless. Retention would not help: Prometheus's and Loki's memory follows active series and ingestion, not days kept. - The testbed runs it too, as a layer of its own on top of layers 1 and 2 (what production has under it), measured against the testbed's bar. Production's nodes run NixOS with linuxPackages_latest and the sandbox runs WSL's kernel, so only the testbed proves the modern eBPF driver on NixOS's kernel. With no Loki there, its spec reads the Falco pods' logs. - The testbed has no Kyverno or monitoring, so its values switch off the PolicyException and the ServiceMonitor: Argo CD refuses a whole sync that holds a PolicyException whose CRD is missing. - If the layer breaks the bar, VM sizes stay as they are. Falco goes to the testbed's not_run, the driver's proof on NixOS is one recorded run by hand (TestbedFalco alone on a fresh testbed), and "Before the first production deploy" in CLAUDE.md says so (my call: the bar protects this workstation, and the driver's load is what needs NixOS). - The sandbox's node shares WSL's kernel with the workstation and every Docker container, and the probe sees all of them, never Windows (WSL 2 is a VM of its own). The sandbox keeps every event and alert as production does: what the workstation's own processes trigger stays in the sandbox's Loki. Falco's metadata knows only the k3d node's containerd, so those events carry no Kubernetes namespace. - Only the clean-baseline check counts events with a Kubernetes namespace, so the workstation's activity during a run cannot fail it. - A workstation process that turns out noisy is accepted in values-dev.yaml with its reason, never in values.yaml. - Production alerts from the first deploy. Its workloads that the sandbox never runs (cloudflared, wireguard, tailscale, Matrix, jellyfin, Ceph's daemons, kube-vip, Renovate's initContainer) may fire rules the sandbox never saw. - Alerts are grouped by rule and namespace, so one noisy rule is one notification. - "Before the first production deploy" adds a review of Falco's events in the first days, with each one accepted (with its reason) or fixed. - No silence and no dashboard-only period: a detector nobody hears does not detect (my call).

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
• system/falco: a wrapper chart of falcosecurity/falco, at the latest stable chart and app version, pinned (chart 9.2.2 and Falco 0.45.2 when this was written; check upstream when building). It runs in namespace falco:
  • the modern_ebpf driver: CO-RE, so no kernel module or headers. WSL's 6.18 kernel has BTF, and the NixOS nodes' kernels do too;
  • container metadata from containerd's socket. The chart's container collector already lists k3s's /run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock; no k8s-metacollector;
  • json_output, with priority: warning;
  • base_syscalls set if the measured CPU calls for it.
  • Kubernetes plumbing:
  • The namespace is privileged in Argo CD's templatePatch. It stays in the mesh like Loki's (Alloy) and kured's: Falco takes no webhook call and needs no host network, so only Prometheus's scrape needs its allow.
  • A PolicyException with homelab/reason (privileged, hostPID, host mounts).
  • An AuthorizationPolicy allow for Prometheus on the metrics port (scripts/check-mesh-policies).
  • Egress: none beyond the default.
  • system/loki/files/falco-rules.yaml: the alert rules above, from Falco's JSON fields (priority, rule, output_fields: container, pod, namespace). Grouped by rule and namespace, so one noisy rule is one notification.
  • Dashboard Security: a panel of Falco events by priority, rule and namespace.
  • Wiring: Argo CD's lists in the sandbox, testbed and production values; test/scopes.yaml (a new label falco, and system/falco/** mapped to it); the guide docs/how-to-guides/runtime-detection.md (reading an event, accepting one with a reason, what to do on an alert); CLAUDE.md (15g done, 15g-2 planned, "Before the first production deploy" naming what only the sandbox and the testbed proved).
  • No secret is created: nothing to add to the rotation catalog.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
• Offline: the render passes scripts/ci-check (policy, mesh, env-config, backup groups: no PVC). An offline test checks that falcoctl's artifact install and follow are off, the driver is modern_ebpf, and every accepted exception carries a reason.
  • Sandbox, e2e spec Falco (labels sandbox, falco):
  • in a namespace of its own, it runs a pod, opens a shell in it and reads /etc/shadow;
  • it proves the events reach Loki with their rule names, and that the deployed alert expressions select them. The Trivy Operator's spec uses the same pattern.
