  • Sandbox, clean baseline: after a full suite on a fresh sandbox, no error-or-above event remains that is neither the spec's own nor accepted.
  • Testbed, spec TestbedFalco (labels testbed, falco): Falco is ready on all three nodes, its driver loaded, and it logs an event a test pod triggers.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Blocking or responding (15g-2).
  • Tetragon, falcosidekick, k8s-metacollector.
  • Falco's Kubernetes audit plugin: 15c reads the audit log.
  • Falco on the workstation.
  • Shortening Prometheus's or Loki's retention in the sandbox.
  • The Localhost seccomp profile for Woodpecker's Buildah steps that would allow seccomp-default (15d's deferred minor): its own step, 15h.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Killing or restarting a real workload because of a rule.
  • An alert stream so noisy that alerts get ignored. The baseline must be clean before merge.
  • A detector that stops without anyone knowing.
  • Rules or drivers fetched from the internet at runtime.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Exact rule names, the accepted exceptions, and FalcoStalled's window.
  • The vendored ruleset files and their versions.
  • Requests and limits from the measurement.
  • Whether base_syscalls is needed.

docs.title: Step 15h: a seccomp profile for Buildah, and seccomp-default on
Why
docs.text:
kube-bench's 4.2.14 asks for the kubelet's seccomp-default: a pod that names no seccomp profile then gets RuntimeDefault instead of none. Step 15d left it off (docs/how-to-guides/cluster-scan.md, deferred minor 15d → 15h). With the flag on, TestWoodpecker failed: Woodpecker's step pods name no profile, and RuntimeDefault refuses the unshare Buildah's chroot isolation needs to build an image.

Every workload of ours already sets RuntimeDefault itself (policy, 15b-1). Two kinds of pod still run with no seccomp filter:

  • Woodpecker's step pods, which run whatever a pipeline author writes.
  • Pods that nothing of ours renders: k3s's own pods in kube-system, and Istio's generated Gateways (deferred minor 15b).

The step pods matter most: they run code from people other than the admin.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• seccomp-default is on in the kubelet of every environment: the nodes (infra/_modules/metal) and the sandbox's k3d node.
  • Buildah steps keep working. They get a Localhost profile (homelab/buildah.json), which is RuntimeDefault plus only the syscalls Buildah's chroot isolation needs inside a user namespace.
  • Every other step pod gets RuntimeDefault, as all other pods do.
  • A pipeline author does nothing. A pipeline copied from docs/how-to-guides/woodpecker.md builds unchanged, with no backend_options line.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• The Security Profiles Operator. It would be one more component running all the time just to place one file on the nodes.
  • Profiles for other workloads, or profiles tighter than RuntimeDefault.
  • Buildah's other isolation modes (oci, rootless). Only --isolation chroot with vfs is supported, as today.
  • The Gateways' own profile. That stays deferred minor 15b, for 15b-2; seccomp-default covers it at runtime anyway.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A failure must never widen access. If the mutation does not happen (Kyverno down: its webhooks are failurePolicy: Ignore), the step pod gets RuntimeDefault and the build fails. It must never run unconfined.
  • A pipeline cannot choose Unconfined itself. Pod Security baseline, enforced on namespace woodpecker, refuses it. Check this; do not assume it.
  • A pipeline cannot give the Buildah profile to another image either. Woodpecker lets a step set backend_options.kubernetes.securityContext.seccompProfile, Localhost included, and no *_ALLOW_FROM_STEP setting turns that off. Without a guard, once the file is on every node, any step could ask for it.
  • No syscall goes into the profile because it "might" be needed. Each addition is one that Buildah was seen to need.

docs.title: Decided
docs.text:
1. The flag. - --kubelet-arg=seccomp-default=true goes in infra/_modules/k3d/k3d.yaml and in infra/_modules/metal/flake/profiles/k3s-server.nix. - The comments saying "not seccomp-default" are replaced. - TestScanHardeningFlags asserts the flag is present, where it now asserts it is absent.

2. The profile. A JSON file in the repository: infra/_modules/metal/flake/seccomp/buildah.json. - It is shipped the way audit-policy.yaml is: one file for the nodes and k3d. - On the nodes, NixOS places it under the kubelet's seccomp root as homelab/buildah.json, with tmpfiles or similar, so pods reference localhostProfile: homelab/buildah.json. - On k3d, infra/_modules/k3d/main.tf mounts it at the same path in the server node, as it mounts the audit policy. Changing the mount rebuilds the sandbox's cluster: one just dev-fresh. - Its base is the RuntimeDefault profile of the containerd embedded in k3s v1.37.1. The sandbox (rancher/k3s:v1.37.1-k3s1) and the nodes (nixpkgs' k3s_1_37) run the same k3s minor, and so the same containerd; check the patch versions match. The file records the k3s and containerd versions it came from. - The additions are found by running buildah build --isolation chroot (the TestWoodpecker pipeline) under the base profile and adding each refused syscall, or argument condition, until the build passes. The spec and the profile's commit list each addition with the step that needed it. - Expected additions are the namespace and mount calls that RuntimeDefault allows only with CAP_SYS_ADMIN, such as unshare, mount, umount2, pivot_root and setns. The measurement decides.

3. The mutation. (Plan: a native MutatingAdmissionPolicy, admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1, served by k3s 1.37.1, in platform/woodpecker beside the guard; in-tree, so it needs no webhook and no Kyverno. What follows about Kyverno is superseded.) A Kyverno mutating policy, in system/kyverno beside the existing policies or in platform/woodpecker. The builder picks; prefer Kyverno 1.19's CEL MutatingPolicy if it mutates on admission without the background controller (still off). - It matches pods in namespace woodpecker that Woodpecker's agent creates for steps (by the labels the Kubernetes backend sets; read them off a live step pod), with a container whose image repository is quay.io/buildah/stable. - It sets the pod-level seccompProfile to {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: homelab/buildah.json}. - It does not override a profile the pod or container already sets: a step whose author sets RuntimeDefault keeps it. - The image match is accepted as is. Anyone who picks the Buildah image gets the profile, whatever they run with it. The profile only adds namespace syscalls, in a pod already in its own user namespace (WOODPECKER_BACKEND_K8S_USER_NAMESPACES), unprivileged. Today the same pod runs with no filter at all. - scripts/ci-check policy still passes. If it runs the Kyverno CLI on renders, the mutation gets a CLI test there too.

4. The guard (my call, from the builder check). A native ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with its binding, enforced now (validationActions: [Deny]), not a Kyverno rule: - It applies to pods in namespace woodpecker. - It refuses a pod or container that names localhostProfile: homelab/buildah.json unless every container and init container in the pod uses an image from repository quay.io/buildah/stable. - It refuses any other Localhost profile there too: only this one exists. - It is in-tree, so the API server evaluates it itself (failurePolicy: Fail, no webhook). It holds while Kyverno is down and does not wait for 15b-2's Enforce. Kyverno stays in Audit for everything else. - If the mutation and the guard disagree about what a Buildah step pod is, the step fails. Test the agent's real step pod, including the clone step and any init containers the backend adds. - Its home is beside the mutation.

5. Falco (15g). Buildah's unshare under the new profile must not add Critical or Error events to the sandbox's clean baseline. If it does, accept it in accepted, with the reason, narrowed like the memfd entry (namespace, image, process).

docs.title: Proofs
docs.text:
• Offline:
  • TestScanHardeningFlags: the flag is on in both files.
  • The profile is valid JSON, its default action is an error action, and it lists the base's syscalls plus the documented additions.
  • The policy matches a Buildah step pod and leaves a non-Buildah step pod, and a pod that sets its own profile, unchanged (a Kyverno CLI test or a rendered fixture).
  • The guard's CEL is checked against the same fixtures, if a tool can evaluate it offline. Otherwise the sandbox spec proves it.
  • Sandbox (Ginkgo, test/e2e):
  • Woodpecker builds and pushes as today, with seccomp-default on.
  • A new spec shows the other side:
    • a non-Buildah step, or a pod shaped like one in namespace woodpecker, cannot unshare under RuntimeDefault;
    • the Buildah step pod's spec carries the Localhost profile;
    • a pod asking for Unconfined in woodpecker is refused by Pod Security;
    • a non-Buildah pod asking for homelab/buildah.json in woodpecker is refused by the guard.
  • Labels and test/scopes.yaml: a change to the profile, the k3d mount, or the policy runs the Woodpecker specs.
  • Full suite (just dev-fresh): every pod without its own profile now has RuntimeDefault. That includes k3s's kube-system pods, the Gateways and every Woodpecker step. Nothing else may break.
  • Testbed, once by hand:
  • The profile file is at its path on every node.
  • The kubelet runs with the flag.
  • A pod with the Localhost profile can unshare -U while a RuntimeDefault one cannot.
  • A plain Buildah pod under the profile builds a small image with --isolation chroot and vfs (my call, from the builder check). Production's newer kernel (7.0 or later) may take other syscall paths than WSL's 6.18, such as clone3 or the new mount API. Any syscall it needs there is added, and recorded as "needed on NixOS's kernel".
  • Woodpecker itself does not run on the testbed.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• docs/how-to-guides/cluster-scan.md: 4.2.14 is fixed.
  • docs/how-to-guides/woodpecker.md: Buildah steps get the profile by themselves, and other images cannot unshare.
  • CLAUDE.md: roadmap 15h done, and the 15d text that says "not seccomp-default".
  • deferred-minors.md: remove the 15d row, and add this PR's own rows.
  • The production list in CLAUDE.md: a containerd bump on the nodes can change RuntimeDefault. The profile was derived from one version, so review it when k3s's containerd changes its default profile.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Where the policy lives and its exact kind.
  • The tmpfiles mechanism on NixOS.
  • The precise label selector for step pods.
  • How the syscall additions are measured: audit-mode profile (SCMP_ACT_LOG), strace, or trial and error.

docs.title: Step 12b-1: production's nodes on the hardware
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-11, with a PXE spike on the hardware the same day. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review. Builds on 12a (docs/installation/testbed.md, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-02-testbed-design.md, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-04-power-design.md): the same node flake (infra/_modules/metal), nixie, lab cluster enroll|kubeconfig|upgrade|shutdown|startup, now on real machines.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Step 12b brings production up on the three mini PCs, split so each part changes one thing (user):

  • 12b-1 (this spec): the nodes. NixOS installed from the network, one k3s cluster of three servers behind the API's VIP, and the machine-level proofs that only real hardware gives: the disks' fsync latency, a node going away, every node losing power at once.
  • 12b-2: the platform through Argo CD (Ceph, Istio, OpenBao, Kanidm, monitoring, backups to R2), with the power cut repeated with Ceph before any real data.
  • 12b-3: every app, the public path (Cloudflare Tunnel), the first just infra deploy production, then lab backup enable.

Production is "ok" when every app in the plan runs there, including those the sandbox and the testbed never ran for lack of resources (Matrix, Jellyfin, cloudflared, WireGuard, Tailscale, Renovate, the blog) (user). Immich, the teaching app (step 18), a NAS or a second disk come after (user).

docs.title: The hardware (user, read by the spike)
docs.text:
All three are cabled to the TP-Link Archer C64 (192.168.0.0/24, its DHCP .100–.249), on mains power, no UPS.

Node Machine CPU RAM Disk MAC (eno1) homelab-1 (192.168.0.11, init_host) HP EliteDesk 800 G4 DM 35W i5-8500T, 6 cores 16 GB /dev/nvme0n1, SK hynix BC901 256 GB 38:22:e2:2c:dc:35 homelab-2 (192.168.0.12) HP EliteDesk 800 G3 DM 35W i5-7500T, 4 cores 16 GB /dev/nvme0n1, Samsung MZAL8256HDJD 256 GB 10:62:e5:16:d2:ca homelab-3 (192.168.0.13) HP EliteDesk 800 G3 DM 35W i5-7500T, 4 cores 16 GB /dev/nvme0n1, Samsung MZAL8256HDJD 256 GB 10:e7:c6:0f:63:a0

Names, addresses and init_host are (Claude's call): the G4 starts the cluster because it carries it alone for its first minutes; afterwards the three are equal servers. Both disk models are DRAM-less OEM NVMe drives without power-loss protection.

One disk per node stays for now; a second disk is decided together with the NAS idea (user). The layout stays upstream's (infra/_modules/metal/flake/disks.nix): ESP 1 GB, root 64 GB (NixOS, k3s, etcd, images, logs), the rest (173.5 GB, measured) a raw partition rook-data for Ceph in 12b-2. No LVM: Ceph takes a raw block device.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• just infra deploy production's metal path, i.e. the unit infra/production/metal (written in this step, like infra/testbed/metal), installs the three machines from the network with nixie, enrolls them into one k3s cluster and writes infra/production/kubeconfig.yaml. In this step it runs alone (terragrunt apply in that unit), not the whole deploy.
  • The nodes resolve names quickly despite the ISP modem's DNS interception (below), and so do pods through CoreDNS.
  • The fio numbers that decide whether etcd and Ceph can share one disk.
  • A node going away moves the API's VIP; the cluster keeps answering.
  • Every node cut at once comes back by itself.
  • kube-bench on the hardware (just testbed-scan's Job, on production's kubeconfig), the before-production list's item.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Ceph, Argo CD and everything above k3s: 12b-2 (Claude's call: production's Argo CD syncs the whole platform at once, with no layer allow-list like the testbed's, and adding one only for this step would fork production's config).
  • A UPS (its own step) and a second disk or NAS.
  • Secure Boot with signed boot (lanzaboote): later, if wanted; with disks unencrypted it protects little.
  • A BIOS administrator password: none (user agreed after the trade-off). Anyone at the machine can take the NVMe out and read it (LUKS set aside in 15d), so the password guards little and a forgotten HP password is hard to reset.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Wiping a disk that is not one of these three: nixie serves PXE on the home LAN, so only hosts.json's MACs may be installed, and the run is started by hand.
  • Leaving the workstation's Hyper-V firewall open after the install.
  • A docs line implying the testbed proved the hardware path, or that the cut proves Ceph (12b-2 repeats it).

docs.title: 1. Before the install: the BIOS, on every machine
docs.text:
A checklist in the installation docs, done by hand:

  • BIOS updated to HP's latest for the model (G4: Q21, G3: P21). Found on homelab-3: P21 Ver. 02.15 (2018-01-31), which kept no change made in F10 (Secure Boot, Power State); updated to 02.50 (2024-07-14), it kept them.
  • Secure Boot off ("Legacy Support Disable and Secure Boot Disable"): nixie's iPXE is unsigned and the firmware refused it ("Selected boot image did not authenticate"). homelab-1 and homelab-2 had it off already.
  • Network boot (UEFI IPv4) and Wake-on-LAN on (user: done), Wake-on-LAN booting to the network and the NVMe first in the normal boot order (decision 6).
  • After Power Loss: Previous State (Last State), so a cut machine boots when power returns (12a-3).
  • F12 starts a network boot by hand on these HP machines, if Wake-on-LAN does not (the startup menu ignored one USB keyboard).

docs.title: 2. PXE from the workstation (spike 2026-11-11)
docs.text:
nixie runs in WSL (mirrored networking) on the laptop, which reaches the Archer over Wi-Fi. It answers as ProxyDHCP beside the Archer's DHCP (UDP 67, 69, 4011; TCP 80 and its API on 5000). WSL sees no LAN broadcast until Hyper-V firewall rules for WSL (VM creator {40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}) allow those ports inbound; with them, a ProxyDHCP server booted the flake's installer into RAM on homelab-1 and homelab-2, about 500 MB over Wi-Fi in under two minutes.

  • The docs give the two New-NetFirewallHyperVRule commands (UDP 67, 69, 4011; TCP 80, 5000) before the install and Remove-NetFirewallHyperVRule after it, run by the person in an administrator PowerShell.
  • nixie gets the laptop's LAN address (--address), as the testbed gives it the bridge's.
  • The person starts the run; nixie wakes the machines and installs them in parallel (the testbed goes one at a time only because three installs at once ran WSL out of memory; real machines install from their own memory).

docs.title: 3. The disk path
docs.text: The disk's path goes in the environment's config.json (a field such as disk, /dev/nvme0n1 for production), which disks.nix reads after a node's own hostConfig.disk and before the default /dev/sda. hosts.json stays nixie's file: nixie keeps only mac_address, ip and machine_id_hash when it rewrites it, so any other field there would be lost. This settles the before-production note about disks other than /dev/sda. The docs' hosts.json example, which shows disk, is corrected.

docs.title: 4. DNS (Claude's call)
docs.text:
The ISP's ZTE modem intercepts every UDP/53 query leaving the LAN: negative answers come back REFUSED after 6–13 s. The Archer (192.168.0.1) forwards over DoH and answers in about 50 ms. network.nix gives the nodes 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 over UDP, and k3s's CoreDNS forwards to the node's resolvers, so both nodes and pods would hit the 6-second answers.

  • The nodes' DNS comes from config.json (network.dns, a list): production names the Archer (["192.168.0.1"]). Without the field the nodes keep today's servers, so the testbed is unchanged (its NAT has no interception).
  • CoreDNS reads the node's resolv.conf, so it follows.
  • The proof is a measurement: an NXDOMAIN and an AAAA-less name answer in under a second from a node and from a pod.
  • Fallback, if the Archer's single DoH upstream proves unreliable: DNS over TLS from the nodes (systemd-resolved) and CoreDNS forwarding over TLS. Not built now.

docs.title: 5. The production SSH key
docs.text: infra/production/metal/authorized_keys gets production's own key: a new ed25519 key with a passphrase, made by the person (ssh-keygen), loaded into the agent (ssh-add) for the install, lab cluster and the specs. It replaces the placeholder.

docs.title: 6. Boot order, the install record, and never reinstalling a live node (Claude's call)
docs.text:
• Boot order (upstream's option 2, docs/installation/production/prerequisites.md):
  • Wake-on-LAN boots from the network (HP: S4/S5 Wake on LAN = "Boot to Network"), and the normal boot order puts the NVMe first. nixie wakes the machines it has not recorded and installs them with no one pressing F12. A machine switched on by its button, or by power returning after a cut, boots its NixOS.
  • A woken node that finds no nixie must fall back to its NVMe. The VIP spec below wakes a node and checks that it does, which is the thorough test upstream asks for.
  • The install record (upstream's way): nixie writes each machine's machine_id_hash into the repository's infra/production/metal/hosts.json, and the person commits it after the install. infra/_modules/metal already leaves that field out of the flake's input. A recorded host is skipped even when it is unreachable, and nixie does not start when every host is recorded, so the record in git is what keeps a live node from being reinstalled, from any checkout.
  • The testbed keeps its record in .state/testbed/ (scripts/testbed-nixie), because its VMs are reinstalled often and a commit per reinstall would mean nothing. Production installs rarely, and its record must outlive the workstation.
  • Production therefore needs no copy of hosts.json; the disk's path lives in config.json (decision 3).
  • Reinstalling a node is deliberate: delete its machine_id_hash, commit, then run.

docs.title: 7. Production's SSH host keys (Claude's call)
docs.text: The keys are trusted on first contact, as on the testbed, but only during the install and only for hosts.json's addresses on the home LAN. The accepted risk is someone on the LAN impersonating a node in the minutes between the install and the first contact. Generating host keys ahead of time and installing them with nixos-anywhere would add key material to keep and rotate, which this does not justify. The docs say how to check a key's fingerprint on the machine's console later (ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub).

docs.title: 8. What runs on the cluster in this step
docs.text: k3s with this repository's flags, kube-vip for the API's VIP (192.168.0.10), nothing from Argo CD. Production's config.json has no slow_control_plane: the hardware runs k3s's defaults. That is the point of measuring here.

docs.title: Proofs
docs.text:
• The install: terragrunt apply in infra/production/metal installs the three nodes and writes the kubeconfig, and all three are Ready. The first run is the RED: nothing is installed.
  • The nodes: the testbed's node specs run on production: the nodes, secrets encrypted in etcd, and the seccomp profile's file and flag. They are labelled testbed today. The builder decides how they run against production: shared specs labelled for both, or production specs reusing the same helpers.
  • The VIP moving (Claude's call): production's version of TestbedVIPMoves stops a node over SSH, and Wake-on-LAN from the workstation starts it again. That proves Wake-on-LAN over the laptop's Wi-Fi, a before-production item.
  • If the node does not wake, the spec fails and names Wake-on-LAN as the cause; the person presses the power button.
  • It and the power cut stop nodes, so they carry a label that just test e2e --env production never selects by default (for example hardware-proof). Once 12b-2 and 12b-3 hold real data, a routine run against production must never power off a node.
  • DNS: the measurement above, as a spec.
  • fio, by hand and recorded in the docs, per node:
  • etcd's pattern (fio --rw=write --ioengine=sync --fdatasync=1 --bs=2300 --size=22m), whose 99th percentile fdatasync must stay under 10 ms;
  • sequential and random 4k throughput on the rook-data partition, before Ceph takes it.

A node over 10 ms is a finding: 12b-2 then decides between etcd's tuning, a second disk, or Ceph's limits before sharing. - kube-bench: just testbed-scan's Job against production, its FAILs against .cluster-scan-accepted.yaml. - A power cut: the person switches off the three machines' power strip, and switches it on again. Every node boots by itself (Last State), etcd and the API at its VIP come back, and lab cluster sees three Ready nodes. Measured: how long. Acknowledged writes are checked in 12b-2, with Ceph and a database.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• docs/installation/production/:
  • the BIOS checklist;
  • the Hyper-V firewall commands;
  • the SSH key;
  • the disk's path in config.json, and hosts.json's committed record;
  • the DNS field;
  • the fio numbers.
  • docs/concepts/pxe-boot.md: PXE from WSL (mirrored) and the firewall rules.
  • CLAUDE.md:
  • 12b-1 done;
  • the before-production items this settles: PXE on a real LAN with a router's DHCP, Wake-on-LAN, UEFI boot order, the disk path, kube-bench on hardware;
  • what stays for 12b-2.

docs.title: BIOS as found ready (2026-11-11)
docs.text: All three on HP's latest BIOS the person found, with Secure Boot off (read from the installer: SecureBoot = 0): homelab-1 Q21 Ver. 02.33.00 (2026-02-03), homelab-2 and homelab-3 P21 Ver. 02.50 (2024-07-14). After Power Loss, Wake-on-LAN and the boot order were set as decision 1 says.

docs.title: Matrix on tuwunel
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-12. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review. A step of its own between 12b-2 and 12b-3: Matrix is an app, so production deploys it only once the stage is all (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-12-production-platform-design.md). It must reach master before that switch, or production deploys the old Dendrite first.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Replace the only app chart, apps/matrix/ (Dendrite and Element Web from two third-party charts, the domain written in its values because neither chart templates it), with one app-template file like every other app. Upstream did the same (checked 2026-11-12): tuwunel and FluffyChat in apps/matrix.yaml. Dendrite is in maintenance mode.

What Matrix is for is not decided yet (user: a homelab to learn the apps), so the defaults are the safe ones, and each is one setting to change later.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• apps/matrix.yaml (app-template) (Claude's call, as upstream):
  • the server: tuwunel (ghcr.io/matrix-construct/tuwunel, the latest stable pinned) at matrix.<domain>;
  • the web client: FluffyChat (ghcr.io/krille-chan/fluffychat) at chat.<domain>;
  • the domain from global.baseDomain;
  • server_name matrix.<domain>, with .well-known for clients.
  • Sign-in through Kanidm only (Claude's call): tuwunel's identity provider with a KanidmOAuth2Client matrix in namespace matrix (PKCE). No password login, no open registration.
  • Federation off (Claude's call): allow_federation = false and no route for it, so only homelab accounts chat. The egress entry for 8448 goes.
  • In the sandbox too: in values-dev.yaml's apps list, with a spec proving an account signs in through Kanidm and sends a message. The old chart never ran there.
  • LAN only (user, 2026-11-12): chat. and matrix. on the LAN Gateway. matrix leaves 15f's public map (system/istio-system/values.yaml) and chat leaves system/public-scan's targets. From outside, use the VPN. Upstream publishes every host through its Tunnel's wildcard (Kanidm included); this fork's 15f does not. A public Matrix, with Kanidm public, is step 13's decision.
  • Backups: the data volume daily, as Matrix's was.
  • The old chart removed: apps/matrix/, its entries in scripts/check-backup-groups, test/scopes.yaml and the docs. CLAUDE.md's Portability line about Matrix's domain goes too.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Federation, bridges (Telegram, Messenger), voice and video calls (TURN): one setting or one step each, once wanted.
  • Moving data: production never ran the old Matrix.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Production deploying Dendrite before this reaches master. The stage stays platform until then.
  • A half-public Matrix. Today chat. (Element) is on Gateway public while the server is LAN-only, so the client loads from outside and can do nothing. Sign-in goes through Kanidm, which is LAN-only until step 13.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• tuwunel's cache and memory settings, the client's config.json, the resource limits. Upstream's are a starting point.
  • How the spec drives FluffyChat's or the API's SSO flow: the API (/_matrix/client/v3/login with m.login.sso) through Kanidm's form, as the other SSO specs do, is enough.

docs.title: Step 12b-2: production's platform, in stages
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-12. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review. Builds on 12b-1 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-11-production-nodes-design.md): three NixOS k3s servers on the HP mini PCs, nothing from Argo CD yet.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Bring production's platform up on the hardware before any app, so each layer is checked on its own:

  • Ceph on the nodes' rook-data partitions;
  • the mesh, the Gateways, OpenBao, Kanidm, Forgejo, monitoring and logs;
  • backups to R2.

Then repeat the power cut with real Ceph-backed data, before the apps and their data arrive in 12b-3.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A stage switch for a new cluster's first deploy (user: option B). infra/production/argocd writes a stage on Argo CD's cluster Secret (the GitOps Bridge pattern of 14g). With platform, the apps ApplicationSet generates nothing, while root deploys system/* and platform/*. With all, the default, everything deploys as today.
  • The first production deploy, with the stage set to platform, from a release on master (just infra deploy production: lab infra forgejo verify, apply, sync, push, the bootstrap). Argo CD switches from the seed to ops/homelab on Forgejo.
  • Ceph healthy on the hardware: three OSDs on rook-data (173.5 GB each), two replicas, and a volume written on one node read back on another.
  • The platform's specs pass on production: what the sandbox proves, run against production where the spec can (Smoke for the platform's apps, Argo CD, the mesh, OpenBao, Kanidm SSO, logs, monitoring).
  • An alert on etcd's disk, following 12b-1's finding (homelab-1's disk, accepted and watched (user)). It fires when a member's WAL fsync p99 stays over 10 ms, or when the leader changes too often.
  • A power cut with data: writes acknowledged before a cut of every node are intact after it, on Ceph. Forgejo's database, OpenBao's raft and a plain Ceph volume, like the sandbox's TestNodePowerCut.
  • Backups: Velero to R2 runs, lab backup enable is run once, and a restore of one volume from R2 is proven.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Apps (apps/*): 12b-3, by switching the stage to all.
  • Immich, the teaching app, a NAS, a second disk.
  • A UPS.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Lowering the stage from all to platform on a cluster that runs apps. The apps ApplicationSet would delete every Application, and with them their volumes. The bootstrap refuses it: the stage only moves forward.
  • Real data before the cut with data has passed. The person's own data waits for 12b-3.
  • A routine deploy that needs the stage set. Unset keeps the cluster's stage, a new cluster gets all, and only a person moves it.

docs.title: 1. The stage (user: B; details Claude's call)
docs.text:
• The variable: HOMELAB_PRODUCTION_STAGE=platform|all reaches infra/production/argocd as an input. cluster-secret.sh writes it on Secret argocd/in-cluster as the label homelab/stage (sandbox and testbed always all).
  • Unset, it keeps the label the cluster already carries; only a cluster with none gets all. So 12b-2's repeated deploys never move the stage by accident.
  • Generators: whatever deploys an app requires homelab/stage: all:
  • the apps ApplicationSet's clusters generator;
  • root's generator for apps/* directories (Matrix, the only app chart);
  • system/public-scan, whose targets are the public apps.

root's other directories keep their selector. - New clusters only: a label added to a selector would, on an existing cluster, delete its apps until the Secret carries it (CLAUDE.md's three-release rule). Production has no apps yet, and the sandbox's and testbed's bootstrap applies the Secret before the ApplicationSets. The plan proves the order on the sandbox, whose apps must survive the change. - Forward only: the bootstrap reads the label already on the cluster and refuses platform where it is all.

docs.title: 2. The release path
docs.text:
lab infra forgejo verify deploys only origin/master with checks passed and its pull request's sandbox passed, plus the testbed's proof mark (release_proof: testbed). So 12b-2 runs in this order:

  1. The branch (stage switch, etcd alert, specs).
  2. Its PR into dev.
  3. A dev → master release: a fresh sandbox, and just testbed for the mark.
  4. The deploy from master.

docs.title: 3. What the first deploy needs from the person
docs.text:
These come from the before-production list; the plan's install task asks for each:

  • Cloudflare:
  • check that the state on R2 is complete;
  • delete the local unencrypted copies (.state/production/cloudflare/terraform.tfstate and .pre-r2);
  • rotate the Cloudflare tokens they held (lab secrets rotate for OpenTofu's entries).
  • The GitHub App's key for Renovate (HOMELAB_GITHUB_APP_KEY). Without it, Renovate waits for its Secret, which is harmless.
  • Telegram's bot, optional: Alertmanager runs without it.
  • The state passphrase (~/.config/homelab/state.env), cf auth login, and the production SSH key in the agent.

docs.title: 4. The etcd alert (Claude's call)
docs.text:
Prometheus already scrapes etcd on every node (job kube-etcd, port 2381). The rules go beside the other node alerts in system/monitoring-system, warning severity:

  • EtcdSlowDisk: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket[10m])) > 0.010 for 1 hour, per instance.
  • EtcdLeaderChanges: more than 3 leader changes in an hour.

They tell when 12b-1's accepted disk must be fixed, by CLAUDE.md's options.

docs.title: 5. The cut with data (Claude's call)
docs.text:
A production spec labelled hardware-proof, like 12b-1's ProductionPowerCut.

  • Before the cut, it writes and records:
  • a marker in OpenBao;
  • a commit pushed to a scratch repository in Forgejo (its database on CloudNativePG, three instances on Ceph);
  • a file on a scratch Ceph volume, written with sync.
  • The person cuts the power strip (nodes and router) and switches it back on.
  • After the cut, it reads each back. Recovery is measured, as in 12a-3 and 12b-1: every node Ready, every pod ready, the data intact.

docs.title: 6. Public parts in the platform stage (Claude's call)
docs.text:
• cloudflared and external-dns deploy in 12b-2 with nothing behind them: their public targets are apps (blog, excalidraw, Element, ntfy), which come in 12b-3.
  • public-scan comes with the apps (decision 1): with no target it would only report failed scans.
  • Alerts: ntfy's path comes with the apps too, so until 12b-3 alerts reach Telegram (if set) and Alertmanager's page.

docs.title: 7. Side effects while the platform is brought up (Claude's call)
docs.text:
• Renovate: its GitHub App key is not given until 12b-3. Renovate waits for its Secret, harmlessly, and no daily pull request labelled sandbox starts a CI sandbox meanwhile.
  • kured: removed (found while building, 2026-11-12). Its sentinel was needs-restarting --reboothint, a RHEL tool NixOS lacks: the shell's 127, negated by !, says "reboot needed", so kured would reboot the nodes in turn forever. NixOS nodes change only through lab cluster upgrade, which already reboots when the kernel, initrd or modules change, drains first and waits for Ceph between nodes, which kured does not. Upstream keeps kured, with a NixOS sentinel comparing /run/booted-system to the system profile, because it rebuilds nodes by hand; this fork automates that rebuild. Bring kured back, with upstream's sentinel and a night window, only if nodes ever update outside lab cluster upgrade (system.autoUpgrade).
  • The rotation CronJob: stays suspended until a release builds lab's image, as today.

docs.title: 8. Accounts and test data on production (Claude's call)
docs.text:
• No test accounts or test clients on production. The SSO specs need the sandbox-only smoke client and the dev-* accounts, with known credentials. On production the person signs in to Grafana, Argo CD and Forgejo with their own account, made by scripts/onboard-user.
  • The cut's scratch data (a Forgejo repository, an OpenBao marker, a Ceph volume) is deleted by the spec once read back.
  • The cut runs before lab backup enable, so none of it reaches R2.
  • The same cluster carries on: 12b-1's install continues into 12b-3, with no reinstall.

docs.title: 9. Fixes found while bringing the platform up (user)
docs.text:
• Every fix goes through a pull request into dev and a dev → master release with the sandbox's check (the ruleset and verify require it). Fixes are batched into releases to save CI time.
  • The testbed's mark is needed only when a fix touches infra/testbed/release-paths.yaml's paths or the testbed's components; verify reuses an earlier mark otherwise.
  • --skip-proof=<reason> only for a fix the testbed's VMs cannot judge, such as a Ceph OSD on the real NVMe disks. It is recorded as production/skipped.

docs.title: Proofs
docs.text:
• The stage, offline:
  • with platform, the rendered apps ApplicationSet selects no cluster;
  • with all (and by default), as today;
  • the bootstrap refuses all → platform.
  • The stage on the sandbox: just dev passes, and the sandbox's apps survive the selector change.
  • The release: the sandbox check, and just testbed's mark.
  • On production:
  • Argo CD synced;
  • Ceph HEALTH_OK with three OSDs, and the cross-node volume;
  • the platform's specs (Smoke for the platform's apps, mesh, OpenBao, SSO, logs, monitoring);
  • Velero's backup to R2 and a restore;
  • the etcd alerts loaded;
  • the cut with data.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• docs/installation/production/deployment.md: the stage, and the first deploy's checklist.
  • CLAUDE.md:
  • 12b-2 done;
  • the before-production items it settles (Ceph, OpenBao, Forgejo on Ceph, Velero to R2, Loki and Alloy on the nodes, Argo CD's switch to Forgejo, the mesh on the nodes, the cut with data), each checked against the list.

docs.title: Step 10f: Argo Workflows and Argo Events replace Woodpecker
docs.text: Status: design agreed in chat 2026-11-13, written spec awaiting review. Branch: feat/argo-ci (PR into dev).

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The homelab's in-cluster CI, for repositories in Forgejo's org ci, moves from Woodpecker (step 10e) to Argo Workflows driven by Argo Events. Woodpecker never ran a real pipeline (only the tests' probe), so nothing migrates: it is removed before the first production deploy, which then never carries it.

Why Argo (chosen by the user, 2026-11-13, after comparing Tekton, Forgejo Actions and Woodpecker):

  • Forgejo Actions would teach GitHub Actions' syntax, which this repository's own CI already uses every day, and its runner still needs Docker or Podman: on Kubernetes a privileged Docker-in-Docker pod, against Pod Security and step 15h. Its Kubernetes backends are community experiments.
  • Tekton (Pipelines-as-Code, Chains) has more of a CI built in: pipelines in the repository, status on pull requests, signing and provenance by a controller. Argo Workflows has none of the three and this step builds them, but it is a CNCF graduated project with a wider community, a general workflow engine (batch, the teaching app's sessions later, step 18b), SSO with groups built in, one family with Argo CD and Argo Rollouts, and part of CAPA, which the user's Golden Kubestronaut goal counts. Revisit Tekton if it graduates and joins that list.
  • The homelab still picks what is best for itself; certifications only break ties. Exam-only setups (kubeadm, Cilium) go to the teaching app's extension, not here.

GitHub Actions stays this repository's CI. Argo serves repositories hosted on Forgejo (the blog, Backstage's app, later ones); a public repository that wants outside contributions is better served by GitHub Actions (forks, keyless signing, free runners), decided per repository.

This step comes first in the order agreed 2026-11-13, before production: CI (this step), then OpenTelemetry, then Backstage (built by this CI, its templates creating repositories with this CI's golden path), then the blog with Argo Rollouts (its repository from Backstage's template, its image from this CI, canary through Istio).

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A push to a repository in org ci builds its image with Buildah, unprivileged; the default branch pushes it to zot as registry.<domain>/<repo>:<commit sha>, signs it and attests its provenance; Forgejo shows the result as a commit status (pull requests show it too).
  • Pipelines are a golden path: templates in this repository (WorkflowTemplates, reviewed and rendered like any chart), never pipelines written in the built repositories. A repository chooses only parameters.
  • Nothing a ci member pushes can run arbitrary pod specs: the controller accepts only Workflows that reference the templates (workflowRestrictions.templateReferencing: Strict).
  • People sign in to Argo's UI with Kanidm (SSO, groups), as with every admin tool.
  • Everything Woodpecker held in the repository goes: chart, Forgejo OAuth client, rotation entries and kinds, backup group, egress row, Falco and Kyverno exceptions, scan acceptances, homepage tile, tests, docs.
  • In the sandbox too, proven by e2e specs.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• This repository's CI (stays GitHub Actions), ops/homelab (only receives deploys).
  • The blog's and Backstage's repositories and pipelines (their own steps); a pipeline per language (tests, linters): the golden path builds images only, more templates come with the repositories that need them.
  • Pull requests from forks or strangers: only ci members' repositories run.
  • An artifact repository (S3) and archived logs: pod logs already reach Loki (Alloy), the UI's logs last as long as the pods, images and everything attached to them live in zot, and files pass between steps on the Workflow's own volume (below). An S3 artifact repository comes with the first pipeline that produces files other than images (test reports, binaries), choosing then between R2, the sandbox's versitygw, or Garage on the NAS of the Ideas.
  • A layer cache: Buildah on vfs rebuilds every layer. When builds get slow, Buildah's registry cache (--cache-to, --cache-from in zot) is the first option; it touches the storage driver, so it is its own change.
  • Argo Rollouts (its own step), Argo CD Image Updater (Renovate or a commit bumps image tags).
  • Enforcing image signatures (step 15b-2 switches Kyverno to Enforce).

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• A privileged pod, a Docker daemon, or a step choosing its service account, node or host users.
  • Webhook payloads trusted without authentication.
  • A signing key readable by a workflow pod (it signs through OpenBao, below).
  • A second CI kept "for now" beside Woodpecker's removal.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Latest stable releases, pinned (2026-11-13: chart argo-workflows 2.0.18 with Argo Workflows v4.1.6, chart argo-events 2.4.28 with Argo Events v1.9.11, from https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm). v4.0.0 to v4.0.4 had an SSO RBAC crash (CVE-2026-42183); 4.1.6 is past it.
  • Every rule in CLAUDE.md applies: securityContext or a PolicyException with its reason, homelab/backup on every PVC, ambient mesh with an allow per namespace, egress denied unless listed, secrets in OpenBao through ESO, every secret in the rotation catalog, settings from config.json (hosts as <host>.{{ .Values.global.baseDomain }}), test/scopes.yaml entries for new components.
  • Step 15h's Buildah seccomp profile (homelab/buildah.json) and its native admission policies carry over to the namespace where builds run; the profile itself does not change.

docs.title: Components and namespaces
docs.text:
Path Namespace Holds platform/argo-workflows argo-workflows the controller and Argo Server (UI, https://ci.<domain>, LAN Gateway), Kanidm client argo-workflows platform/argo-events argo-events Argo Events' controller (no validating webhook) platform/ci ci the EventBus, the Forgejo EventSource and Sensor, the WorkflowTemplates, the Workflows and their pods, their ExternalSecrets, the seccomp admission policies

Workflows run only in ci (the controller's namespace list or --managed-namespace, builder's call): the controller and server stay where no pipeline runs.

docs.title: From a push to a Workflow
docs.text:
1. lab infra forgejo sync keeps an org webhook on ci (push and pull request events, JSON) pointing at the EventSource's Service in namespace ci, sending Authorization: Bearer <secret>; the secret is generated in OpenBao (ci/generated/webhook, platform/generated-secrets), and sync reads it there. Forgejo's webhook.ALLOWED_HOST_LIST: private already admits the in-cluster address.
  2. A webhook EventSource checks the bearer secret (authSecret); Argo Events has no Forgejo or Gitea source, so the Sensor reads Forgejo's JSON itself.
  3. The EventBus is JetStream (its minimum replica count; check whether the sandbox can run fewer).
  4. The Sensor filters push to any branch and pull request opened/synchronized, and creates a Workflow from workflowTemplateRef: pipeline with the repository, commit, ref and event as parameters, through its own service account (create Workflows in ci, nothing else).

docs.title: The golden path (platform/ci/templates/)
docs.text:
WorkflowTemplate pipeline (the only entry point the Sensor uses), built from smaller templates others can reuse later:

  • the Workflow's volume: one PVC per run from volumeClaimTemplates (homelab/backup: none, the default storage class: Ceph RBD in production, csi-hostpath in the sandbox), deleted with the Workflow; steps run one after another, so ReadWriteOnce is enough. It carries the source from clone to build and the image's digest and SBOM to signing;
  • clone: Forgejo over the in-cluster address with the ci bot's token (read), at the commit;
  • settings: optional .ci.yaml at the repository's root with only known keys (context, containerfile, image), defaults ., Containerfile or else Dockerfile, the repository's name; anything else fails the run; a repository with neither file and no .ci.yaml ends as success with nothing built;
  • build: Buildah (quay.io/buildah/stable, pinned, the version step 15h measured or a newer one re-measured), chroot isolation, vfs, in a user namespace (hostUsers: false in the template's pod spec), under homelab/buildah.json; pull requests build only; the default branch pushes registry.<domain>/<repo>:<sha> to zot as its machine account ci (the existing htpasswd user, now a Secret in namespace ci);
  • SBOM (default branch only): an SPDX SBOM of the pushed image (Syft or Trivy, pinned; the builder picks), as the lab image has since step 15e;
  • sign and attest (default branch only): cosign signs the pushed digest and attests the SBOM and an SLSA provenance predicate the pipeline writes (builder: Argo Workflows in this cluster; the workflow's name, template, parameters; materials: the repository at the commit, the base images' digests Buildah reports), both with an OpenBao transit key through cosign's hashivault:// KMS, authenticated by the workflow pod's service account token (OpenBao role ci-signer, audience openbao, policy: sign with that key only). The key never leaves OpenBao; keyless signing is out because public Fulcio does not trust this cluster's tokens;
  • exit handler: a commit status (pending at the start, then success, failure or error, linking the run in Argo's UI) through Forgejo's API with the ci bot's token.

Workflows carry ttlStrategy (kept 7 days after completion) and podGC (pods deleted on success; failed pods kept with their Workflow for debugging); the builder picks the exact values.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
• lab infra forgejo sync: drops Woodpecker's OAuth2 application (deleting it if present) and gains the org webhook and a bot user ci-bot (member of ci's team developers: write, for statuses and clones; its token in OpenBao ci/forgejo-token, refused if it signed in with Kanidm, like deploy/argocd; a local user, so the Kanidm groupTeamMapRemoval never touches its membership). The Kanidm groupTeamMap stays.
  • Argo Server: --auth-mode=sso, Kanidm OIDC client argo-workflows (confidential; homelab_groups from claimMap like the other admin tools; PKCE if Argo Server sends it, otherwise the client allows its absence: check), SSO RBAC by service accounts with workflows.argoproj.io/rbac-rule: homelab-admins full on ci's Workflows, homelab-editors submit from the templates, resubmit, view and logs, homelab-users view only (the three groups every admin tool matches); nobody else. Argo Server keeps no session of its own beyond its cookie.
  • The controller: workflowRestrictions.templateReferencing: Strict, so a Workflow submitted through the UI or API must reference ci's templates.

docs.title: Seccomp, Pod Security, mesh, egress
docs.text:
• 15h's MutatingAdmissionPolicy and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy move to platform/ci, bound to namespace ci. Argo adds its own containers to every pod (the init and wait containers, argoexec), so "every container is Buildah" no longer identifies a build: the mutation matches pods of the build template (a label only templates in this repository set, which templateReferencing: Strict keeps out of anyone else's reach) whose main container is quay.io/buildah/stable with hostUsers: false; the validating policy still refuses a Localhost profile to every other pod in ci. argoexec under homelab/buildah.json (RuntimeDefault plus four syscalls) is expected to work; the e2e spec proves it.
  • Pod Security baseline on ci, restricted where possible elsewhere; exceptions with reasons (Buildah's root in a user namespace, as Woodpecker's).
  • Mesh: argo-workflows, argo-events and ci join it; allows: the Gateway to Argo Server, Forgejo to the EventSource, Prometheus to the metrics ports; ci's pods call Forgejo, zot, OpenBao and the API server (EXTRA in scripts/check-mesh-policies where renders cannot show it).
  • Egress: ci gets 80/443 (base images, a build's downloads), as woodpecker had; the controllers need none.
  • Falco: the Buildah memfd exception moves to namespace ci.
  • Trust: in the sandbox the templates trust the local CA through the ConfigMap homelab-dev-ca (trust-manager copies it into ci; values-dev.yaml), never by skipping TLS verification as Woodpecker's sandbox pipeline did. In production, ci's pods reach git. and registry.<domain> through public DNS: that they land on the LAN Gateway is checked before relying on it, as for the rotation CronJob (CLAUDE.md's production list carries it).

docs.title: Secrets and the rotation catalog
docs.text:
Secret Where Rotation the webhook's bearer secret ci/generated/webhook generated, class 1: new value, sync updates Forgejo's webhook, the EventSource restarts ci-bot's Forgejo token ci/forgejo-token Forgejo token with overlap (the existing method) zot's ci password its existing path zot's htpasswd and the Secret in ci change together; waits for no running Workflow in ci Kanidm client argo-workflows kaniop Secret the existing kanidm-client kind, class 2 the signing key OpenBao transit ci-signing manual, with the reason: a new key version needs Kyverno's public key updated first

The kinds woodpecker-agent and woodpecker-token, the entries woodpecker.agent, woodpecker.admin-token and forgejo.woodpecker-oauth, and idle: woodpecker go; class 2's "wait for no running pipeline" reads ci's running Workflows instead. OpenBao's initialize stanzas gain the transit engine, the key and the role ci-signer (production has not started yet; a sandbox built before this step needs just dev-fresh once).

docs.title: Verification of images
docs.text: A Kyverno verifyImages policy (Audit, like verify-lab-image) checks registry.<domain>/* against the transit key's public key (published in the chart, exported once from OpenBao; the builder chooses how it reaches the policy without a manual copy if one exists, otherwise a documented step), and requires the provenance and SPDX attestations.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Argo keeps no lasting volume (Workflows live in etcd for 7 days; each run's volume goes with it, homelab/backup: none); JetStream's storage, if it has one, is none too (an event lost in a restart is a push to repeat). Woodpecker's daily group entry goes.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Offline (test/offline): renders of the three charts (restrictions on, SSO on, no Woodpecker anywhere), the seccomp policies against fixtures of an Argo build pod and of other ci pods (replacing TestWoodpeckerSeccompPolicies), the catalog and generated-secrets wiring, scripts/check-* updated.

E2e (test/e2e, labels from test/scopes.yaml, sandbox and testbed where they apply):

  • CI: a fixture repository pushed to ci (a two-line Containerfile) builds, pushes to zot, is signed and attested (cosign verifies the signature, the provenance and the SBOM with the public key), its Workflow's PVC is gone once the Workflow is deleted, and Forgejo shows a success status; a pull request builds without pushing; a repository whose .ci.yaml has an unknown key fails with a failure status; a webhook without the bearer secret creates no Workflow.
  • CISeccomp: the build pod runs under homelab/buildah.json; another ci pod naming a Localhost profile is refused; RuntimeDefault refuses unshare (the 15h specs, moved).
  • CIRestrictions: a Workflow without a template reference is refused.
  • SSOArgoWorkflows: admin, editor, viewer, outsider (like SSOKiali).
  • TestRotation covers the new entries where they are scheduled.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: docs/how-to-guides/in-cluster-ci.md replaces woodpecker.md (bring a repository, .ci.yaml, reading a run, who signs in); architecture overview, secrets rotation, supply chain, runtime detection, cluster scan and backup guides lose Woodpecker; CLAUDE.md's roadmap gains 10f (done when merged) and the agreed next steps (OpenTelemetry, Backstage, blog with Rollouts), and its "before the first production deploy" list trades Woodpecker's unproven points for Argo's.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text: The exact controller and server values, TTL and podGC numbers, JetStream sizing, how the public key reaches Kyverno, the label the seccomp mutation matches, the provenance predicate's fields, and whether Argo Server's UI host stays ci.<domain> (the default here) — each recorded in the plan.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry: the Collector replaces Alloy, traces into Tempo
docs.text: Status: designed in chat 2026-11-14; the builder check's four questions are settled below (decisions 10 to 13). Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks the builder's own, open to review. Builds on step 9 (Loki and Alloy), 15c (security logs), 15g (Falco) and the threat model (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-14-threat-model-design.md).

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The homelab moves its telemetry pipeline onto the vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry Collector, the standard the community converges on and the one the user is learning (OTCA), and starts collecting traces. Grafana Alloy (itself a distribution of the Collector) goes: one agent per node, not two. Loki 3 ingests OTLP natively and Tempo stores the traces, so nothing in between is Grafana-specific.

(user) This is learning by doing: traces are collected the way the community usually does it, not to answer a question the homelab already has. The sandbox is short of resources, so the Collector replaces Alloy at once, with no period of running both: what breaks is fixed.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. The OpenTelemetry Operator runs the Collector; Alloy is removed from system/loki.
  2. Every log Alloy collects today reaches Loki through the Collector over OTLP: pod logs, OpenBao's audit lines, the API server's audit log, Kubernetes events. Falco's events keep arriving as Falco's pod logs.
  3. Traces reach Tempo from the Istio Gateways (Envoy, through Istio's Telemetry API) and from the platform tools that export OTLP themselves, and Grafana links a log line to its trace and back.
  4. Every alert, dashboard panel, retention rule and test that reads logs works on the new labels.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Metrics through the Collector: Prometheus and its scrapes stay as they are; the Collectors' own metrics are scraped like any component's.
  • Auto-instrumentation: the Operator can inject SDKs into pods (Instrumentation), but no app needs it yet; Backstage, the next step, is the first.
  • Tempo at scale: no object storage, no replication, no metrics-generator (service graphs, span metrics); worth it with apps of our own.
  • Traces inside the mesh: ambient's ztunnel makes no spans (L4 only); spans between services need waypoints, which stay an idea.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• An OTLP endpoint reachable from outside the cluster, or by namespaces that have no reason to send (the threat model's rule: nothing new is published).
  • Audit lines lost: a line read while Loki is unreachable still arrives after a restart of the Collector, as with Alloy's write-ahead log (LogsSurviveLokiOutage). Their 60 days hold unless measured otherwise, and then CLAUDE.md's rule applies (shorten to 45, then 30 days; never grow the volume).
  • A Collector configuration only one person can read: every pipeline commented as the Alloy configuration was.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. (user) Approach A: the Operator manages two Collectors, the agent and the gateway.
  2. The agent: an OpenTelemetryCollector in mode daemonset. It reads /var/log/pods and /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log on its node (filelog, with the container operator for containerd's format), keeps its read positions on the node (file_storage on a hostPath, so a restart resumes where it stopped, as Alloy's positions did), adds the pod's metadata (k8sattributes), and exports the logs to Loki's OTLP endpoint itself (decision 10).
  3. The gateway: an OpenTelemetryCollector in mode deployment, one replica. It receives OTLP traces (from the Gateways' Envoy and the tools) and exports them to Tempo, and watches Kubernetes events (k8sobjects, which a single replica watches once) and exports them to Loki.
  4. Rejected: the opentelemetry-collector chart without the Operator (two ways to configure a Collector once Backstage needs the Operator anyway, and it skips what OTCA covers); one DaemonSet doing everything (events need leader election across the DaemonSet, apps would send to their node's address, and no single place samples or processes traces).
  5. (user) No parallel run. The Collector replaces Alloy in one change; the sandbox shows what breaks.
  6. (user) OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions for labels. Loki indexes the resource attributes it indexes by default (service_name, k8s_namespace_name, k8s_pod_name, k8s_container_name, the workload's name, …) and keeps the rest as structured metadata. Queries, alerts, dashboards and tests are rewritten to them; nothing keeps the old names namespace, pod, container, app, job.
  7. (user) Traces as usually done: the Istio Gateways through Istio's Telemetry API with an opentelemetry extension provider pointing at the gateway Collector, and the platform tools that export OTLP (Argo CD, Grafana; Loki, Tempo, Kanidm and others where their charts or configuration allow it, each found by the builder).
  8. (Claude's call) The audit streams are named by service.name: k3s-audit for the API server's file and openbao-audit for OpenBao's audit lines, which the agent tells from OpenBao's other output as Alloy did (JSON with "type":"request" or "response"). Loki's 60-day retention selects them by service_name. Kubernetes events get service.name kubernetes-events.
  9. (Claude's call) The otelcol-k8s distribution, the Collector project's own build for Kubernetes: it has every component above and less than contrib, so a smaller image to scan and fewer components to trust. Version 0.165.0 (the latest), the Operator chart 0.129.0 (Operator 0.162.0); the builder checks the Operator accepts that Collector version and pins the newest pair that works.
  10. (Claude's call) Tempo from grafana-community's chart 3.2.1 (Tempo 3.1.1), single binary, a PVC (homelab/backup: none, like Loki: telemetry is not worth restoring), 7 days of traces in production and 1 day in the sandbox; Grafana gets a Tempo data source (uid tempo), traces linked to Loki's logs by trace_id, and Loki's lines linked to their trace.
  11. (Claude's call) Where things live: system/opentelemetry (the Operator, both Collectors and their allow policies), system/tempo, and system/loki without Alloy.

  12. (Claude's call) Sampling: every Gateway request in the sandbox; in production a fraction small enough for Tempo's volume (the builder proposes it, e.g. 10%, through the Telemetry API's randomSamplingPercentage).

  13. (Claude's call, from the builder check) The agent sends logs to Loki directly, with a persistent queue. Its OTLP exporter's sending_queue is stored in file_storage on its hostPath, beside its read positions, so lines read during a Loki outage survive the agent's restart, as Alloy's write-ahead log did; LogsSurviveLokiOutage keeps proving it. Logs never pass through the gateway, so the gateway needs no volume; Kubernetes events, which only it watches, are queued in memory (an event lost in an outage plus a restart is accepted, as they are not audit).

  14. (Claude's call, from the builder check) The Gateways write access logs (Istio's Telemetry API, JSON to stdout, the request's trace_id among the fields), read by the agent like any pod's log: they are the log lines that link to the Gateways' traces in Grafana (a derived field on trace_id). The homelab's traffic is small; the measurement in decision 12 covers them.
  15. (Claude's call, from the builder check) Loki's volume is measured, not assumed. OTLP adds structured metadata to every line; the agent drops the attributes no query uses (file paths, ids nothing reads), and the plan measures the bytes per audit line against step 15c's budget (7.3GiB of 10Gi for 60 days on one node). If it no longer fits, CLAUDE.md's rule applies: shorten the audit period, never grow the volume.
  16. (Claude's call, from the builder check) The Gateways' traces go over the mesh. The Gateways (namespace istio-system, outside the ambient data plane) already reach meshed apps with their own identity, which allow-gateways matches; their OTLP export to the gateway Collector is an ordinary upstream cluster and should do the same, so the Collector's allow admits them by identity. If the sandbox shows it cannot, the fallback is a port exception like forgejo-db-status (permissive on OTLP's port, a NetworkPolicy admitting only the Gateways' pods), recorded in the threat model's entry points.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Every rule in CLAUDE.md: latest stable versions pinned; homelab/backup on every PVC; a securityContext or a PolicyException with its reason (the agent reads host paths as root, as Alloy did: it inherits Alloy's exception and namespace privileged); a test/scopes.yaml entry for each new component; the mesh's allow per namespace.
  • The mesh and webhooks: the Operator's admission webhooks are called by the API server, so its pods carry istio.io/dataplane-mode: none and its NetworkPolicies let 15008 in; a webhook that mutates pods must not block pod creation cluster-wide while the Operator is down (failurePolicy: Ignore, as ESO's and Kyverno's).
  • OTLP stays inside (threat model): no route to the gateway Collector; its AuthorizationPolicy admits only the agents, the Gateways' namespace and the tools that send; no egress to the internet.
  • Resources: the sandbox is short already. Alloy goes (about 125Mi); the agent, the gateway, the Operator and Tempo must fit with small requests in values-dev.yaml, measured under the suite.
  • The first sync: the Collectors are custom resources whose CRDs come with the Operator, so their Application waits for them like the other operators' (SkipDryRunOnMissingResource only where a cycle needs it, as CLAUDE.md says).

docs.title: What changes outside the new components
docs.text:
• system/loki: Alloy's subchart and its PolicyException removed; Loki's OTLP ingestion configured (otlp_config: which resource attributes become labels; the default set unless a query needs another); the retention selector on service_name.
  • The Loki ruler's rules (system/loki/files/*.yaml: 11 audit, 2 Falco, 1 public scan) and the dashboard "Security": stream selectors to the new labels. The bodies stay the original lines, so the | json stages are unchanged.
  • Istio (system/istio-system): the extension provider in meshConfig and a Telemetry resource for the Gateways.
  • Argo CD's and Grafana's tracing settings; Grafana's data sources.
  • system/argocd's templatePatch (namespace privileged moves from Alloy's namespace to the agent's), .cluster-scan-accepted.yaml (Alloy's accepted findings become the agent's), test/scopes.yaml, system/egress if anything sends out (nothing should).
  • Docs: docs/how-to-guides/logs.md and security-logs.md (the queries people type), the runtime-detection guide, CLAUDE.md's lines on Loki and Alloy, a new guide for traces.
  • Comments naming Alloy (OpenBao's audit device, k3d's audit mount, Falco's values).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Offline: renders of both Collectors (pipelines, receivers, exporters), the Operator's webhook settings, Tempo's PVC label, the retention selector, every ruler rule parsed with its new selector (the existing offline tests, rewritten), no Alloy left anywhere.
  • Sandbox:
  • the existing specs rewritten to the new labels: Logs* (pod logs, events, the audit streams, LogsResumeAfterRestart now proving the agent's file_storage), SecurityLogs*, Falco, the monitoring specs that read logs;
  • a new spec: a request through the LAN Gateway leaves a trace in Tempo, and its access log line carries the same trace_id;
  • LogsSurviveLokiOutage kept: lines read during an outage arrive after the agent restarts (decision 10);
  • a new spec: the gateway Collector refuses OTLP from a namespace that has no reason to send.
  • test/scopes.yaml: the logs family selects the specs above for changes to system/opentelemetry, system/tempo and system/loki.

docs.title: Production, unproven
docs.text: Added to CLAUDE.md's list for the first deploy: the agent on the NixOS nodes' log paths, three agents' volume into one gateway, Tempo's volume at the chosen sampling, the Gateways' trace headers through Cloudflare.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Each tool's tracing configuration beyond Argo CD and Grafana, and which tools have none.
  • The Collectors' resource requests, measured, and the attributes the agent drops (decision 12).
  • Whether Loki needs extra resource attributes indexed for a query the rewrite finds (keep the default set otherwise).
  • The production sampling rate.

docs.title: Measured (the sandbox, 2026-11-15)
docs.text:
• Memory: the agent used 365Mi (Alloy 220Mi), the gateway 56Mi, the Operator 71Mi, Tempo 189Mi: about 460Mi more than Alloy. The node reached 92% under the suite and k3s restarted once; GOMEMLIMIT at about 80% of each limit and smaller sandbox limits (the agent 256Mi, the gateway 128Mi, Tempo 256Mi) followed.
  • Loki's volume: an audit line averaged 1418 bytes (k3s-audit) and 1773 bytes (openbao-audit); OTLP added 213 and 448 bytes of labels and structured metadata (15% and 25% before compression). The receiver's scope and the file's name (about 100 bytes a line) are dropped by the agent; what remains repeats line after line and compresses well, so the audit streams' 60 days stay within step 15c's budget (7.3GiB of 10Gi) and the period is unchanged.

docs.title: The homelab's threat model
docs.text: Status: a draft for review, 2026-11-14. The user asked for it in chat on 2026-11-14: review what is or will be exposed (Kanidm for Headscale, Matrix, the step-13 VPS) before it is, rather than one service at a time. Decisions marked (user) were made in chat; (Claude's call) marks proposals open to review. Nothing here is built yet: each gap names the step that would close it.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: One place that says what the homelab protects, from whom, where an attacker could come in, what already stands in the way, and what is missing, so that each later step (OpenTelemetry, Backstage, the blog, 12b-3, 13, 18b) is checked against it instead of discovering its own risks late. It is a living document: a step that adds an entry point updates it.

docs.title: What is worth protecting
docs.text: Asset Where Losing it means Every secret OpenBao (raft on a PVC), its unseal key in production's encrypted state on R2 everything below Personal data Actual Budget, paperless, OpenCloud, Matrix, (Immich, step 17) privacy of the family's documents, money, files, chats Identity Kanidm (people, groups, OAuth2 clients) every app's sign-in The deploy path GitHub master → lab infra forgejo push → ops/homelab → Argo CD (cluster-admin) the whole cluster The signing key OpenBao transit ci-signing what Kyverno trusts as built by the golden path Backups R2 (Velero, Kopia), the OpenBao snapshot recovery after any of the above The home network the Archer C64, the family's devices a foothold beyond the homelab

docs.title: Who it is protected from
docs.text:
• The internet at large (scanners, botnets, credential stuffing): the realistic threat for anything public.
  • A compromised dependency (an image, a chart, a GitHub Action, a Renovate update): the supply chain.
  • A device on the home LAN (a compromised laptop, phone or IoT device): the network is flat today.
  • A member of org ci or of homelab-editors acting beyond their role, or whose account is taken over.
  • Later, strangers running code on purpose (the teaching app, 18b).

Out of scope (user, 2026-11-14): a targeted attacker with physical access to the house (the disks are unencrypted, an accepted risk since 15d), and the providers themselves (Cloudflare, GitHub, AWS, Kanidm's and Argo's maintainers).

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text: # Entry point Today Planned E1 Public apps through the Cloudflare Tunnel (blog, excalidraw, ntfy) only rendered (12b-3) Kanidm for Headscale (13); Matrix if federated E2 The LAN Gateway (every admin app, Kanidm, Forgejo SSH) sandbox production (12b-3) E2c Backstage (Backstage-1, LAN Gateway only): homelab-admins and homelab-editors sign in with Kanidm; it reads the cluster (no Secrets, ConfigMaps, logs or exec), Argo CD (read-only) and the repository Argo CD syncs; its token creates repositories in org ci sandbox (Backstage-1) production once its image is released E2b OTLP into the gateway Collector (traces from the Istio Gateways, Argo CD, Grafana) sandbox (OpenTelemetry step) inside the cluster only: allow-otlp names the senders, nothing routes to it E3 The nodes' own ports from the LAN (SSH, the API server, etcd, the kubelet, flannel's VXLAN) production's nodes E4 The step-13 VPS (SSH, WireGuard, Headscale, DERP/STUN on a public address) none 13 E5 The supply chain (images, charts, Actions, Renovate's pull requests) GitHub, the sandbox E6 The in-cluster CI running a Containerfile (org ci) sandbox (10f); Backstage's template creates repositories there (admins only, Backstage-1) 18b's learners E7 The workstation's admin path (admin kubeconfigs, the state passphrase, SSH keys, Cloudflare and GitHub sessions) in use E8 Accounts outside the homelab (GitHub, Cloudflare, AWS, the domain's registrar) in use AWS (13)

docs.title: What already stands in the way
docs.text:
• No inbound port at home (CGNAT, double NAT): the internet reaches the homelab only through the Tunnel, which connects outbound.
  • The public surface (15f): Gateway public admits only an allow-list of namespaces and hosts, every public route is proxied, Cloudflare's WAF managed rules and one zone rate limit, nuclei weekly from inside. ntfy denies by default, has no sign-up and no attachments.
  • Identity: Kanidm OIDC with PKCE for every app; apps with personal data admit only their access group.
  • Inside the cluster: ambient mesh with strict mTLS and default-deny AuthorizationPolicy per namespace (6b, 6c), default-deny egress for pods (6d-2), Pod Security baseline enforced and restricted audited by Kyverno (15b-1), seccomp-default (15h), secrets encrypted at rest in etcd (15d), OpenBao behind ESO with per-namespace stores (8a).
  • Supply chain (15a, 15e): pinned versions, gitleaks, Trivy on new images in pull requests, the Trivy Operator on running images, lab's image signed, 10f's images signed, zizmor on the workflows, push protection on GitHub.
  • Deploy path (10c): production deploys only origin/master whose checks and sandbox passed, pushed by a user only the workstation holds.
  • Detection (15c, 15g): the API server's and OpenBao's audit logs with alerts, Falco, the Trivy alerts, every alert to ntfy and Telegram.
  • Recovery (11a, 11b): daily off-site backups with a write-only R2 token, restores only by command, every new cluster read-only until lab backup enable; every secret rotatable by its official method.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text: Ordered by what a person running this homelab would lose, most first. Each names a proposal and the step that would carry it.

docs.title: G1. Kyverno only audits (15b-2 not done)
docs.text:
Pod Security restricted, pinned images, allowed registries and the image signatures (verify-lab-image, verify-ci-images) report but block nothing. 10f's final review showed the cost: the build pod broke a restricted rule and nothing noticed until a reviewer read it.

The window is small, though: every workload from git already passes the same policies in the pull request's basic check policy, Pod Security Admission enforces baseline (privileged, host paths and namespaces, dangerous capabilities) whatever Kyverno says, and the native admission policies (the build's seccomp, ci-workflow-arguments) refuse on their own. What Audit leaves open is what no render shows (pods an operator makes: Ceph, CloudNativePG, Trivy's scans, the golden path's steps) and the image signatures, which only someone already able to create pods could get around.

Decision (user, 2026-11-14): production starts in Audit (12b-3) and switches to Enforce (15b-2) after a short window of reading its own PolicyReports: production runs workloads the sandbox never does (cloudflared, the VPN routers, jellyfin, Ceph's daemons, kube-vip, Renovate's initContainer), whose reports exist nowhere else, and the skip results show which PolicyExceptions are still used and which can go. Enforcing before 12b-3 would risk refusing those pods on the first deploy. During the window:

  • an alert on a new fail result in a PolicyReport (today only PolicyException changes outside Argo CD alert), so the window does not depend on someone reading the reports;
  • nothing new is published and nobody outside the household joins org ci;
  • Enforce comes before step 13 at the latest, and within about two weeks when the reports are clean; it also needs who may create a PolicyException restricted, the golden path's pods rendered for the policy check (10f's deferred minor) and the first release's signatures (lab's image) verified.

docs.title: G2. The nodes' cluster ports are open to the whole LAN (E3)
docs.text:
infra/_modules/metal/flake/profiles/k3s-server.nix opens 2379 and 2380 (etcd), 10250 (the kubelet) and UDP 8472 (flannel's VXLAN) to any address; only the metrics ports are limited to the nodes and the pod network. etcd and the kubelet require client certificates, but flannel's VXLAN is neither encrypted nor authenticated: any LAN device that sends to UDP 8472 can inject packets into the pod network as if from a pod, around the mesh's policies for anything outside it. SSH and the API server (6443) are open to the LAN too, which is how the workstation reaches them.

Proposal (Claude's call): limit 2379, 2380, 10250 and 8472 to the nodes' addresses (and 10250 to the pod network for the metrics scrape), like the metrics ports already are; set SSH to keys only explicitly (PasswordAuthentication and KbdInteractiveAuthentication off: no user has a password today, which is all that stops it). A small change to infra/_modules/metal, proven on the testbed (it gates releases there anyway). Restricting 6443 and SSH to the workstation needs a fixed admin address: it comes with G6.

docs.title: G3. Kanidm on the internet (step 13, E1)
docs.text:
Headscale's OIDC sign-in needs Kanidm reachable from the internet, through the Tunnel. Kanidm is the key to every app, and its admin API shares the host with its login.

Proposal (Claude's call), all preconditions of publishing it: - passkeys only for every person (Kanidm's credential policy on the groups: no password, no TOTP-only sign-in); today no policy is set; - only the paths Headscale's OIDC flow needs on the public host (a path allow-list at Gateway public, as 15f's host allow-list), the rest (admin API, account recovery) LAN only; - alerts on Kanidm's failed sign-ins from Loki, as 15c does for OpenBao; - a rate limit on its sign-in paths: the Free plan's one rule already covers the whole zone, so either a separate host with its own rule (a paid plan) or a limit in Kanidm or at the Gateway; - whether Cloudflare Access goes in front of it (13 already asks), weighed against signing in twice.

docs.title: G4. The VPS (step 13, E4)
docs.text:
The first machine with a public address, and the WireGuard hub that routes back into the home.

Proposal (Claude's call): SSH reachable only through the tailnet (no public port 22), the VPS's own firewall (nftables) with only WireGuard, Headscale and DERP/STUN, Headscale ACLs by least privilege, the hub's AllowedIPs towards the home limited to the Gateway's VIP (not the whole LAN), automatic NixOS updates, and the periodic nmap 13 already plans. The VPS holds no secret that opens the cluster.

docs.title: G5. The flat home network (E3)
docs.text:
The nodes share the LAN with the family's phones, laptops and IoT devices: a compromised device reaches every node port (G2) and the LAN Gateway's admin apps (behind Kanidm), and a compromised node reaches every device.

Proposal (user, 2026-11-14): OPNsense is not worth it for the public apps (no inbound port; the Tunnel connects outbound), but it, or a managed switch with VLANs and OpenWrt, would separate the homelab from the home, filter the nodes' own egress and serve DNS over TLS for the whole LAN. Recorded in Ideas, decided with the UPS or step 13's hardware.

docs.title: G6. The workstation is the strongest admin path (E7)
docs.text:
It holds production's admin kubeconfig (a client certificate valid for a year), the state passphrase (which guards the unseal key and the R2 credentials), SSH keys and the Cloudflare and GitHub sessions. The 15a scan already found unencrypted Cloudflare state there (listed for the first deploy).

Proposal (Claude's call): kubectl through Kanidm OIDC (short-lived tokens, group-based RBAC, the audit log naming the person), with the admin certificate kept offline for break-glass; hardware-key 2FA on GitHub, Cloudflare, AWS and the registrar (a checklist in the docs, not code); the state passphrase out of a plain file (a password manager or pass). A step of its own after 12b-3.

docs.title: G7. What the in-cluster CI runs (E6)
docs.text:
Org ci's members are trusted, but the build runs their Containerfile with zot's credentials in its environment (10f deferred minor), and any repository may publish under another repository's name (deferred to 15b-2). Backstage's templates and 18b's learners widen who that is.

Proposal: the two deferred minors before anyone outside the household joins org ci; 18b keeps its own design (Ideas: sandboxed runtime, quotas, its own nodes).
